item.title: [SCMP] Pacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.

These public statements come ahead of a highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York City on the weekend to discuss AI safety.

Yet despite converging on the language of restraint, Silicon Valley’s AI leaders remain locked in a high-stakes and costly tech race against each other – and with China – with no clear winner in sight.

These dynamics, both domestically between industry players and globally between the world’s two AI superpowers, make it highly unlikely that a slowdown will happen any time soon, analysts told the South China Morning Post.

“Even the US companies themselves cannot agree on that,” said Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego and an expert on Chinese elite politics. “So certainly the US and China will not agree on that.”

It has been four years since Washington imposed wide-ranging controls on the export of advanced semiconductor technology to China, citing national security concerns. Yet Chinese AI models from the likes of DeepSeek and Moonshot AI continue to be competitive with their US counterparts in price and capability.

This, in turn, threatens the trillion-dollar valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic as they head towards initial public offerings, as well as challenging US claims of global AI leadership – an explicit priority of US President Donald Trump, who outright dismissed the calls for a slow down in AI development.

“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a hoax,” he wrote on social media last week, raising questions about whether the world can pace AI without the support of one of its most powerful leaders.

The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share

Oskar Galeev, Concordia AI

What is driving calls to slow down?

There have long been concerns about the existential risks of AI. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, winners of the Turing Award computer science prize and widely regarded as the “Godfathers” of AI, have both warned that the technology could eventually displace all humans, with Hinton saying earlier this month that a 10 per cent chance of AI killing all humans within a decade was not an “unreasonable” estimate.

While such concerns are legitimate, what sets apart the recent statements by industry leaders such as Amodei and Altman was that their AI safety proposals also served commercial and geopolitical ends, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

Sun pointed to Amodei’s recent essay “We Must Pace the Frontier”, in which the Anthropic founder warned that a swarm of AI agents could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, potentially causing “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage”.

While the essay laid out why Amodei believes pacing is needed, it also devoted a large part to advocating for tighter restrictions on China’s AI industry. These included US semiconductor chip export controls and a “crackdown on unauthorised distillation by companies” in “autocratic” China.

“Amodei explicitly connects pacing with preserving a US lead over China,” Sun said. That made it “difficult” for Chinese policymakers to view the move as “politically neutral”, the Tsinghua fellow added, even if Amodei acknowledged that “[global] pacing will require cooperation with China”.

Reaction in China to Amodei’s essay was dismissive, with many accusing the tech CEO of using the guise of AI safety to shape the rules governing the sector and to entrench Anthropic’s position as an industry leader.

Last week, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, People’s Daily, published a commentary accusing the US of seeking to monopolise frontier AI development, while a DeepSeek engineer invoked Nazi Germany in a blog post that criticised OpenAI and Anthropic for their latest pacing calls.

China was likely to draw a sharp distinction between AI safety and efforts it viewed as “AI containment”, according to Wei Sun, principal analyst for AI at Counterpoint Research. Beijing has recently unveiled new AI initiatives that call for greater AI safety measures and international cooperation on AI governance, including a new “AI Safety Governance Framework” standards document for the industry released last week.

Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, said the Chinese government had demonstrated that it increasingly cared about AI safety. But it would still require the US to deal with it on an “equal footing”, he said, rather than as a subordinate being dictated to by a stronger power.

“The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share,” he said.

Existential risks, practical realities

Geopolitics aside, even getting the US to pace its own industry would be a challenge, according to UC San Diego’s Shih. While the Anthropic and OpenAI founders have raised alarms about the existential risks of AI, they have also been rebuffed by fellow industry titans including Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who dismissed such worries as “complete nonsense” at an event last week.

There are questions over how a pacing mechanism would be enforced given high levels of mistrust between US AI companies.

As Karen Hao chronicled in her award-winning 2025 book Empire of AI, Altman and Musk helped found OpenAI in 2015 because they did not trust Google to develop AI safely. Six years later, Amodei and other former OpenAI executives and researchers left to start Anthropic after losing trust in Altman to develop AI safely.

Musk, founder of Grok model developer SpaceXAI – formerly xAI – took Altman to court earlier this year after having long accused the OpenAI CEO of prioritising profits over AI safety.

Qian Zilan, a research scholar at the independent AI governance think tank GovAI, said US AI leaders claimed that they wanted to build safe AI but did not trust others to do the same. This created pressure to continue building powerful AI systems, driven by fears that slowing down would cede ground to a rival who would deploy a system with far fewer safeguards.

Further intensifying these dynamics are the massive investments being made by US and Chinese companies in underlying AI infrastructure, such as chips and data centres, with the pace of spending not slowing down.

According to a Morgan Stanley report published earlier this month, capital expenditure by Chinese AI hyperscalers was forecast to jump 121 per cent year on year in 2026 to 995 billion yuan (US$142 billion), outpacing the 41 per cent growth among US peers.

China has long been a laggard in terms of AI investment, but recent successes, including DeepSeek’s breakthrough moment in January 2025 and growing policy support from Beijing, have spiked investment levels.

Still, even as the gap narrowed, China was set to spend only around 17 per cent as much as the US on AI infrastructure over the five years to 2030, Morgan Stanley estimated. Given that China’s AI spending was a much smaller share of its economy than the US, it would not likely slow down its investment momentum, Lu Ting, managing director and chief China economist at Nomura Securities, said at a Fortune event in Guangzhou last week.

“I think the key question in China is whether it can obtain chips, how many chips it can get, and how many Nvidia chips it can buy,” he said.

With China not showing signs of slowing down, the US want to maintain its pace over fears of China fully catching up, said Shan Hui, chief China economist at Goldman Sachs, at the same event. “The next 12 to 18 months will not slow down, and may even accelerate, especially in terms of AI infrastructure,” she said.

Adding to investor frenzy is the rush from both leading American and Chinese AI companies to go public. Despite its high-profile safety warnings, Anthropic itself was still expected to go public later this year, with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, Axios reported earlier this month, citing multiple sources.

In China, Kimi developer Moonshot AI has reportedly been valued at US$50 billion in an ongoing funding round and confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, people with knowledge of the matter told SCMP earlier this month.

Meanwhile, GLM developer Z.ai, which is listed in Hong Kong, announced plans earlier this month to raise an additional US$5 billion through a combination of new shares and convertible bonds, just two months after raising US$4 billion in a share placement.

According to Tsinghua’s Sun, the new influx of capital and unprecedented investor interest made a collective slowdown difficult. “If one frontier company deliberately slows the development of its most capable models while its competitors continue to move ahead, it risks losing market share, capital, talent and technological leadership,” he said, adding that this also applies to countries.

Genuine safety fears

While there were legitimate concerns about the feasibility of pacing AI development, recent incidents involving AI agents demonstrating unprecedented cyber hacking capabilities had “captured the attention of both policymakers and the public”, said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent months released details about how their models hacked into other companies’ internal systems through “agentic swarms” that went undetected for weeks.

Besides industry warnings, calls for greater safeguards have also intensified among US and European politicians after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his role at Anthropic earlier this month and accused the companies of “gambling with our lives” with their plans to accelerate AI development.

Central to their plans was recursive self-improvement (RSI), Coxon warned, which involved automating the AI research and development process itself with the use of AI – a controversial practice that some experts say could lead to humans losing control of AI entirely.

Still, both American and Chinese AI industry leaders have in recent months described RSI as imminent. Given the AI hacking incidents, calls for restraint from industry should not be dismissed as “regulatory theatre,” said Counterpoint Research’s Sun, as the arguments for AI safety had become “much more concrete.”

According to Singer, AI’s growing threat to both US and Chinese interests and humanity as a whole could ultimately be what overrides geopolitical and commercial incentives to continue racing ahead.

“At this stage, voluntary pacing isn’t just feasible, it’s pragmatic [in] the face of serious risks,” Singer said. “Regardless of whether a model is developed in San Francisco or Shanghai, they can create risks that transcend borders.”

Even in its attacks on Amodei and Washington’s hawkish tech policy towards China, the People’s Daily commentary nonetheless called on Washington to work with Beijing to “manage risks through dialogue and communication” and “promote AI to benefit mankind”.

Wang Shengyu, a research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, said China’s dominant national security apparatus may be more sympathetic to calls for a slow down given the risks of AI expanding from cyberattacks to bioweapon development.

Last week, China’s top intelligence official Chen Yixin called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the emerging technology in an article published in a journal run by the country’s Cyberspace Administration.

“Once the benefits and risks of frontier AI become concrete enough to create real policy trade-offs, the final judgment is likely to rest with President Xi [whether to slow down AI development]”, Wang said.

As the Xi-Trump meeting nears, experts cautioned against expecting a sweeping agreement on AI, saying any breakthrough would focus on narrower areas where US and Chinese interests overlapped.

A good deliverable from the summit would be for the two sides to agree to have more AI dialogue in future, while finding out what the common concerns over AI risks were, said Tsinghua’s Sun.

There are early signs that this may be possible. Following Sunday’s meeting, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said that the US and China had discussed a “US-China AI dialogue” mechanism and further meetings to discuss AI-related issues.

He added that the US side would “want a shared vision of common goals and threats” with China, including a proposed “notification mechanism” between the two countries.

“Just like any cross-border activity, moving from opaque to more transparency between the No 1 and No 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent said.

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Bangkok’s World Gourmet Festival, where top chefs share the kitchen
item.description:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration
item.content:encoded:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration

Beyond now commonplace four-hands dinners and chef residencies, the World Gourmet Festival presents a unique set of challenges. Chefs must traverse language barriers, unfamiliar ingredients, and sky-high expectations from some of the industry’s most trained palates. For many, this tests more than culinary skill; it also challenges adaptability and creativity.

Josiah Citrin, chef-owner of restaurants Mélisse and Citrin in Los Angeles, acknowledges the pressure this event brings. “The expectation is always high, but that’s what makes these events exciting,” he explains. “In the kitchen, food becomes its own language quickly. Once you start cooking together, you find a rhythm, and that’s part of the fun of doing these events around the world.”

This balancing act – maintaining one’s gastronomic identity while embracing the unknown – is central to the festival’s spirit.

Pastry chef Puyachart “Boy” Puttawong of Saneh Jaan in Bangkok frames the goal precisely. “A successful collaborative menu should allow guests to recognise each chef’s individual personality while still experiencing a clear and harmonious connection from the first course to the last.”

Weaving a comprehensive throughline that connects each course, rather than jockeying for attention, helps diners understand the interplay between both cuisines and each chef’s culinary ethos. “Our intention is not to make every dish taste Thai, but to allow Thai culinary knowledge and ingredients to become part of the creative conversation,” Puttawong stresses.

Creating a cohesive dining experience amid such diversity can be daunting. Chefs must develop a menu together that reflects their individual styles while maintaining culinary continuity across courses. “Menu development begins with understanding each chef’s strengths,” remarks chef Pilaipon “Toi” Kamnag of Saneh Jaan. “Compromise doesn’t mean weakening anyone’s culinary identity; it’s about making thoughtful adjustments.”

Clavijo stresses the importance of listening rather than competing for space on the same plate: “I wouldn’t really call it ‘compromise’. If both chefs are trying to prove their identity in every single course, the guest feels that tension. A good partnership requires enough confidence to know when to speak and when to let the other person speak.”

Communicating can be a challenge in itself, with chefs from so many different countries taking part. But for many involved, food serves as a universal tongue, reducing friction.

Thanh Vuong Vo, executive chef of Coco Dining in Ho Chi Minh City, shares his perspective: “In a professional kitchen, communication goes beyond spoken language. You communicate through technique, timing, gestures, tasting and repetition,” he says. “If there is a difference in interpretation, we taste together and use the food itself as the common vernacular.” This fluidity allows chefs to communicate through actions and shared experiences rather than relying solely on verbal exchanges.

Zee Zheng, chef-owner of Fabula in Shanghai, observes, “I believe a chef is simply a messenger of nature. My role is to act as a bridge – connecting dishes while weaving in subtle local touches that add a sense of discovery.

“It’s all about both chefs working together to allow the ingredients to speak for themselves; that is what defines high-level cuisine.” This synergy cultivates an environment where innovation thrives despite the pressures of the event.

Ingredient-led approaches

Despite the challenges, one of the event’s most exciting aspects is the opportunity to experiment with niche Thai ingredients, from produce to proteins. For the chefs involved, these ingredients offer both inspiration and a challenge. Says Vo, “I want to understand the Thai ingredients and techniques first, then see how they can enter my own culinary language naturally.”

His goal is to create something that feels like a genuine conversation between Vietnam and Thailand, rather than simply combining ingredients from both countries. “Understanding their role in Thai cooking allows me to incorporate them into my own cuisine in a meaningful way while keeping the Vietnamese perspective at the heart of my cooking.”

This mindset of exploration is essential for chefs seeking to create dishes that resonate with both their own background and the local culture.

Clavijo’s approach at his restaurant, El Chato, is deeply rooted in Colombia’s ecological variety, and he sees Thailand as a mirror rather than a contrast. “Even though Colombia and Thailand are far apart, there are many similarities in our ingredients as both countries share a tropical climate,” he says. “Rather than forcing Colombian and Thai cuisines together, I prefer to find natural connections and let the products guide us.”

Julien Royer, chef-owner of Odette in Singapore, echoes this sentiment, emphasising the importance of understanding local flavours. “My culinary ideology revolves around the principle that ingredients are a reflection of terroir. My grandmother, Odette, was the one who taught me that respect for seasonality,” he says. For Royer, cooking with Thai ingredients is about respect and balance – finding a natural connection between two cuisines and letting them meet on equal terms.

The costs and benefits of participation

While the festival offers significant exposure and brand building, it also comes with sacrifices. Chefs must balance their responsibilities at home with the demands of such high-profile events. Citrin acknowledges this cost, stating, “Leaving your restaurant means leaving your team, your business, and your family. It has to have a meaningful purpose that extends beyond that one single event.”

Clavijo agrees, explaining that collaboration must go further than mere visibility. “The real value is exchange,” he says. “The lasting benefits of meeting other chefs, discovering new products, and creating ongoing relationships are what make these experiences worthwhile for chefs and attendees alike.”

A celebration of gastronomy

The World Gourmet Festival mirrors the evolving culinary landscape in Bangkok and Asia. As local chefs collaborate with international talents, they bring new perspectives and techniques to the fore. “As Thai chefs, we are proud to be part of the hosting city,” says chef Toi. “Bangkok is no longer simply a destination where international cuisine is presented; it has become an active and influential participant in the global culinary conversation.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why younger Filipinos are warming to China despite maritime tensions
item.description:
Inside a car wash lounge in the southern Philippine city of Davao, Shenilane Formento scrolls through messages on her Chinese-made Oppo phone as she waits for a customer to pay.

Formento, 29, has worked as a cashier for about a year. She follows developments in the South China Sea through news reports shared on her social media feeds, including frequent confrontations between Philippine and Chinese forces in the disputed waters.

While she found such incidents “disappointing”, she ultimately thought better of Beijing than Washington, which she blamed for the high energy prices affecting the Philippines and the rest of the world.
item.content:encoded:
Inside a car wash lounge in the southern Philippine city of Davao, Shenilane Formento scrolls through messages on her Chinese-made Oppo phone as she waits for a customer to pay.

Formento, 29, has worked as a cashier for about a year. She follows developments in the South China Sea through news reports shared on her social media feeds, including frequent confrontations between Philippine and Chinese forces in the disputed waters.

While she found such incidents “disappointing”, she ultimately thought better of Beijing than Washington, which she blamed for the high energy prices affecting the Philippines and the rest of the world.

“That’s why I prefer China to the United States. Just look at what is happening … because of the US-Iran war – fuel prices are skyrocketing,” she said.

Formento’s views point to a broader contradiction in how Filipinos see China: even as Beijing remains distrusted over its actions in the disputed waters, younger Filipinos are more likely than older generations to view the country favourably.

A new survey released on July 15 by the US-based Pew Research Centre found that 47 per cent of Filipinos aged 18 to 34 viewed China favourably, compared with 44 per cent of those aged 35 to 49 and 27 per cent of those 50 and older.

The survey also found that 61 per cent of Filipinos aged 18 to 34 had confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 32 per cent among those 50 and older.

The findings stand out against a long-running pattern of distrust towards Beijing, according to Social Weather Stations (SWS), a Philippine polling organisation.

SWS has measured Filipinos’ trust in China annually since 1994 and quarterly since 2012. Beijing recorded a positive net trust rating in only nine of 74 surveys, with its rating falling to a record low of minus 54 in 2024 on a scale ranging from plus 100 to minus 100.

China’s net trust rating remained negative in 2025 and 2026, while the US, Japan and Australia recorded higher levels of trust among Filipinos.

Pew’s findings do not establish why younger Filipinos have more favourable views of China, but experts point to how they encounter the country in everyday life, as well as a generational shift in perceptions of its economic and political rise.

“As I see it, younger Filipinos encounter China in many different ways. They see Chinese technology and consumer products, entertainment, travel content, and social media posts about life in China,” said Jan Robert R Go, associate professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

“This is where I find the idea of ‘everyday China’ useful. By this, I mean the China that people encounter in their daily lives, often outside formal politics and diplomacy. These experiences may give younger Filipinos a wider range of impressions of China.”

But Go cautioned against interpreting more favourable views of China as evidence that younger Filipinos are turning away from the US.

“I find the 61 per cent figure particularly interesting because it suggests we should be careful about assuming that attitudes towards China all move together,” he said.

“Someone can have confidence in Chinese leadership on the world stage, appreciate Chinese popular culture, and still distrust China on territorial issues.”

Indeed, the Pew survey found that 76 per cent of Filipino respondents overall named China as the country’s top threat, while 86 per cent said they were very or somewhat concerned about territorial disputes involving China and neighbouring countries. Pew did not provide age-group breakdowns for those questions.

Arnaud Leveau, a geopolitics professor at Paris Dauphine University, said the coexistence of these views was among the most notable findings.

“Strategically, this tells us something about the emerging generation in Asia. The political landscape may become less binary. Younger citizens may be willing to recognise China’s power and even aspects of its leadership while refusing to accept Chinese pressure on their sovereignty,” Leveau said.

Generational memory could also help explain the gap, he said.

Older Filipinos grew up in an environment in which the US occupied a particularly central strategic and cultural position, while China was more distant, poorer and associated with communist rivalry.

Younger Filipinos have instead grown up with an economically powerful and technologically sophisticated China that is deeply integrated into Asian trade and supply chains.

“Their China is the China of smartphones, digital platforms, high-speed rail, electric vehicles, large cities and a major Asian consumer market,” Leveau said.

“For younger Asians, China’s rise is already part of the normal international landscape. They did not experience the transition from a US-dominated regional system in the same way as older generations. Multipolarity is not a disruption for them; it is increasingly the world they have always known.”

Edmund Tayao, a law professor at the San Beda University Graduate School of Law in Manila, urged caution in interpreting the Pew findings without comparable polling from Philippine research organisations, saying he would prefer surveys from two or three of the country’s most respected polling groups.

He also pointed to social media as a potentially important influence on respondents’ views, saying the dominance of online content and what he described as China’s “vigorous campaign” could shape perceptions, particularly when users might struggle to distinguish reliable information from misinformation.

Tayao said some Filipinos might also view China favourably because they were impressed by the speed of its development and hope the Philippines could achieve similar progress.

Such exposure, Go said, did not necessarily mean younger Filipinos were becoming more sympathetic to Beijing on political questions.

“I also wouldn’t assume this makes younger Filipinos apolitical,” he said. “They may simply be responding to China through a wider range of experiences.”

Go noted that it was too early to say whether the age gap represented a lasting generational shift.

“What we do not know yet is whether that difference will remain as younger Filipinos grow older,” he said, adding that developments in the South China Sea, economic conditions, domestic politics and media coverage could all change how Filipinos viewed China.

“So, for now, I would treat the age difference as an important pattern to watch. We need to see whether it appears consistently over several years before calling it a permanent generational change.”

item.title: [SCMP] China hawks grumble over Trump’s lavish welcome planned for Xi state visit
item.description:
Hours before President Xi Jinping’s aircraft lands at Joint Base Andrews, Washington is preparing for a scene that seemed unthinkable in recent years: his American counterpart waiting on the tarmac for the leader of a country that much of the US national security establishment regards as its foremost strategic adversary.

While the Donald Trump administration is betting on warmth, deals and stability with Beijing, recent public surveys show that American anxiety over China has eased from its 2024 peak.

But the China hawks who helped shape the debate have spent the week warning that the ceremony risks obscuring a more familiar reality: Beijing remains a rival, and the issues that have defined that rivalry have not gone away.
item.content:encoded:
Hours before President Xi Jinping’s aircraft lands at Joint Base Andrews, Washington is preparing for a scene that seemed unthinkable in recent years: his American counterpart waiting on the tarmac for the leader of a country that much of the US national security establishment regards as its foremost strategic adversary.

While the Donald Trump administration is betting on warmth, deals and stability with Beijing, recent public surveys show that American anxiety over China has eased from its 2024 peak.

But the China hawks who helped shape the debate have spent the week warning that the ceremony risks obscuring a more familiar reality: Beijing remains a rival, and the issues that have defined that rivalry have not gone away.

They are making that case from outside the room. Since Trump returned to the White House, the chorus has lost resonance inside the building and with the public. The US president has disputed their arguments himself while calling Xi a “great gentleman”.

Roger Wicker, a Mississippi Republican who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, told senators on Tuesday that “quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome”.

Wicker reminded Trump that “his guest” sought to dominate his “neighbours and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America”.

He also demanded the “America first” president raise reports during his meeting with Xi about Chinese satellite imagery allegedly used in Iranian strikes that killed American troops.

Michigan Republican John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, wrote to Trump on September 18, saying that China remained “the United States’ foremost foreign adversary and greatest external threat”.

Enabling Iran to use the images to hit US forces was “tantamount to an act of war” and should bring “the most severe consequences”, the letter continued. Beijing’s objections to Taiwan arms sales should be “rejected out of hand”.

Democrats, too, have focused on what they see as the gap between the pageantry and the underlying tensions.

Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons, Jack Reed, Mark Warner, Elizabeth Warren and Andy Kim said on Tuesday that China presented “a greater threat to American security and prosperity than ever before”.

They also cited the Iran imagery and AI chips, accusing Trump of “rolling out the red carpet for President Xi and hosting closed-door dinners so his billionaire friends can strike deals”.

The objections are not confined to Capitol Hill. Outside Congress, China hawks and former government officials have been making a parallel case, focusing less on the policy details than on what the lavish welcome says about the balance of power.

Conservative commentator Gordon Chang, who regularly appears on Fox News, warned on social media that many would see the welcome “as the US acknowledging China as the world’s No 1 power”.

“Xi, after all, did not greet Trump on his arrival in Beijing in May. This special treatment will make Xi even more arrogant,” he said.

Trump has already waved him off, taking a shot during an interview with Fox in April. “You know, I listen to this Gordon Chang. He has no idea what he’s talking about. We have been very tough on China. Tough but fair.”

But Rush Doshi, who ran China policy on former president Joe Biden’s National Security Council, reads the choreography of the visit as evidence of a deeper imbalance in the relationship.

In a Substack post on Monday, Doshi noted that the honours planned for Xi exceeded those Trump received during his visit to Beijing.

“Trump will be waiting for him … then comes a flyover by a B-2 and four F-22s and a meeting between Melania Trump and [China’s first lady] Peng Liyuan,” Doshi wrote, noting that nothing quite like that happened when the US leader went to Beijing in May.

“Xi wasn’t waiting for him, there were no flyovers, and there was no meeting of the first ladies,” he observed, adding that “reciprocity” was the Trump administration’s “watchword”.

“The asymmetry in pageantry reveals something about an overall asymmetry in the relationship.”

For Doshi, the ceremony is a window into how the relationship itself may be changing. He argues that Beijing believes it has gained leverage through rare earth export controls, while the Trump administration has increasingly prioritised stability.

He predicts that the meeting is unlikely to produce many major deliverables – perhaps an extension of the trade truce, some agricultural and energy purchases and an AI dialogue. On Taiwan, “Trump’s informal, unscripted remarks may be as consequential as any formal change”, he argues.

China hawks have had less say over the tone and choreography of policy towards Beijing in the second Trump White House.

Paul Heer, a former US national intelligence officer for East Asia, wrote this week that even the remaining China specialists inside the administration, including “hawks … probably frustrated with Trump’s more accommodative approach … have yet to forge a policy consensus”.

The public mood has shifted too.

A Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey released on Monday found Americans rating China at 39 on a 0-to-100 feeling thermometer, up from 26 in 2024.

Fifty-seven per cent said they favoured “friendly cooperation and engagement” with China, while 40 per cent wanted to limit China’s power. The share describing Chinese territorial ambitions as a “critical threat” fell to 41 per cent from 52 per cent in 2022.

“There’s not a bipartisan consensus among the public in favour of a competitive containment approach,” said Craig Kafura, the council’s director of public opinion and foreign policy.

The hawks want a harder line. Other China specialists are asking a different question: whether the welcome is anything more than a show.

Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute called the welcome “unusually conspicuous,” but said it did not “necessarily reflect the real substance of the relationship”.

That Xi was making his first state visit to Washington in more than a decade “helps explain why former officials and China hawks are objecting to the optics. In their minds, China is the enemy,” he said.

According to Simon, the test will be whether the administration’s negotiating positions are tougher than Trump’s rhetoric.

“On AI, for example, the administration continues to confront China over advanced technology even as Trump has pursued a less restrictive approach to some chip exports,” he said.

Simon also noted that Washington was still pressing Beijing on fentanyl precursors, even as China announced new export controls on related chemicals.

In Simon’s view, the question that matters is less “why is Trump being so nice to Xi?” than whether the cordiality produces “concrete US gains, and what happens when the personal relationship collides with unresolved structural disputes”.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s local acts feel left out of live music boom: ‘missing middle’
item.description:
Kuala Lumpur is making it easier and cheaper to bring international music stars to the city, hoping that a bigger concert calendar can help Malaysia capture more of Southeast Asia’s booming live-music economy.

But as more global acts come to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysian musicians are asking whether the concert boom is creating more opportunities for local artists too.

Fuad Alhabshi of Malaysian rock band Kyoto Protocol said local bands once routinely benefited when major international acts came through Kuala Lumpur, including opportunities to play support slots.
item.content:encoded:
Kuala Lumpur is making it easier and cheaper to bring international music stars to the city, hoping that a bigger concert calendar can help Malaysia capture more of Southeast Asia’s booming live-music economy.

But as more global acts come to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysian musicians are asking whether the concert boom is creating more opportunities for local artists too.

Fuad Alhabshi of Malaysian rock band Kyoto Protocol said local bands once routinely benefited when major international acts came through Kuala Lumpur, including opportunities to play support slots.

His band has opened for Muse, Death Cab for Cutie and The Killers.

“Of late, I feel there has been a worrying trend of foreign acts opting not to have a local opening act,” he said.

Fuad said venues that could accommodate crowds of between 200 and 500 people were disappearing, creating what he described as a “missing middle” for Malaysian musicians trying to graduate to larger stages.

Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh has argued that the city’s booming concert calendar shows a strong demand for live entertainment.

According to Communications Ministry figures, Malaysia hosted more than 450 concerts nationwide last year, up from 408 in 2024, 335 in 2023 and 104 in 2022. The live-events industry contributed nearly US$422 million to the economy in 2025.

“This shows that there’s a real appetite for concerts here,” Yeoh said in May.

Live Nation Malaysia expects Kuala Lumpur to host 25 international music performances across six major venues throughout 2026, attracting more than 500,000 fans from Malaysia and across the region.

But Fuad said the problem was bigger than a lack of suitable venues for smaller acts.

He said stagnant wages and limited disposable income forced concertgoers to become increasingly selective, particularly as expensive international tours competed for their entertainment budgets.

“In the end, I think it still falls back to the structurally low disposable income of the median Malaysian,” he said.

For Indonesian punk band Dongker, Kuala Lumpur already has many of the ingredients needed to become a regional music hub, being affordable and easy to reach from neighbouring countries.

“I think it is very possible,” the Bandung-based band said in a statement, pointing to Malaysia’s location at the heart of Southeast Asia and its proximity to Indonesia, the region’s largest music market.

The band added that Kuala Lumpur’s cost of living was low enough for audiences to comfortably cover food, accommodation and transport on top of concert tickets.

But what looks like an attractive destination at first glance becomes more complex on closer inspection.

Dongker, currently in Malaysia for a mini tour, said cross-border movement between the Malaysian and Indonesian music scenes was already well established, especially among independent and underground musicians.

The band pointed to acts such as Daighila, Piri Reis, Moneybag and Pasca Sini, all of whom have performed in Indonesia, with Indonesian bands making the reverse trip just as often.

Dongker said Malaysian musicians including Noh Salleh, Masdo and Yuna had built audiences in Indonesia, adding that Singapore-born Malaysian rapper Alyph had also made inroads.

“Malaysia is one of the most accessible countries for alternative and indie musicians from around the world,” the band said, adding “Malaysia’s music ecosystem will grow quickly.”

Kuala Lumpur is trying to break into an increasingly competitive regional market.

Singapore has already established itself as a leading Southeast Asian stop for global artists, with Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Ed Sheeran and Mayday drawing tens of thousands of visitors to the city state in 2024, proving the sector’s economic potential. Bangkok and Jakarta are also vying for a share of international bookings.

Turning up the incentives

Malaysia has responded with a package of federal incentives spearheaded by the Communications Ministry.

Under its Concerts and Events in Malaysia Incentive (Cemi) programme, organisers of qualifying large-scale events attracting more than 15,000 attendees can claim back up to 30 per cent of eligible Malaysian expenditure, capped at US$368,000.

The scheme, administered by MyCreative Ventures, is designed to stimulate the local economy and attract international acts.

To qualify, productions must spend at least 20 per cent of eligible expenditure locally and ensure Malaysians make up at least 30 per cent of their crew. Organisers can claim an additional US$24,500 for featuring local artists if ticket sales exceed 60 per cent of capacity 30 days before the scheduled event.

Alan Foo and Johnson Lowe, the chairman and deputy chairman of the Arts, Live Festivals and Events Association, have lauded Cemi as a sign of growing alignment between government and industry.

“This grant gives our industry the momentum to do just that with structure, vision and urgency,” Foo said at the scheme’s launch in April 2025.

The ministry has also overhauled regulations governing foreign performances under its Puspal Guidelines 6.0, revising blackout dates, speeding up approvals for smaller events and introducing pre-approval requirements for foreign artists’ promotions and ticket sales.

Local councils have followed suit: Kuala Lumpur City Hall has halved the security deposit for foreign concerts to US$3,680 while keeping the cap at US$2,450 for local concerts.

But Fuad questioned whether the growing investment and attention directed towards international performers was being matched by efforts to develop Malaysian artists, noting that major record labels were increasingly tilted towards promoting foreign acts.

One way to redress that imbalance would be to harness the growing presence of Southeast Asian musicians in Malaysia to promote cross-border exchanges, he suggested.

But this would only be a success “if the domestic industry is able to take that experience and put a considerable amount of effort into developing home-grown capabilities across the value chain”, Fuad said, pointing not only to performers but also event organisers, distributors, songwriters and producers.

‘Controlled’ experience

Attracting more international acts to Kuala Lumpur is unlikely to stop Malaysians travelling abroad to see them, however.

Aaron Matthew, a 45-year-old trader based in the city, said the restrictions governing live performances in Malaysia diminished their appeal.

“Why pay so much for a ‘controlled’ performance or experience?” Matthew said. “If I can afford it, I’d pay for the full experience in a foreign country where the artist is allowed to perform their true self as much as possible.”

Malaysia’s live-music scene has weathered a string of controversies over regulation and management in recent years.

In 2014, the Future Music Festival Asia was abruptly cancelled on the final day of the electronic dance music festival after six attendees collapsed and died. Postmortem and toxicology results released two months later attributed the deaths to severe heatstroke.

The most prominent controversy to date came in 2023, when the government cancelled the final two days of the Good Vibes Festival after Matty Healy, frontman of the British band The 1975, criticised Malaysia’s anti-LGBT laws on stage before kissing a male bandmate.

The incident prompted authorities to require organisers of foreign concerts to have a “kill switch” that can shut off performances if necessary.

Matthew questioned whether the current concert boom represented sustainable demand, suggesting social media had turned some shows into “must-go” events driven by fear of missing out rather than genuine fandom.

Those who felt otherwise should embrace “Jomo”, or the “joy of missing out”, he joked.

While Matthew said he preferred smaller, more intimate shows to large-scale spectacles, he conceded that one November performance could tempt him: “I might attend the MCR concert. There’s a ticket waiting, but I don’t know.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trump praises Takaichi for doing ‘tremendous job’ ahead of Xi’s visit to US
item.description:
US President Donald Trump praised his strong relationship with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in New York on Tuesday, days before he is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The talks, held on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, came at a time when relations between Beijing and Tokyo show no signs of thawing.

Both leaders hailed their good working relationship, with Takaichi saying the two countries looked forward to deepening ties.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump praised his strong relationship with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in New York on Tuesday, days before he is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The talks, held on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, came at a time when relations between Beijing and Tokyo show no signs of thawing.

Both leaders hailed their good working relationship, with Takaichi saying the two countries looked forward to deepening ties.

Trump lavished praise on the Japanese leader, saying she had “done a tremendous job” and was “going to go down in history”.

“It’s an honour to be with her. She’s a friend of mine. We’ve gotten to know each other very well over the last period of time,” Trump said at the start of talks.

He added that he kept a close eye on Takaichi’s approval ratings and was “pleased” with what he saw, describing her as “tough and smart”.

Refraining from naming specific countries or crises, Takaichi said the meeting came as the security environment in Asia had become “so severe”, adding that her bilateral meeting with the US president “shows the world the strength of the Japan-US alliance”.

Takaichi thanks Trump for Japan-US alliance support

She also thanked Trump for his commitment to the alliance and told him that the cabinet reshuffle she carried out last week, which replaced 10 of her 18 ministers, had left his administration’s main interlocutors in Tokyo untouched.

“All of your counterparts have stayed on,” she told him, naming Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa and Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi.

This represented a continuity, Takaichi said, that would allow policymakers on both sides to deepen their personal ties and make the alliance “unshakeable”.

She also told Trump that the two countries were making headway on economic security cooperation, pointing to artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical minerals. “There are a lot of issues I’d like to discuss,” she said, without going into specifics.

UN address takes aim at Beijing, avoids naming China

Takaichi did not mention Beijing or Taiwan in her first address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, but much of the speech appeared to answer the pressure Beijing has put on Tokyo since her remarks on Taiwan in November last year.

When she turned to the rule of law, she repeated the language that Tokyo uses to describe Beijing’s activity in the East China Sea and around Taiwan.

“Any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are contrary to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and must never be tolerated anywhere in the world,” she said.

The venue carried its own weight, since Beijing had already taken the dispute to the UN.

Weeks after the row began, China’s ambassador Fu Cong wrote to Secretary General Antonio Guterres accusing the prime minister of violating international law, and the letter was circulated to every member state as an official General Assembly document.

That same month, the Chinese embassy in Tokyo posted on social media the charter’s so-called enemy state clauses, written to constrain the Axis powers after the second world war.

The embassy said founding members such as China could take military action without Security Council approval against a former enemy state that renewed a policy of aggression.

Beijing returned to the clauses in August, when foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian endorsed a remark by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that Japan was still an “enemy state” under the charter.

Takaichi used the podium in New York to demand their removal, citing a 2005 resolution in which member states had pledged to drop the references.

“In accordance with this resolution, these clauses must be deleted,” she said, adding that she wanted to “strongly emphasise this position” because Japan took “pride and honour” in its 70 years of work at the UN.

She also pushed back on Lin’s accusation, made at the same briefing, that her government was steering Japan away from pacifism and towards remilitarisation.

Japan had contributed to peace for seven decades “as a peace-loving nation under its exclusively defence-oriented policy”, she said near the end of the speech, and “this policy will remain unchanged in the future”.

The economic side of the dispute also surfaced when the prime minister spoke on critical minerals. She told delegates that “concerns about arbitrary export restrictions are growing throughout the international community”, in a clear reference to China’s rare earths export controls.

Beijing banned exports of dual-use items, a category that includes rare earths, to Japanese military users in January.

A month later, it placed 20 Japanese entities under export controls, among them the aerospace units of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Kawasaki Heavy Industries.

Souring ties

Ties between China and Japan soured dramatically after Takaichi in November suggested Tokyo could deploy its military forces in the event of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait.

Beijing viewed her comments as a sign of Tokyo’s desire to return to its pre-war path of militarism. It has since urged its citizens to avoid travelling to Japan and has restricted exports of rare earths and related materials to the country.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not see Taiwan as an independent state but are opposed to any unilateral change in the status quo.

As the Chinese trade curbs continue to bite, Tokyo has sought to appeal to Washington – its long-time ally – to urge Beijing to ease its rare earth restrictions against Japan. Trump reportedly discussed Japan with Xi during their sit-down in Beijing in May.

Against that backdrop, the US, Japan and South Korea announced a new trilateral consultation on economic security on Monday aimed at strengthening supply chains and cooperation on critical technologies.

Without naming China, the three governments pledged to oppose economic coercion, non-market practices that produce harmful overcapacity and arbitrary export restrictions. They also reaffirmed the importance of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, sending a coordinated message ahead of Trump hosting Xi at the White House on Thursday.

The Trump-Takaichi talks came a day ahead of Xi’s arrival in Washington, his first state visit to the US in more than a decade. Xi is expected to hold talks with Trump on Thursday.

The South China Morning Post understands that Japanese officials have grown anxious about how forcefully Trump would discuss Japan with Xi and how hard he would press the Chinese leader on China’s measures against Tokyo this time.

Tokyo, viewing Trump as “flirtatious” with Xi, was worried he would “go soft” on Beijing, one source said.

Timing of meeting between two leaders crucial, analyst says

Jeremy Chan, a senior analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group, said Trump’s meeting with Takaichi was particularly significant given its timing – on the eve of Xi’s arrival in the US – and the signal it sent about the continued strength of the US-Japan alliance.

“Tokyo’s ties with Washington remain remarkably strong given how frayed the US’ ties have become with so many other erstwhile allies and partners,” he said.

“For Takaichi, this meeting will allow her to be the last person to speak with Trump before he meets Xi and she will use it to underscore to Trump the centrality of Japan to his broader goals in Asia.”

Chan suggested that while Takaichi would likely not directly ask for Trump’s support in persuading Xi to ease pressure against Japan, she would emphasise the damage Chinese rare earth export restrictions are doing to US companies that rely on Japanese suppliers for key inputs.

“Takaichi will want to remind Trump of the value of the US-Japan alliance and everything that Japan has done to support his policy agenda,” Chan said.

item.title: [SCMP] Brazil’s Lula backs China peace push at UN, tells US his nation is ‘no one’s backyard’
item.description:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva renewed his backing on Tuesday for a peace initiative he launched with China to end the war in Ukraine, using his opening speech at the UN General Assembly to take thinly veiled aim at the United States over tariffs, military pressure and access to critical minerals.

Speaking in New York just days before Brazilians vote in a tight presidential race, Lula described the war between Russia and Ukraine as a five-year humanitarian drama that “continues to claim lives”.

There will be “no winners on the battlefield” and “diplomacy is the only option”, he told the assembly, pointing to “the Group of Friends for Peace, created by Brazil and China”, as proof that “there are forces in the international community willing to work for dialogue”.
item.content:encoded:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva renewed his backing on Tuesday for a peace initiative he launched with China to end the war in Ukraine, using his opening speech at the UN General Assembly to take thinly veiled aim at the United States over tariffs, military pressure and access to critical minerals.

Speaking in New York just days before Brazilians vote in a tight presidential race, Lula described the war between Russia and Ukraine as a five-year humanitarian drama that “continues to claim lives”.

There will be “no winners on the battlefield” and “diplomacy is the only option”, he told the assembly, pointing to “the Group of Friends for Peace, created by Brazil and China”, as proof that “there are forces in the international community willing to work for dialogue”.

Beijing and Brasilia launched the group at the UN in September 2024, gathering representatives from 17 developing countries behind a call for a negotiated settlement. China received no criticism in the address.

Lula framed the appeal within a wider indictment of the UN, telling delegates its credibility had “never been so low” and that members were “hostages to the immobility of a Security Council that does not fulfil its role”.

“War is not the continuation of politics by other means. It is the total bankruptcy of politics,” he said.

Criticism of US foreign policy

The United States was not named during the speech but was the clear target of several passages.

In one, Lula described the proximity of Latin America and the Caribbean to “the world’s greatest military power” as inescapable, “especially in a context of resurgent hegemonic temptations”.

“Brazil does not fit in anyone’s backyard,” he said.

He also rejected foreign military involvement in fighting organised crime, months after Washington designated Brazil’s two largest gangs, the Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho, as terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials had opposed the designation.

Brazil “will not outsource the responsibility of defending our borders”, the president declared. “We do not need aircraft carriers watching over our waters.”

Lula instead pointed to a proposal he had personally handed to US President Donald Trump for cooperation against arms trafficking and the laundering abroad of money by Brazilian criminal groups.

He paired those warnings with a message to the foreign powers competing for Brazil’s rare earths, a contest in which Washington and Beijing are the main players.

Brazil holds the critical minerals and rare earths “that the world needs to carry out the energy transition”, the president told delegates, and those resources will be exploited for the benefit of the Brazilian people.

Foreign access to them, in his words, “will have as a mandatory counterpart the generation of value in our territory, the transfer of technology and the supply of strategic national sectors”.

The remarks came six days after Lula signed a national critical minerals policy into law.

It offers up to 7 billion reais (US$1.4 billion) in incentives for domestic processing and creates a council under the presidency with powers to vet changes of control at mining companies and international agreements involving strategic minerals.

The issue has become a campaign flashpoint since April, when US-based USA Rare Earth agreed to buy Serra Verde, owner of Brazil’s only commercial rare earths mine, for about US$2.8 billion. Lula’s ruling Workers’ Party called the deal an attack on national sovereignty.

Lula’s main challenger, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, has taken the opposite line.

The Trump ally argued that Brazil should position itself as an alternative supplier for a US still dependent on China, and a memo bearing his campaign’s branding, reported by the South China Morning Post this month, proposed a rare earths supply chain with Washington designed to isolate Beijing.

The new rules apply equally to Chinese capital, which has been flowing into Brazilian mining at a record pace. Brazil was the top global destination for Chinese investment last year, receiving US$6.1 billion, and Chinese investment in mining more than tripled, according to the Brazil-China Business Council.

The largest pending Chinese bet is MMG, controlled by state-owned China Minmetals, which agreed in February last year to buy Anglo American’s Brazilian nickel operations for up to US$500 million. That is the kind of change of control the new council is empowered to review.

Brazil is also on course for a record in exports this year “despite the tariff barrage against our economy”, according to Lula. Exports reached US$250.9 billion between January and August, the highest on record for the period, while sales to China rose 15 per cent to US$77.1 billion and accounted for 30.7 per cent of the total, trade ministry data showed.

A tradition that puts Brazil before the US

Brazil has opened the General Debate every year since 1955, a custom that places its president at the rostrum immediately before the leader of the United States, the host country. Trump spoke after Lula on Tuesday.

That running order produced an unexpected thaw last year, when Trump and Lula crossed paths backstage and embraced after months of trading barbs publicly over US tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Brazilian goods, which Trump tied to the trial of former president Jair Bolsonaro over a coup plot.

Trump told the assembly minutes later that they had shared “excellent chemistry”, opening a thaw that led Washington to roll back much of the tariff package.

The combative tone of Lula’s speech this year, aimed squarely at US geopolitical decisions of recent months, was followed by a brief encounter on the floor.

As the hall emptied after Trump’s address, as it usually does once the US president finishes speaking, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio quickened his pace to reach Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, the SCMP observed.

Rubio was accompanied by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, first lady Melania Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. He pointed towards Lula as he spoke to Vieira. Their words were inaudible, but Vieira appeared to answer with a hand gesture suggesting the conversation would have to wait.

Brazil’s foreign ministry and the US State Department had not responded to requests from the SCMP for comment on the exchange by the time of publication.

Lula left UN headquarters at around the same time and went straight to John F. Kennedy International Airport for his flight back to Brazil. It was a break with his practice of holding a press conference after addressing the assembly.

Tariff dispute

No bilateral meeting between the two presidents is scheduled this year, according to Brazil’s foreign ministry.

Relations have soured again since July, when the US Trade Representative imposed a 25 per cent tariff on some Brazilian goods. The action followed an investigation that targeted Brazilian policies on digital trade and electronic payments, among other areas.

Lula addressed that directly in his speech, vowing that Brazil “will not give in to pressure from multinationals that want to privatise our PIX”, the free instant payment system run by the central bank.

He also described the World Trade Organization as “on life support” and warned that “when governments capitulate before those who use tariffs as weapons of coercion and blackmail, the consequences are dire”.

A source on the Brazilian side confirmed to the SCMP that negotiations with US officials are ongoing and that, to keep the talks going, Vieira is expected to remain in the country until the end of the month.

Vieira is scheduled to attend the G20 trade ministers’ meeting, which is set for September 30 and October 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the source said.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump defends Iran war, touts ‘America is back’ agenda in UN speech
item.description:
US President Donald Trump addressed the global community on Tuesday morning with a speech that sought to justify his war with Iran, touted how he has “made peace” and argued that his “make America great again” policies benefit the world.

His speech before the UN General Assembly came as the world grapples with years of conflict in Ukraine, Iran, Gaza, Sudan, Yemen and Lebanon, with no relief in sight.

“I can report to you with pride that America is back, and our country is stronger today than ever before,” he said. “Our country is doing better than ever before, and our future is very, very bright.”
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump addressed the global community on Tuesday morning with a speech that sought to justify his war with Iran, touted how he has “made peace” and argued that his “make America great again” policies benefit the world.

His speech before the UN General Assembly came as the world grapples with years of conflict in Ukraine, Iran, Gaza, Sudan, Yemen and Lebanon, with no relief in sight.

“I can report to you with pride that America is back, and our country is stronger today than ever before,” he said. “Our country is doing better than ever before, and our future is very, very bright.”

In a speech that seemed at times more suited to a US campaign stop than the global community, he touted his record on cutting crime, encouraging US innovation, ending illegal immigration and enacting US tax cuts, selling them as wins for the global community.

“While others have talked, I have acted. While others have spoken of peace, I have made it,” he added. “The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit and momentum of a newly energised and a very powerful United States of America.”

Trump largely kept to his prepared comments, other than a tirade against the “rogue” UN International Criminal Court and against critics of artificial intelligence.

“This is the group that came up with the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, the Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax, climate change, open borders,” he said.

“Whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins. And we’re leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

The relatively on-message address – which even included a few kudos to the UN for passing favoured resolutions – was in sharp contrast to last year’s UNGA speech. Twelve months ago, he riffed on the UN escalators and teleprompters, its substandard building materials and environmental policies that “kill all the cows”.

Trump spent a significant part of his remarks laying out his case for his war of choice in Iran.

But even as Trump has called the Iranian leadership “vicious,” “violent” and “scum” on social media, his administration has teased a possible meeting this week with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is also attending the General Assembly.

Both sides were being coy, however. Shortly before boarding his plane in Tehran, Pezeshkian said Iran was wary of more talks, having twice been attacked by the US and Israel during active negotiations.

‘To the victor belong the spoils’

Trump also highlighted on Tuesday his administration’s strategy for ending violence, instability and foreign interference in the western hemisphere, a region increasingly contested on the economic front with China, which has invested billions of US dollars.

He revisited the US military operation in January that captured then-Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and said Washington was “working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future”.

Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodriguez sat motionless and stern-faced as Trump referred to her government and did not applaud him at any point, a South China Morning Post correspondent in the hall observed.

Trump praised an oil agreement signed with Rodriguez’s government last month, which he said covered 65 billion barrels.

“It was a war, but it’s perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” he said. “To the victor belong the spoils.”

The deal gives the US 55 per cent of the effective output of 17 oilfields, including the right to buy oil at cost. Several of those fields had been operated or targeted by Chinese firms such as Sinopec, while Chinese lenders are still owed at least US$10 billion by Caracas, according to analysts.

Trump said the operation proved “the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere”, adding that Washington would use its military might when necessary.

Without naming a specific country, he accused previous administrations of letting the region be “infiltrated by hostile foreign adversaries” and mocked Venezuela’s imported hardware.

“Venezuela had the finest equipment in the world from other countries, and guess what? It didn’t work [against US forces],” he said.

Caracas relied on Russian missile systems and Chinese-made radars that Beijing had promoted as capable of detecting stealth aircraft.

Trump also called drug cartels “the ISIS of the western hemisphere” and claimed US strikes on alleged drug boats had cut seaborne drug flows by 97 per cent. The campaign has killed at least 231 people since September last year, according to US Southern Command.

He described Mexico as “the epicentre of the cartel violence” but praised ties with its government, which has repeatedly rejected US military action on its soil.

The US president also predicted that Cuba’s communist government “will fall”, prompting the Cuban delegation to walk out of the hall.

“Communism will never be coming to America, but freedom will be coming to Cuba,” he said, “and safety and security will be coming to Mexico.”

Greenland and the UN succession

Trump’s speech came as his poll figures hit new lows at home and abroad. According to a Pew survey in June, a median of just 23 per cent of adults from 36 nations expressed confidence in his leadership of global affairs, citing tariffs, Gaza, Iran, Greenland and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Even as Trump has repeatedly slammed the United Nations, questioning its purpose and inability to solve conflicts, he has relished the opportunity to address a large audience on a prominent stage.

This year’s speech went ahead without the technical mishaps of last year, when an escalator halted as Trump and his wife, first lady Melania Trump, stepped onto it on their way to the hall.

His teleprompter then failed for roughly the first 15 minutes of his 57-minute address, and he complained about the UN several times from the podium.

UN officials later said a White House videographer had accidentally triggered the escalator’s emergency stop and that the teleprompter was operated by the White House.

Trump nonetheless called the episodes “triple sabotage”, adding a claim that the sound in the hall had failed.

In the days before this year’s general debate opened, the South China Morning Post saw UN staff working to rule out a repeat. On Monday, security officers were seen testing the escalator, the teleprompter and the earpieces that carry the audio feed from the podium microphone.

In his address, the US president claimed the Pentagon had no shortage of munitions, called on Russia and Ukraine to “stop the killing” without mentioning that Moscow had invaded, and gave a shout-out to his wife.

Trump also met with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark after his speech and signed a deal allowing a larger US military presence on the world’s largest island, territory he has long coveted, that ‌could end a stand-off over the strategically located and mineral-rich territory.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday morning that the deal allows Washington “to put as many military bases as we need in order to defend everything”, adding that the US will screen potential investors in Greenland to block those linked to China or other adversaries that are not North Atlantic Treaty Organisation members.

He also called for UN financial reform, slamming the UN’s human rights activities.

“With all the genuine atrocities in the world, the UN’s top human rights officials spend their time criticising the United States for protecting our children from transgender mutilation and transgender insanity,” he said. “The craven hypocrites of [the] Human Rights Council have little to say about the persecution of Christians.”

In his last major speech to the 193-member global body, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres opened the assembly with a plea for “a world built on interdependence”.

“The fault lines in our world are widening,” he said, citing wars, climate change and artificial intelligence, among other crucial issues.

The UN assembly comes as speculation heats up about who will replace Guterres when his second five-year term ends on December 31.

No clear successor has emerged but the issue may well be on the agenda when Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping hold their summit on Wednesday in Washington. The US and China are the UN’s largest funders and most powerful Security Council members.

Guterres on Tuesday also called for AI superpowers, widely viewed as the United States and China, to start a dialogue on the technology’s future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War.

AI is expected to be a significant issue during the Trump-Xi sit-down following a pre-summit meeting on Monday between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in New York.

In an apparent dig at Trump, Guterres said superpowers must realise “that their power isn’t so super” and military power alone can’t secure peace.

item.title: [SCMP] Why small quakes in Malaysia’s Sabah could be sounding seismic alarms
item.description:
A series of small earthquakes beneath Keningau, an inland district of Sabah in Malaysian Borneo, is drawing attention to a part of the state where scientists say the faults are poorly understood and the consequences of a larger quake could be devastating.

The latest, a magnitude-3.4 tremor on September 3, was felt in several parts of Keningau, prompting staff at the district office to suspend a meeting and move to a designated safe area. No serious damage was reported.

The tremor was one of several weak earthquakes recorded around Keningau since 2023, raising questions about efforts to strengthen monitoring, development and disaster planning in the area.
item.content:encoded:
A series of small earthquakes beneath Keningau, an inland district of Sabah in Malaysian Borneo, is drawing attention to a part of the state where scientists say the faults are poorly understood and the consequences of a larger quake could be devastating.

The latest, a magnitude-3.4 tremor on September 3, was felt in several parts of Keningau, prompting staff at the district office to suspend a meeting and move to a designated safe area. No serious damage was reported.

The tremor was one of several weak earthquakes recorded around Keningau since 2023, raising questions about efforts to strengthen monitoring, development and disaster planning in the area.

A stronger earthquake in the region could trigger landslides and debris flows, cutting off roads and other vital infrastructure, experts say.

Sabah has focused much of its earthquake monitoring and preparedness on Ranau, a district near Mount Kinabalu where a 2015 earthquake killed 18 people, triggered landslides and caused widespread damage.

But about 100km southwest of Ranau, the similarly mountainous Keningau and Tambunan valleys were identified as seismically active in federal planning guidance in 2018. Geologists say both lie within the Crocker fault zone, a network of geological faults in Sabah’s mountainous interior associated with earthquake activity.

Yet neither Keningau nor Tambunan appears on the government’s published list of mapped active fault zones or areas where developers must check for earthquake risks before building.

It is unclear how extensively the two districts have been mapped and monitored for seismic risks, as the Minerals and Geoscience Department (JMG) did not respond to questions from This Week in Asia.

“Sabah’s seismic hazard is broader than Ranau alone, our scientific understanding of Sabah’s earthquake sources has not yet caught up with the level of development and exposure that now exists in the state,” said Felix Tongkul, a geologist at Universiti Malaysia Sabah (UMS), who has studied faults in the state for more than three decades.

The September 3 tremor was not an isolated event. Mohd Hisham Mohd Anip, director general of the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia), listed six weak earthquakes in the Keningau area since April 2023, ranging from magnitude 1.4 to 3.4.

“What makes Keningau scientifically interesting is not its magnitude, which was small, but the fact that several small earthquakes have occurred there over recent years,” Tongkul said.

Mohd Hisham told This Week In Asia on Friday that the sequence showed local seismic activity “associated with the release of tectonic energy”, with the “possibility of recurring earthquakes”.

Of MetMalaysia’s 80 seismic monitoring stations, 28 are in Sabah and concentrated around the Mount Kinabalu area. Keningau has one at the local meteorological station.

“For now, the current station network is sufficient for monitoring seismic activity on a regional scale,” Mohd Hisham said.

The 13th Malaysia Plan, a national development blueprint covering 2026 to 2030, does not list any new stations in the works. Rather, MetMalaysia will upgrade one station in Sandakan and four others across Sabah.

By contrast, when a series of tremors rattled Segamat in Johor – a state with no history of damaging earthquakes – last August, two new stations were announced in November, along with four to be upgraded under the plan’s first implementation phase.

Seismic records

In November 2025, Johari Abdul Ghani, then acting Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability minister, said the JMG had mapped 11 active fault zones nationwide between 2016 and 2020, four of them in Sabah: Lobou Lobou and Mensaban in Ranau, and Lahad Datu and Tabin in Lahad Datu.

“Ranau is relatively well studied, whereas places such as Keningau, Tambunan and parts of the interior are much less well characterised,” Tongkul said.

Six fault-movement benchmark stations had been installed in Sabah, Johari said. No fault in Keningau or Tambunan appeared on the list.

This contrasts with the 2018 guideline from PlanMalaysia, the federal town planning department under the Ministry of Housing and Local Government, which names both Keningau and Tambunan as seismically active.

Arthur Joseph Kurup, who took over the portfolio in December 2025, announced 18 additional early-warning systems for Sabah in June. He said four of the 34 systems nationwide were in Sabah, two of them in Kundasang.

The ministry also planned to table a proposal earlier this year to strengthen the 2017 hazard map underpinning Malaysia’s seismic building standard, including new active fault-mapping.
