Sabah has held disaster-preparedness exercises since the 2015 earthquake, but publicly posted programmes have largely centred on Kundasang and Ranau. In October 2024, the National Disaster Management Agency (NADMA) and the Sabah government held drills on landslides in Kundasang involving more than 70 personnel from various agencies.

In June, a community disaster-risk initiative in Kundasang included an earthquake simulation, early-warning and evacuation procedures, and landslide-risk mapping.

NADMA and the Sabah Fire and Rescue Department did not respond to questions regarding earthquake contingency plans, preparedness and public education.

Hidden faults

Rodeano Roslee, dean of science and technology at UMS, said the geology of the interior left little doubt about the source.

According to Rodeano, Keningau and Tambunan lie within the Crocker fault zone and normal faults have been documented cutting young river gravels near Keningau with displacements of several metres. Some faults may also be hidden beneath valley sediments.

“We know enough to recognise Keningau and Tambunan as fault-controlled and potentially active areas, but not yet enough to quantify the hazard of individual faults with the confidence required for detailed risk-based planning,” he said.

This uncertainty, he said, had consequences for things such as fault setbacks (a legal buffer zone between a known active geological fault and human structures), predicting how violently the ground would shake in future earthquakes, and the design of critical infrastructure and high-occupancy buildings.

Rodeano said this did not mean development in these two districts should stop, but rather that “the level of geological investigation should be proportional to the consequences of failure”.

The potential risk to Sabah’s mountainous interior is not limited to structural damage from an earthquake itself but also includes secondary hazards like landslides and debris flows, which can cut off vital road and infrastructure links.

Rodeano said the 2015 Ranau disaster showed that Sabah’s danger could extend well beyond the initial shaking, with destabilised slopes and rockfalls causing immediate casualties and loosened debris later capable of being swept into debris flows by heavy tropical rain.

He urged Sabah authorities to shift to statewide fault mapping, better earthquake monitoring and checks on vulnerable areas, and stronger infrastructure planning.

“The recent Keningau earthquakes are not grounds for alarm, but they are grounds for investigation,” Rodeano said.

item.title: [SCMP] Constructive. Strategic. Stability. Chinese state media spell out Xi-Trump summit aim
item.description:
The Communist Party’s flagship newspaper has set the tone for the summit on Thursday between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, calling for the two sides to build on the “constructive strategic stability” agreed upon during Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing.

The Chinese government and state media have also spelled out Beijing’s “red lines” days ahead of the high-stakes event in Washington.

The leaders will provide “strategic guidance” on how the two powers can develop a stable relationship during this week’s summit, according to a front-page article published by People’s Daily on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Communist Party’s flagship newspaper has set the tone for the summit on Thursday between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, calling for the two sides to build on the “constructive strategic stability” agreed upon during Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing.

The Chinese government and state media have also spelled out Beijing’s “red lines” days ahead of the high-stakes event in Washington.

The leaders will provide “strategic guidance” on how the two powers can develop a stable relationship during this week’s summit, according to a front-page article published by People’s Daily on Tuesday.

The newspaper cast a rosy light on the state of China-US ties since the pair last met in Beijing during Trump’s trip four months ago, saying that “positive factors in bilateral interactions continue to increase”.

Xi’s visit this week was aimed at “keeping the positive momentum going”, an article posted on Chaoyang Shaoxia, a social-media channel widely believed to be affiliated with the Chinese foreign ministry, said on Tuesday.

The ministry, Chinese embassies and ambassadors posted videos in both Chinese and English to social media on the same day, highlighting that “from Beijing to Washington DC, the China-US relationship must stay on course towards constructive strategic stability”.

At their meeting in Beijing, Xi and Trump agreed to maintain “constructive strategic stability”, although the White House statement on the talks also included demands for “fairness and reciprocity”.

Beijing has emphasised that the concept should guide China-US relations “over the next three years and beyond” – at least for the remainder of Trump’s presidency – which state media echoed on Tuesday.

“Managing ‘Taiwan independence’ is a key part of building constructive strategic stability between China and the US,” the front-page People’s Daily piece noted, framing pro-independence forces as a “common enemy” of Beijing and Washington.

“The US side must handle the Taiwan question with the utmost caution and take concrete action to safeguard the stable development of China-US relations and peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait,” it warned.

It also reiterated that “Taiwan, democracy and human rights, the path and system and development rights are four red lines” for Beijing.

“These are the guardrails and safety net for China-US relations,” said the article, which was published under the byline Guo Jiping, a pen name used for editorials which express the Communist Party’s position on major international matters.

Beijing considers Taiwan to be part of China and has not renounced the use of force to bring the self-governed island under its control.

Most countries – including the US – do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The South China Morning Post reported on Saturday that the Trump administration was considering delaying the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

The Guo Jiping commentary also argued that having the “correct strategic understanding” was “the first button that must be fastened properly” in building China-US constructive strategic stability.

It warned that the “root” of all problems in the bilateral relationship laid in the “cold war mentality” that was held by some in the US, who viewed China as a strategic rival and hyped a narrative of strategic competition.

“China and the US should be partners and friends. This is what history teaches us, and what reality requires,” it added.

The Chaoyang Shaoxia article said China’s overall national strength had “comprehensively” increased since Xi’s last state visit to the US in 2015 and its international influence had also “steadily” risen.

After more than a decade, Washington should understand that “cooperation between China and the US is greater than their differences, there is no benefit in testing each other’s limits, and decoupling from China is even less realistic”.

Instead, the US was urged to “focus on expanding cooperation” to “serve the common interests” of both nations.

Chinese policymakers have repeatedly said in recent months that the concept of “constructive strategic stability” does not deny the existence of competition between China and the US but calls for avoiding full-scale confrontation and maintaining dialogue to manage the countries’ differences.

“Economic and trade cooperation should continue to serve as the ballast and propeller” of the relationship, the Guo Jiping article said.

As part of preparations for the summit, the two governments held a round of trade talks in New York over the weekend. They also agreed to establish dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI), while China stepped up purchases of US soybeans in recent days. Beijing on Tuesday added two drug precursor chemicals to its export control list for North America.

Chaoyang Shaoxia said that as the technology continued to develop, competition between China and the US in AI was inevitable.

“But what we seek is a race in which each side strives to catch up and both advance together, rather than a life-or-death, zero-sum struggle that exhausts both sides,” it said.

“By steadily breaking the ice and building trust in lower and moderately sensitive areas, even if each step forward is only a small one, we can help ensure that global technology advances in a positive direction and benefits the world.”

The People’s Daily article called on the two countries to make AI a “new frontier” of cooperation.

It also said China-US constructive strategic stability would serve as a “precious public good” for the whole world.

The article described the concept as a solution to the “Thucydides Trap”, a theory in which a rising power and an established hegemon are destined for war. The article described the theory as being rooted in a zero-sum narrative of confrontation drawn from the West’s history.

“Major powers bear special responsibilities,” it said.

“China and the US should … properly handle regional flashpoints with a strong sense of responsibility by doing more practical and beneficial work to promote peace talks and reconciliation,” it added, referring to conflicts in the Middle East, the war in Ukraine and tensions on the Korean peninsula.

It argued that the back-to-back multilateral gatherings of the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 summit in Miami in December would create a “historic linkage” to help coordination between the two countries.

“The year 2026 is bound to be a historic and landmark year in China-US relations that carries forward the past and ushers in the future,” it said.

item.title: [SCMP] Were the Serbian military’s new robot dogs built using Chinese technology?
item.description:
Cutting-edge Chinese technology could gradually be becoming part of Serbia’s weapons systems with the appearance of robot dogs in a Serbian military drill on the weekend soon after the opening of a Chinese robotics factory in the Balkan country, according to observers.

Robodogs equipped with machine guns, grenade launchers and rocket launchers were among the major weapons systems unveiled at Serbia’s Pobednik 2026 large-scale tactical live-fire exercise on Sunday.

The event involved its army, air force, air defence, special forces and military police and, according to Serbian media reports, the robodogs were designed to enter dangerous areas and secure entry routes for special forces, operations that were part of the military drill.
item.content:encoded:
Cutting-edge Chinese technology could gradually be becoming part of Serbia’s weapons systems with the appearance of robot dogs in a Serbian military drill on the weekend soon after the opening of a Chinese robotics factory in the Balkan country, according to observers.

Robodogs equipped with machine guns, grenade launchers and rocket launchers were among the major weapons systems unveiled at Serbia’s Pobednik 2026 large-scale tactical live-fire exercise on Sunday.

The event involved its army, air force, air defence, special forces and military police and, according to Serbian media reports, the robodogs were designed to enter dangerous areas and secure entry routes for special forces, operations that were part of the military drill.

The robodogs’ debut comes only a few weeks after Europe’s first factory for mass-producing humanoid robots and robotic dogs began production in the western Serbian city of Sabac.

During factory’s opening ceremony on August 29, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that the country would unveil domestically produced combat robots in action “in 15 days”.

The robot factory was jointly established by Taiwan-headquartered automotive supplier Minth Group and mainland Chinese robotics company AgiBot.

AgiBot, which provides technological support for the Sabac factory, said that the company “neither manufactured nor sold” the quadrupedal robots involved in the military drills, and that the products it developed and sold were intended exclusively for civilian purposes.

However, Minth Group, which actually operates the factory, did not respond to the South China Morning Post’s request for comment.

While the US is thought to be a leader in robodog technology, military exports are strictly controlled.

This leaves China as the most likely source of Serbia’s robotic dogs, given the two countries’ existing defence collaboration and China’s 80 per cent share of global robodog production.

“[One can] only assume the dog robots were manufactured in Sabac,” said Vuk Vuksanovic, lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy education at King’s College London.

“The issue remains: how advanced is the Serbian defence system, and does it allow integration of Chinese robotics, given that Serbian defence procurement is not always based on long-term strategic planning.

“For China, the main reason for these transactions is to win new defence markets, and Serbia can be used as a potential short cut to European defence markets.”

China is one of the world’s largest suppliers of parts for uncrewed platforms, often with the potential for both civilian and military uses, and is rapidly integrating robotics technologies into its own military.

During a military parade in Beijing in September last year, the People’s Liberation Army showcased robodogs equipped with combat rifles and reconnaissance gear.

China also unveiled similar robotic dogs during February’s World Defence Show 2026 in Saudi Arabia, potentially in an attempt to drum up overseas sales. On display was the PF-070 system, which carries four anti-tank guided missiles.

Martin Sebena, a lecturer at the University of Hong Kong who specialises in China-Europe relations, said there was “both industrial and geopolitical logic” to the countries’ “intense collaboration” on drone production, with the Serbian Ministry of Defence explicitly describing China as a partner in air defence and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV).

“Together with robotics, this gives rise to a dual-use industrial cluster,” Sebena said. “On the geopolitical side, production in Serbia can be seen as hedging, as it allows AgiBot to localise production in Europe in case import restrictions are imposed on it in the future.

“Robotics production has the cover of a Sino-Serbian strategic partnership and goes in line with Serbia’s recent military purchases from China, which has become Serbia’s largest arms supplier.”

Sebena said that given the UAV precedent, the integration of Chinese robotics technology into the Serbian military “could go quite far”.

“The Chinese have first sold drones to Serbia, then helped it develop its own UAV systems until the Serbians were able to produce UAVs themselves,” Sebena said.

“The same could repeat here, with the Chinese providing the know-how, platform and software, and the Serbian side adapting the technology and integrating it into their military.”

Serbia is a major customer for China’s arms industry, buying 6.8 per cent of Beijing’s arms exports between 2021 and 2025 – the second-biggest buyer after Pakistan, which accounted for 61 per cent, according to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Belgrade’s recent military drill also featured other Chinese-made weapons systems, showing intelligence collection using CH-95 long-range reconnaissance and strike UAVs and tackling swarms of low-flying drones and combat aircraft with the HQ-17AE short-range surface-to-air missile system.

Chinese weapons systems play a particularly significant role in Serbia’s air defence network, which reportedly operates Chinese-made HQ-9 long-range and FK-3 surface-to-air missile systems.

Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said Serbia would likely integrate Chinese robotics, sensors, AI, autonomy software and networking technologies into its drone-enabled formations.

Meanwhile, China saw Serbia as a “strategic European manufacturing and technology partner” that was politically receptive to Chinese investments and technology transfers, she said.

“I expect cooperation to be deepened gradually over the next three to five years, especially in drones,” Odgaard said.

“The opening of the robotics factory and recent military cooperation suggest growing institutional links.”

Odgaard added that Serbia was likely to balance these ties against its relations with the EU and other partners, which could mean that “incremental integration” and co-production were more likely than wholesale dependence on Chinese military robotics.

Stefan Vladisavljev, programme director at the Serbia-based Foundation BFPE for a Responsible Society, said Belgrade traditionally maintained a policy of military neutrality, which did not limit its cooperation with different actors.

“As Serbia and China have developed their relations over the span of the past two decades, an increased amount of military-type equipment has been purchased from China,” Vladisavljev said.

“With the development of military technology, now we are entering a phase in which Serbia – in order to build its own capacity – is purchasing new types of equipment.”

item.title: [SCMP] Taiwan coastguard’s rare missile firing reveals deepening links with navy
item.description:
Taiwan’s coastguard fired a supersonic anti-ship missile during a military exercise last week, an unusual move by a civilian law enforcement agency that analysts say could be aimed at complicating potential war plans.

The drill matters not only because it highlights the growing integration between the agency and Taiwan’s navy, experts argue, but also because missile-armed coastguard vessels would add another threat the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would have to account for in a conflict.

On Friday, the Anping-class coastguard patrol vessel Qijin launched a home-grown Hsiung Feng III, or HF-3, which hit a decommissioned navy frigate more than 100km (62 miles) away, according to local media. The coastguard also fired an HF-2, an older subsonic anti-ship weapon, during the drills, which involved Taiwan’s army, navy and air force.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan’s coastguard fired a supersonic anti-ship missile during a military exercise last week, an unusual move by a civilian law enforcement agency that analysts say could be aimed at complicating potential war plans.

The drill matters not only because it highlights the growing integration between the agency and Taiwan’s navy, experts argue, but also because missile-armed coastguard vessels would add another threat the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would have to account for in a conflict.

On Friday, the Anping-class coastguard patrol vessel Qijin launched a home-grown Hsiung Feng III, or HF-3, which hit a decommissioned navy frigate more than 100km (62 miles) away, according to local media. The coastguard also fired an HF-2, an older subsonic anti-ship weapon, during the drills, which involved Taiwan’s army, navy and air force.

This means at least three named vessels of the coastguard’s 12-ship Anping class have now fired Hsiung Feng missiles, underscoring a broader effort to turn them into an additional pool of naval strike platforms.

Based on the navy’s Tuo Chiang-class corvette, the vessels are designed to be armed with up to 16 HF-2 and HF-3 anti-ship missiles upon wartime mobilisation.

John Bradford, executive director of the Yokosuka Council on Asia-Pacific Studies and a former US Navy officer, said the developments made long-standing arrangements between the coastguard and navy more visible while also showing that their cooperation was taking new forms.

“The two forces are definitely getting closer, learning to cooperate and identifying ways to complement each other,” he said. “What was going on before is becoming more visible while they are simultaneously doing things never done before.”

The practice of arming coastguard vessels with anti-ship missiles is unusual internationally, as coastguards are generally associated with law enforcement, safety and patrol duties rather than military and long-range strike missions.

There is some precedent, however. During the late Cold War, the United States Coast Guard fitted some Hamilton-class vessels with Harpoon anti-ship missiles. The Mellon patrol vessel fired one in January 1990 before the capability was removed.

Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration remains a civilian agency in peacetime, but its wartime role is built into the island’s defence framework.

The island’s National Defence Act allows the government to bring the coastguard into the military order of battle during a conflict. A 2021 special defence procurement law went further by funding wartime weapons and related support systems for coastguard vessels under a peacetime-to-wartime conversion programme.

Beijing has taken a different route towards integrating its coastguard with the military.

In July 2018, the China Coast Guard was transferred from civilian administration to the People’s Armed Police, placing it within a structure under the Central Military Commission. Beijing’s Coast Guard Law, which took effect in 2021, also allows the agency to carry out defence operations under the commission’s orders.

Its director, Zhang Jianming, is a former navy officer. The PLA Navy has also transferred ships to the coastguard, including 22 Type 056 corvettes from 2021, with their missile and torpedo launchers removed.

Beijing has also deployed coastguard formations during major exercises around Taiwan, including Joint Sword in 2024 and Strait Thunder-2025A, using them for patrols, inspections and other law-enforcement operations – moves seen as possible rehearsals for a blockade.

That said, Simona Grano, head of Research Area China-Taiwan Relations at the University of Zurich, cautioned against viewing Taipei’s approach as an attempt to replicate Beijing’s model. While the mainland had integrated its coastguard into a military command structure, Taiwan retained a civilian coastguard in peacetime and was preparing it for wartime operations, she said.

“The institutional models and the political purposes are quite different,” she said.

Taipei’s preparations date back at least to 2005, when the Wei Hsing patrol vessel fired an HF-2 during the annual Han Kuang military exercises.

Within the Anping class, the Anping fired an HF-2 in 2022 and the Bali fired an HF-3 in 2024, while an unidentified vessel of the class fired two HF-2s in 2025, according to a navy report to lawmakers.

The approach became more visible during this year’s Han Kuang iteration in August, when the Bali was fitted with Hsiung Feng missiles and operated alongside navy Kuang Hua VI missile boats in a coastal-strike drill involving the navy’s newly established Littoral Operations Command.

There is no indication the exercise changed the coastguard’s wartime command arrangements, but it showed a coastguard patrol vessel operating alongside navy missile boats in a strike role.

Those operational preparations have been accompanied by moves to strengthen links between the navy and coastguard leadership.

Hours after Friday’s drill, Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling said a navy flag officer would fill the coastguard’s restored third deputy director general post, describing the move as part of closer cooperation between the two services.

The position was restored under legislation passed in June, with the government citing peacetime-to-wartime conversion and the coastguard’s expanding military-related duties among the reasons for adding another deputy.

A Taiwan coastguard expert, speaking anonymously because he was not authorised to comment publicly, said that arming coastguard vessels with anti-ship missiles could help close the gap between law enforcement and military responses if a confrontation involving mainland Chinese warships escalated into armed conflict.

However, the expert said the approach also risked blurring the line between law enforcement and military action, complicating crisis responses.

For the PLA, this would mean treating some Taiwanese coastguard “white hulls” – not just naval “grey hulls” – as potential anti-ship missile threats, the expert added.

Despite that added complexity, Bradford said the missile-armed coastguard vessels would not fundamentally change the military balance.

“Given the size of the PLA Navy and [PLA] Air Force, these are not going to be a game-changer,” he said. “Yet in naval warfare, every opposing vessel adds risk to your plan and forces you to make increasingly difficult choices.”

Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not see Taiwan as an independent state, but most are opposed to changing the status quo by force.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Xi and Trump use their leverage to actually make progress?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fifth part of a series, Fan Chen and Orange Wang look at the negotiating chips and areas where progress might be made.

There will be some powerful bargaining chips on the table when Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet in Washington this week.

Both sides have economic and geopolitical leverage, and according to one analyst the negotiations will be as much about what they have chosen not to do to avoid retaliation.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fifth part of a series, Fan Chen and Orange Wang look at the negotiating chips and areas where progress might be made.

There will be some powerful bargaining chips on the table when Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet in Washington this week.

Both sides have economic and geopolitical leverage, and according to one analyst the negotiations will be as much about what they have chosen not to do to avoid retaliation.

Others pointed to critical areas where the two powers are locked in fierce competition but could instead be working together – from artificial intelligence and military dialogue to trade and biosafety.

But analysts agreed that keeping bilateral ties on a stable track would be a priority at the summit, and that was likely to be helped by a “tacit understanding” between Beijing and Washington on sensitive issues such as Iran and Taiwan. North Korea is also expected to be on the agenda.

Since Trump visited China in May, both countries have seen that the leverage they hold actually “works”, according to Taiyi Sun, an associate professor of political science at Christopher Newport University (CNU) in Virginia.

He said rare earths and critical minerals remained a key bargaining chip for China, while America still had leverage from its advanced semiconductors and related technologies.

Sun noted that Washington still had options, including another tariff increase based on its Section 301 trade investigation and its delayed US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan.

Likewise, he noted that Beijing had room to adjust its commitments to buying American oil, planes and agricultural products.

“What looks like goodwill today can become leverage tomorrow,” Sun said.

But he said that while both capitals had powerful tools at their disposal, “neither can use them without expecting significant retaliation”.

Expectations have been low for the presidential talks – the second face-to-face encounter between Xi and Trump this year.

Still, Sun said artificial intelligence “could produce one of the summit’s least expected outcomes”, suggesting the US and China might share the strongest interest in preventing “catastrophic misuse or loss of control” of the emerging technology.

AI governance has become a prominent part of the strategic rivalry between the world’s two largest economies.

The issue has been in the spotlight in recent days, with warnings that the technology could create an extinction-level event for humanity and heated debate over slowing down development of advanced models.

In marathon talks in New York on Sunday, US Trade Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng agreed to set up a dialogue on artificial intelligence with a “shared vision of common goals and common threats”. The US said a bilateral Board of Trade was also operationalised during the talks.

Strengthening communication on AI will be a key goal of the Xi-Trump talks, according to Zhao Minghao, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University.

He said the two sides were likely to discuss domestic regulatory approaches and notification mechanisms for shared threats such as terrorism and transnational criminal groups using AI for malicious purposes.

“They may also explore communication protocols for major AI risk events, including a US-China emergency hotline for critical AI incidents,” Zhao said, adding that these proposals were already under discussion through unofficial channels.

Earlier this month, the Trump administration accused Chinese firms of stealing and copying American models through “industrial-scale distillation campaigns”. In response, Beijing said Washington was seeking a “monopoly” on the technology and warned of countermeasures.

Huang Ping, assistant dean of the Chinese University of Hong Kong- Shenzhen’s School of Public Policy, said that given the timing, the US accusations would boost its leverage in the discussions on AI.

He said a US-China dialogue mechanism on AI was of “very high” urgency, noting that they had clear differences over the definition of security and the purpose of regulation.

But he remained “cautiously optimistic” about outcomes of the AI talks, saying he expected a statement on principles, a follow-up working mechanism and preliminary arrangements in some areas.

According to Huang, Beijing and Washington were likely to discuss the rules, pace and boundaries of their AI rivalry. But he noted that their technological advantages, market interests and industrial growth remained the biggest issues – highlighting the clash between China’s low-cost, open-source ecosystem and an American commercial model that relies on closed-source, high-priced services.

Ahead of the summit, China’s top diplomat Wang Yi on Thursday urged Washington to stick with its commitment to “constructive strategic stability” in the relationship during a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Zhao from Fudan said reinforcing and acting on that commitment would be Beijing’s “primary goal” for Xi’s US trip – his first state visit to the country since 2015.

Both sides agreed to the concept in May, though the White House in its statement included US demands for “fairness and reciprocity”.

Political scientist Zhu Zhiqun, from Bucknell University in Pennsylvania, said both the US and China “genuinely desire a stable and constructive relationship”.

He also noted that Trump valued his personal relationship with Xi, seeing their rapport as key to stabilising bilateral ties.

“When facing serious internal and external challenges such as rising gas prices and a prolonged war in Iran before the November midterm election, the last thing Trump wants is a rocky relationship with China,” he said.

Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, expected Trump to “express further support” for constructive strategic stability when he met Xi.

“With the Russia-Ukraine war grinding on and the Middle East morass expanding, Trump aims to preserve a tactical thaw between the two countries,” he said, adding that Xi was also likely to avoid a personal rupture with Trump.

According to Sun from CNU, China has gained leverage since the Iran war began in February by avoiding using its “enormous purchasing power in the global energy market” and not adding more pressure on international oil prices.

“I see that restraint partly as a favour to Trump – reciprocity for Trump’s restraint on issues that Beijing cares about,” he said, pointing to the US president putting the latest Taiwan arms sale on hold.

“There is a tacit understanding between Trump and Xi on this front,” Sun added. “Neither side needs to publicly announce a quid pro quo for such an understanding to function.”

Taiwan has long been “the first red line” for Beijing in managing its ties with Washington.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The South China Morning Post reported on Saturday that the US was considering postponing major arms sales to the island until after November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, citing Beijing’s strong opposition to the deal and US defence industry constraints.

The SCMP also reported on Thursday that the two sides were discussing possible announcements to strengthen military ties during Xi’s visit to the US.

A potential trip by Trump to China to attend the Apec gathering could provide an opportunity for another face-to-face meeting with Xi, as well as a chance to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

The SCMP reported earlier this month that China was willing to broker a leaders’ meeting between Pyongyang and Washington and would support all credible efforts leading to resumed dialogue.

Zhao from Fudan said it was possible that Trump and Xi had already discussed this in May, and that there had been further talks between Beijing and Pyongyang during Xi’s subsequent visit to North Korea in June.

“As a result, I think Trump himself remains very interested in pushing for a new summit with North Korea’s top leader – and Shenzhen is a very likely location,” he said, adding that Pyongyang would be looking to improve its international standing with such a meeting.

But he noted that China’s influence on its neighbour was limited and that friction between Washington and Seoul – following the recent cancellation of joint military drills – could stall diplomatic progress with Pyongyang.

Wyne from the International Crisis Group noted that some of Trump’s advisers would likely be “wary of making China a diplomatic intermediary”.

“Trump himself, though, would likely have little – if any – objection given his affinity for strongmen, his frustration that South Korea did not assist US efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and his hope that another tete-a-tete with Kim could burnish his peacemaking credentials by helping de-escalate tensions across the Korean peninsula,” Wyne said.

According to Sun, North Korea is not a Chinese bargaining chip. “China can help open the door, but it cannot simply deliver Kim,” he said.

There have been efforts to build positivity ahead of Xi’s trip to Washington, with the two governments signalling progress in discussions on reciprocal tariff cuts covering some US$30 billion in trade on each side and on counternarcotics cooperation.

Zhao said extending the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea in October was likely to be the “most realistic deliverable” from this week’s talks.

“This summit is vital for how China and the US coordinate their economic and trade relations and operationalise mechanisms such as the trade and investment councils,” he said.

Meanwhile, growing warnings over AI-enabled biosecurity threats have fuelled calls for the two powers to work together in the health sector.

Yanzhong Huang, a senior fellow for global health at the Council on Foreign Relations, said health issues were “unlikely” to be a summit focus, with fentanyl a possible exception.

“That does not mean there are no urgent issues between the two sides. Pharmaceutical supply-chain resilience, China’s rise in biotech, dual-use research, and AI’s application to health are increasingly treated as health-security challenges,” Huang said.

“US-China health cooperation is possible, but it will remain narrow and ad hoc,” he said, adding that given the lack of trust, formal cooperation in sensitive areas was unlikely and “joint R&D even more so”.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s UN Security Council bid tests non-aligned diplomacy
item.description:
Indonesia’s bid for another term on the United Nations’ premier security body stands a good chance of success given Jakarta’s growing global engagement, analysts say, but its balancing act between competing powers could complicate efforts to speak for the Global South.

Jakarta’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that it would launch its campaign this week for a fifth term as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for 2029–2030.

The ministry said it was seeking the seat to represent the priorities of developing countries at the UN’s most powerful body and that its campaign would focus on peacekeeping, preventive diplomacy, conflict prevention and civilian protection.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s bid for another term on the United Nations’ premier security body stands a good chance of success given Jakarta’s growing global engagement, analysts say, but its balancing act between competing powers could complicate efforts to speak for the Global South.

Jakarta’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that it would launch its campaign this week for a fifth term as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for 2029–2030.

The ministry said it was seeking the seat to represent the priorities of developing countries at the UN’s most powerful body and that its campaign would focus on peacekeeping, preventive diplomacy, conflict prevention and civilian protection.

“Indonesia aims to act as a bridge builder, establishing common ground, maintaining dialogue within the council and seeking practical solutions. We will also bring the voice and priorities of the Global South,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Yvonne Mewengkang told reporters on Thursday.

“Indonesia [also] wants a Security Council that delivers results. It might sound overly ambitious, but why not? That is precisely what Indonesia aims to bring: an effective and responsive Security Council,” she added.

The council has 15 members: five permanent members with veto powers – China, France, Russia, Britain and the United States – and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.

Indonesia has previously served four terms on the council: 1973–1974, 1995–1996, 2007–2008 and 2019–2021.

Rifki Dermawan, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Andalas in Padang, West Sumatra, said the country’s bid stood a good chance considering its active global engagement under President Prabowo Subianto.

“Popularity does matter,” he said, adding that securing the seat could help strengthen Prabowo’s goal of making Indonesia an active contributor to the international community.

Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo has visited nearly 30 countries and attended a number of high-profile summits to position Jakarta as an active mediator and independent middle power.

Apart from joining Brics as its first Southeast Asian member, Prabowo has actively advocated for the Global South at international forums such as the G20, emphasising fairness and strategic autonomy for developing countries.

Radityo Dharmaputra, a foreign-policy analyst and lecturer at Surabaya’s Airlangga University, said the odds of a fifth term on the council “are in Indonesia’s favour”, adding that Jakarta was one of the most consistent contributors to UN peacekeeping troops.

He said Indonesia was expected to push hard for Palestinian statehood, humanitarian access and for any stabilisation mission to remain anchored in a UN mandate rather than in a US-led framework.

“On Ukraine, I would expect Indonesia to present itself as a bridge builder calling for a ceasefire and dialogue,” Radityo added.

However, Indonesia will still need to mount a strong diplomatic campaign, taking lessons from the Philippines’ defeat by Kyrgyzstan last June. Manila lost to Bishkek for a non-permanent seat by a wide margin of 142 to 49 votes – a loss partly resulting from Manila’s treaty alliance with the US, which worked against it among non-aligned nations.

Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate international relations professor at Jenderal Achmad Yani University, said that while Indonesia stood a good chance of getting a seat, the UN might look to consider other countries. He pointed out that former Indonesian foreign minister Retno Marsudi was appointed UN special envoy on water in November 2024.

The Security Council bid also reflected the “personal ambition” of Prabowo, who had often sought high-profile arenas to “showcase his leadership”, Yohanes added.

A voice for the Global South?

Rifki said a seat on the council might not automatically make Indonesia the voice of the Global South due to Jakarta’s mixed positions on several international issues.

“Jakarta’s external approaches under Prabowo have been confusing for many Indonesians. Many have criticised his unclear direction in exercising foreign policies,” he said.

“How can Indonesia support the freedom of Palestine while sitting side-by-side with Israel on the ‘Board of Peace’, a problematic organisation led by [US President Donald] Trump?”

Indonesia strongly supports Palestinian independence and a two-state solution, maintaining that it will only formally recognise Israel as a sovereign state once Palestinian statehood is established.

In January, Indonesia joined Trump’s “Board of Peace” to oversee post-war governance, reconstruction and demilitarisation of the Gaza Strip, but Prabowo later suspended his country’s participation.

Rifki said that Indonesia’s ability to exert influence on behalf of the Global South would also be constrained by the “privileges of veto power” held by the five permanent members of the council.

“To make the council more effective, reform is a must,” Rifki said.

Critics have long called for reform of the council as its permanent members, in place since 1945, each wield a veto power that often paralyses its ability to resolve international conflicts and crises.

Apart from sharp disagreements among nations on how to expand the council, amending the UN Charter governing its make-up would require a two-thirds majority in the UN General Assembly as well as ratification by two-thirds of member states – including all five permanent members of the council.

Radityo said that other countries might see Indonesia as a “fence-sitter” or a “hypocrite” for championing Palestine’s statehood while remaining neutral on Ukraine. Indonesia had consistently framed the Ukraine war “as a tragedy to be ended through dialogue rather than as an act of aggression”, he said.

Abstaining from votes would be harder to hide on a 15-member council than in the General Assembly, Radityo said.

“So ambiguity becomes much harder to maintain,” he said, adding that Indonesia could contribute credibly as a non-Western, non-aligned voice in humanitarian areas – such as helping with prisoner exchanges, returning deported Ukrainian children and ensuring nuclear safety in war zones like Zaporizhzhia.

“By 2029, the council may be dealing with monitoring a ceasefire rather than the war itself,” Radityo said, adding that Indonesia’s peacekeeping experience would serve it well should this outcome come to pass.

For Prabowo, winning the council seat would indicate “to the world and to the domestic audience that Indonesia is respected”, he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Home at last? Why house arrest for Malaysia’s Najib is no done deal
item.description:
Malaysia’s former prime minister Najib Razak appears to have entered the home stretch of his years-long bid to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest.

The 73-year-old has spent nearly two years fighting to serve his sentence at home, after claiming a royal order issued alongside his 2024 sentence commutation granted him that privilege.

The 2024 decision had already halved his 12-year prison sentence and reduced his fine – to 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) – for misappropriating funds from SRC International, a former unit of state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s former prime minister Najib Razak appears to have entered the home stretch of his years-long bid to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest.

The 73-year-old has spent nearly two years fighting to serve his sentence at home, after claiming a royal order issued alongside his 2024 sentence commutation granted him that privilege.

The 2024 decision had already halved his 12-year prison sentence and reduced his fine – to 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) – for misappropriating funds from SRC International, a former unit of state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).

Najib must first settle that fine before he can be released from prison, but even if he manages to raise the funds, his future is far from certain.

Malaysia has no law governing house arrest and the rules for Najib’s detention are still being worked out.

Here’s what we know so far about how it will work, what Najib needs to do to go home – and why he could yet find himself back behind bars.

Crowdfunding freedom

Najib was granted his request for house arrest on Friday, when the Federal Territories Pardons Board, chaired by King Sultan Ibrahim, agreed to let him serve the remainder of his six-year SRC sentence – until August 23, 2028 – at home.

He must first pay the fine, however, and comply with the pardon’s other conditions. Any breach would void the arrangement and see him returned to prison, according to the official statement announcing the decision.

His supporters in Umno – the Malay nationalist party he led for nine years until his government was ousted in the 2018 election – have already started passing the hat around. A solidarity fund launched by the party raked in 1 million ringgit within a single day, with many supporters reportedly chipping in 10 ringgit or 50 ringgit apiece.

Attorney General Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar said on Monday that Najib’s family had yet to pay the fine, which must be settled with the Kuala Lumpur High Court registrar before any transfer from prison can go ahead.

Yet even once the money was paid, the process “may take some time”, Dusuki said.

Najib’s lawyers have said raising the money is complicated because a “significant part” of his assets, bank accounts and properties remain frozen or subject to government enforcement proceedings.

Decree deja vu

The pardon Najib was granted in 2024 by then king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah not only cut his jail sentence and slashed his initial 210 million ringgit fine, it was also accompanied by a separate decree Najib’s lawyers insisted allowed him to serve the balance of his prison term at home.

The document did exist, but the High Court ruled in December that it was unenforceable since house arrest had not been deliberated at the Pardons Board meeting and Malaysian law contained no provision for carrying it out. Najib then withdrew his appeal in April.

Article 42 of Malaysia’s Federal Constitution gives the king broad powers to grant pardons, reprieves and respites.

But the text does not spell out precisely how far that clemency can go, according to Malaysian constitutional lawyer Andrew Khoo.

“The actual ambit of the Pardons Board, in terms of the scope of the clemency that may be granted, is not specified in the constitution or in regulations connected therewith,” Khoo said.

“Given that this provision relies on the historical royal prerogative that has been received by convention, it could be argued that there are no limits to the scope of the clemency.”

Home as a prison

Malaysia still has no law specifically governing house arrest, leaving authorities to look to existing prison rules for a way to make Najib’s new arrangement work while the government develops separate legislation on home detention.

Police and prison officials have assessed Najib’s residence in the upmarket Langgak Duta neighbourhood of Kuala Lumpur, local media reported on Monday, with a mobile police station deployed nearby.

Authorities said the bungalow had not yet been formally confirmed as his detention site.

“One possible technical way the prison authorities can enforce a house arrest is to designate Najib’s house as a prison,” Malaysia-based constitutional lawyer Lim Wei Jiet said.

Such an arrangement could also subject Najib to prison-style restrictions, Lim said, including limits on electronic devices, food and who he can meet.

“There are restrictions … I’m not sure whether that is in line with the idea of a house arrest,” he said.

Back behind bars?

Even a successful move home would only cover Najib’s SRC sentence, relating to some 42 million ringgit that was transferred into his personal accounts.

In December, the High Court convicted him in a separate 1MDB case involving 2.3 billion ringgit (US$564 million) and sentenced him to a further 15 years in prison.

Justice Collin Lawrence Sequerah rejected Najib’s claim that the case was a politically motivated witch hunt, pointing instead to “cold, hard and incontrovertible evidence” against him and ordering the new prison term to begin only after his SRC sentence ends.

Najib is currently appealing that conviction, but as things stand, he would be legally bound to return to prison in 2028.

“If he remains convicted in the 1MDB matter and his house arrest period has finished, he has to go back to the normal prison,” Lim said. “Unless, of course, there is a further clemency bid by him which is successful.”

Pardon the politics

Friday’s pardon decision followed a strong year at the ballot box for the United Malays National Organisation. Its Barisan Nasional coalition swept 48 of 56 seats in Johor in July, then took 18 of 36 in Negeri Sembilan the following month – more than any other bloc.

Umno continues to press for its former president’s release, ensuring the issue remains one of the most sensitive in the party’s uneasy governing partnership with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition.

That has never sat well with the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key coalition partner for Anwar and one of Najib’s fiercest critics over 1MDB. Tensions flared again following the house-arrest decision, with DAP secretary general Anthony Loke offering his resignation as transport minister in protest.

Political scientist Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid called Najib’s house arrest “a double-edged sword” for Umno.

“Malay voters are now divided,” he said. “Some who have supported Umno all along will continue to do so, but floating voters [such as] those without any party loyalty will likely distance themselves from Umno [even] further.”

While house arrest for Najib could “marginally improve Umno’s prospects” in some of its traditional strongholds, it also risked alienating middle-class Malay and anti-corruption voters, Ahmad Fauzi said.

item.title: [SCMP] The US-China tech war has evolved since the last Xi-Trump summit. Who has the edge now?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fourth part of this series, Sylvia Ma looks at the economic and technological levers available to both in their protracted rivalry.

For years, Huawei Technologies has served as a central battleground in the contest between the world’s two largest economies. As Washington tightens restrictions, the Chinese tech giant continues to find new ways forward – to the point that “becoming Nvidia” is now an internal goal.

Days before President Xi Jinping’s trip to the United States for a high-stakes meeting with his American counterpart Donald Trump, Huawei announced a major technological breakthrough: a system that it said was capable of enabling up to 1 million processors to operate as a single, unified computer.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fourth part of this series, Sylvia Ma looks at the economic and technological levers available to both in their protracted rivalry.

For years, Huawei Technologies has served as a central battleground in the contest between the world’s two largest economies. As Washington tightens restrictions, the Chinese tech giant continues to find new ways forward – to the point that “becoming Nvidia” is now an internal goal.

Days before President Xi Jinping’s trip to the United States for a high-stakes meeting with his American counterpart Donald Trump, Huawei announced a major technological breakthrough: a system that it said was capable of enabling up to 1 million processors to operate as a single, unified computer.

The announcement followed earlier semiconductor advances, namely the Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture, which aim to deliver high-performance chips without relying on the most advanced lithography tools, whose sale to China remains restricted.

Ahead of the Xi-Trump summit, Huawei rotating chair Xu Zhijun last week voiced a widely shared hope among entrepreneurs that the world’s two superpowers could “coexist and get along in a peaceful way” and that government actions would avoid interfering with normal, innovation-driven market competition.

“With increasing geopolitical tension, those days [of globalisation and full competition] are leaving us,” Xu said, asserting that enterprises were now trapped in a reality where “you cannot buy what you want to, you cannot sell what you want”.

As geoeconomic competition continues to reshape US-China relations, the sources of leverage available to Washington and Beijing are also coming under scrutiny.

Four months after Trump visited the Chinese capital in May, when both sides agreed to work towards “constructive strategic stability”, traditional economic levers, such as pledges to order Boeing aircraft, have almost flatlined. At the same time, the technological contest has accelerated, spanning China’s push to catch up in artificial intelligence and semiconductors and Washington’s drive for self-reliance in rare earths – one of Beijing’s main trump cards.

“The more interesting change is that both sides appear increasingly conscious that their leverage is reciprocal,” said Matteo Giovannini, a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation. “Neither side has a decisive advantage without imposing significant costs on itself.”

While the US still holds the leading-edge chip advantage, it is now treating it as a bargainable asset rather than a hard wall

Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis

Chasing the AI frontier

Since May, Chinese AI developers have increasingly sought to combine powerful open-weight models, whose parameters are made available for developers to download, modify and run, with a broader domestic hardware base to reduce reliance on Nvidia chips.

When Moonshot AI launched its 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 in July, it made the weights available to developers. The model was soon adapted to run on Alibaba Group Holding’s Zhenwu M890 and Huawei Technologies’ Ascend 910C chips, while new models from Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, and Alibaba – owner of the South China Morning Post – have followed.

Paul Triolo, a partner and technology policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said the release of such “capable models” had “arguably” narrowed the gap at the frontier.

Although the US still leads in proprietary frontier models, Washington has increasingly shifted its focus to how Chinese developers gain access to those capabilities. A report released by three US government agencies earlier this month accused six Chinese AI firms of using “distillation” – a technique in which a smaller system is trained on responses generated by a more powerful one – to extract capabilities from American-developed models.

China’s Ministry of Commerce rejected the allegations of “aggressive, malicious” AI distillation as groundless, warning that Beijing would retaliate if Washington weaponised the claim to stifle the country’s tech sector.

Elly Rostoum, a senior fellow with the tech policy programme at the Centre for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), disagreed that China’s progress could be explained solely by distillation, calling such claims “short-sighted”.

“Even if they distil it, they are smart enough to take the technology, distil it and build on it within six weeks – in such a short time – as we’ve seen with Moonshot AI,” she told a media briefing last week.

Meanwhile, Joe Khawam, managing director of legal and AI policy at the Law Reform Institute in Washington, said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had weighed sanctions over distillation, some policymakers could favour a diplomatic solution given the risk of Chinese retaliation.

“One of the big questions is how truly important distillation is for specific Chinese AI companies to maintain their position as fast followers in frontier AI models,” he said.

Yao Xu, secretary general of the Centre for Global AI Innovative Governance at Fudan University, said the two countries held leverage in different parts of the AI technology ecosystem. “The United States has the chips, but lacks effective planning and public persuasion,” he said.

“China can do better at planning and securing public trust in policy, but we lack the chips.”

The battle over advanced semiconductors

Although the US retains a major advantage in cutting-edge chips, Chinese players have spent the past four months bolstering the domestic hardware ecosystem underpinning the country’s AI models.

“The US has a lot of leverage around ... [the] ecosystem for advanced chips,” Kevin Allison, a senior fellow with the tech policy programme at CEPA, told the same media briefing. “China has yet to catch up, although it’s been making progress kind of under pressure from US export controls.”

Unable to access the machines capable of extreme ultraviolet lithography – the cutting-edge chipmaking technology dominated by Dutch giant ASML – Chinese companies such as Huawei and Alibaba’s T-Head division are pursuing alternative ways to improve performance.

Huawei, for instance, anticipates a major domestic shift towards its AI infrastructure for model training next year, as its Ascend processors gain ground on Nvidia in China despite supply bottlenecks.

Washington continues to bar Chinese firms from accessing the most advanced Nvidia chips, even after approving sales of the H200 model, and has yet to close loopholes that allow remote access to processing power hosted in overseas data centres.

In early August, Bloomberg reported that US regulators were reviewing how Chinese AI companies accessed Nvidia chips through computing power rented overseas.

“While the US still holds the leading-edge chip advantage, it is now treating it as a bargainable asset rather than a hard wall,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis.

Alex Capri, a senior lecturer at the National University of Singapore’s business school, said he expected the coming Xi-Trump talks to renew interest in Beijing’s push to secure relief from export controls on high-end chips and lithography equipment. That could include Washington extending its suspension of the “50 per cent affiliates rule”, which would otherwise expand tech export restrictions to overseas subsidiaries that are at least 50 per cent Chinese-owned. The suspension is set to expire in November.

As foreign memory-chip giants increasingly devote production capacity to high-bandwidth memory, which supports AI computing, Chinese manufacturers such as Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC) and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) have continued expanding their presence in conventional memory, strengthening China’s domestic memory supply chain.

Data released by Counterpoint Research last month showed that YMTC had entered the world’s top three NAND suppliers by shipment volume for the first time, accounting for 14 per cent of global bit shipments.

Leverage beyond rare earths

Beyond AI models and chips, both the US and China have increased their use of restrictions and export controls across technology and other supply chains, creating additional sources of potential leverage.

On the American side, the regulatory dragnet is expanding rapidly into downstream hardware.

The Federal Communications Commission expanded its Covered List in July to include foreign-made advanced robotic devices and connected power inverters. It is also reportedly drafting a ban on new Chinese-made optical transceivers used in data centres, with officials aiming to publish and implement the measure later this year.

Analysts at Bernstein described the recent US ban on new foreign-made mobile robots as “the formal beginning of US-China decoupling in robotics,” in a note published last month.

Although China’s robotics industry remained reliant on US AI chips and simulation platforms, it had moved faster in scaling training datasets and acquiring high-value data, the analysts said. Data would consequently be Beijing’s “base case” response, with rare earth magnets potentially serving as an escalation lever, they added.

China accounts for about 60 per cent of global rare earth mining and nearly 90 per cent of processing, according to the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies. As the world’s leading producer of rare earth elements, it has long used critical minerals as a strategic lever in its protracted trade conflict with the US.

Washington has accelerated efforts to reduce its rare earth dependence, with Elon Musk earlier this month touting the Cybercab’s rare-earth-free motor, although analysts regarded the development as only a slight step towards meaningfully weakening China’s leverage across industries.

At the federal level, USA Rare Earth secured access to up to US$1.6 billion in US government funding in June to build out a domestic mine-to-magnet supply chain – though Rostoum of CEPA said China had “a 20-year head start in going around the world” on a “shopping spree” to secure critical minerals.

“The Chinese definitely have the upper hand when it comes to rare earths,” she told the media briefing last week.

Beyond rare earths, analysts also pointed to China’s ability to leverage its position in global manufacturing and supply chains.

“As the US seeks to de-risk from China, Beijing retains considerable leverage through the depth and scale of its industrial ecosystem, something that is much harder to replicate quickly than individual supply chains,” said Giovannini, also a fellow at the University of Hong Kong’s Asia Global Institute.

“The key question ahead of the meeting is therefore less about which side has more leverage and more about which side is willing to bear greater economic costs in exercising it.”

Additional reporting by Coco Feng, Iris Deng, Howard Liu, Vincent Chow and Wency Chen

item.title: [SCMP] AI poses new national security threat, outgoing Hong Kong deputy police chief warns
item.description:
Retiring deputy police commissioner Andrew Kan Kai-yan has said artificial intelligence (AI) poses a new threat to national security in Hong Kong, with the force turning to the emerging technology to help combat the issue.

Kan raised the alarm after state security minister Chen Yixin warned last week of rising national security risks posed by AI. The senior mainland Chinese official also called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the technology.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined plans in his annual policy address last week to adopt an AI risk‑governance strategy, focusing on combating the use of such technologies in criminal activities and formulating safety‑management guidelines for AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
Retiring deputy police commissioner Andrew Kan Kai-yan has said artificial intelligence (AI) poses a new threat to national security in Hong Kong, with the force turning to the emerging technology to help combat the issue.

Kan raised the alarm after state security minister Chen Yixin warned last week of rising national security risks posed by AI. The senior mainland Chinese official also called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the technology.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined plans in his annual policy address last week to adopt an AI risk‑governance strategy, focusing on combating the use of such technologies in criminal activities and formulating safety‑management guidelines for AI agents.

Kan, 57, who headed the National Security Department, began his pre-retirement leave on Tuesday after 35 years on the force.

Discussing the new threat, the outgoing police official said he had seen overseas examples of AI agents launching attacks on critical infrastructure and other companies’ computer systems, as well as generating misinformation.

Anti-government forces could also use AI to commit crimes related to national security, he said.

“I totally agree … that AI poses a new security threat to national security,” he said. “We have been working to improve our capability in AI in this aspect. I can also tell you one of the tactics to combat AI crime is using AI.”

Kan pointed to AI tools used to help screen social media posts to identify potential “soft resistance” against the government as an example.

“As computers and AI become more powerful, the chances of successfully hiding your criminal intent or criminal acts are actually getting slimmer. So, it’s better not to test the law,” he warned.

The police official also said that anyone who used AI to commit crimes should be held responsible.

Kan said the current legislation was adequate for now to tackle such threats, but he did not rule out the need for new legislation in the future.

“Maybe in the future we need new laws,” he said. “Of course, technology grows very fast. We do not know next year or five years later, what the world will be.”

Discussing the relevant legislation, he cited Section 50 of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, which governs acts of endangering national security in relation to computers or electronic systems, saying that authorities had anticipated AI-related threats while drafting the law.

He also pointed to the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance, which safeguards critical infrastructure and banking systems from attacks.

In his announcement of Hong Kong’s first five-year blueprint last week, Lee touched on plans to enhance the legal system and enforcement mechanisms to safeguard national security.

Kan said the four main national security threats that would require vigilance over the next five years were soft resistance, home-grown terrorism, foreign influence and espionage.

Earlier this year, national security police raided three independent bookstores over allegations that they had displayed or sold titles with seditious intent.

The deputy police chief said his officers had actually read the books and sought legal advice from the Department of Justice before taking enforcement action. “There is no such thing as blind enforcement or making arbitrary arrests,” he said.

Kan also rejected the idea of publishing a banned books list with book titles or ISBNs, arguing booksellers were responsible for ensuring the books they were selling complied with local national security legislation and comparing the situation to how restaurant owners needed to ensure food safety.

“If we issue a banned books list today, and tomorrow you publish another book that turns out to be illegal after our investigation, you’ll say, ‘hey, why are you arresting us if it wasn’t on the list?’ This simply cannot resolve the problem,” he said.

He suggested that sellers read the books before offering them and seek legal advice if in doubt. “If you say it is not easy to get legal advice … then don’t sell it,” he said.

“If you say, ‘you will not publish the book list, and I don’t know where the red line is’ – I feel this is a bit of … soft resistance,” he said, adding that there was a clear definition of sedition under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance.

Kan said more people were engaging in soft resistance, which had become even more discreet and underground after the enactment of national security laws.

He added that people used different platforms, including cultural, arts and online media, to spread misinformation, incite hatred and instigate public resentment towards the local and central governments.

On the distinction between soft resistance and freedom of speech, he said that the key determining factors were whether the expression was intended to incite others and whether the criticism was based on concrete facts.

On September 11, three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil were sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail for inciting subversion.

Kan said that whether it was legal to commemorate the anniversary of the Tiananmen Square crackdown on June 4 in the future should be judged on a case-by-case basis.

He said that when evaluating applications for protests, police assessed threats to national security, public order and safety, as well as the potential impacts on the freedoms of others.

“Of course, if the rally or protest you join is explicitly taking up the mantle of the alliance’s ideology, or ideas aimed at opposing China and destabilising Hong Kong, then you really need to think twice about whether you’ll end up breaking the law,” he said.

Commenting on the effectiveness of putting bounties on wanted persons who had breached national security laws, Kan said: “Justice may be delayed, but it will not be denied.

“Just because they haven’t returned now does not mean they never will … world politics can change drastically.

“Will those sheltering you today betray you tomorrow? I wouldn’t rule it out. It’s certainly not impossible. When you beg others for protection and shelter, what happens to you once your usefulness runs out? We shall wait and see.”

Kan also noted that national security police had arrested people suspected of handling funds or donations on behalf of absconders, largely cutting off their means of survival.

Asked whether he would join the Committee for Safeguarding National Security after retiring, he said he wanted to take a good rest and spend time with his family first, adding that he did not have any current plans for the future.

item.title: [SCMP] Analysts tip a stronger hand for China ahead of Xi-Trump summit in Washington
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the second part of a series, Fan Chen looks at Beijing’s stronger position going into the high-stakes visit.

Beijing is poised to begin this week’s summit with Washington from a position of strength, bolstered by a flurry of recent diplomatic outreach.

Chinese confidence could be further reinforced by the United States’ latest push to make headway on conflicts in Ukraine and Iran – wars that observers say Washington may need Beijing’s cooperation to help resolve – even if a near-term truce remains unlikely.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the second part of a series, Fan Chen looks at Beijing’s stronger position going into the high-stakes visit.

Beijing is poised to begin this week’s summit with Washington from a position of strength, bolstered by a flurry of recent diplomatic outreach.

Chinese confidence could be further reinforced by the United States’ latest push to make headway on conflicts in Ukraine and Iran – wars that observers say Washington may need Beijing’s cooperation to help resolve – even if a near-term truce remains unlikely.

Just weeks before his Washington trip, Chinese President Xi Jinping embarked on one of his most intense overseas itineraries, paying a state visit to Egypt after wrapping up the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

Xi also attended the Brics summit in New Delhi last weekend, marking his first trip to India in seven years. In his address, the Chinese president took a veiled swipe at US policies and urged the bloc’s members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.

Through a joint declaration, the two-day summit also forged a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” policies – all without naming Washington.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, noted that Beijing’s diplomatic blitz strengthened its hand ahead of the second US-China summit of the year.

“Xi’s visit to Egypt – a major Middle Eastern power – underscores China’s rising influence in the region,” he said.

“As Washington is currently entangled in conflict with Iran, this serves as a reminder to the US that it cannot overlook China’s regional clout when managing its bilateral ties with Beijing.”

Amid escalating conflicts in the Middle East, Xi used his first Cairo visit in a decade to urge the countries of the region to build a self-led security model and “take charge of their own future”.

Observers noted that the approach nudged the countries in the region away from Washington, without committing Beijing to a role as a replacement security guarantor.

US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that Xi would visit on September 24 and that they would have “a lot of good things to discuss”. Beijing has yet to confirm the trip, in line with its practice of leaving official travel announcements to the last minute.

Wu added that Beijing’s diplomatic whirlwind highlighted its focus on Asia and the Global South, showing its expanding reach as a global power and standing in sharp contrast to a US administration that has alienated traditional allies.

His view was echoed by Ali Wyne, International Crisis Group’s senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations.

As Trump undermined US alliances, Xi was building “China’s portfolio of transactional alignments”, Wyne said, although he added that Beijing was “unlikely to establish a coherent counterbalancing coalition”.

“Still, the Trump administration’s foreign policy enables Beijing to present itself as a more stabilising force than Washington.”

According to Wyne, while Xi would avoid upstaging or upbraiding his counterpart, he might enter the Washington summit far more confident than in May, buoyed by Trump prioritising their relationship over allegations of Chinese election interference and support for Iran.

Patricia Kim, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Brookings Institution, said Xi’s multiple tours showed that China had other important relationships and diplomatic options. They aimed to portray Beijing as “increasingly central to a more multipolar international order”, she said.

“The message Xi wants to project is that Beijing can engage Washington without making the US the centrepiece of its foreign policy.”

In Bishkek, Xi praised the SCO approach of peaceful coexistence “without alliance, confrontation or targeting any third party”, taking a veiled swipe at the US military alliance system.

Bloc leaders – representing Central Asian states, Iran, Russia, Pakistan, India and Belarus – condemned military strikes on Iran as international law violations and backed Tehran’s right to a peaceful nuclear programme, directly countering US demands for total nuclear abandonment.

Meanwhile, pressed by November’s midterm elections and the approaching summit with Beijing, Washington has also stepped up efforts to resolve the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

Following a phone call on Tuesday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump said, though not for the first time, that he thought his Russian counterpart wanted to make a deal to end the war in Ukraine.

The call came after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held more than three hours of “highly useful” talks with Putin on Saturday. Both sides have signalled optimism and that plans for next steps could be expected soon.

Witkoff and Kushner travelled to Kyiv on Sunday for talks aimed at resuming Russia-Ukraine negotiations – their first visit to the Ukrainian capital after numerous trips to Moscow since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022.

While no breakthrough was announced, Witkoff said he was “confident there would be a good resolution”.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian, European and US officials would meet to continue talks, while reiterating his call for a trilateral meeting involving Russia and the US.

Zelensky also said he expected the war with Russia to continue into the winter.

On Wednesday, Trump addressed the Middle Eastern front where the US has been deeply embroiled since February. The war with Iran would end immediately after the midterms, he said, and hinted that negotiations “could possibly happen”.

Surging oil prices and broader inflation from the US-Israel war in Iran have plunged Trump’s approval ratings to new lows, stoking Republican fears of what the midterms may bring.

Though neither conflict has a clear end in sight, analysts say that Washington might need China’s cooperation to resolve them, giving Beijing a stronger hand ahead of the Xi-Trump talks.

According to Zhu Junwei, director of Chinese think tank Horizon Insights, Trump – unable to resolve the conflict in Iran – is pursuing alternative wins in North Korea and Ukraine to project a “can’t stop winning” narrative in a bid to distract voters and boost his political prospects.

“None of these crises can be resolved quickly. If Trump wants quick, tangible wins to boost his midterm prospects, he is likely to need China’s help,” she said.

“Even if he approaches this by applying pressure, it fundamentally comes down to needing Beijing’s cooperation.”

Trump has repeatedly signalled a desire to revive personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, saying he expected to meet him later this year after scaling back last month’s US-South Korea military drill, widely seen as a conciliatory gesture.

On Thursday, the South China Morning Post reported exclusively that China was willing to broker a leaders’ meeting between Pyongyang and Washington and would support all credible efforts leading to resumed dialogue.
