Zhu also noted that calming the Ukraine and Middle East conflicts – even if impossible overnight – “ultimately benefits Beijing, regardless of its impact on US-China rivalry, as it significantly improves China’s external environment and creates new opportunities”.

Sun Yun, director of the China programme at US think tank the Stimson Centre, echoed this view, saying that China could help the US resolve both conflicts and describing Beijing’s role as a potential bargaining chip in broader US-China talks.

However, both Sun and Wyne of the International Crisis Group noted that Beijing was not the main driver behind Trump’s pre-summit rush to resolve both conflicts.

“While the Trump administration would indeed have more diplomatic bandwidth were it to freeze the Russia-Ukraine war and reach a fresh ceasefire with Iran, it has not prioritised China policy nearly as much as many observers had anticipated when Trump retook office,” Wyne said.

Even though Putin might view Trump as a more favourable interlocutor than his predecessor Joe Biden, Moscow “is unlikely to weaken its relationship” with China for a fragile US truce under Trump, knowing American leadership was likely to revert to a hostile stance towards Moscow, he added.

Even without major deliverables, the summit could still prove useful if it maintained a cordial rapport between the leaders and sustained a “tactical thaw”, Wyne stressed.

According to Kim from Brookings, the leaders’ meeting was “unlikely to produce a significantly expanded bilateral agenda or result in a fundamental reset” of ties. Instead, the focus remained on extending the trade detente and sustaining leader-level diplomacy as the main buffer against further deterioration, she said.

Zhu noted that while Trump aimed to stabilise ties with China, an overall hawkish US bipartisan consensus meant there was “still a long way to go” towards achieving “constructive strategic stability” – the framework introduced at the Beijing summit in May.

“A single summit cannot resolve every issue; if this meeting yields partial economic and trade agreements and temporarily manages differences, it should be viewed as a success.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore minister Chan Chun Sing’s Mandarin diplomacy strikes China chord
item.description:
Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state.

Videos of Chan at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum quoting ancient philosopher Mencius, or Mengzi in Mandarin, have gone viral on platforms such as Weixin and Baidu, with users hailing his command of the language and knowledge of Chinese thought.

Observers say that through resonating with the hosts, Chan managed to convey Singapore’s sterner message of a call for major powers to build trust instead of coercion, though there is a risk that linguistic bonds may raise the expectation for Singapore to sympathise with Beijing’s interests.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state.

Videos of Chan at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum quoting ancient philosopher Mencius, or Mengzi in Mandarin, have gone viral on platforms such as Weixin and Baidu, with users hailing his command of the language and knowledge of Chinese thought.

Observers say that through resonating with the hosts, Chan managed to convey Singapore’s sterner message of a call for major powers to build trust instead of coercion, though there is a risk that linguistic bonds may raise the expectation for Singapore to sympathise with Beijing’s interests.

At the summit on Wednesday, attended by delegates from nearly 100 countries and helmed by Chinese defence chief Dong Jun, Chan spoke mostly in English but switched to Mandarin occasionally and cited Mencius, saying: “Power may compel others to comply. But in the end, it is trust that truly wins others over.”

Social media users also drew comparisons between Chan and US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, praising the former for displaying wisdom which exceeded that of a counterpart helming the military of a much larger country.

On Chan’s use of Mandarin, a Weixin user commented: “This minister is not an ordinary person; he knows Chinese culture like the back of his hand.”

Many also said Chan’s Mandarin was proof that the language and Chinese culture were gaining traction on the global stage.

The Singapore minister also urged superpowers to shoulder higher expectations from smaller states, stressing that countries should strengthen their own security but not at the expense of others.

“The more responsible major powers are, the less concerned small countries will be,” he said in Mandarin.

Singapore welcomed China’s aspiration to be a “responsible major country”, Chan said, adding that Beijing’s “reform and opening up” policy had contributed greatly to regional and global prosperity.

“As the People’s Liberation Army approaches its centenary, there is much potential for it to make a positive contribution to global stability and security,” he said.

Diplomatic move?

Observers hail Chan’s use of Mandarin and historical references as a clever diplomatic move, showcasing an appreciation and understanding of China and its culture.

Stefanie Kam, an assistant professor at S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), described Chan’s switch to Mandarin as deliberate and a “clear effort to show cultural awareness and diplomatic tact”.

“For a defence minister to quote an old Chinese classic like this is quite strategic; it makes it hard for the Chinese audience to disagree because they would be disagreeing with their own classic,” she said.

Adam Liu, a political scientist and assistant professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, pointed out that Chinese leader Xi Jinping often quoted ancient Chinese teachings.

“Speaking in Mandarin and drawing on Mencius is a way of saying: I am addressing you in your own idiom, on your own terms. That tends to land well,” he said.

While Chan’s Mandarin switch-up was largely well received, some netizens were unimpressed, arguing that it should be expected that Chan – who hails from a country where 74 per cent of citizens were of Chinese ethnicity – would be fluent in Mandarin.

As English strengthens its hold as the main language for Singaporeans, the government has reinforced the importance of maintaining a bilingual edge, implementing measures such as public speaking contests and cultural workshops. According to a 2020 census, the use of Mandarin as the language most frequently spoken at home fell from 35.6 per cent in 2010 to 29.9 per cent in 2020.

Dylan Loh, associate professor of foreign policy at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University, said the speech showed Singapore’s bilingualism and an ability to code-switch.

“Beyond citing Mencius specifically, the broader context in which it was used is also important,” he said. “The message was respectful and paid compliment to Chinese history and philosophical heritage.”

But Loh said the code-switch was not necessarily a strategic move in itself, noting that leaders had in the past done the same at various forums.

Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, warned that the Chinese public could view affirmations of culture and ethnic similarities as synonymous with political alignment.

While using a Chinese philosophical expression “may be tactically helpful to smooth ties”, Chong said it could also “create disappointment when a person or the entity they represent take positions that diverge from prior expectations associated with race, culture and politics”.

On Chinese social media, some users interpreted Chan’s speech as veiled criticism of the United States, though observers note the script was vague and aligned with Singapore’s foreign policy.

In his speech, Chan said: “We must work even harder to strengthen our domestic fundamentals, rather than try to externalise our domestic issues.” He also illustrated Singapore’s journey to the global stage since its independence in 1965, through which “leaders avoided exploiting foreign policy for political gain”.

While Chan did not explicitly name a country, some online users who appraised Chan’s speech likely interpreted the reference to winning by force as implying American actions, Kam said.

Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and coordinator at the China Programme at RSIS, said Chan’s speech was broad and in line with the city state’s “pro-Singapore” policy.

“It’s not surprising the Chinese read this as a reference to the US, but the case that China’s domestic issues are not absent in its foreign policy can also be made,” he said. “If you look past the idioms, which are obviously for the Chinese audience, it’s general and mostly speaking on principle.”

Liu said Mencius’ quote was consistent with Singapore’s non-alignment. “The hope is for an international order built on trust, rules and moral principles, which is a position one can hold without pointing at anybody.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why the Global South keeps its doors wide open to Russia
item.description:
Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met some 18 heads of state.

Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few.

The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met some 18 heads of state.

Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few.

The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war.

Tellingly, however, the main thrust of discussions led by the Russian president had a different focus: fuel, trade and transit.

Here’s why Russia is deepening ties with many partners in the Global South – and what these meetings tell us about the impacts of Western efforts to isolate Putin.

Fuel and energy

Fuel and energy security is becoming a mutual concern for both Moscow and its partners in the Global South. Ukraine’s deliberate offensive campaign targeting Russia’s oil refining capacity has resulted in noticeable fuel shortages in the country.

It has forced the Russian government to import refined fuel from countries it has traditionally exported to, such as Belarus, Turkey and India.

At the same time, the Kremlin continues to push for the expansion of its energy exports. This includes finalising the contract to build the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which intends to deliver 50 billion cubic metres (1.77 trillion cubic feet) of natural gas annually from Russia to China via Mongolia.

Last week, Russia also signed a deal to establish a new strategic oil reserves hub in Vietnam.

Moscow is also expanding cooperation on nuclear power, which was part of the discussion agenda with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Vietnam’s President To Lam (during his state visit to Russia), and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Deeper ties

The ongoing sanctions war between Russia and the West has made its economic and trade relations with the Global South pivotal for the country’s survival and future development.

Two friendly interstate bodies, in which Russia plays core roles, are becoming especially important. The first is Brics, a group of 11 economies comprising Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.

The Brics economies now account for about 40 per cent of global gross domestic product. Last year, mutual trade turnover between Brics member states exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time.

The second is the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. This is a political and security bloc spanning countries in Europe, Asia and the Indo-Pacific. According to Putin, Russia’s trade turnover with the SCO exceeded US$400 billion in 2025.

Overall, Asia accounted for 73.4 per cent of Russia’s trade turnover last year. It’s no surprise that Moscow’s trade links with Asia featured in almost every conversation in Bishkek, Vladivostok and Delhi.

Bypassing disruption

Despite its friendly ties with Iran, Russia and its clients aren’t immune from the ongoing disruption to transport and trade routes through the Middle East. To mitigate these risks, Russia is actively lobbying two relatively new transcontinental transit networks.

The first is the 7,200km (4,470-mile) combined rail-road-maritime International North-South Transport Corridor. This route connects Russia’s Baltic Sea ports with Mumbai in India, via the Caspian Sea and Iran.

Russia reportedly discussed this route with the Indian and Iranian delegations this month.

The second is the 5,600km (3,480-mile) maritime Northern Sea Route, which connects Asia’s ice-free ports with Russian and European ports as part of a maritime passage across the Arctic Ocean.

In August, Beijing launched commercial operations along this route for the first time.

Political signalling

Russia walked away from this month’s diplomatic blitz with some clear wins. In addition to securing US$7.7 billion worth of investments in Vladivostok, along with some lucrative deals with Vietnam, Putin could also claim some political success.

First, although challenging at times, Putin’s interactions with his counterparts showcased how Moscow’s relationship with major non-Western international players remains a geopolitical constant, even in the fifth year of the Ukraine war.

For leaders of emerging centres of global influence, whether India’s Modi, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto or Vietnam’s Lam, interacting with Russia forms part of their countries’ foreign policy approach based on the notion of “strategic autonomy”.

This sends a powerful signal to the United States and its allies, amid the latest round of high-level consultations involving the CIA and US Treasury chiefs and their Russian counterparts.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump sent his own personal envoys to Moscow and made a follow-up phone call to Putin.

Second, Russia and its core partners in Asia jointly signalled they would continue to maintain strategic partnership links. This includes the question of importing Russia’s fossil fuels, nuclear power and other goods, and exporting processed fuel back to Russia.

Fuel security is particularly relevant to the Russian authorities’ attempts to stabilise the domestic situation. The Kremlin is under pressure to mitigate the aftershocks of the escalating war with Ukraine amid coming parliamentary elections from Friday to Sunday.

Concerns persist

Still, many in the Global South remain concerned about the growing impact of what seems to be becoming a forever war in and over Ukraine.

The latest round of tit-for-tat attacks against merchant shipping in the Black Sea triggered fears of grain and wheat shortages.

In mid-November, China will host the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. This is tipped to be a possible venue for the first trilateral meeting between Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump.

Here, Moscow might feel increasing pressure to settle the war by political means from its partners. These countries don’t want to feel the effects of the sanctions war between the West and Russia, let alone be dragged into it.

Alexey D Muraviev is senior research fellow at the School of Arts and Humanities at Edith Cowan University. This article was first published by The Conversation.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
item.description:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.
item.content:encoded:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.

Concerns about AI run the gamut from autonomous weapons, mass unemployment and machine-driven cyberattacks to deepfake-fuelled misinformation, algorithmic bias and a dangerous overreliance on automation.

South Korea has seen all this – and decided now is the time to hit the accelerator.

Under President Lee Jae Myung’s “AI for All” initiative, the government is preparing to hand every citizen free access to artificial intelligence, integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices and daily lives in a way few countries have attempted.

“The idea is to substantially lower barriers to access so that the benefits of the technology are distributed evenly rather than enjoyed by only some people,” Seoul’s Ministry of Science and ICT said in a statement to This Week in Asia.

The government, which has a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current financial year, has allocated an additional 250 billion won for the roll-out through 2027.

A beta version is set to launch later this month, introducing free, unlimited-access general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by three consortiums – led by telecoms giants SK Telecom, KT and Kakao – using hundreds of state-of-the-art Nvidia B200 graphics processing units lent to them by the government.

From next year, officials envisage the temporary trial will become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility, eventually connecting to government systems to allow citizens to book doctor’s appointments, go house hunting, get tax advice and the like, all through AI intermediaries.

To manage the risks involved, Seoul is relying on its landmark AI Basic Act, which came into force in January, to ensure human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments and clear watermarking of synthetic content.

Meanwhile, a state-funded AI Safety Institute has been tasked with serving as a technical watchdog to evaluate the pitfalls and ensure that public AI utilities remain trustworthy, secure and answerable to the citizens who use them.

“Going forward, the government plans to establish an autonomous reliability-assurance system”, the ICT ministry said in its statement, adding this would be based on the seven “AI Ethics Principles” it laid out last month: accountability, human-centredness, privacy protection and fairness among them.

South Korea hopes its “AI for All” push will help it become one of the world’s three leading AI powers, alongside the United States and China, with the government seeing the technology as an antidote to a shrinking workforce and as a way to strengthen its export-driven economy.

But the same society racing to put AI in every pocket is also confronting the consequences of what that means, as workers worry about automation eliminating jobs, police struggle to combat a surge in deepfake crimes and educators watch a generation’s reading scores slide.

Sovereignty is another concern. Of the roughly two-thirds of South Korea’s 51.6 million people who have tried or regularly use AI, 23.45 million are active users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, 8.45 million of Google’s Gemini and 2.41 million of Anthropic’s Claude, according to government figures.

Yet access to these platforms cannot be guaranteed, as the ministry noted in its statement.

“As we saw recently, foreign AI services can have their availability limited at any time depending on decisions made by foreign governments or companies,” it said, in a possible nod to Washington’s recent attempts to block access to the newest models.

In July, Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon unveiled plans for South Korea to develop its own cybersecurity-focused AI model by the end of this year, following the US clampdown.

Brewing with bots

At Unicup Coffee, an independent cafe vying for business against 11 low-cost chain rivals in Busan International Finance Centre, owner Bae Kyung-han, 31, credits AI with helping him beat the competition.

What began a year ago as a cost-saving experiment, with Bae teaching himself how to use generative AI to create promotional posters and menu images, has since taken over nearly every part of the business.

“It’s now running my research, proposal developments, communications and advertisements,” he said, adding that the AI system – his only office-based “colleague” – had also orchestrated a shift in focus towards bulk orders instead of walk-in customers.

Five employees handle customer orders, serving some 13,000 people a month and generating card sales that are, according to Bae, roughly double those of his competitors.

He has also built a second business around the technology, registering as a vendor under one of the government’s chosen AI consortiums to teach novices how to ask better questions of their chatbots.

“The biggest advantage of AI in the workplace is that it reduces the psychological burden of managing people,” Bae said, describing the relief of no longer having to coordinate schedules, repeat instructions or manage employees’ feelings.

“With AI, I can ask questions whenever I need to and revise plans whenever I want to. It’s just more efficient.”

Yet he is still sceptical of the government’s AI strategy, questioning whether domestically developed models – even ones that are provided for free – would actually be able to wean people off premium foreign made tools.

“People who are used to using AI would likely pay for a more expensive US-based model like ChatGPT rather than use a free domestic service,” Bae said.

That is, unless the models were specialised and purpose-built for specific problems, as opposed to another general-purpose chatbot.

“That changes the conversation,” Bae said. “That could do wonders for businesses like mine.”

Elsewhere, at a jobs fair in Seoul’s Yonsei University, technology companies crowded the floor, competing for the attention of soon-to-be graduates before they had even finished their degrees.

Kwon Il-geun, an electronic engineering student hoping to work at semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix, said AI proficiency had never been more important.

“My skills in using AI tools have nearly doubled in the past year,” he said, comparing the shift to the first industrial revolution or the arrival of the personal computer. “This is just part of the changing times.”

No juniors needed?

Not everyone is sharing in the spoils, however. The number of young South Koreans aged 15 to 29 who were in work dropped by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to the central bank, which estimated that 94 per cent of that decline was in sectors highly exposed to automation, including publishing, IT services and computer programming.

And the Korea Development Institute, a government-run think tank, projected in July that AI could wipe out roughly 256,000 jobs a year within the next decade.

This has had a knock-on effect on students’ ambitions, with enrolment reportedly falling at academies teaching graphic design and coding, even as institutions preparing young people for stable public-sector careers enjoy booming interest.

At the SKY Entrance Exam Academy in Seoul, enrolment in its military and policy preparation track is up 70 per cent year on year.

Yun Ji-sang, a recent school leaver, is among those preparing to commit himself to five years of officer training and a military career of 15 years minimum.

“Some people think this is a long time to be trapped inside the military, but I just view it as a long time of having a stable job,” he said, noting that it was also one that came with a pension.

The number of young South Koreans in employment fell by 143,000 in August compared to the year before, the Chosun Daily newspaper reported on September 9, marking the 46th straight month of decline for those aged 15 to 29.

Meanwhile, the number of civil servants being recruited nationwide increased this year for the first time in five years, according to the Ministry of Personnel Management.

“I used to want to live as an entrepreneur who would travel abroad frequently and live freely,” Yun said. “But what use is that when we are constantly worrying about making a living?”

Conventional wisdom surrounding which jobs were most at risk from automation had been flipped on its head by the rise of generative AI, said Ko Hak-soo, a law professor at Seoul National University.

“When ChatGPT first emerged three or four years ago, there was widespread concern that jobs involving workers with relatively low levels of education … would be at highest risk,” he said.

“But now, there is a much stronger view that jobs requiring a great deal of human labour may actually be relatively safe while professional occupations, especially entry-level and junior workers in these fields, might gradually disappear.”

New roles were likely to emerge as AI became more integrated into workplaces, Ko said – while warning there was “little understanding of the reality of the shifting labour market”.

Kim Myuhng-joo, executive director of South Korea’s AI Safety Institute, said the disruption was already under way.

“Until just a few years ago, programmers were extremely highly valued, and their salaries were rising rapidly,” he told This Week in Asia. “But AI companies are increasingly using AI for coding … without needing as many junior-level developers.”

Kim further voiced concerns that a new cohort of workers coming of age in the “AI for All” era might never develop the skills needed to operate without the technology.

“In less than 10 years, we could see a new generation entering the workforce that is overly dependent on AI,” he said.

“Companies may expect these new employees to have the capabilities of previous generations, but they … could end up becoming people who are incapable of doing anything without AI.”

AI-fuelled abuse

South Korea’s most visceral fears surrounding AI stem not from the threat of rogue tech, however, but from the recent reality of criminal misuse.

The Nth Room case of 2020 – in which encrypted social media channels were used to produce, sell and distribute sexually exploitative material and blackmail victims – and subsequent scandals led to the country strengthening its deepfake laws in 2024.

Producing such material can now result in seven years behind bars or a 50 million won (US$37,000) fine, while possessing or knowingly viewing it can mean three years in prison or a 30 million won penalty.

Yet police still recorded 1,553 deepfake-related offences last year, accounting for over 35 per cent of all reported cybersex crimes, according to statistics presented at a recent forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea.

In the first half of this year alone, police apprehended 419 suspects for deepfake offences, 17 of whom were physically detained while awaiting trial.

The National Office of Investigation said in a statement that officials were “developing police response technologies at a pace that exceeds the speed at which technology itself is evolving”, including by expanding forensic video expertise and the use of AI-assisted detection tools.

Won Eun-ji is less convinced that technology alone will solve the problem. As director of Team Flame, which investigates digital sex crimes, she has spent much of this year infiltrating roughly 50 Telegram chat rooms alongside investigative outlet Newstapa, documenting how AI tools have swelled the ranks of anonymous perpetrators and lowered the age of victims.

“Even today, many initial leads in these investigations often come from victims themselves,” she said. “The police need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities.”

Kim, of the AI Safety Institute, said the government needed to prepare for the unintended consequences of increasing access to AI.

“Once AI becomes embedded in society, it is difficult to remove it,” he said, describing it as “an irreversible change”.

“We need to conduct thorough impact assessments from the beginning, considering what effects the technology might have and whether it could be misused, abused or overused.”

To combat crime, Kim said he would support police undercover investigations “depending on the circumstance” alongside greater use of invisible watermarking to trace AI-generated content back to its creator or means of distribution.

“Online platforms should take more active steps to identify online crimes” and prevent abuse material from being circulated, he said, adding the children “need to receive education on these issues as part of broader civic education and AI literacy”, starting in primary school.

Generation chatbot

Yet in the classroom, an upside-down hierarchy of knowledge has begun to emerge, according to Moon Sung-ho, the 16-year-old editor-in-chief of Tokipul, an independent student-run newspaper.

“In many cases, students actually know more about AI than teachers, resulting in students using AI to complete all of their assignments while teachers don’t really know how to stop them,” he said.

Song Keun-sang was among the educators who protested last year against the government’s short-lived 1.2 trillion-won plan to roll-out AI-powered textbooks.

“Once we actually tried using AI in the classroom, we realised that it wasn’t as useful as we had expected,” said the fifth-grade teacher at a school in South Chungcheong province.

While good teaching pushes students to learn more about the world, AI short-circuits this process, according to Song.

“It simply gives you the answers,” he said. “It doesn’t have much educational value.”

Song had once thought that AI might be useful to help isolated students or those struggling to make friends, but that changed after a child in neighbouring North Chungcheong province died by suicide following conversations with a chatbot.

“I wonder whether it is really beneficial for students to be exposed to chatbots that constantly cater to them and reassure them,” he said. “They are essentially designed to tell you what you want to hear, so you will never be challenged or face disagreements.”

The effects of this may already be starting to be felt. South Korean 15-year-olds topped global reading charts in 2006, as measured by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment.

Yet in 2025 they posted their lowest average reading score since the country first began taking part in the assessments in 2000, the OECD reported earlier this month.

“Other countries are starting to ban social media and other online devices for adolescents, but South Korea is moving in the exact opposite direction,” Song said. “We can already expect serious declines in academic achievement and literacy skills.”

The more pressing concern for him, however, is social rather than academic.

“Cooperation and communication between students ultimately develops the skills they will need to succeed in society later on,” he said, predicting that interacting with AI chatbots might make it “much more difficult to form relationships with other people.”

Moon has seen this happen among his own classmates and friend group, who once went to internet cafes and played football together, while also asking for help with homework assignments.

“Students these days increasingly ask AI chatbots about these questions,” he said. “It feels like it’s become more difficult to talk with people.”

This Week in Asia contacted South Korea’s Ministry of Education for comment on this article.

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
item.description:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.
item.content:encoded:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Under contracts signed by non-Chinese entities, models have been trained on cutting-edge Nvidia processors housed thousands of miles, away outside the reach of US authorities, he said.

That critical lifeline could be on the verge of collapsing.

Washington is reportedly moving to expand its tech blockade from physical hardware to cloud networks. As the US Congress weighs legislation to restrict foreign remote access and executive agencies review cloud-leasing loopholes, China’s AI sector faces its most severe choke point since the chip bans began.

The impending US crackdown threatens to reshape the global AI ecosystem, challenging Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, squeezing Nvidia’s international revenues and forcing Beijing into an acceleration of its domestic chip push.

The cloud escape hatch

Developing AI infrastructure across borders has long been common practice among Chinese developers looking to bypass hardware bans while avoiding US regulatory hurdles, according to observers.

“For a long time, Chinese AI companies have circumvented chip export bans by leasing overseas data centres,” said Arisa Liu, chief director and research fellow at Taiwan Industry Economics Services, a unit of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research. “[This] has indeed contributed a significant amount of overseas market demand to Nvidia.”

To make good use of these remote servers, some Chinese teams have taken extraordinary measures to overcome technical bottlenecks. Chinese engineers personally carried hard drives storing 80 terabytes of data from Beijing to Malaysia to train an AI model at a local data centre, saving months of digital transfer time, The Wall Street Journal reported last year.

Driven by the global AI boom, demand for high-performance computing power has sent global cloud rental rates soaring.

Leading AI infrastructure provider Nebius Group raised rental prices on certain Nvidia chips by roughly 30 per cent in June, with a further 21 per cent increase to come into effect on October 1. Hyperscaler rates for Nvidia’s A100 processors rose to US$3.75 per hour in late August, up from US$3.71 a month earlier, according to tracking firm Silicon Data.

To maintain secrecy and navigate cross-border payments, some Chinese teams have even executed cloud-leasing transactions via blockchain-based smart contracts and paid in cryptocurrency to keep both parties hidden behind anonymous digital wallets, the Journal reported in 2024.

However, the regulatory net in Washington is rapidly closing.

The administration of US President Donald Trump was reviewing remote access arrangements and was working on policies to curb it, according to reports by Bloomberg and The Information. In January, the US House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which, if signed into law, would expand American export controls to remote cloud computing access.

“If the US passes and implements relevant legislation that extends restrictions from physical chips to cloud leasing, Nvidia’s overall sales growth momentum will inevitably be curtailed to some extent,” Liu said.

Legal experts noted that current compliance remained a grey area. Currently, there are “no regulations or similar provisions in place to restrict or prohibit” such remote access, said Hong Jiayang, managing partner of US law firm Joint-Win Partners.

The only measure that came close to banning the practice was the “AI Diffusion Rule”, said Hong, who focuses on trade compliance. The regulation, which requires US cloud service providers to exercise caution when providing cloud services for Chinese AI models, was introduced by the Biden administration in January 2025 but rescinded by the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) after Trump came to power.

The Remote Access Security Act “was introduced for a similar purpose”, Hong said. However, once it goes into effect, “the businesses of cloud service giants such as Oracle and Amazon.com will be significantly impacted, which is bound to provoke a strong backlash”.

Even if the US did not enact legislation to regulate cloud services, the BIS could “theoretically impose penalties on data centres and even model developers that use illegally smuggled chips” on the grounds of “General Prohibition 10”, which penalises transactions conducted with knowledge that a violation has occurred, Hong explained.

“Hi-tech companies should avoid becoming entangled in such legal liabilities at all times,” he added.

Southeast Asia’s data centre boom

If Washington closes the cloud computing loophole, the immediate shock waves will hit Southeast Asia, one of the world’s fastest-growing data centre hubs.

Local data centre capacity in the region was projected to expand at 35 per cent each year from 2023 through 2028, outpacing the global average of 15 per cent, according to market intelligence platform Speeda.

Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – Tencent Holdings and TikTok owner ByteDance, have spent years building out regional infrastructure to serve the Chinese market.

Asian hyperscalers preferred the region for several reasons, including “competitive development costs across construction, equipment and human capital; and lower operating costs”, according to Vivian Wong, lead analyst for APAC at DC Byte, a market consultancy in the data centre industry.

If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market

Alex Cordovil, Dell’Oro Group

“If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market … Southeast Asia is the natural first step for that expansion, given proximity, existing business ties, land and power availability,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group, a market research firm in the telecommunications, security and data centre industries.

Beyond local demands, the region has attracted international workloads, “including from Chinese internet and cloud companies”, Cordovil said. “Export controls are part of that picture: certain accelerator architectures are only available outside mainland China, so workloads that depend on them naturally gravitate to locations where that supply is accessible.”

The region also offers competitive energy economics.

In Southeast Asia, electricity prices average US$118 per megawatt hour (MWh), with the lowest in Indonesia at US$60 per MWh, according to Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy focusing on the energy, chemicals, renewables, metals and mining.

While higher than China’s average industrial rates - between 600 yuan (US$89) and 700 yuan per MWh, and half that in energy-rich regions like Inner Mongolia and Guizhou – Southeast Asia remains cheaper than US hubs like northern Virginia and Silicon Valley, where prices range between US$70 and US$120 per MWh. In comparison, European centres like Germany and Ireland see prices ranging between €150 (US$174) and €250 per MWh, according to state-backed media China Energy News.

Should remote access become a constraint for certain customers in Southeast Asia, it would “likely create a transient imbalance between supply and demand in the region”, he said, adding that the imbalance was expected to be “short lived” as demand was deep.

Wong held a similar view, saying that “any released capacity is likely to be taken up relatively quickly by other customers”.

The domestic bottleneck

For Chinese AI firms, losing overseas cloud access will lay bare a troubling reality: despite heavy state investment, domestic hardware is not yet fully equipped to handle frontier model training at scale.

Despite China’s push for self-sufficiency in chips, the country’s most advanced AI models are still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP previously reported.

The AI development life cycle involves training and inference – the use of a trained model to generate new content. Systems such as DeepSeek-V4 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 have been successfully adapted to Chinese hardware for inference work only.

For now, the most advanced Nvidia chips remain unavailable in China, including the B200, B300, H100 and H800. Chinese firms either use Nvidia chips they have in inventory or gain access through cloud computing.

The H200, the latest of Nvidia’s Hopper-series chips but a generation behind the Blackwell family, was approved for import by both Washington and Beijing but is only available in small quantities.

ByteDance and Tencent Holdings each received about 10,000 H200s and a few other Chinese customers obtained shipments of a similar size, the Financial Times reported in August.

“There is a massive gap between this quantity and the actual demand of such top-tier tech giants, which often consume tens of thousands or even over 100,000 advanced [graphics processing units],” said Liu of the Taiwan institution.

Nvidia in late August reported that shipments of H200s to China accounted for less than 1 per cent of its US$89 billion data-centre revenue in the quarter that ended July 26. However, it said it did not expect any data-centre computing revenue from China in the following quarter.

Liu added that even though Nvidia’s income might be temporarily curtailed if the US imposed the ban on remote access, “this shortfall may be partially offset by massive orders from other international tech giants” given strong AI demand globally.

Accelerating self-reliance

If the US bans Chinese companies from renting Nvidia-powered data centres overseas, it may lead to higher domestic rental rates, the Shenzhen-based data centre broker noted. For now, rates for B300 chips outside China are two to three times higher than local prices, not including differences in electricity costs.

Even if there were no restriction on renting overseas data centres, replacing Nvidia with domestic chips was “the main trend”, said a semiconductor designer at one of China’s biggest chipmakers, who requested anonymity.

“Who knows if Nvidia processors have back doors,” the person said. Nvidia has repeatedly said that there are no back doors, kill switches or spyware in its products.

Some Chinese teams have started using local chips for AI training. In June, Meituan released LongCat-2.0, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that it said was fully trained and run on a 50,000-card domestic computing power cluster, without naming the supplier.

Huawei Technologies’ rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun expected a major domestic shift towards its AI computing infrastructure for model training next year.

The semiconductor design engineer said the best domestic AI chip currently was the Ascend 950 from Huawei Technologies, not only for its performance but for the whole ecosystem from architecture to networks. Huawei announced last week that the next-generation Ascend 960DT, designed for model training, will be ready in the first quarter of 2027, nine months ahead of schedule.

However, transferring training workloads from Nvidia to domestic chips is a steep engineering bottleneck. The hurdles included the software ecosystem, as Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) platform has long been the industry standard for AI development, the SCMP reported in August.

Migrating existing workflows to Huawei’s Ascend chips could add at least 50 per cent to training time and cost, according to researcher James Wang.

Still, China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade. The supply of advanced-node wafers made using 7-nanometre processes and below was projected to grow at 46 per cent annually between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a recent report.

That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035 from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank.

As Washington moves to extend its tech blockade from hardware shipments to virtual server networks, Chinese AI developers may soon lose their refuge in the cloud. What remains to be seen is whether the squeeze will stall China’s frontier AI ambitions or simply accelerate its push towards technological self-sufficiency.

item.title: [SCMP] Boeing’s 200-jet China deal could hinge on Trump-Xi talks: industry insiders
item.description:
When President Xi Jinping travels to Washington later this month, he is likely to hop over the Pacific on a Boeing 747 jumbo jet. He will also hold the fate of the American planemaker’s much-touted China deal in his hands.

Beijing agreed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft during US President Donald Trump’s visit to China in May. But the deal has yet to materialise – and the negotiations could depend on the outcome of Xi’s coming meeting with Trump in the Oval Office, according to industry insiders.

With key details still needing to be agreed – especially the time frame for any purchases – the final deal was likely to be shaped by the broader economic and political bargaining between the two presidents, they said.
item.content:encoded:
When President Xi Jinping travels to Washington later this month, he is likely to hop over the Pacific on a Boeing 747 jumbo jet. He will also hold the fate of the American planemaker’s much-touted China deal in his hands.

Beijing agreed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft during US President Donald Trump’s visit to China in May. But the deal has yet to materialise – and the negotiations could depend on the outcome of Xi’s coming meeting with Trump in the Oval Office, according to industry insiders.

With key details still needing to be agreed – especially the time frame for any purchases – the final deal was likely to be shaped by the broader economic and political bargaining between the two presidents, they said.

“It’s all about the three Ws: whether, when and what,” said a retired aviation executive, who previously oversaw fleet management and engineering at one of China’s largest state-owned airlines.

“With Trump’s Beijing trip in May and the 200-jet deal announcement, the ‘whether’ part is now agreed upon … But a call on when to place actual orders needs to be determined by Chinese trade officials, a vice-premier or even needs a nod from the top leader.”

In May, China agreed to purchase at least 200 Boeing planes as a key deliverable from Trump’s state visit – the country’s first deal with the US aviation giant for nearly a decade.

At the time, China’s Ministry of Commerce said aviation was an area where both nations could deepen “mutually beneficial, win-win” cooperation, adding that the two presidents had reached an “important consensus”, without elaborating.

The White House, meanwhile, called the 200-jet deal an “initial purchase”, with Trump claiming that China could commit to buy up to 750 aircraft if certain conditions were met.

The deal has appeared to stall in the months since. No details have been released regarding the number or models of Boeing aircraft involved, nor which Chinese airlines will be placing orders.

No Chinese government agencies have provided updates on the deal’s status. There have not been any related announcements from Chinese airlines, either.

But the silence does not mean the deal is off. Xin Qiang, a professor with Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, said Beijing had been facing growing domestic calls to buy from Boeing in recent months – and that Xi’s US trip could present an opportunity to advance the deal.

“Many US-focused analysts and government departments have since this year made stronger recommendations to the top leadership [to place orders with Boeing],” Xin said.

“With Xi’s coming visit to Washington – which in itself is a sign of continued easing of tensions – the decision to advance the purchase makes perfect sense,” he added. “The reality is that there are very few high-end industrial products – Boeing aircraft being a prime example – that China has the need to buy and the US is able to sell.”

In May, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg cautioned that “official orders” from China “will come later in the year”, as the company was still working to iron out specifics with Chinese clients.

“My primary objective was to reopen that [Chinese] market … and we accomplished that,” said Ortberg, who was part of the US business delegation that accompanied Trump on his trip to Beijing.

“I think people focused a bit too much on the initial quantity,” he continued. “The order is a good start.”

In July, Ortberg told CNBC that Boeing was in the process of finalising the contracts. “China will allocate the total quantity to individual airlines, then we negotiate the contracts with individual airlines,” he said. “We are in the process right now. We will have contracts here shortly.”

A source with flag carrier Air China confirmed the airline was involved in discussions over a potential Boeing order.

“We are involved in this, but it is not something on which individual airlines can make a final decision – it requires coordination and advancement by the National Development and Reform Commission,” the source said, referring to China’s top economic planning body.

Beijing was currently maintaining a “silent period” regarding the deal status, the person added. “Our approach is to proceed and be ready, without making public comments.”

The last time China bought from Boeing was in 2017, when a US$37 billion, 300-plane contract was announced during Trump’s first state visit to Beijing.

But the US firm was later frozen out of the world’s second-largest economy, as US-China tensions rose and Boeing experienced a string of safety issues. In the meantime, China has directed huge orders to the company’s European rival, Airbus.

Airbus has landed a series of fresh contracts in China in recent months, with Chinese airlines including China Eastern, China Southern, Air China, Xiamen Air and Spring Airlines signing formal agreements for hundreds of European-made aircraft.

Switching wholesale to Airbus, however, would not be easy for China. Several Chinese airlines – including China Eastern-owned carrier Shanghai Airlines and Air China subsidiary Shandong Airlines – have all-Boeing fleets. These carriers have needed new aircraft for years to renew their ageing stock, according to independent aviation analyst Li Hanming.

“China does need Boeing,” said the retired airline executive, who declined to be named as he was not authorised to speak with the media. “The art of the deal [for Beijing] is to balance commercial need with geopolitical bargaining.”

For some market observers, one of the concessions Beijing will want to extract before proceeding with any Boeing deal will be securing supplies for China’s domestically made C919 passenger jet.

While the C919 is assembled in China, many of the plane’s parts are sourced from overseas – including the Leap-1C engine, which is produced by CFM International, a consortium between America’s GE Aerospace and France’s Safran.

In May, China’s commerce ministry said the US would “provide China with adequate supplies of engines and spare parts” for its aviation firms. The Boeing deal could be tied to firming up that guarantee.

For the executive, the coming Xi-Trump meeting could provide an opportunity for “breakthroughs” in such negotiations. “What’s better than the two presidents meeting face-to-face again?”

Additional reporting by Zhu Wenqian

item.title: [SCMP] Former WTO head Pascal Lamy on the EU’s China choice: get a rebalance, or go protectionist
item.description:
Pascal Lamy served two consecutive terms as director general of the World Trade Organization from 2005 to 2013. Before that, he spent decades in various French government roles, contributing to the building of the European Union. He was chief of staff to European Commission president Jacques Delors from 1985 to 1994, and European trade commissioner from 1999 to 2004.

Here, he discusses Europe’s trade tensions with China, the continent’s growth potential problem and the WTO’s need for stronger enforcement mechanisms.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Pascal Lamy served two consecutive terms as director general of the World Trade Organization from 2005 to 2013. Before that, he spent decades in various French government roles, contributing to the building of the European Union. He was chief of staff to European Commission president Jacques Delors from 1985 to 1994, and European trade commissioner from 1999 to 2004.

Here, he discusses Europe’s trade tensions with China, the continent’s growth potential problem and the WTO’s need for stronger enforcement mechanisms.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

In France, many have expressed doubts about the future of free trade. Former finance minister Eric Lombard said last year that free trade is dead, killed by the US and China. Do you agree?

No, free trade is not dead. And by the way, I never ever use the expression “free trade”. I’ve been in this business for decades now, and I’ve never used this expression, which is for one simple reason: it is misleading. Trade is never free. It is either more or less open. Free trade is not dead, it was never born.

The question is whether the previous decades we’ve seen, which have consistently moved in the direction of more open trade – this being evidenced by the growth of the volume of international trade – whether this volume is still growing or not.

If you look at the numbers, which we have to do, especially if we discuss trade, trade is still growing in volume. This means that trade is more open than it used to be. But there is a catch: the growth of international trade, at least benchmarked against the growth of the economy, has slowed.

The slowdown can be attributed to many reasons. Starting with the main factor, which is the fragmentation of production systems that has led to the global supply chains that now span the world. The expansion of the supply chain, the fragmentation of production, has limits. It is efficient and productive at some stage, for some products in some conditions.

But we’ve probably reached a stage where the efficiency gains stemming from the multi-localisation of production systems are slowing, with decreasing yields, like any productivity curve. At some stage you reach a level where economies of scale are less important than at the beginning of the process.

Reason No 2 is that trade openness trends are now counterbalanced by trade-restricting attitudes among a number of international trade players, given the United States’ position and the huge growth of China’s exports and surplus. There are also growing reactions in some places to the expansion of international trade for social or environmental reasons. Its growth is slowing because of various reasons, but overall, international trade is still expanding.

So what, in your view, are the main problems facing the global trade system?

As Europeans, we have three problems in global trade today. A small one, a medium-sized one and a big one.

The small one is the US. The US has embarked on a protectionist crusade, which stems from the deep belief by US President Donald Trump that tariffs are the Swiss army knife of the 21st century economy, which is not so. The ones who pay the price for that at the end of the day are US consumers. But even if he makes a lot of noise about his attempt to de-globalise the planet, this will not happen.

Then we have the medium-sized problem, which is that the World Trade Organization, the international institutional engine for opening trade, is not working in the way it used to work.

This is mainly a problem of organisation. The fact that the US de facto left the WTO. The fact that although a new dispute-settlement system has replaced the previous one, it does not work with the US. The fact that all decisions, including on minor issues, are still taken by consensus, and that the secretariat is not allowed to exercise its potential authority based on its first-class expertise. And that third one, in my view, is the main reason.

The WTO has not been able to develop new trade-opening agreements in areas where international trade has moved a lot – digital trade for instance, which matters a lot for services – and we should always remember that international trade is goods plus services, plus the invisible part of international exchange trade today, which is about trillions of pieces of data.

Then we have a big problem, which is China, which is a problem for every country. It’s a huge problem for us Europeans because we have a mega trade deficit, growing in an unsustainable way. And for the European Union, addressing this problem is a very tough task.

The main reason behind it is the macroeconomic imbalance of China, which is structural, which Chinese authorities have not addressed, do not want to address, although they’ve been saying for many years that Chinese growth should be rebalanced – with more domestic consumption.

China already has plans to make itself self-sufficient in food – why not in services too later?

It is not happening, and we are in a situation where industry in China produces twice as much as it consumes in industrial goods, hence the debate about overcapacity.

China now has comparative advantages in most of the supply chains in manufacturing. Not yet in agriculture, and not yet in services. But I believe China wants to get there, following a policy developed by the Chinese government, mostly since 2010.

China already has plans to make itself self-sufficient in food – why not in services too later? Because of the strategic concept that China has to become more self-reliant. In energy, in manufacturing, in technology, China has, so far, been formidably efficient in constructing self-sufficiency; other sectors will come.

This is a major systemic problem, because trade opening has always been based on the theory of comparative advantage. I do something better than you do. You do something better than I do. We have a rational interest to trade, which is, by the way, the philosophical basement of the WTO.

The WTO is built with the mission of promoting open trade because opening trade is a good way to create growth and welfare, because it is based on the efficiencies stemming from the exchange of comparative advantage, the international division of labour.

This game seems to be over with China today. China has gained comparative advantages all along the industrial production chain for various reasons. Some of which are legitimate. They have a huge market. They have a formidable education capacity, and this is something where they have built their own comparative advantage, and they have a political regime that allows a level of strategisation, coordination, multilayered intervention, which is incredibly efficient.

This has a lot to do with the political regime, and this is something, of course, that we Europeans would hesitate to emulate for a variety of reasons. China also uses its state-owned sector, its state-owned banks, its budget to heavily subsidise sectors – which is not in the spirit of a fair international division of labour – benefiting from the fact that WTO disciplines on subsidies, state support and state ownership, have remained very weak.

This is the situation we Europeans now have to face. It’s not just a bit different from what it was before, where maybe we could adjust the recipes here and there with a bit more or a bit less of anti-dumping or countervailing duties. The size of the deficit is now out of reach of the normal instruments which the WTO provides to regulate trade and absorb import shocks. With China trade dynamics, we are entering a new world, a new paradigm, which opens a lot of questions about WTO disciplines.

The French government’s high commission for strategy and planning has called for 30 per cent tariffs on all Chinese imports, and Paris and Berlin have expressed a desire for fast measures rather than long WTO-style investigations. Is China right that the EU is turning protectionist, and would Brussels be better off saying so openly, telling Beijing it has no choice if it wants to keep its industry?

You are absolutely right, we Europeans are reaching a moment of truth with trade and China. Either we can convince China to rebalance the system and decrease its exports or we will have to go protectionist. Let’s test the willingness of China to seriously address the problem. This is the first option and in my view, the good option, provided China shows signals that it is ready to address the problem. This is Plan A. We need a Plan A, but we also need a Plan B.

Some in the US argue it was a mistake to let China into the WTO. You were the one who closed the EU’s bilateral accession deal in Beijing in May 2000. With hindsight, was the mistake letting China in, or was it what the West failed to write into the terms? Would you sign the same text today?

Yes and no. I think letting China into the WTO was the right thing to do precisely because it brought about an exchange of comparative advantage, and China wanted to join the WTO to benefit from an insurance policy against export restrictions. China paid a high price for subscribing to this insurance in opening its economy.

China opened its economy as a developing country, roughly three times more than its developing country equivalents at the time and more than Russia 10 years later. The maximum tariff China accepted on goods was 10 per cent.

China made a big effort, which led to a big divide within the Chinese leadership: between those who said [former paramount leader] Deng Xiaoping was right, we have to open to better combine Chinese characteristics and Western characteristics, and this is the way to go to grow China more rapidly, represented by [former premier] Zhu Rongji.

And then there was another camp, more conservative within the leadership, that thought that opening trade with Western countries might make China more vulnerable. The first camp won and China opened its economy, which became very profitable for the rest of the world during the next 10 years.

There was an end to that, which roughly coincided with the aftermath of the 2008 crisis, where the Chinese government switched back to a more ideological approach. Self-sufficiency became the new strategic priority to reach total strategic autonomy in the future.

The Chinese economy was, from then on, run on a geopolitical basis, not on a geoeconomic basis. China then pushed, very successfully, to go from low-wage value addition, which was a comparative advantage 25 years ago, to where China is now, competing with the US on the frontiers of technology.

To answer your question, we were right to let China in, and we were wrong not to reinforce the WTO’s rules on subsidisation and state support before China entered. The reason we did not do that – “we” being the big shots at the time: the US, EU and Japan – was we thought that we might end up restricting our ability to support our champions such as Airbus or Boeing, or Japan’s programmes to foster innovation.

We were subsidising a small part of our economy, and we mistakenly remained defensive. We did not forecast how large a part of the Chinese economy would remain de facto under state control and support. Or the importance of the state-owned sector, which had actually shrunk in the first 10 years after China joined the WTO and then grew again from 2010 on.

We did one thing right, which was letting China in, which benefited everybody for quite a bit of time, but we did not properly identify the risk that China’s state-owned system would drive the economy in such an efficient way, including in subsidising a strategic industry heavily at the beginning, then creating a lot of competition. The best example is what we see in electric vehicles, which were heavily subsidised at the start, and now there’s cutthroat competition within China until the system stabilises with maybe a handful of surviving producers.

How do you see the current EU-China negotiations, with Brussels demanding “tangible progress” by October? Can both sides still avoid a trade war? Some argue China and the EU are already in one. Do you agree?

First of all, I don’t think we should use the word “war” about trade. I’m talking to you from Ukraine, I was a naval officer in my youth. I know the meaning of the word “war”, and we shouldn’t use it lightly.

We have trade frictions, we have trade disputes, we have trade tensions. There are trade tensions between China and the US. There are trade tensions between the US and Canada that were triggered by Trump because he thinks Canada should become a new US state. We have trade tensions between the EU and China, which stem from the fact that we have such a huge and growing deficit with China.

The European Union today still has a trade surplus as a whole. What does this mean? This means that, overall, the EU, in what is traded today, can compete with the rest of the world. We have a trade surplus vis-a-vis the US. We have a trade surplus with many of our trade partners, except with China. If you remove €350 billion (US$407 billion) of trade deficit between the EU and China, we have a big trade surplus, which means that we are competitive with anybody on this planet except China.

Now there are reasons for that, which I can totally understand. It stems from what I describe as Chinese organisation: they’ve been extremely good at gaining a comparative advantage all along the supply chain, including, for instance, in critical materials, which is extremely important for electrification and the economy.

Of course, China did not do it for the pleasure of doing it. China built a comparative advantage in critical materials because China wanted to electrify, and the reason China wanted to electrify was that it wanted to be less dependent on oil or coal or gas imports.

We Europeans have to try to convince China that it is in their interest, as it is in our interest, to reduce our trade deficit massively

It’s not because China suddenly became a believer in the necessity to reduce emissions – although I’m happy that China is doing this. China built the comparative advantage in rare earths to become less dependent on fossil fuel imports. They built this control, which now gives them a monopoly that they can weaponise.

We Europeans have to try to convince China that it is in their interest, as it is in our interest, to reduce our trade deficit massively, not just by €10 billion or €20 billion. We have a €350 billion trade deficit, and this cannot be addressed by a little bit of this or a little bit of that. The problem is the magnitude of the problem.

Either we can convince China to address this problem, which will need a lot of unilateral market power exercised by the Chinese side to export less, or we will have to look for other options. I hope we do not have to do this. I interpret the Sefcovic mission [aimed at rebalancing trade] and the time between now and the October deadline as a test of whether China is serious about addressing this or not.

As usual, the EU gave priority to negotiation, consultation, discussion. We are not the US, and nobody wants to play Trump on the EU side, we are not brutal. We try to understand problems. We try to address this peacefully, respectfully and through negotiation. But if that does not work, we have to look at other options.

Europe says it wants to be neither dependent on the US nor overwhelmed by China. Is a third position actually available, or does reducing exposure to one side mean aligning with the other?

Solving this issue will not, by itself, solve Europe’s No 1 problem, which is growth. The EU’s growth potential is half of that of the US, one-third that of China and one-quarter that of India. This is a worrying situation, and one we will have to work hard on to improve our competitiveness. But becoming more competitive will not solve our China trade problem, given its magnitude and the threat it represents to the survival of some of our production systems.

How did we get here, to this level of trade imbalance? Is that a story about Chinese competitiveness or industrial policy?

It is overall competitiveness, all along the supply chain, which leads to this. If you have a competitive advantage all along the supply chain, there is no more fair trade. You are absolutely right, this is the result of Chinese competitiveness.

Chinese competitiveness has various sources, which I mentioned: the size of the market, the organisation of the state and its capacity to subsidise efficiently. It’s not just subsidising, because you can subsidise inefficiently too. The Chinese system has learned to use subsidising efficiently, giving the industrial policy a coherent logic: what strategic priorities, what the state does, in which sector, what the regions do and what the municipalities do. There is a lot of competition within. It’s a formidable mix of non-competition, which is the state, and competition, which is a part of the economy.

What would China have to do to prove that it is a defender of multilateralism and free trade?

Beef up domestic consumption. Stop pushing, pushing and pushing for increasing manufacturing, which is way beyond the consumption capacity of Chinese consumers. Chinese households have a saving rate that is way too high, coming from the fact that they want to hedge against old age, children’s education spending, pensions and so on, so China also needs to create somewhat of a welfare state.

Secondly, import more, export and subsidise less. Or in the case of subsidies, renegotiating the WTO rules on subsidies – what we in the EU call “state aids” – to level the playing field, which is now heavily unbalanced in the subsidisation capacity between China and Europe. And convince China to invest more in Europe in areas where tech transfers and ownership arrangements are doable, which was China’s position 30 years ago. Boosting Chinese investment in Europe is, in my view, part of the solution.

item.title: [SCMP] Could Chinese explorers have settled New Zealand before the Maori?
item.description:
For generations, the narrative of New Zealand’s human settlement has held that Polynesian voyagers – the ancestors of the Maori – arrived and settled the islands in the 13th century, followed by European explorers in the 17th century.

This timeline underpins New Zealand’s history and its political model. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and about 540 Maori chiefs, served as New Zealand’s founding document, paving the way for Britain to claim sovereignty and incorporate the country into the British Empire.

Outside the halls of universities and government institutions, two independent researchers are on a quest to discover pre-Maori Chinese presence in New Zealand.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, the narrative of New Zealand’s human settlement has held that Polynesian voyagers – the ancestors of the Maori – arrived and settled the islands in the 13th century, followed by European explorers in the 17th century.

This timeline underpins New Zealand’s history and its political model. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and about 540 Maori chiefs, served as New Zealand’s founding document, paving the way for Britain to claim sovereignty and incorporate the country into the British Empire.

Outside the halls of universities and government institutions, two independent researchers are on a quest to discover pre-Maori Chinese presence in New Zealand.

Citing underwater shipwrecks, carbon-dated structures and anomalous artefacts as evidence, scholar and author Sheng-Wei Wang has proposed a theory that a Chinese “treasure ship” fleet met its end there around 1435-1436 owing to the impact of a meteorite.

Wang also contends that Chinese mining and trading activities date back to 190BC, challenging the accepted 13th-century Maori settlement timeline and suggesting that these pre-European contacts have been overlooked or suppressed.

While mainstream academics and Maori groups voice scepticism, Wang and others argue that acknowledging this lesser-known history could reshape New Zealand’s national identity and improve its relations with China.

Speaking this month at the Commonwealth of World Chinatowns conference in Penang, Malaysia, Wang raised the question of whether fleet leader Zheng He died in New Zealand during his final voyage.

Zheng was a Chinese admiral who led seven massive naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean during the early Ming dynasty.

While Zheng is widely believed to have died in 1433 in Calicut, or today’s Kozhikode, a coastal city in southern India, after setting sail in 1431, his exact fate was still unverified, Wang said.

“We know that Zheng disappeared during the seventh voyage. There were different kinds of proposals about what happened to him.

“Could he [have died] while he visited the Americas? Or in India near Calicut – he was ill, and because the weather was so hot that his body couldn’t be brought back to China? Or just like in this case that he died because of the unexpected tragic event?”

Wang said a meteorite was believed to have crashed in the Tasman Sea, southwest of New Zealand.

“My estimate of the date is around 1435 or 1436, when a squadron of the Ming Treasure Fleet reached New Zealand after they explored the Americas during their seventh voyage to the Indian Ocean and beyond,” she said, adding that the impact carbonised all the ships in the harbour.

“One of the possibilities is that the whole fleet disappeared there, which may have included Zheng because there is no satisfactory evidence to show where or when he died,” she said. “There was no convincing record, so I am proposing that.”

Wang’s research draws on field surveys by the late independent British surveyor T.C. Bell, who used magnetic anomaly surveys to detect underwater and buried structures throughout New Zealand. The method measures local variations in the Earth’s magnetic field to locate metal objects.

“When Bell went to New Zealand for surveys in 2003, 2006 and 2017 … he was able to detect 78 shipwrecks of various dimensions,” she said.

“Twenty-four of them are of the super-junk or treasure-ship size. They are around over 100 metres (328 feet) in length, about 40-something [metres] in width, and all these large ships are characterised by their unique double-fluke anchors.”

The specialised Chinese anchor consisted of a central wooden bar connected to two huge rocks, Wang said, and was designed to cut into the sea floor to secure the ship in place.

She proposed a route for Zheng’s last voyage that “went to America for several months and came back by rounding the southern part of South America, Cape Horn. They followed the Humboldt Current, then the [South] Equatorial Current and they could have gone to Asia”.

“Naturally they would have been brought westward to New Zealand.”

Wang described the seventh fleet as on its way back to China. Carbon dating results indicated a Chinese presence in New Zealand predated the seventh Ming voyage, extending from as early as 190BC through 1600, Wang said.

She pointed to a “scrub-covered, small-moated Chinese fort platform” at Governors Bay, South Island, which was carbon-dated to 190BC, and the years 800 and 1600.

“In my opinion, in Bell’s opinion, [New Zealand] became the headquarters of Chinese business trading ships.”

“There were already many Chinese who had lived there for thousands of years,” Wang said, explaining they were attracted by “coal mining and other metallic ores in New Zealand”, including “very rich ores” of gold and silver.

She also noted the presence of canals, smelter sites and barrack blocks that she believed bore Chinese characteristics.

“It is clear that a Chinese presence in New Zealand started at least from 190BC and lasted until the tragic [meteorite] event took place,” she said. “The next wave of Chinese immigration started in the 19th century.”

Wang also cited stone carvings as possible evidence, with a massive gateway rock on the North Island bearing an elephant petroglyph and linear script.

“New Zealand does not have native elephants, and the Maori had no history of carving elephants either,” she said. “Even the Europeans did not do much elephant carving. This is very interesting. But the Chinese knew elephants.”
