It ended up like this.” After that, I left the radio station and started my company, Shya-la-la Workshop.

ONE DAY, WE were shooting in a train station – it was too noisy for sound recording – so I could shoot freely. Leslie was annoyed at me for distracting him. My shutter was too loud, but I kept going. I explained to him, “I’m only scared of Wong Kar-wai, not you. Because he hired me, only he can fire me.” He looked at me for a long moment, then said, “I like your attitude. When we get back to Hong Kong, you’ll work for me.”

HE MEANT IT. From that day until he died, I shot almost every photograph of Leslie for his work, his concerts, behind the scenes, albums and tours. He was the most considerate person I’ve known in this industry. He remembered everyone’s habits, every name, if you took milk in your coffee. He looked after the whole crew, from driver to delivery boy. We travelled together for concerts, shot in countries I’d never been to. I still think about him.

FOR In the Mood for Love (2000), Wong Kar-wai gave me one instruction: the film is about red. He gave me some music to listen to, and that was it, initially. So, in 1999, I went to Tokyo, bought 40 or 50 different rolls of film, shot test after test and laid every print in front of him. He picked one: an old, obscure film – barely still in production, its colour deeply reddish. I called the manufacturer; they were closing the following month because nobody was buying their film any more. “How many rolls remained,” I asked. “Two hundred,” they said. I bought every single one.

THAT PHOTO FILM was made in the 1960s or 70s, and its dyes were slowly failing – that’s why my shots for In the Mood for Love look the way they do. After we finished the film, there was none left anywhere in the world.

THERE ARE PEOPLE who I learned almost everything from. One, of course, is Wong Kar-wai, who gave me access to everyone, all these famous faces. I learned how to crop a photograph by watching him on the monitor. But another one of my real teachers is William Chang Suk-ping – the famous production designer and art director. Even now, we work together regularly. Just the other day, I was on a shoot, with William beside me. I learned what makes a picture by watching what Wong Kar-wai and William chose to keep and what they threw away. I don’t think of my work as mine alone. It is a long conversation with two people I deeply respect.

IN 2010, FOX came to Hong Kong to make a Chinese film – my feature-film directorial debut, Hot Summer Days. Stars such as Jacky Cheung, Maggie Cheung Man-yuk, Nicholas Tse Ting-fung and Daniel Wu Yin-cho all appeared in it, for very little money, as a favour to me because we had 20 years of trust.

DIRECTING FELT LIKE another universe. You have to think about logistics, 80-people crews, egos, dangerous rigs, scenes and even the crew lunches! I’ve made more films since. I still shoot fashion campaigns, recently for Chanel and Bottega Veneta, and – fingers crossed – I am now writing a television drama.

MY FIRST BOOKS came about because cultural curator Shelly Verthime told me at a dinner many years ago that she wanted to make a book. One day, in 2015, she called from Hong Kong International Airport, so I put a hard drive with every photo I owned into a taxi and sent it to her, at the terminal. She spent a year and a half editing alone. An investor funded the printing and an exhibition in Shanghai, in 2017. My shows in Japan (in Tokyo and Kyoto), the books (Chaos [2020], Solace [2024], Is [2026] and more) – they happened all because someone pushed. I never start these things myself.

MY WORK HAS been in the Mori Art Museum, in Tokyo, and in the V&A, in London. I don’t think about it much. I’ve done it already, and the future is more exciting to me than the past. What I still love is being on set – the mess, the crew eating together, the gossip, the waiting. I think the universe already has a script written. My job is only to follow my heart and see what page it turns to next.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Ode to the horse: 5,000 years of human-equine connection on display in new Kazakh museum
item.description:
On the scenic drive east from Almaty, in Kazakhstan, along the old corridor of the A351 highway, towards the Charyn Canyon National Park, and the Xinjiang border beyond that, sits an unassuming museum run by an unlikely duo.

Nurbol Baimukhanov, 50, is an independent, published researcher of shezhire – traditional Kazakh genealogies, historically memorised and passed down through generations – and an award-winning documentary producer who speaks in equal parts archaeology and mysticism. His son Ilyas, 23, with a MacBook tucked under his arm and an eye for systems, is pursuing a master’s in management at Satbayev University, the nation’s oldest technical institute.

On a quiet stretch of the A351, father and son have built a showcase dedicated to the ancient Botai, the multi-hyphenate people of the Eurasian steppes – hunter-gatherer-herder-settlers – who some archaeologists believe were among the first to domesticate the horse more than 5,000 years ago.
item.content:encoded:
On the scenic drive east from Almaty, in Kazakhstan, along the old corridor of the A351 highway, towards the Charyn Canyon National Park, and the Xinjiang border beyond that, sits an unassuming museum run by an unlikely duo.

Nurbol Baimukhanov, 50, is an independent, published researcher of shezhire – traditional Kazakh genealogies, historically memorised and passed down through generations – and an award-winning documentary producer who speaks in equal parts archaeology and mysticism. His son Ilyas, 23, with a MacBook tucked under his arm and an eye for systems, is pursuing a master’s in management at Satbayev University, the nation’s oldest technical institute.

On a quiet stretch of the A351, father and son have built a showcase dedicated to the ancient Botai, the multi-hyphenate people of the Eurasian steppes – hunter-gatherer-herder-settlers – who some archaeologists believe were among the first to domesticate the horse more than 5,000 years ago.

Located around 70km from Almaty, the Ush Qiyan Open-Air Museum sits near the village of Akshiy, in the Enbekshikazakh district – the kind of place most travellers pass without noticing.

Opened this summer, it rises from the flat landscape as three circular log dwellings with sloping roofs – constructed from more than 1,000 logs, the exhibition brochure proudly proclaims – and is designed to evoke what some researchers believe are among the oldest known permanent settlements of the steppes.

Ush Qiyan receives no government funds, has launched no grand marketing campaign – it is just a father, his son and their semi-domesticated horse named Ayan grazing outside.

“Kazakh culture is, first and foremost, the culture of the horse,” says Nurbol. “In gratitude to these beautiful animals, we built this museum as a temple of knowledge to enlighten people.”

Before there were empires and criss-crossing trade routes, before valiant steeds carried armies across continents and monks towards enlightenment, there was a culture that first looked at a wild horse and saw something more than prey.

It is believed that the Botai people lived in what is now northern Kazakhstan, in the 4th and 3rd millennia BC. Mighty they were not.

As far as archaeologists could detect, the Botai built no cities, wrote no epics and erected no monuments that would survive the centuries and catch the eye. Instead, what they left behind were traces of dwellings, scattered pottery and the bones of horses – thousands upon thousands of them, now housed at the North Kazakhstan Regional Museum of History and Local Lore, in Petropavl.

Archaeologists around the world now widely believe that the Botai were the first to domesticate the horse, though the claim is debated each time new evidence comes to light. Experts argue that the proof is in the bones, which show signs of bit wear on the teeth, from the bridle gear used to control them, and in the residue of mare’s milk found in their pottery, leading them to theorise that the Botai were not just hunting horses, but riding them, milking them and living alongside them. If true, it would be one of the most consequential partnerships in human history. Migration, trade, warfare, the spread of ideas and empires – all of it would eventually travel on horseback.

And yet, there is a twist. Genetic research suggests that the animal the Botai domesticated is actually the ancestor of the Przewalski’s horse – the stocky, pot-bellied wild horse that still roams parts of Central Asia. In other words, the first horse believed to be part of human culture eventually returned to the wild, rather than develop into the modern steeds we see today.

Ush Qiyan attempts to capture this paradox – the last wild-horse species being descended from domesticated ancestors, raising questions around whether the breed is truly wild or simply feral – telling a complicated story about a partnership that was formed, dissolved and formed again, as the modern horse, tamed later in the Early Bronze Age, became the engine of human history.

It all started with Ayan, a stallion who seems to straddle both worlds. In the spring of 2021, Nurbol went looking for a light-hued horse in the Altai mountain range, in eastern Kazakhstan. He had no particular reason for doing so; he says he simply, suddenly, felt like having one.

A friend had told him about a remote village with no internet and a horse bearing a rare isabelline colour. Having negotiated a price, it took Nurbol three nights by truck to take Ayan back to Almaty.

“He was born wild, near Lake Zaysan,” says Nurbol.

Ayan is, according to Nurbol, a Zhabe – one of Kazakhstan’s oldest horse breeds, distinguished by its stout frame, thick neck, muscular croup and substantial body weight. But with a pale, almost metallic coat that glows golden in sunlight, Ayan is no ordinary Zhabe.

Whether the isabelline colouring is genetically possible for this breed is another matter, but Nurbol is not a man to let science get in the way of a good story.

“It was a sign from above,” he says, referencing the heavens. “Our horse bears all the hallmarks of an ancient celestial horse. It has a powerful mind and transmits information telepathically.”

Separating fact from fiction is a secondary concern for Nurbol.

He is a researcher whose published works focus on history, archaeology and ancestry. At the same time, he is a believer who sees little boundary between myth and reality. In his telling, Ayan the horse is both a living animal and the latest chapter in a legend that began with the Botai people and culture five millennia ago.

“In the Chinese epic Journey to the West, the White Dragon Horse came from the West,” says Nurbol, noting that, in the text, “the tale of the monk [Tang Sanzang] who met a White Dragon Horse happened somewhere in our area. [Kazakhstan] is a land of legends where myth and reality intertwine”.

Ayan eventually inspired the construction of Ush Qiyan, which began in the summer of 2024. It took about two years to finish, building only in the warmer months, with a small crew, and involved no architects or contractors in the conventional sense – just workers stripping bark from logs under a punishing sun.

“Construction was not easy,” Nurbol recalls. “It was very hot. People were breaking down like matchsticks.”

All the logs had to be processed and cut by hand, following what Nurbol dubs “experimental archaeology” – a scientific approach to understanding how ancient nomads built their dwellings, and the physical labour involved. It was, in his words, an attempt to recreate not just the look of the Botai world, but the toll it took.

Money for the project came entirely from the Baimukhanovs, and though that choice was deliberate, it had consequences. Nurbol remembers days when, due to a lack of funds, “we were idle and wondering how to raise money to continue construction. [But] this was our conscious choice, and we are pleased with the result”.

Ilyas was born in Almaty and grew up tagging along on his father’s scientific expeditions across Kazakhstan. Ush Qiyan, in some ways, is the culmination of a childhood spent among artefacts and open landscapes. Now in his early adulthood, Ilyas speaks with the composure of someone a decade older.

“My father and I are like-minded people,” he says. “I represent the younger generation, a new perspective.” While Nurbol supplies the vision, the younger Baimukhanov thinks about sustainability, management systems and visitor services.

His own “eureka!” moment came years earlier, in the Botai region of northern Kazakhstan, where he met the influential archaeologist Viktor Fedorovich Zaibert, who discovered, excavated and opened the Botai settlement site in 1980, in the Aiyrtau district. In doing so, Zaibert gave the world some of the earliest evidence for horse husbandry and domestication. “He [was] an amazing person,” Ilyas recalls. “He told fascinating stories about history.”

What struck him were the traces of ancient circles still visible in the earth – the outlines of dwellings long gone – and the bones and pottery scattered across the ground, some more than 5,000 years old.

“I am happy to have interacted with such a great archaeologist and seen the artefacts in person. It’s unforgettable,” says Ilyas. Zaibert died in 2022, but his influence, legacy and memory live on in the log walls of the museum.

A visitor to Ush Qiyan moves through the three log structures, each roof shaped like an inverted basket, echoing the ancient yurts of the early nomads. Inside, scientific replicas of nomadic dress from various periods, made from materials such as hide, bone and leather, created for the 2018 documentary Equus: Story of the Horse, which Nurbol co-produced, hang alongside other props. Installations showing reconstructions of historical dwellings and horse sculptures fill the spaces between, and films are screened for guests who want to linger.

In another room, Daniyar Sarbassov, a 36-year-old artist from the Bayanaul district, showcases his work: castings of horses, mostly.

“Daniyar is our friend,” says Nurbol. “He’s a talented sculptor with great potential.” But the connection to the museum runs deeper than friendship. Sarbassov’s horses are not decorative – they carry, as Nurbol puts it, “the code of the Great Steppe”.

One of his pieces, an aluminium-and-bronze statue titled Zhuyrik (2022), was sculpted earlier, in his studio, when Sarbassov had no knowledge of Ayan, or the world Nurbol was building. But when he spotted the ivory-coloured horse, something shifted. “After seeing Ayan, I decided that this work would be better placed at the entrance of the museum,” he says.

In Sarbassov’s description, Zhuyrik is not simply a horse running.

It is “a creature that merges with the wind and moves together with the air”. Its smooth surface catches the natural light from the structure’s oculus as it shifts throughout the day, seemingly dissolving the boundary between the horse’s body and the surrounding space.

“A truly swift horse is difficult to perceive in its entirety,” he says. “Its speed is often experienced through the impression, trace and sensation of movement left in our memory.”

As its metallic shine echoes Ayan’s coat, Sarbassov calls it “a spiritual symbol of the museum”. He hopes it will remain there permanently, and that visitors will find their own meaning in the work: “One viewer may see freedom in the image of a horse, another may be reminded of their ancestors, while a third may discover an entirely different meaning. My hope is that they will pause for a moment to reflect on their own history, their homeland and their place as human beings within this vast expanse of time.”

Outside, Ayan grazes, unaware of the symbolism attached to him. Nurbol considers him the living echo of the story Ush Qiyan exists to tell: the wild horse that came to humans, changed their world and still carries that independence in its blood. Whether that story belongs to history or to myth is, by now, beside the point.

Between them, a father and son have built a temple to the horse, raised by hand, off the beaten track. “We live in a complex era of digital technology; it’s difficult to be surprised by anything,” says Nurbol. “But at the same time, we look to the future without forgetting the past. Our museum is like a time machine.”

But a time machine moves forwards, too. More visitors will be drawn by the same road that connected cultures. Ush Qiyan sits beside it, ready to welcome those who pause on their way to somewhere else. “The Great Steppe has always been a place of meeting,” says Nurbol. “We are open to dialogue with the world.”

item.title: [SCMP] Paul French lifts veil on final months of China’s last emperor in the Forbidden City
item.description:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.
item.content:encoded:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.

In 2018, his City of Devils: A Shanghai Noir was a Kirkus Reviews’ “Best Book of the Year”. In 2024, Her Lotus Year: China, The Roaring Twenties and the Making of Wallis Simpson received much coverage and quotably upbeat reviews (“Her Lotus Year stays in the mind as a bright, shining, lively snapshot,” says The Spectator. “Delightful to read.”).

Now, it’s the turn of Puyi in The Last Emperor of China: Twilight of the Forbidden City, which falls into a royalty subgenre that French calls “doomed monarchy”.

Although he’s writing – primarily – for a Western audience, as a category, it has promising global reach. Earlier this year, French was told by his Chinese publisher that only one other foreigner has shifted (and signed) more books in China: British author and historian Simon Sebag Montefiore, whose 2016 work on those quintessential doomed monarchs, The Romanovs: 1613-1918, was a massive hit.

Puyi, of course, didn’t meet his doom with an execution in a cellar. He was six years old in 1912, when the Manchu empire ended and the new Republican government decided to leave him behind the walls of the Forbidden City – an oddity, roaming around the “Great Within”, attended by eunuchs (“teapots without spouts” was the local term). With his peculiar upbringing and background, that child would grow into the adult who, during the second Sino-Japanese war (1937-1945), would become his country’s “Great Traitor”.

French, who was a language student in 1980s Beijing and lived in Shanghai for many years before returning to Britain in 2014, had been marinating this story for a while. He sensed that – “a bit like Wallis Simpson”, the American socialite whose relationship with Britain’s King Edward VIII led to his abdication – people sort of knew about Puyi but not really. He’d been struck by the blank stares he met when he mentioned him to Chinese-language students at a couple of British universities.

French realised that it’s been almost four decades since he, along with many others, had been “blown away” by the Bernardo Bertolucci epic, The Last Emperor (1987), which was – an amazing achievement – filmed inside the Forbidden City.

While he was wondering how to tackle the topic, he wrote an article about Puyi’s wife, Wanrong, in 2024, for this magazine. “Wanrong is so beautiful and there are so many pictures of her and I thought it would be fun,” he says. “I did mention, in a couple of lines, that she’d had a tutor and this was one of the things the film had missed.”

In fact, Joan Chen – who played Wanrong in the film – makes a single reference to her tutor as a “Miss Windsor”. Bertolucci, who co-wrote the screenplay with his brother-in-law, Mark Peploe, knew Wanrong was educated but not by whom, so they made up a name with British royal resonance. Wanrong’s tutor, however, was not British. Isabel Ingram was an American “mishkid” – a child of missionaries – born in Peking (Beijing) in 1902 and educated at Wellesley College, in Massachusetts, in the US.

After the PostMag piece came out, French was contacted by a man called Kenneth Mayer, who told him he was Ingram’s grandson. “He said, ‘Thank you so much for noticing Isabel; no one else does,’” French recalls. “And then he said, ‘By the way, you really should read her diary and she has some letters from this Johnston guy …’”

French was staggered. He hadn’t known about the diary, and the “Johnston guy” was Reginald Johnston, Puyi’s Scottish tutor, played in the film by Peter O’Toole.

Johnston had written a memoir which, in its 486 pages, makes a single reference to “the Empress’s American friend who had been her teacher of English both before and after the Empress entered the Forbidden City as a bride”; and his letters and journals had been destroyed after his death in Edinburgh, in 1938.

Diary! Letters! Such finds are history’s gold dust. Even better, Ingram, who died in Virginia in 1988, had typed up all of it. (French, who revels in his North London unacademic blokeishness, makes some cheerfully unrepeatable comments about the trials of handwritten research materials.) Once he’d read the Ingram documents, he knew he had his book. Ingram was 20 when she became Wanrong’s tutor, in October 1922. A few months later, on December 1, Wanrong, aged 16, married Puyi, also 16.

French decided to focus The Last Emperor of China on the 23 months between that five-day wedding – “the last burst of imperial pageantry Peking would ever see”, he writes – and the couple’s expulsion into the “Great Without” on November 5, 1924, which brought an end to more than 500 years of (occasionally interrupted) dynastic occupation of the Forbidden City.

Apart from sporadic chunks of necessary context, the book is like a wonderfully evocative play with four principal performers – a middle-aged Scottish man, a young American woman and two teenage Manchu royals – on a spectacular stage.

French says he’s only too aware that he joins a long line of Puyi biographers, but what Ingram brings to his version is the voice of modernity. Formal lessons with Wanrong, who had a golden fountain-pen and silver inkwell, rarely took up more than an hour or two. Afterwards, there would be hair-braiding, hat-selecting, wardrobe-rummaging, dancing to gramophone records, chocolates and cigarettes.

Ingram’s language – “I love her for life”; “cute little thing”; “the Empress is still darling”; “he nearly died on the spot” – could be that of a Californian blogger, and the film these scenes evoke isn’t the Bertolucci drama; it’s Clueless, in every sense. Her diary also testifies to Puyi and Wanrong’s genuine friendship as they go cycling and kite-flying and dog-walking around their vast, mouldering compound. Many happy photographs are taken.

For French, Ingram is an important witness to the growing intimacy between the newlyweds. As he says, a great debate among biographers concerns Puyi’s sexuality and whether he was asexual or homosexual. Famously, on his wedding night, the last emperor had sloped off to the Hall of Mental Cultivation for a think.

“He’s 16!” says French, and goes on to note that “the single most surprising thing [in the diary] is when Isabel writes about ‘the curtain being drawn’ and there are no lessons today … Obviously, like all young people, they work out what goes where”.

But Puyi and Wanrong’s isn’t the only unexpected romance in the book. It becomes clear through his letters that Johnston, 28 years older than Ingram, is attracted to her. French believes he was “heartbroken” when she refused him, which is why her name was never mentioned in his memoir. Perhaps. (On the other hand, this reader thinks it was more about Johnston’s considerable, publicity-hogging ego.)

At any rate, Johnston’s letters to Ingram veer in tone from housekeeper (“I am sorry to hear chewing gum has been introduced into the palace”) to stalker (“Who is the young man you kept looking at so earnestly all the time?”). Eventually, he becomes self-deludingly creepy. “Did you explain to the Lockharts how and why you refused to let me kiss you when we were on the Emperor’s swing together?” he writes. “And yet it would only have been a remote, innocuous fatherly salutation!”

By then, the quartet had broken up. On November 5, 1924, several hours after the early-morning palace coup, Ingram was taken by rickshaw to the Forbidden City as usual, but was barred from entering. At the Gate of Divine Prowess, the commandant told her that Wanrong had gone into the “Great Without” “hatless, coatless, baggage-less”. Ingram, who would leave China in 1927, never saw her dressing-up companion again.

In the Bertolucci film, when soldiers arrive to evict Puyi and Wanrong, they are playing tennis. In real life, he was peeling her an apple, that ancient symbol of expulsion, in the Palace of Gathered Elegance. Soldiers took a – distinctly unhappy – photo, which is in the book, of his abandoned bedroom: an adolescent muddle of kung fu novels and toys.

“Once they go outside the gilded cage, they’re lost,” says French. “You could write another book about Puyi in Manchuria and try and get into the psychology of what happened to that relationship when he’s manipulated, with no advisers, and she knows that they’ve made a horrendous mistake and slips into opium abuse.”

In this immensely readable book, however, French steps only briefly beyond the palace gates and into that future when Puyi was crowned the emperor of Japan’s puppet state, Manchukuo, in 1934 – another doomed monarchy.

Another sombre note is the contrast between Ingram’s spirited diary and the fate suffered by Wanrong in the final summary, which is heart-wrenching.

Puyi survived and, in the 60s, made several return visits to the Forbidden City. Premier Zhou Enlai liked to keep an eye on him.

Asked what he thinks of Puyi now, French replies, “I do take the Zhou Enlai line. He’s supposed to have invited Puyi to a lunch and told him, ‘You weren’t to blame for becoming emperor and what happened then. But you can be blamed for what happened after.’”

item.title: [SCMP] Up in smoke: why Southeast Asia failed to halt the haze
item.description:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.
item.content:encoded:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.

Repeated, prolonged exposure to haze wreaks havoc in the human body, triggering inflammation, asthma attacks and other respiratory problems.

“That is already a signal that their body is not simply being irritated,” Asma said. “It is having a clinically significant response to the exposure.”

Left unchecked, that exposure can scar lungs, cause cardiovascular illness and lead to cancer, as PM2.5 particles small enough to cross into the bloodstream spread the damage far and wide.

In Sarawak, the Air Pollutant Index (API) Malaysia uses climbed as high as 519 this week, surpassing a level so hazardous it triggered a state of emergency in the Bornean state’s Serian district that was lifted only once the air was clear enough to breathe.

Singapore, which had gone three years without air quality breaching unhealthy levels, restarted daily haze alerts and in the Philippine capital, more than 2,000km (1,240 miles) from the wildfires, schools were forced to shut their doors.

Climate experts warn of a meteorological double-whammy conspiring to make this the hottest year on record for Southeast Asia. “Super El Nino” – a massive warming of the Pacific Ocean that chokes off regional rainfall – is being stacked on top of a developing positive Indian Ocean Dipole, which cools regional waters, further cutting off moisture.

Together, they act as a force multiplier, fuelling droughts, heatwaves and wildfires from Indonesian Borneo and Sumatra to the Mekong nations of Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.

Extreme weather is only part of the story, however. The fuel for the fires is the land cleared, year after year, for palm oil, pulpwood, corn and sugar cane, on plantations that drain water from the region’s peatlands until they become as dry as tinder.

It’s agribusiness vs the atmosphere, observers say – and for now, agribusiness is winning, despite decades of Asean pledges, a real-time satellite-powered fire-detection system and US$1.5 billion in funding to tackle the crisis that has yet to be raised.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, facing an electorate once again struggling to breathe, called on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to take action. “Asean ministers must seriously look at it”, he told reporters, “because it is affecting lives, particularly of children and babies”.

The crisis is also decimating some of the world’s greatest stores of biodiversity. Pitiful photographs from Kalimantan of rescued pangolins curled into defensive balls and orangutans with their fur singed orange-black have refocused the world’s attention on the issue.

But climate advisers warn against a convenient narrative taking hold: that this is simply the fault of this year’s “super El Nino”, rather than the businesses making billions from the burning.

“El Nino and dry conditions are risk multipliers, not the root cause,” said Renard Siew, a climate change specialist at the Centre for Governance and Political Studies in Kuala Lumpur.

“We cannot govern El Nino away,” he added. “But we can manage land better, prevent fires, enforce regulations and reduce the underlying vulnerability. Climate change is effectively making the consequences of weak governance more severe.”

History repeats

By far Southeast Asia’s worst haze offender is its most populous nation and largest economy.

Indonesia’s peatland fires began alarmingly early this year, with hotspots detected way back in January – months before the typical dry season burn.

More than 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) have burned so far and police have named 138 arson suspects, including eight companies implicated in forest and land clearance.

But arrests are of little comfort to the families forced to live under a cloud of toxic haze.

Lina Rose, a mother of four in Sarawak, has had to keep her children indoors for most of the recent school holidays.

“I’m worried about my child who has asthma,’’ she said. “The sky looks so gloomy that you think it’s going to rain, but then it doesn’t.”

Residents hark back to 2015, when Indonesia’s worst haze crisis in decades – fuelled by the same slash-and-burn clearance for palm oil and pulpwood – released thousands upon thousands of tonnes of carbon into the atmosphere and blanketed tens of millions of people, from Sumatra to Singapore, in choking smog for months on end.

Jakarta, faced with international fury, labelled that year’s crisis a “crime against humanity of extraordinary proportions” and belatedly signed on to an Asean road map promising haze-fire skies by 2020.

But that deadline came and went – and still the haze continued. A second road map followed in 2023, with a new target year of 2030. Yet few believe this new framework will be any more effective than the first.

The reason comes down to Asean’s modus operandi: consensus and non-interference are not conducive to policing environmental crime across borders, analysts say.

Meanwhile, the palm oil, pulp and paper conglomerates whose business models depend on cheap land clearance have every incentive to keep enforcement weak.

“The fundamental shift has to be from ‘managing haze’ to preventing the conditions that create it,” Siew said. “That means stronger land-use governance, better fire prevention and peatland management, clearer accountability across supply chains and much greater investment in local capacity.”

To its credit, the newer haze-control road map does “contain something its predecessor lacked”, according to Dominique Nicky Fahrizal, a legal expert and researcher at Indonesia’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies – namely, measurable indicators, “including zero days at the highest alert level for two consecutive years”, as well as pledges to reduce burned area by 10 per cent and hotspots by 5 per cent, with a midterm review due in 2028.

But the mechanisms for holding anyone accountable remain weak.

“The consensus principle and the related ‘Asean Way’ approach have led to the creation of mechanisms that are ambitious but have been described as toothless,” said Helena Varkkey, an associate professor of political ecology at the University of Malaya. “This is because the mechanisms often lack strong operationalisation or punitive measures.”

Sanctions would not work, Fahrizal said, as Asean members would never agree to impose them on one another, adding that the latest road map “is not a binding instrument” with reporting done by member states themselves.

Asean’s consensus-based approach has allowed Jakarta to commit to haze-free targets with no penalty attached to missing them. After 2015, it did impose a moratorium on peatland clearance and created an agency to restore affected areas, eventually rehabilitating some 1.6 million hectares (6,177 square miles).

But Indonesia also produces more than half the world’s palm oil and its industry has found ways to adapt, securing permits for “sustainable” farming on the one hand while surreptitiously clearing protected areas on the other. The peatland restoration agency, for all the good it did, was dissolved last year.

Fahriza said the most “realistic” option for enforcing anti-haze measures was to employ independent, third-party verification of data that could be reviewed collectively to impose “consequences for reputation and access to financing”.

Absent that, Asean’s credibility – and relevance – would “ultimately be judged by the citizens breathing the smoke, not by the number of documents signed”, he said.

Patchwork fixes

Advocacy groups are done waiting for another of the bloc’s road maps to fail.

On Monday, Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights called for the region’s latest haze crisis to be treated as a “human rights emergency”, urging Asean member states to use an October summit in Vietnam to close enforcement gaps and hold corporate offenders to account by forcing companies to publish fire and land-use information for independent scrutiny.

Some smaller-scale bilateral cooperation has also emerged. Thailand and Laos signed a data- and resource-sharing agreement on Wednesday aimed at pre-empting wildfires before they spread, echoing a similar arrangement Bangkok struck with Myanmar last month.

External pressure is building too, with mixed results. The European Union’s threatened ban on palm oil linked to deforestation has been delayed to 2027, after Indonesian objections and Brussel’s own need to lock in a new trade deal amid rising US tariffs.

Then there are the built-in weaknesses in Asean’s own crisis-response tools: under the bloc’s latest haze agreement, accepting emergency firefighting help from abroad remains entirely voluntary.

“At the moment, the arrangement exists, but ultimately it cannot function without the explicit invitation of the host country,” Varkkey said.

“This should be a scientific decision, when the haze is bad enough to warrant external help, not a political one.”

Singapore perhaps best captures the tension between profit and public safety: its companies are heavy investors in Kalimantan’s palm oil sector, yet its people – the region’s wealthiest – no longer tolerate haze imported from beyond their borders.

The city state’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 lets it prosecute companies for haze pollution regardless of where the fire was lit, a legal reach that was tested after the 2015 pollution crisis when six companies, including Indonesia’s Asia Pulp & Paper Group, were investigated – a move Jakarta called an affront to its sovereignty.

As of 2021, four of the cases remained open, Singapore’s environment minister told parliament. There has been no public confirmation of their closure in the years since.

Meanwhile, Singapore still wheezes whenever Borneo burns.

Wildlife photographer Eddie Vanderloot, 47, has learned to recognise a tight chest and itchy eyes as unmistakable signs that the air has turned.

“Constantly planning activities around the air quality gets tiring and it’s hard not to feel worn down by it,” he said.

“Even with all the windows closed, a mask on, an air purifier and air conditioners switched on, the haze still affects me for hours.”

item.title: [SCMP] Golden years: in Southeast Asia, growing old is big business
item.description:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.
item.content:encoded:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.

Carers wheeled and walked eight fellow residents to the dining table before breaking into song. Goaded into a speech, Fung kept it brief: “I’m very happy to be here.”

The home, a refurbished two-storey bungalow, is one of a growing number of assisted living facilities springing up as Singapore’s population ages. The city state officially became a “super-aged” society this year, with more than one-fifth of its population over 65.

These facilities offer a much-needed middle ground for older people who can no longer live independently but do not require the round-the-clock medical care of a nursing home.

Staff help residents with daily tasks such as dispensing medication and writing letters, while some facilities include memory care units for those experiencing cognitive decline.

Assisted living is a nascent but fast-growing segment of Singapore’s multibillion-dollar silver economy. The government has provided more than 1,100 such flats since 2021, and private real estate operators are also increasingly entering the market.

For residents like Fung, what matters most is feeling part of a community, keeping their independence and being treated with dignity. Despite her early-stage osteoporosis, she moves around the home without a walking frame, sometimes forgoing afternoon sessions of mahjong to journal in her room instead.

“I’m fitting in little by little – I’ve learned to get to know more of the residents and our different timetables,” she said. “I told my family I’ll probably stay here until the time comes.”

For fellow resident Soo Soo Cheng, 90, her single room is a world away from the six-bedded ward she shared at her previous nursing home. “It was like a dormitory and nothing private like this. I was getting really uncomfortable,” she said.

Now she spends her days in a bright orange armchair by the window, walking frame within reach, while carers take care of tasks like printing copies of bills and helping her to bed when her spine acts up.

“I’m thankful for a place like this, where I can do things on my own and yet never have a dull moment,” she said. “Time seems to fly.”

A middle ground

Southeast Asia is ageing rapidly and its social welfare systems are increasingly grappling with a thorny question: what happens to the people who can no longer manage entirely on their own, but do not need a hospital bed?

Assisted living – offering medical and social care scalable to residents’ needs – has emerged as an answer.

It was designed for people whose needs fell somewhere between the intensive clinical care of a nursing home and what a domestic helper, who cannot reasonably be expected to manage a medical emergency, could provide, said Janice Chia, founder of Ageing Asia, a Singapore-based social enterprise focused on the business of growing old.

In Singapore, more people are ageing alone – an estimated 83,000 by 2030, according to the Ministry of Health – while shrinking family sizes are increasing the caregiving burden shouldered by adult children.

“Assisted living provides independence and privacy without the seeming unpopular burden of managing foreign domestic helpers,” said Kelvin Tan, who heads the applied ageing studies programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

Options in the city state range from government-run flats to private luxury apartments, with monthly bills ranging anywhere from three to five figures, depending on location, room size and level of care required.

In 2021, Singapore introduced community care flats aiming to support independent ageing in a social environment. Five such projects have launched so far.

The Housing Development Board announced in July that from its sixth project, launching in October, the eligibility age for assisted-living public housing estates would be lowered from 65 to 55, alongside lower fees aimed at improving affordability.

Estimated fees for a 15-year lease – currently S$40,000 to S$49,000 (US$31,400 to US$38,500) for a basic package – will drop to between S$26,000 and S$28,000 from next year, according to Vanguard Healthcare, which operates the developments.

“The cost is a big advantage for average Singaporeans looking for an accessible offer,” Tan said.

Private operators are also scaling up their operations. St Bernadette Lifestyle Village, which runs eight facilities island-wide, offers a mid-tier option priced from S$3,000 to S$6,000 a month.

Care homes were “less a business venture than a necessity”, said founder Belinda Wee, who has observed elderly residents growing unsettled in nursing homes due to a lack of socialising. About 80 residents lived in St Bernadette’s homes last year, up from 19 in 2023.

Well-heeled pensioners gained a luxury option last month with the opening of Perennial Living, a S$260 million, 195,000 sq ft development in northeastern Singapore featuring a hydrotherapy pool, a traditional Chinese medicine clinic and a karaoke lounge.

A basic package for a 330 sq ft studio flat starts at S$8,000 a month, while a 565 sq ft two-bedder costs more than S$13,000.

The hefty price tag has raised concerns about the affordability of retirement, though experts note the project is aimed squarely at the upper end of the market.

Chia said its prices should be viewed in the category of premium hospitality and care, rather than general assisted living.

Sign-ups have been gradual and interest has been “positive”, according to Perennial Holding’s chief executive Pua Seck Guan, who projected a 30 per cent occupancy rate after a year and 80 per cent after two.

More new entrants were expected to join the assisted living sector, Chia said, as Singapore’s shift from live-in caregiving to mainstream services gave firms the confidence to invest. But she urged regulators to pace approvals carefully given the dearth of healthcare workers.

Singapore needed to recruit about 6,000 nurses, healthcare professionals and support staff every year to meet demand, the Health Ministry said in 2024. It previously estimated that a healthcare workforce of 82,000 would be needed by 2030.

“This figure is the one worth dwelling on, because it shows care capability cannot simply be commissioned. Sites can be approved considerably faster than carers can be trained, deployed and retained,” Chia said.

Ageing in luxury

With its circular driveway and plush lobby, Perennial Living looks more like an upscale hotel than a home for the elderly.

The development aimed to set a “new benchmark for senior living in Singapore”, Pua said – reflecting a surge in luxury senior living facilities across Asia as operators recognise their target demographic wants more than just care and medical services.

More than US$500 billion is expected to pour into the silver economy across six Southeast Asian markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines – by 2030, according to Ageing Asia.

Retirees today were wealthier, healthier and more assertive than any generation before them, the social enterprise said in a report released last month, making the business of ageing the Asia-Pacific’s “largest commercial opportunity”.

“Baby boomers, the biggest savers of all generations, have spent their lives making choices and are expected to hold onto that autonomy into their older age,” it said.

At Homerly International Senior Living in Thailand, residents walk long, tree-lined avenues within a large, serene gated community, accompanied by nurses, with their pets padding along behind them. The resort, which provides assisted living and nursing care, is one of hundreds of retirement communities popping up across a country with abundant land and a growing healthcare workforce.

A month’s stay – including round-the-clock medical care, physiotherapy, pool villas shaded by trees and two staff members in attendance – starts at US$2,200, with the top-end pool villas commanding a price tag of around US$4,500.

“Here you’re not a patient, you are a resident. We treat people with dignity,” general manager Rene Pisters said. “You have somebody with you all the time if you need it and the feeling that if something happens to you, there is a nurse sitting here.”

Malaysia is seeing a similar boom in luxury homes for the elderly, driven by changing expectations of ageing, according to N. Raaj Selvarajan, group chairman of regional healthcare infrastructure investor Hemrish Group and founder of its flagship senior living brand Sukha Golden.

Residents increasingly wanted privacy, wellness and access to care without the institutional feel traditionally associated with elderly care, he said.

Demand for its luxury Sukha Senior Resort has surged since it opened in March last year – all rooms are fully occupied, with interested residents placed on a waiting list.

Capitalising on the boom, Selvarajan said plans to expand regionally were under way, with projects in Indonesia and Vietnam in the pipeline. “The opportunity is not simply that Asia is ageing; it is that people want to age differently,” he said.

Crossing borders

For Singaporeans who feel priced out of their own super-aged society, homes for the elderly have become an unlikely engine of Malaysia and Thailand’s recent tourism boom, as families shop for similar care standards at a fraction of the cost.

The Straits Resorts Medini, a retirement home in Johor just a 15-minute drive from the border, has built its business around Singaporean demand.

“Consistent and encouraging” is how founder Elvira Tan describes cross-border interest in the facility, which offers rooms from S$4,300 a month, bundling in personalised care and grooming services, arts activities and social programmes.

Industry insiders expect the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Rapid Transit System Link, set to open in January, to further boost demand.

“You can obtain the most expensive level of care in Malaysia for about one-third the price of the same level of care in Singapore,” said Kashif Ansari, group CEO of real estate market intelligence group Juwai IQI.

Cultural familiarity and the absence of a language barrier eased the transition for would-be residents considering homes across the causeway, he added.

“Families with a senior who needs potentially years or even more than a decade of care, naturally want the highest quality service and the lowest cost they can possibly obtain,” he said. “Malaysia has a real competitive advantage in this sector and operators hope to make the most of it.”

Money goes further in Thailand too. Facilities in Bangkok and Chiang Mai are attracting a growing number of Asian retirees, including from Singapore and Hong Kong, looking for care comparable to what they can get at home at a fraction of the cost.

Thailand hopes the care and wellness industry will become a defining part of its economy in the years ahead, as more people grow old and spend money on a curated retirement.

Care standards were high, Homerly’s Pisters said, adding that his company helped elderly residents with bureaucratic hurdles such as visas and bank accounts.

“The demand is huge, and it will only get bigger,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
item.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
item.content:encoded:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.

But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.

While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.

That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.

Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.

“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”

The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.

Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another

Seth Goldstein, Morningstar

Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.

While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.

“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.

The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.

Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.

The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.

“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.

Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.

Can Tesla do without China?

At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.

Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.

Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.

Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.

Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.

China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.

“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.

“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”

Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.

Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.

Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.

Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.

And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.

The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised

Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney

Between Washington and Beijing

Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.

Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.

Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.

The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.

But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.

Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.

How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.

“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”

She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”

Tesla lays the first bricks

Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.

It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.

Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.

CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.

Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.

“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.

Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.

SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.

Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.

However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.

While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.

Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’

However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.

“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”

Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.

A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.

Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.

“There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research.

Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said.

Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added.

These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026.

Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11.

“The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said.

Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO.

“China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Thailand’s bid to wire the world’s AI revolution
item.description:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.

“They are essential to our daily life. They are in all electronics you are using,” said WellTek founder Jennifer Deng, who established the Thai subsidiary of her China-based Jiangxi Welgao Electronics in Ayutthaya two years ago.

Thailand is now Southeast Asia’s No 1 producer of PCBs – often described as the nervous system of modern electronics, channelling essential signals through increasingly complex arrays of semiconductors, resistors and capacitors – and the fifth largest in the world.

Deng’s US$75 million WellTek plant, built in under a year, is the first of two planned for Ayutthaya, a major Thai industrial zone once dominated by Japanese carmakers and global electronics giants, now being rewired for the artificial intelligence age.

Circuitous success

Malaysia may lead the field in lucrative semiconductors and Vietnam in electronics assembly, but PCBs give Thailand its competitive advantage in Southeast Asia’s race for tech relevance.

Its rise in this niche owes as much to the trade wars triggered by Washington as it does to the smart timing of Thai authorities in welcoming global companies seeking new bases away from the tariff line of fire.

“The market demanded movement to Thailand,” Deng told This Week in Asia from WellTek’s Ayutthaya headquarters, where workers in crisp company polo shirts hustled down corridors beneath posters bearing the mantra “Conscience and Altruism”.

Over the next few years, Deng not only wants to build a second factory but treble output to more than 3.6 million square metres (38.8 million sq ft) of PCBs per year.

Thailand’s existing PCB industry gave it a head start over rivals, she said, explaining that “Europeans and Americans all requested we are outside of China, and our main partners are here in Thailand.”

Narit Therdsteerasukdi, secretary general of Thailand’s government-run Board of Investment, told an investor forum on Wednesday that the country was at a “turning point”.

Investment in the PCB and electronics component sector topped US$10 billion over the past three years, he revealed, calling this proof of how Thailand should pivot its economy.

“We need to restructure our economy … and the electronic industry, especially PCBs, is a very good example [of how to do it],” he said. “The key question is where do we go from here?”

For Narit, the country’s future growth depends on climbing the value chain, backed by a higher-skilled workforce trained for the AI age.

Printed fortunes

PCBs are a rare success story in a decade of patchy industrial policy that has left Thailand a regional growth laggard.

Many of the ideas floated to accelerate growth through new manufacturing chains and a splurge of foreign investment have been delayed, watered down or scrapped entirely on contact with the reality of delivering big infrastructure projects in a politically febrile kingdom.

Trade dispute and fuel-price spikes from distant wars have further hurt an economy that expanded just 2.4 per cent last year – a relative crawl compared with Vietnam’s 8 per cent.

Yet around 60 per cent of all new investment into Southeast Asia’s PCB industry has flowed into Thailand since 2023, according to the Thailand Printed Circuit Association.

Phutana Daoruang, the association’s general manager, said Thailand already had the PCB infrastructure, built up by a dozen or so Taiwanese firms, when Donald Trump’s first presidency fired the starting gun on companies fleeing US tariffs.

Thailand’s location and logistics networks, tax breaks, industrial estates and skilled workforce allowed the new factories to plug straight into electronics clusters like Ayutthaya, with the upgraded deep-sea port at Laem Chabang – a two-hour drive away – providing a maritime gateway to China.

“We pitched to compete with Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam as the fundamental infrastructure was already here,” Phutana told This Week in Asia.

“Thailand is quite suitable, we are quite strong in logistics and electricity supply is stable – especially compared with Vietnam and Malaysia.”

There are now around 50 PCB companies in the country, forming a sector that meets a modest 5 per cent of world demand but is eager to capture more of a global market forecast to reach US$100 billion in the coming years.

The ambition is to export eight to 10 times more PCBs than Thailand currently does – reaching roughly US$18 billion to US$25 billion in trade volume and a 20 per cent global market share.

Lofty as that sounds, it may not be impossible given the trillions of dollars flowing into data centres that need increasingly complex layers of PCBs.

“It’s quite complicated and uses very specialised material,” Phutana said of PCB manufacturing. “Thailand has the fundamentals to do it.”

Running hot

AI has changed the stakes for PCB manufacturers. A PCB destined for use with an AI accelerator card – roughly the size of a sheet of A4 paper – is a very different beast from the boards that are found inside car key fobs.

Densely layered with winding copper traces that resemble an illuminated cityscape from above, these boards must survive extreme heat and power loads while shuttling vastly more data at far higher speeds, providing the physical foundations for the AI chips crunching numbers across the region’s data centres.

Thailand has attracted billions of US dollars of data-centre investment in recent years on the promise of booming AI demand – so much, so fast that the capital is arriving well ahead of the physical buildout of centres themselves.

But data centres are voracious consumers of water and electricity while creating comparatively few jobs, and domestic critics argue that beyond a handful of landlords, Thailand risks getting the environmental costs without the economic rewards.

Delta Electronics Thailand, the local arm of the Taipei-headquartered “grid to chip” manufacturer that became the first company on the Thai stock exchange to be valued above US$100 billion in February, is now eyeing a bigger prize – the power and cooling systems that keep those centres humming.

In the Thai electronics world, Delta is the gatekeeper to the big data-centre contracts – and as it grows, Thailand and its PCB makers are desperate to keep it on side.

“Thailand is moving beyond cost competitiveness towards higher-value industries,” Delta said in a statement, pointing to “advanced engineering talent, energy infrastructure readiness and supply chain depth” as the areas that, with “continued progress” and “pro-business policies”, could give the country a lasting regional edge.

Not everyone shares that confidence. Analysts the world over have grown increasingly nervous about an AI investment bubble and what its bursting might do to countries that have calibrated their industrial strategy on the boom continuing.

Even Delta admits to being “mindful” of “tariff uncertainty, engineering talent gaps, supply chain constraints, intensifying competition in AI infrastructure” and the difficulty of scaling manufacturing “while maintaining quality and profitability”.

Down on the factory floor, the constraints are more immediate. PCB manufacturing demands “a crazy amount of water each day”, according to Thailand Printed Circuit Association chief Phutana – and it needs to be “high purity”, competing directly with the needs of households and other industries.

“The next wave of investment is there. Everyone in AI servers and data centres is looking for new land to expand their facility.” he said. “The customers cannot wait.”

Layered on top of water constraints is a supply squeeze on laminates – the non-conductive, rigid base material that forms the physical foundation of circuit boards – and essential chemicals, a knock-on effect of the US-Israel war on Iran disrupting imports.

Thailand’s Board of Investment says it is exploring ways to free up more water and power, but critics argue the country is sprinting ahead of its own capacity to sustainably keep pace.

Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director at environmental monitor and advocacy group EEC Watch, said automation had killed the jobs case for hosting PCB plants at all.

Relocation incentives meant most equipment was imported, he said, with little technology transfer or upskilling of local workers – turning Thailand into an “assembly line” for foreign capital rather than a genuine beneficiary.

“The factories that come here don’t use as much labour as they used to,” he said. “If they come from Chinese capital, they barely hire Thai workers at all. Blue collar [workers] are Myanmar, white collar are Chinese.”

Despite the scepticism, there is a more hopeful reading – one rooted less in job numbers than in opportunity.

Thailand’s education system produces precious few science, technology, engineering and mathematics graduates each year and PCBs may be one of its rare growth industries suited to hiring them.

“Thailand faces a severe shortfall in meeting the surging demand for PCB and electronics workers,” said Panisa Harnpathananun of the National Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Policy Council in Thailand.

She estimated the sector would need roughly 225,000 high-skilled workers over the next five years, against the around 1,100 electronics engineers Thai universities produced in 2024.

“This deficit is driven by an ageing population and a structural educational mismatch,” Panisa said.

Plans are afoot to close that gap, including a “sandbox” scheme to fast track engineering degrees and proposals to retrain redundant car industry workers for PCBs and semiconductors.

In a country short on other engines of growth, Panisa said PCBs might offer “the most critical opportunity and the strategic careers” its graduates were likely to find.

item.title: [SCMP] A rural city, once known for livestock, now provides China’s AI computing fuel
item.description:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.

As the global artificial intelligence boom fuels a scramble for more computing power and electricity, the same climate that has sustained Ulanqab’s pastoral economy is turning this Inner Mongolian city into one of China’s most coveted industrial assets.
