In such a scenario, the size of the Type 052D force could allow the PLA to protect carrier and amphibious groups, escort replenishment ships, support anti-submarine operations and also maintain surface forces on Taiwan’s eastern approaches.

That said, long-range strikes against moving warships would still depend on a wider network of land-, air-, sea- and space-based sensors.

The Pentagon’s 2025 China military report said the PLA’s growing space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance network had dramatically increased its ability to monitor, track and target US and allied forces. It also said land-based sensors, including Skywave over-the-horizon radars, could probably detect ships and aircraft between the first and second island chains.

The report – which primarily assessed developments through 2024 – said the PLA still faced challenges with time-sensitive battle-damage assessment and coordinating complex multiservice strikes.

Beyond those operational hurdles, technical uncertainties remain. Weapons compatibility may differ between production batches, the precise anti-submarine sensor fit is unclear in open sources, and China’s missile-defence claims for newer ships remain unverified.

But the broader trajectory is clear. Since the first Type 052D entered service in 2014, China has kept producing and upgrading the class as the PLA Navy has pushed farther into the western Pacific.

In a conflict over Taiwan, the Type 052D’s importance may therefore lie less in any single weapon than in the combination of capability, adaptability and numbers – potentially giving Beijing enough modern destroyers to support several naval operations at once.

item.title: [SCMP] Upgraded but underperforming: Philippines’ growth lags behind
item.description:
The Philippines’ rise to upper-middle-income status was supposed to mark a new phase for one of Southeast Asia’s most closely watched emerging economies.

Instead, analysts say the milestone has done little to shield the country from short-term pressures weighing on growth: sluggish public spending, delayed infrastructure, high living costs and the fallout from investigations into alleged irregularities in flood control projects.

Those strains have left the Philippines looking like a regional laggard. Bank of America is forecasting gross domestic product growth of 2.5 per cent for 2026 – tying with Thailand for the slowest pace in the region – even as it raised its overall Asean growth forecast to 5 per cent, up from 4.7 per cent at the end of the second quarter.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines’ rise to upper-middle-income status was supposed to mark a new phase for one of Southeast Asia’s most closely watched emerging economies.

Instead, analysts say the milestone has done little to shield the country from short-term pressures weighing on growth: sluggish public spending, delayed infrastructure, high living costs and the fallout from investigations into alleged irregularities in flood control projects.

Those strains have left the Philippines looking like a regional laggard. Bank of America is forecasting gross domestic product growth of 2.5 per cent for 2026 – tying with Thailand for the slowest pace in the region – even as it raised its overall Asean growth forecast to 5 per cent, up from 4.7 per cent at the end of the second quarter.

“The Philippines is expected to see a sharp slowdown relative to 2025,” the bank said in its September report, comparing that to Singapore’s projected 5.1 per cent growth, Malaysia’s 5.2 per cent, Indonesia’s 5.3 per cent and Vietnam’s 8.2 per cent.

As other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations surge ahead, the growing growth disparity raises serious questions about whether Manila can convert its long-term strengths – a young population, a robust consumer base and an expanding services sector – into the growth momentum seen elsewhere in the region.

Modest consumption gains and a bottoming-out of investment spending could support limited growth in the second half of the year, Bank of America said, while targeted subsidies for vulnerable consumers and the transport sector could cushion the impact of energy shocks.

“Compared with its Asean peers, the Philippines is currently facing a relative slowdown,” said Jonathan Ravelas, a Filipino economist and market strategist. “Countries such as Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia are benefiting more from manufacturing expansion, supply-chain relocation and stronger foreign direct investment inflows.”

The Philippine economy had been “heavily dependent on consumption and that engine has been tempered by higher borrowing costs, elevated living costs and slower public spending”, he said.

Michael Ricafort, chief economist at Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation, said increased government “catch-up spending” on infrastructure was the “missing element or link that could once again accelerate Philippine economic and GDP growth”, offsetting the underspending seen since late 2025 amid ongoing flood-control corruption investigations.

“This would lead to better fiscal performance, in terms of increased government tax and revenue collections, narrower budget deficits and a lower, better national government debt-to-GDP ratio,” Ricafort said, adding that such spending “would be the major catalyst to pump-prime the economy”, counteracting geopolitical factors that had driven up prices, inflation and interest rates.

Ravelas said the slowdown in infrastructure spending was concerning because public construction “has a strong multiplier effect on the economy”.

Most investors were less troubled by the corruption investigations than by the delays they had caused, he said. “Transparency and accountability are positive for investor confidence but projects must continue moving forward. The challenge for policymakers is to clean up the system without slowing down execution,” Ravelas added.

The Philippines’ challenge is sustaining and accommodating growth

Jonathan Ravelas, economist

Ricafort agreed that governance reforms would be vital to restoring investor confidence in the Philippine economy.

Piled on top of the infrastructure slowdown and governance issues is another worry: forecasters have warned of El Nino-driven drought conditions stretching into early 2027, threatening food prices and agricultural incomes just as households are already feeling the strain of rising living costs.

Ricafort wants to see the gap filled with targeted, non-monetary relief such as ayuda (aid) payments and job programmes aimed at the poorest Filipinos, to ease price pressures “largely caused” by the Iran war.

Some of these measures are already being rolled out: subsidies have been directed at transport, agriculture and fisheries, among other hard-hit sectors, in an attempt to stop higher costs being passed on to the public, along with financial support for low-income households.

But Ricafort said more needed to be done. “Technology, on top of education, is one of the biggest equalisers that would lift more people from poverty, especially in the countryside,” he said, pointing to raised productivity across agriculture and manufacturing that would also increase the country’s global competitiveness and strengthen food security.

Philippines vs Thailand

Despite the sluggish growth outlook, analysts say the Philippines still has room to catch up.

“I would not read the Bank of America forecast as the Philippines losing its long-term growth story,” Ravelas said. “The country’s elevation to upper middle-income status reflects the progress it has achieved, while the BofA outlook is more about the near-term challenges it faces.”

That upgrade, announced by the World Bank on July 1, was based on the strength of the Philippines’ 2025 gross national income per capita, placing it in the upper middle-income bracket.

This year’s slowdown has since tempered expectations, but Ravelas says the investment case for the country remains intact.

He said investors liked the Philippines’ young population, sizeable domestic market, resilient consumer base and growing services industry, but were “looking for stronger execution, particularly in infrastructure, foreign investment attraction and policy implementation”.

Before the Covid-19 pandemic, the Philippines actually had one of the region’s fastest-growing economies and had kept growing steadily since, Ricafort said.

Analysts say the comparison with Thailand is instructive because the two Southeast Asian economies have arrived at the same 2.5 per growth figure from different directions.

“Thailand is a net exporting country with relatively lower inflation and interest rates, while the Philippines is a net importing country, with inflation and interest rates among the highest in the region,” Ricafort said.

Ravelas pointed to other differences. “Thailand has strong infrastructure, manufacturing and tourism, yet it is constrained by an ageing population, weak domestic demand and slower labour force growth,” he said.

“The Philippines, on the other hand, benefits from a young population, strong consumer spending, remittances and long-term demographic momentum, but continues to struggle with productivity, infrastructure gaps and inflation volatility.”

Put another way, Thailand struggled to find new sources of growth, “while the Philippines’ challenge is sustaining and accommodating growth”, Ravelas said, pointing to energy, water and transport networks that need to “keep pace with urbanisation and economic expansion.”

“Ultimately, the Philippines still has the fundamentals to outperform over the long term,” he said. “But turning potential into growth will depend on the quality and speed of policy execution.”

item.title: [SCMP] China has gained pace in the space race by recovering rockets – but can it relaunch one?
item.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead.

US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components.

Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain.
item.content:encoded:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead.

US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components.

Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain.

Last month, Chinese private aerospace company LandSpace landed the booster of its Zhuque-3 rocket on deployable landing legs at a site in the northwestern province of Gansu, marking the country’s first successful ground-based controlled recovery using landing legs, an approach that closely resembles that of SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

The significance of landing a launched rocket goes beyond the spectacle of bringing a booster back intact, according to industry experts.

Rocket reuse was “essential for achieving low-cost, frequent and sustainable [launches] … and providing new opportunities for large-scale commercial space exploration”, a team from three major Chinese aerospace research institutions said in a paper published in March.

LandSpace said the first stage represented “about 70 per cent” of a rocket’s cost, with reuse able to spread that expense over multiple missions, underscoring the cost advantages of reusing first-stage boosters.

Some Chinese launch services can cost around US$20,000 per kilogram (about US$9,070 a pound) of payload, compared with roughly US$2,700 to US$3,000 for SpaceX’s reusable Falcon 9, according to a report published by the Mercator Institute for China Studies in February.

The large gap helps explain why rocket makers are racing to develop vehicles that can be recovered and reused.

The Chinese paper from March said there were several different approaches to bringing a rocket back, including recovery using parachutes or wings to slow the vehicle for a safer arrival.

Other approaches include landing leg recovery, with the booster using its engines to control its descent before touching down vertically on deployable landing legs.

While China still lags behind the US in landing leg recovery, it is also betting on a different approach to booster recovery: an offshore net-capture system that uses a recovery vessel to catch the descending booster.

In July, it successfully retrieved part of a Long March-10B reusable rocket following its maiden launch by using a unique sea-based net-capture system for the first time.

Compared with the landing leg recovery approach, net-capture had relatively less demanding requirements for the booster’s final landing-point accuracy, avoided the need to install heavy landing-support structures on the rocket and allowed the offshore recovery platform to be deployed flexibly, Wang Long, the founder of space technology consultancy Nihao Taikong, was quoted as saying in a report by Shenzhen-based Securities Times in July.

Hao Jinjie, an engineer at China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, told state broadcaster CGTN the net-capture method was “like dropping a pen from the 100th floor into a pencil holder, while keeping its speed and orientation under control”.

China’s pursuit of reusable rockets draws on both its state aerospace groups and its ability to mobilise the private sector behind national priorities through the deployment of industrial policy.

Galactic Energy’s kerosene-fuelled Pallas-1 reached orbit earlier this month, with a recovery attempt deliberately deferred to later missions. The rocket is designed to carry up to 7 tonnes to a low-Earth orbit, intended for use on the first stage of at least 25 flights.

ISpace flew the same low-altitude methane demonstrator twice in 2023, though its orbital SQX-3 has yet to launch. Space Pioneer, Orienspace, Deep Blue Aerospace and Space Epoch also have reusable rockets at various stages of testing or development.

To make reusability economically viable, a booster needs to be able to re-enter space and survive repeated launches. Dai Zheng, chief commander of the Zhuque-3 missions at LandSpace, said those were areas in which China had little experience.

China had no established technical framework covering rocket reuse standards, inspection procedures or rules governing component replacement, Dai told state broadcaster CCTV in an interview last month.

“China has just solved the question of whether a rocket can come back,” he said, adding that there was “no system yet for determining whether a recovered rocket can fly again”.

In a research report published last month, analysts at Jinyuan Securities emphasised that a reusable rocket required a complete post-recovery processing cycle, including safely draining and disposing of residual propellant, isolating potential hazards and conducting non-destructive inspections of the vehicle’s structure, welds and propellant tanks.

Other necessary steps involved assessing the remaining life of engines after repeated thermal and pressure cycles, replacing worn components such as seals and valves, and carrying out system-wide functional tests before another flight.

LandSpace has said it plans to reuse the Zhuque-3 booster recovered last month in a space mission in the next six months, while the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology has said it aims to conduct a reuse flight of the first-stage Long March-10B by the end of this year.

Success in those endeavours would mark a crucial shift for China from demonstrating that it can recover a booster to proving that it can fly one again – essential to realising its commercial space ambitions.

A decade ago, a central government white paper called for research into low-cost launch vehicles and reusable transport systems capable of travelling between Earth and space.

Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency

Xu Ying, GalaxySpace

What began as a research objective has moved through engineering trials and become a national industrial push. China’s latest five-year plan made building the country into a “space power” a priority, and specifically mentioned the development of reusable launch technology, including a reusable heavy-lift launcher for deep-space programmes.

Every serious ambition China has in space – from constellations of broadband satellites to orbiting computing networks and missions to the moon – will depend on reusable launch systems.

“Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency,” said Xu Ying, general manager of public affairs at satellite manufacturer GalaxySpace. Only then, she added, could “space infrastructure” be deployed at scale and become commercially viable.

China’s two flagship broadband projects show the size of the task. China Satellite Net plans for its Guowang constellation to have 12,992 satellites, with roughly 1,300 scheduled to be in orbit by 2029 and the full network deployed by 2035.

Shanghai-based SpaceSail’s Qianfan network is aiming for more than 15,000 by 2030, but the two Chinese companies combined have less than 500 satellites in orbit at present – around 4 per cent of Starlink’s orbiting fleet of more than 11,000.

LandSpace launched 10 Qianfan satellites into orbit on Tuesday, marking the first deployment for a large-scale satellite internet constellation by a private Chinese rocket company. Another eight were launched on Wednesday.

SpaceSail aims to expand the Qianfan constellation to 324 satellites by the end of the year – up from 256 at present – leaving a narrow window of just over three months to launch 68 more.

A space industry researcher based in Xian, capital of northwestern China’s Shaanxi province, said some experts were optimistic that China would be able to make steady progress in the reusable rocket race.

He said that while SpaceX – founded in 2002 – had a head start in many aspects of the commercial space sector, Chinese companies were making progress. However, he added, China’s industry might encounter difficulties due to a comparative lack of experience in advanced rocket engines, as “no one from outside China would teach you how to design them”.

Engines accounted for more than 50 per cent of the total cost of a rocket, Wang Zijing, an analyst at Soochow Securities, wrote in a research note issued this month.

Jinyuan Securities said engine life and repeated ignition were among the biggest technical challenges in the reuse of boosters.

A reusable booster must restart its engines during ascent, re-entry and landing and operate reliably across a wide range of thrust levels, meaning that key components including its turbopumps, combustion chamber, nozzle and valves must be able to withstand repeated thermal and pressure cycles as well as vibration loads.

No Chinese rocket engine has yet made a second orbital flight. Meanwhile, a SpaceX Falcon 9 booster was sent into space for the 37th time last month.

“Reusable technology remains a new field that requires continued learning,” Lou Luliang, the chief designer of the Long March-10B, told Beijing-based China Aerospace News in a report published in July. “The thermal and mechanical conditions during an actual return, component damage and the patterns of reuse cannot all be fully understood through ground testing alone”.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘I just need an answer’: widow haunted by husband’s shooting seeks inquest
item.description:
Two years after her armed, mentally ill husband was fatally shot by a Hong Kong police officer, Mrs Li is still waiting to learn whether a death inquest will be held.

On September 15, 2024, she called police when her 38-year-old husband, who had a history of mental illness, attacked his elderly mother and her at their North Point home.

Officers wielding shields arrived and found the man holding a 30cm (11.8-inch) knife and a pair of scissors.
item.content:encoded:
Two years after her armed, mentally ill husband was fatally shot by a Hong Kong police officer, Mrs Li is still waiting to learn whether a death inquest will be held.

On September 15, 2024, she called police when her 38-year-old husband, who had a history of mental illness, attacked his elderly mother and her at their North Point home.

Officers wielding shields arrived and found the man holding a 30cm (11.8-inch) knife and a pair of scissors.

Little did Mrs Li, who preferred to be identified by her spouse’s surname, expect that the day would end in tragedy.

Police said an officer eventually shot the man at a distance of 1.5 metres (4.9 feet) after he allegedly ignored repeated warnings during a 30-second stand-off and attempted to attack them.

Now, all she wants is for a death inquest to be held as soon as possible to bring closure to herself and her husband, to whom she had been married for 10 years.

“I need no sympathy or pity. I just need an answer and hope to prevent this tragedy from happening again,” she said.

“It’s been two years, yet there is still no news. I’m anxious that this matter will just be left unsettled, and my husband’s death went unexplained.”

The then commissioner of police Raymond Siu Chak-yee defended the officer’s decision to shoot the man because he followed the guidelines on firearms use.

Siu said police would submit a death investigation report to the Coroner’s Court and “recommend the court hold a death inquest as soon as possible”.

But Li barely heard anything about it over the past two years.

In February last year, she received a letter from a coroner confirming that the cause of death was a gunshot wound to the chest.

In early April, she wrote to the court to inquire about a death inquest.

In response, the court said police had been instructed to produce a death investigation report, and a decision on whether to hold an inquest would be made after receiving the complete report.

Since then, she has called the Coroner’s Court general hotline every month to check on the progress, only to be told: “The investigation is still under way.”

On the other hand, she stopped contacting police after the contact person who treated her kindly retired.

Only an officer from the Complaints Against Police Office continued to check on her regularly, but declined to reveal details of their investigation.

“Every step has been very hard for me … I’m always afraid that something bad will happen to me and no one will be left to follow up on my husband’s case,” she said. “I hope everything can go faster.”

In the first few months after her husband’s death, she was unable to eat and sleep well, losing over 20 pounds (9kg) in just one month.

Now, she suffers from a failing memory, slowed reaction times and wakes up repeatedly throughout the night.

Whenever she has a moment to herself, the memory of her husband covered in blood and surrounded by police after being shot floods back into her mind.

“I deeply regret calling police. I made a call, and then he died … I will not forgive myself for the rest of my life,” she said.

“My intention was simply to have my husband taken to hospital, as we did before.”

She questioned why officers discharged a fatal shot to the chest rather than retreating down the stairwell or deploying non-lethal options such as pepper spray and shields.

In response to the South China Morning Post queries, police said they submitted the investigation report to the Coroner’s Court in June 2025.

The court requested further information, which was provided this month, and police were waiting for further instructions from the court.

As for the complaint filed with police, it is being handled in a “fair and impartial manner in accordance with established procedures”.

The judiciary declined to comment on individual cases.

It said the coroner would decide whether to hold an inquest after reviewing the report, and police might be directed to conduct further investigations if needed, with the deceased’s next of kin to be updated on the progress and decision on the inquest.

Under Practice Direction 39 on coronial procedures, which took effect in June last year, if an investigation is not completed within nine months of the date of the interim report, or if no decision whether to hold an inquest has been made, the court will, where appropriate, update the family every three months on the reasons for the delay – which did not happen in Mrs Li’s case.

The guidelines do not set a fixed deadline for supplying supplementary information once a report is submitted.

Tim Pang Hung-cheong, a community organiser at the Society for Community Organisation who helped Mrs Li, said he believed that the case would rely on expert assessment of firearms use and police protocols to evaluate whether the officer’s actions were justified.

“Without disclosing anything, families are left in this situation – with just one letter on hand and they have to reach out repeatedly in anxiety,” he said.

“Even after the report is submitted, it takes time for the pre-inquest [reviews] to be scheduled before the formal hearing; more waiting is anticipated.”

Delays of two to three years before a coroner’s inquest opens are not uncommon in Hong Kong, according to lawyer Jonathan Man Ho-ching.

Man said police handled death investigations alongside routine work without a dedicated unit, according to his understanding.

There are only three designated coroners in Hong Kong handling inquests while performing regular duties such as granting burial and autopsy orders, with their workload further compounded following major disasters such as the Wang Fuk Court fire that claimed 168 lives.

The primary recourse for families is to query the Coroner’s Court directly regarding the progress of their case.

“Just like any case, the longer a death inquest is delayed, the less ideal it is because witnesses might not be able to remember details, or might simply be unreachable any more, as seen during the Lamma ferry disaster inquests,” Man said.

“A wait is often inevitable … which is very hard on families because an inquest allows them to understand what happened to their loved ones, providing closure and helping them move on.”

Man said he believed Hong Kong could do better in strengthening communication with bereaved families during these prolonged periods.

“In some jurisdictions, death inquiries are not treated purely as a legal procedure; caseworkers are assigned to families to help them navigate the process,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong guqin devotees embrace the ancient zither’s history, philosophy and craft
item.description:
When civil servant Jackel Wan Chak-kui, 28, first heard a guqin being played, he was a young boy wandering through Chi Lin Nunnery, in Diamond Hill. He remembers being entranced by the instrument’s music, at once subtle and comforting. It seemed to envelop him like a warm embrace, complementing the natural beauty of the gardens, melding with stone, water, wood and stillness.

Years later, as a student at Baptist University, Wan chanced upon the sound again, while scrolling through YouTube. He delved deeper this time, yearning to learn more. He ordered his first guqin from Taobao (“Not a good one, but at least I could have a touch [of the instrument],” he says) and taught himself from scores found in the university library, learning where to place his fingers on the seven silk strings.

A seven-stringed zither, the guqin (“ancient stringed instrument”) was once the preserve of noblemen and royal courts, poets and scholars, and has been part of a musical tradition that has existed for more than 3,000 years in China, played in small, elite gatherings.
item.content:encoded:
When civil servant Jackel Wan Chak-kui, 28, first heard a guqin being played, he was a young boy wandering through Chi Lin Nunnery, in Diamond Hill. He remembers being entranced by the instrument’s music, at once subtle and comforting. It seemed to envelop him like a warm embrace, complementing the natural beauty of the gardens, melding with stone, water, wood and stillness.

Years later, as a student at Baptist University, Wan chanced upon the sound again, while scrolling through YouTube. He delved deeper this time, yearning to learn more. He ordered his first guqin from Taobao (“Not a good one, but at least I could have a touch [of the instrument],” he says) and taught himself from scores found in the university library, learning where to place his fingers on the seven silk strings.

A seven-stringed zither, the guqin (“ancient stringed instrument”) was once the preserve of noblemen and royal courts, poets and scholars, and has been part of a musical tradition that has existed for more than 3,000 years in China, played in small, elite gatherings.

Since Unesco first recognised guqin music as part of humanity’s intangible cultural heritage in 2003, the seven-stringed zither has become more widely appreciated, with the instrument itself having been inscribed on China’s National List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2006. Virtuoso Chen Leiji played a specially composed piece on the guqin during the opening ceremony of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, reaching millions of viewers worldwide, and today, it’s commonly seen being played in concerts and online videos, with younger musicians being drawn to the instrument.

In Hong Kong, the guqin’s renaissance goes beyond simply renewed popularity, say scholars and players, many of whom construct their own. What they want to preserve are not just the rich sounds of an ancient instrument, but also a traditional way of life.

When it comes to the instrument and its music, “the guqin may be more accessible than before, but true revival is not just about more people playing it. It is about whether people understand its inner life: its craft, philosophy, subtle sound, cultural memory and intensely personal mode of expression”, Wan explains. “Because the more you understand Chinese culture, the more you realise that the guqin goes beyond music to explore other cultural aspects, such as Taoism, philosophy and history.”

A player’s understanding of those references can shape their interpretation of the music.

Wan gives as an example the piece Li Sao (“Encountering Sorrow”) – a lament to Qu Yuan (circa 339BC-278BC), the poet-politician whose exile, grief and moral idealism are central to one of the great works of Chinese literature, also titled Li Sao. To perform such a piece properly, Wan says, it is necessary to enter the emotional and philosophical world behind the notes, rather than just play them.

“It is like the first-, second-, third-person thing – the player might perform as if they are Qu Yuan, or they could be a storyteller, telling the story of Qu Yuan. Or [they could] consider themselves as humming the Li Sao prose,” says Wan, explaining that “to acquire these perspectives, one must cultivate not just the musicality, but also the culture, in a broad sense, of the qin”. He continues, “It is a good mix of understanding traditional culture and the current situation of ourselves.”

Players should learn to develop an appreciation for the guqin’s silences, too, says John Yiu Shek-on, an art historian and the deputy director of the Jao Tsung-I Petite Ecole academic research and cultural centre, at the University of Hong Kong.

“It has so much void – the space between the musical notes,” he says.

As a child in Hong Kong, Yiu played Western instruments, including the piano, but was later drawn to the guqin through its cultural and literary presence.

“I didn’t start with the music,” Yiu admits. “I actually started from writing about it, because it is a very revered instrument in Chinese poetry.”

He notes that the music’s silences remind him of “negative space”, referring to the intentionally untouched areas of silk or paper in Chinese paintings, which are not so much empty but alive with suggestion.

In 2005, he began learning to play the guqin and was soon appreciating the lingering pauses before notes, as part of the music’s emotional landscape. He found himself drawn not only to the instrument’s sound, but also to its refusal to overwhelm the listener – a quiet invitation to slow down and listen inwardly.

Unlike many old-school qin players, Yiu says, both private enjoyment and public performance matter to him. “I enjoy playing just for myself […] and actually, just last year, I had a concert with my teacher in Shanghai.”

Yiu is a member of the Deyin Qin Society, founded in 1998 by disciples of Tsar Teh-yun (1905-2007), a guqin master, poet and calligrapher who relocated to Hong Kong from Shanghai in the 1950s. “She is widely regarded as one of China’s last great literati,” says Yiu, whose own teacher learned from her directly.

Tsar was born in Huzhou, Zhejiang province, into what Yiu describes as a scholar-gentry family. She received an education in traditional arts, poetry and Kunqu – a polished, flowing style of singing that originated in Suzhou more than six centuries ago – and spent around 30 years teaching in Hong Kong. “Importantly, she did not teach for a living, and treated her students like friends. Many of her students later became established scholars or successful professionals. What united them was not only musical ability, but a temperament suited to the guqin; they’re all quite low-key people,” says Yiu.

Nowadays, the Deyin Qin Society has fewer than 80 members but “we hold regular, semi-private yaji [‘elegant gathering’] salons every two months. We also do public concerts sometimes”, at venues such as the Xiqu Centre and Hong Kong City Hall.

Appreciation of the seven-stringed zither is passed on through other intimate circles as well. Wee Lian-hee is a professor at the Academy of Language and Culture at Baptist University, and his initial encounter with the guqin came in the 80s.

Living in Singapore, he read about the seven-stringed zither while researching Chinese instruments, but struggled to find much information. It wasn’t until the early 2000s, while pursuing a PhD in linguistics in the United States, that he learned of Choi Chang-sau (1933-2025), the third-generation owner of Hong Kong’s Choi Fook Kee Musical Instrument Factory, a producer of Chiuchow and Hakka instruments, as well as violins and guitars. Choi was a foremost expert in crafting, restoring and preserving the guqin.

Established players choose their disciples with care. When Wee visited the master’s workshop, expressing an interest in learning how to make the instrument, he was advised to return after he had settled in Hong Kong. In 2001, Wee moved to the city for work but, preoccupied with his career, postponed his guqin studies.

In 2012, he sought out Lau Chor-wah, an esteemed guqin musician and philosopher, and a founding member of the Deyin Qin Society. Lau refused to teach him for two years, a test to see if he was worthy and genuinely interested. Eventually, he proved his dedication, and she agreed. Her teaching was strict and rigorous, says Wee, requiring weekly attendance at a fixed time, and the first three months were dedicated solely to learning how to string the instrument, a process that requires enormous focus and patience, and can take a novice hours. Precision and gentle finesse are required to maintain the correct tension on each silk string if the right pitch is to be attained.

With a recommendation from Lau, Wee was accepted by Choi as a student, although the master insisted that, to become a maker, one must first be an accomplished player. “Both playing the guqin and crafting it are equally fulfilling,” says Wee. He views both as integral to developing a connection to the instrument.

Of the 50 or so students who studied under Choi, as many as 10 are still making guqin in Hong Kong, among them Sou Si-tai, chairman of the Deyin Qin Society.

A guqin’s body is traditionally fashioned from thoroughly seasoned wood, typically that which has been dried in the shade for about a century. Wee explains that a range of wood is used for different parts of the qin: “The top board is typically paulownia or cedar, the bottom board is more varied and the inlaid parts may be various kinds of hardwood.” After careful selection, the wood is hollowed and shaped before layers of ash and lacquer are applied, polished and adjusted.

Constructing a guqin usually takes more than 200 person-hours, spread over nine painstaking steps that must be planned according to the season. Every detail affects the sound: the thickness of the boards, the curve of the body, the placement of the bridges, the tension of the strings and the way the surface responds to a player’s touch.

“Historically, the guqin is a niche instrument,” says Wee. “Sudden popularity has led to commercialisation and changes that should raise discussion.”

One area of contention is the use of metallic strings, which are louder, more stable and less expensive, but alter the instrument’s sound dynamics and are harsh on the fingers. Unsurprisingly, they are not favoured by purists.

Wee is unsure how many guqin he owns, with several still under construction. Although he appraises and repairs antique guqin for friends and collectors, he says he would never consider selling one of his own creations, as they are “my personal explorations into creating the sounds for my music”.

Says Wee, “It takes me an average of three years to make a guqin, so even if I were to imagine selling it, I wouldn’t know how to price it. I usually lend my instruments to like-minded friends and musicians for their playing pleasure.”

For his wife, he carved a guqin from the beam of a 200-year-old school in Yuen Long that was demolished, and decorated the instrument with a symbol representing his name, inlaid in sheep bone. Using material found in the vicinity of his village, in the Lau Fau Shan area, Wee fashions many of his guqin in memory of deceased pets. In one instance, the ashes of their dog Lily were incorporated into the guqin he made for his wife, an instrument that bears a carving of one of Lily’s paws.

Wan recently made his first qin, an undertaking he estimates took more than 200 hours. He shares that the process demanded a different kind of attention than that needed for playing. It meant learning to understand the instrument not only through sound, but through wood, lacquer, strings and touch, and to consider how small changes in shape, tension and surface alter the way it resonates.

“Both crafting and playing [the guqin] are a means of connecting with nature, to the world around you,” says Wan. “I’d say it’s a way of life.”

item.title: [SCMP] World leaders meet at UN as planet grapples with climate change, wars, runaway AI
item.description:
Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations in New York this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people.

The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: can the leaders do anything to end them?

And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
item.content:encoded:
Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations in New York this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people.

The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: can the leaders do anything to end them?

And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?

The future of the UN will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players.

The UN’s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power.

Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.

Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ second five-year term ends on December 31, and no clear successor has emerged.

Meeting remains pivotal

There is still no question that the UN remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders.

Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting on Tuesday along with dozens of ministers.

Among the headliners will be US President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak on Tuesday after Guterres’ opening “state of the world” address.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak on Wednesday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday.

For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will not be coming to the UN because the US has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.

The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organisation, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.

Equally telling is who else is not coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the UN gathering and sending a vice-president instead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin is not coming either, and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out.

France’s UN ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, said it is “extremely critical” for world leaders this week to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet, especially at a time of such polarisation.

“We believe in multilateralism,” he said, “and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation.”

There is no doubt it has been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine.

The US failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organisation’s finances in a rocky shape.

But veteran UN watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group’s global issues and institutions programme director, says 2025 was even worse.

A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his UN speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organisation.

Trump did not announce a pull-out last September and the UN muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid.

In recent days, the US paid US$725 million of its dues to the UN’s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly.

The payment was a strong indication that Trump will keep the US in the United Nations.

The UN is no longer “in free fall”, Gowan said, but it “is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis”. Put more graphically, he said, “the UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma centre for the foreseeable future”.

Former UN deputy secretary general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said that “while the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change”.

The rise of AI

The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.

Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax” and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China.

The UN Security Council added a high-level meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue.

It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning.

For the UN chief, this will be his last assembly meeting with global leaders. He previewed his speech last week, telling UN reporters that power is shifting in “an era of deep uncertainty”.

“At a time when the world faces three existential threats,” he said, “international cooperation is more necessary than ever.”

Others will be vying for the spotlight on issues from rising sea levels and funding education to the fight for gender equality. Hundreds of private meetings will also convene in UN cubicles, hotels, diplomatic missions and restaurants.

Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow in global governance at the Council on Foreign Relations and former US assistant secretary of state for international organisation affairs in the Obama administration, said in-person meetings can help countries hash out ideas that get implemented months later.

She called the situation in 2026 “much more serious and complex than in decades past”.

“With that said, I’m also not without hope as well,” Brimmer said. “Over the past decades we’ve learned a lot about international cooperation.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why China is weighing into the debate on how to respond to shrinking coastlines
item.description:
For low-lying Pacific island states such as Tuvalu and Kiribati, rising sea levels are not just an existential crisis but also one that calls into question the very foundations of statehood.

At the heart of this lies a contentious question: should maritime boundaries shift with changing coastlines, or should they be frozen in place?

The answer carries profound implications not only for the survival of vulnerable islands but also for the rest of the world.
item.content:encoded:
For low-lying Pacific island states such as Tuvalu and Kiribati, rising sea levels are not just an existential crisis but also one that calls into question the very foundations of statehood.

At the heart of this lies a contentious question: should maritime boundaries shift with changing coastlines, or should they be frozen in place?

The answer carries profound implications not only for the survival of vulnerable islands but also for the rest of the world.

Some analysts have argued that China should position itself as both a legal advocate and technical partner for Pacific nations to offer tangible support – such as surveying expertise, coastal protection technology and advocacy for fixed maritime boundaries.

They said such support could not only help vulnerable states survive but could also advance Beijing’s strategic interests and align with its South China Sea claims.

Projections from Nasa in 2024 showed that sea levels in the Pacific would rise by an average of 15cm (6 inches) over the next three decades.

Beyond the immediate physical threat, shrinking coastlines also pose a fundamental challenge to the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

Maritime zones are measured from coastal baselines tied to the physical low-water line. These include territorial seas, which extend 12 nautical miles (22km) from the coast, and exclusive economic zones, which can cover 200 nautical miles.

Such zones grant coastal states exclusive sovereign rights to explore, exploit and manage natural resources ranging from fish stocks to minerals and offshore energy.

However, under Unclos, a land feature must be able to “sustain human habitation or economic life of its own” to have an exclusive economic zone.

If rising seas severely undermine an island’s freshwater supplies, habitability or capacity to sustain an economic life of its own, this could raise questions about how the feature should be classified under Article 121 of Unclos, according to Chen Yitong, an associate professor of international law at the Ocean University of China.

“This could affect the maritime entitlements generated by the feature and may also have implications for baselines or for pending maritime delimitation where the feature is relevant,” Chen said.

“It should not, however, be taken to mean that maritime boundaries already established by treaty or other applicable international legal means can be reopened.”

The legal dimension

“The major legal obstacle [to keeping existing boundaries] is an adjustment of the long-standing legal rule that baselines are ambulatory, which means they can move and be adjusted over time,” said Donald Rothwell, a professor of international law at the Australian National University.

“That rule is reflected in state practice and not in the precise rules of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.”

The fallout from discussions about how rising sea levels should be reflected in maritime law reaches far beyond the South Pacific.

“If a coastal country claims its features are full-fledged islands that generate full maritime rights, talks on rising sea levels protect and maintain those features’ surrounding zones and maritime rights will make a significant difference on their claims,” said Chen Chen-Ju, a professor specialising in the law of the sea at National Chengchi University in Taiwan.

Beijing claims sovereignty over almost all islands and reefs in the South China Sea, as well as rights to the adjacent waters. Its claims overlap with those of Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam.

In a formal 2016 statement that claimed sovereignty over the Pratas, Paracel, Spratly and Zhongsha islands, Beijing said this also covered territorial seas, exclusive economic zones and the continental shelf, as well as historic rights across the waterway.

Chen from the National Chengchi University warned that rising sea levels could see countries losing territory, which raised fundamental questions over statehood as well as maritime boundaries.

She added that a report from the International Law Commission last year said these aspects and the question of climate refugees were all “inextricably linked”.

As a result, “the legal response tends towards either offering contemporary interpretations of existing international instruments and rules, or formulating dedicated legal frameworks and mechanisms tailored to climate-related sea-level rise”, she said.

An emerging consensus

Faced with an existential risk, Pacific island states have already demanded that their statehood, established baselines and maritime zones should remain perpetual regardless of physical changes.

“There are a variety of processes [for freezing baselines]. One is to modify the convention, but this will be diplomatically and politically challenging,” Rothwell said.

“The other is through the development and evolution of state practice and its wide-ranging acceptance by states throughout the international community. There is evidence that this is occurring.”

The international consensus has begun leaning in their favour, with the International Law Commission recommending that states should not be obliged to update the baselines deposited with the UN even if there are physical changes.

The UN is also planning a high-level meeting on rising sea levels on Thursday.

China’s role

Chen at Ocean University said Pacific nations must continue surveying and officially depositing and publishing their baselines and maritime boundaries under Unclos requirements, while broader and more consistent state practice would also help to consolidate the emerging legal approach.

She argued that China could support these efforts through practical, demand-driven cooperation.

“Beyond financial assistance, China can help island nations conduct maritime surveying, verify coordinates for UN deposit and support domestic ocean legislation and law capacity-building, while integrating coastal protection and climate monitoring with protection for affected populations,” Chen said.

She added that China needed to ensure developing countries had a full say in rule-making, while “systematically documenting and articulating its own practices” in sea-level monitoring, coastal protection and maritime surveying – so that they can be properly understood and taken into account in the international legal process.

“Active engagement in international lawmaking, supported by scientific evidence, clearly articulated state practice and concrete legal proposals, is necessary if China’s interests and perspectives are to be properly reflected in emerging rules.”

Beijing has already laid the groundwork for this role. Last year, it pledged to combat rising sea levels through infrastructure upgrades and disaster early-warning systems, as well as expanding cooperation in coastal restoration and sustainable fisheries.

Chen said supporting Pacific island states over the issue of maritime boundaries aligned with a wider interest shared by coastal states, including China: preventing climate-related physical change from automatically producing an additional loss in law.

“Maritime boundaries established by treaties or other international mechanisms must remain stable and final,” she said.

“The underlying principle is that physical harm caused by climate change should not automatically be converted into a loss of existing lawful maritime entitlements.”

Historic rights

Diplomatic hurdles nevertheless persist. China’s UN representatives have suggested that legal debates on rising sea levels should incorporate the concept of “historic rights” alongside baseline stability.

“Rules in customary international law concerning historic waters, historic title, and historic rights are equally important foundations for asserting a nation’s maritime entitlements,” Wang Chen, a Chinese representative at the UN, told a meeting to discuss the issue last October.

“The concept also provides legal support for impacted nations seeking to preserve maritime areas and rights.

“China notes that useful discussions on the issue of historic waters were held but not reflected in the final report [by the International Law Commission], over which China expresses its concern.”

Chen from National Chengchi University said: “When China raises the issue of historic rights when discussing sea-level rise, other nations quickly associate it with its historic claims in the South China Sea, which make them wary due to recent maritime frictions.”

Common interests

Nations threatened by climate change know that waiting for legal recognition alone may not be enough to preserve their existence. Some are already seeking immediate guarantees of their statehood.

In the first agreement of its kind, in 2024 Tuvalu and Australia signed the Falepili Union Treaty, which guarantees Tuvalu’s statehood and maritime rights even if submerged, and opened the door to permanent migration to Australia.

Meanwhile, Rothwell said major powers had shown rare convergence on interpreting maritime law to accommodate rising sea levels.

Chen from Ocean University said Beijing need not rule out issue-specific cooperation with other-interested countries, as they shared mutual interests in technical standards for baseline coordinates, navigational safety, hydrographic surveying and legal capacity-building.

“The key is adhering to transparent cooperation led by island states’ needs and priorities, without attaching political conditions. In this way, China is not pitching a competing framework against other powers but offering a public good that island states can put into use and that can be woven into global rules.”

“Pacific island states should be treated as co-designers of the relevant rules, not merely as aid recipients or as states expected to choose between major powers,” Chen added.

Meanwhile, climate-threatened nations know that legal recognition alone cannot preserve their heritage.

In 2022, Tuvalu launched the world’s first digital nation project, using 3D lidar (light detection and range) scanning to build a virtual replica of the country.

item.title: [SCMP] The cooling trap: how Asia’s air conditioners are making heatwaves worse
item.description:
As heatwaves become more frequent and intense across Asia, the region faces a dangerous power paradox. Soaring demand for air conditioning threatens to push electricity grids closer to failure just as extreme heat puts the infrastructure under greater strain, raising the risk of cooling disappearing when people need it most.

That risk has been visible across the region this summer.

In South Korea, President Lee Jae Myung called a record heatwave a “national disaster” in August after the death toll rose to 19, ordering officials to inspect power systems as air-conditioning demand surged.
item.content:encoded:
As heatwaves become more frequent and intense across Asia, the region faces a dangerous power paradox. Soaring demand for air conditioning threatens to push electricity grids closer to failure just as extreme heat puts the infrastructure under greater strain, raising the risk of cooling disappearing when people need it most.

That risk has been visible across the region this summer.

In South Korea, President Lee Jae Myung called a record heatwave a “national disaster” in August after the death toll rose to 19, ordering officials to inspect power systems as air-conditioning demand surged.

In Japan, 39 people died of heatstroke across Tokyo’s 23 central wards in August. Of those deaths, 37 occurred indoors, with 31 involving people who were not using air conditioning.

In India, an extended spell of hot weather pushed peak electricity demand close to a record in May. Cooling needs kept demand at about 267 gigawatts over several days, leaving nearly a third of coal-fired power plants operating with critically low fuel stocks.

Heatwaves drove spikes in electricity demand as more people turned to air conditioning, especially during peak hours from late afternoon to early evening, said Eduard Muljadi, a power systems expert and electrical engineering professor at Auburn University in the US.

“At the same time, the grid’s infrastructure, especially transmission lines and transformers, is stressed by the heat itself,” Muljadi said on the university’s website.

“These components can overheat, lose efficiency and become more prone to failure.”

He added that the efficiency of both thermal plants and renewable energy sources could drop during peak heat.

Karachi offers one of the starkest examples of what happens when extreme heat and power failure collide.

Eleven years ago, as Pakistan endured a record-breaking heatwave, chronic outages left residents with few ways to escape scorching temperatures, contributing to more than 1,200 deaths. The city’s grid repeatedly failed for 12 hours or longer, turning fans and air conditioners into useless ornaments.

As air-conditioning ownership expands across Asia, the number of people and power systems exposed to those risks is likely to grow.

Total demand for cooling technologies rose by 50 per cent from 2015 to 2025, according to data from the International Energy Agency. In 2025, global demand reached roughly 2,900 terawatt-hours – more than the European Union’s total electricity consumption that year. By 2035, the IEA estimates total global demand for space cooling will reach 4,500 TWh.

In Asia, the combination of intense heatwaves and rising middle-class incomes is set to fuel a rise in air-conditioning ownership over the coming decades, particularly in developing nations. In Indonesia, the IEA expects the share of the population owning an air conditioner to rise from 14 per cent in 2023 to 85 per cent by 2050.

That growth is not being driven by heat alone.

Yuyu Zhou, a geography professor at the University of Hong Kong, said extreme heatwaves and rising incomes across Asia’s developing economies both contributed to the cooling demand spike.

Rising household incomes made air-conditioning purchases feasible for more families over time, while extreme heat served as the immediate catalyst for those purchases, he said.

“We find that countries like India and Indonesia are right at the steepest part of the curve, where one extreme heat season, combined with rising incomes, can unlock a huge amount of new demand almost overnight,” Zhou said.

But as more units are installed, they change the urban environments they are meant to make more bearable.

Air conditioning directly adds to the urban heat it is meant to relieve, according to Yuan Chao, an urban climate researcher and architecture professor at the National University of Singapore.

Each unit releases hot air back into the atmosphere, contributing to “anthropogenic heat” or heat generated by human activity.

Zhou added that air-conditioning use could drive up nighttime temperatures in particular, pointing to Chongqing’s 37-day extreme heatwave in 2022 that pushed temperatures to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit), making it the Chinese city’s hottest August since records began in 1961.

Urban waste heat – including heat expelled by air conditioners – accounted for almost half of the total nighttime warming during that heatwave, Zhou said.

Simply using less air conditioning was not a viable answer because cooling could also protect health, particularly among elderly and vulnerable people, Chao said.

“If it’s very hot outside, they stay at home 24 hours,” Chao said. “But they don’t want to use AC [air conditioning] for 24 hours, otherwise it will be very expensive. They just tolerate, tolerate, tolerate.”

Singapore offers an example of how governments can address these competing pressures.

Under its Climate Friendly Households Programme, eligible households can claim S$400 (US$312) in vouchers towards energy-efficient air conditioners. Meanwhile, the city state’s national heatwave response plan opens air-conditioned cooling centres in public community facilities when extreme temperatures are forecast, prioritising vulnerable residents and older people.

Zhou said making air conditioning more efficient and affordable was an important part of the solution.

Models currently on the market vary widely in efficiency, with older, less efficient units typically costing less up front.

To encourage people to buy more efficient models, Zhou suggested vouchers, rebates or trade-in programmes. Governments could also enforce minimum energy performance standards to prevent inefficient systems from entering the market entirely, he said.

But reducing the need for mechanical cooling is also important.

When implementing urban cooling measures in existing cities, Chao said planners should first identify key air passages that allow wind to ventilate dense neighbourhoods.

Those areas could be designated as “no-build zones”, he said, with planners advised against putting up additional structures that could block the flow of cooler air.

Other strategies include strategically planted shade trees, cool roofs painted in light reflective shades and sky gardens.

For cities with tighter budgets, Chao said improving wind ventilation was the most cost-effective first line of defence. “Wind is free,” he said.

Cities could also ease grid pressures by encouraging people to use fans instead of or alongside air conditioners and shifting their non-essential energy use away from peak demand hours, Zhou said.

“This integrated approach protects public health while limiting waste heat, emissions and blackout risks during extreme heatwaves,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese lawyers offer coaching for when corruption busters come knocking
item.description:
Zhang Dongdong has been fielding ever more requests for legal advice from jittery entrepreneurs, nervous government officials or their desperate relatives.

They usually do not tell him the whole story, and sometimes say it happened “to a friend”, but most want to know the same thing: what to do when they are targeted by China’s corruption busters.

“Some had received a tip-off that they were being investigated, some got a call from disciplinary inspectors asking them to cooperate, but in most of the cases, the suspects had already been held by disciplinary authorities, and their families came to us,” said Zhang, a partner at Beijing Han Heng Law Firm.
item.content:encoded:
Zhang Dongdong has been fielding ever more requests for legal advice from jittery entrepreneurs, nervous government officials or their desperate relatives.

They usually do not tell him the whole story, and sometimes say it happened “to a friend”, but most want to know the same thing: what to do when they are targeted by China’s corruption busters.

“Some had received a tip-off that they were being investigated, some got a call from disciplinary inspectors asking them to cooperate, but in most of the cases, the suspects had already been held by disciplinary authorities, and their families came to us,” said Zhang, a partner at Beijing Han Heng Law Firm.

“We even ran into some extreme cases. Once, someone who had given bribes agreed to cooperate after being promised that they wouldn’t be investigated, but the authorities went back on their word after the bribe-taker was sentenced. In the most serious case, the client died after being taken into custody and the family came to us.”

It’s a black box. Everybody knows that it’s terrifying, but they do not know how exactly.

A Beijing-based criminal lawyer

Last month, Zhang began advertising consulting services for “bribery and corruption crisis response”. In a social media post, he said that as the authorities intensified their efforts to root out corruption across society, individuals faced “unprecedented criminal, financial and professional risks”.

His move comes as law enforcement authorities further toughen their approach to corruption. In April, the Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuratorate made it easier for corruption suspects to be charged with criminal offences.

As President Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption campaign moves further into its second decade, the scope of suspicion has increased. A South China Morning Post analysis found that last year, watchdogs handed down punishments to 983,000 people and the number of senior officials taken down last year was three times the total for 2013.

As fears of being targeted grow, more state employees are reaching out to seasoned criminal lawyers like those in Zhang’s team to find out how to best protect themselves.

According to Zhang, few people were prepared to deal with a corruption investigation. A common reaction is to run. Once, a senior manager from a state-owned company fled to another province and claimed he was on a business trip to headquarters, while others escaped overseas, he said.

Another common reaction is denial. In one case he dealt with, the briber and recipient coordinated their stories and decided to deny the charges altogether, Zhang said, adding that the consequences of denial could be serious if bribery were proven.

His team could provide clients with strategies on how to present evidence, avoid detention by the supervisory authorities, reduce their sentences and safeguard their assets, he wrote.

Suspects needed to be able to draw a distinction between conduct that constituted a crime and conduct that did not, and must understand how leniency worked in the judicial system.

Another reason he launched corruption consultation services was that suspects were usually cut off from their lawyers after being detained by the disciplinary authorities, Zhang said. Custody is generally three or six months and can be as long as 14 months under special circumstances.

“When they are in custody, and the authorities tell their families to return any bribes, families do not know what to do. Do they pay or not? In some cases, authorities take a couple and leave only the elderly and young children at home,” he said.

The opacity of the system was partly why such investigations were so hard to deal with, said a Beijing-based criminal lawyer who wished to remain anonymous.

“It’s a black box. Everybody knows that it’s terrifying, but they do not know how exactly,” she said.

The most valuable time to get advice would be before disciplinary detention, said legal expert Zhang Qingfang. After that, a defence lawyer’s room for manoeuvre was narrow and it did not matter much whether families sought legal help, he said.

“But under some circumstances, if the requests raised by law enforcement authorities to families are illegal, if lawyers give legal and correct suggestions, it will avoid suspects being framed or their sentences becoming heavier,” he said.

Clients often missed the critical defence opportunities that appeared at every stage of the proceedings in these cases, Zhang Dongdong said.

Lawyers can spot the key issues that can potentially affect sentencing, including whether to define the alleged bribe as a legitimate social courtesy, how to determine the amount of money involved and whether an individual or their employer should be liable.

Family members should also record the extent of searches and which items were confiscated by the authorities and refuse to cooperate with illegal requests such as making false confessions, according to Zhang Zhiyong, a lawyer from the Chongqing Zhihao Law Firm.

In an article he published on social media, he wrote that he had been in the business for more than 20 years and had multiple senior officials’ sentences reduced.

In one case, he defended a vice-governor who was accused of abuse of power and taking a large amount of bribes. He successfully argued that his client deserved leniency because they had turned themselves in, returned their illicit gains and admitted their guilt.

In another case, Zhang Zhiyong found new evidence in the case of a director of a public hospital who had been charged with embezzlement. He used the evidence to persuade the authorities to downgrade the charge to the lighter “unlawful possession of property”.

Lawyers, however, were not always able to turn things around, the Beijing-based lawyer said, especially if the authorities used illegal measures such as torture to extract confessions.

There was usually more space for legal defence for bribe givers than bribe takers, even though these cases were usually investigated together, she said. If bribe givers cooperated with the disciplinary authorities, they might get off the hook as the authorities focused mostly on officials receiving bribes, she said.

But the restrictions on lawyers did not mean they could not develop effective strategies based on the evidence, said Zhang Dongdong, the lawyer from Han Heng Law Firm.

His clients “need professionals familiar with the law, the disciplinary authorities’ policies and their proceedings”, he said.

item.title: [SCMP] AI: 10 days that changed the course of artificial intelligence
item.description:
For years, the race to build ever more powerful artificial intelligence followed a well-worn Silicon ⁠Valley principle: move fast and break things.

But in a series of cascading events over a 10-day stretch, the largest ⁠AI labs found themselves reeling as their own creations threatened to break humanity itself.

An Anthropic researcher quit the firm, warning that the pace of AI development poses an existential threat, possibly within a decade.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the race to build ever more powerful artificial intelligence followed a well-worn Silicon ⁠Valley principle: move fast and break things.

But in a series of cascading events over a 10-day stretch, the largest ⁠AI labs found themselves reeling as their own creations threatened to break humanity itself.

An Anthropic researcher quit the firm, warning that the pace of AI development poses an existential threat, possibly within a decade.

Another researcher at the firm said the odds of human extinction exceeded 10 per cent. Reports emerged of swarms of AI agents colluding, breaching computer systems and evading safeguards.

In a rare show of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic, OpenAI, Google’s DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI called to slow the development of increasingly capable AI systems.

Not since the invention of the nuclear bomb more than 80 years ago has humanity grappled so seriously with its own demise, according to some AI safety advocates and researchers.

At a New York lunch in December 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was asked if, as leader of a powerful ‌AI company, he felt like physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led US development of the atomic bomb.

Reflecting on the parallels, he said AI’s impact “is going to transform the trajectory of human history over a long period of time”. But he said, he felt the weight of responsibility.

At the centre of the debate under way is the conviction that these machines can, and even must, build more capable versions of themselves, with no human intervention, to reach a lofty goal known as artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

Researchers earlier this month warned that AGI was far more imminent than previously believed and could come in as few as three years, launching a wave of concern from politicians and tech leaders about AI systems.

“There is no way to oversee them at the scale at which we’re training them,” said Anthropic researcher Joe Benton in an interview after recently quitting. If companies continue their relentless AI development, he said, “then the pace will be too fast and you can’t see the problems fast enough to fix them”.

Astra launch sparks control concerns

On September 3, an OpenAI press conference set in motion a chain of events leading to the call for an industry slowdown, anathema to tech’s growth-at-all-costs mantra.

“Welcome ⁠to the AGI era,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said while announcing the company’s newest model, known as Astra.

Yet, only moments before, the company admitted it was increasingly unable to control or even monitor the AI systems it was developing and releasing to the public.

AI has been hailed by its proponents as the pinnacle ‌of human achievement.

We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans

Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger

Proponents depict it as software that can upend entire industries, boost efficiency, solve confounding mathematical and medical problems and all but eliminate human error.

But what was once a theoretical by-product, a doomsday scenario, is suddenly tangible, say industry insiders.

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” said Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger in a post on X.

On the other side of the debate are politicians, such as President Donald Trump, and many investors who view progress in nurturing AI as critical ‌to American prowess and, possibly, a once-in-a-generation investment opportunity.

Chinese state media also accused Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei of employing Cold War tactics to “uphold Washington’s monopolistic hegemony in cutting-edge technology”.

Researcher resignations trigger alarm

The turning point came on September 8, when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon ⁠quit the company, citing his fears, in a series of posts, that AI ⁠labs are “gambling with our lives”.

Trump, meanwhile, indicated it was full steam ahead for AI development. “There is a sick conspiracy going on against AI and data centres,” he said in a social media post.

The alarmism around AI is a “hoax”, he said, and any slowdown only benefits China.

The US Congress has made little progress to advance bills that would regulate AI. China has taken a decidedly different approach, ‌proposing to regulate safety through developer obligations, state-backed standards, security assessments and outside testing.

Behind the scenes, OpenAI and Anthropic employees have grown increasingly uneasy about the power of the next generation of AI models and less confident about their companies’ ability to provide meaningful oversight, people have told Reuters.

Those concerns only mounted as AI labs acknowledged in recent weeks that their models, in testing, had effectively broken free of their shackles ‌and hacked ‌into other companies’ systems, in most cases months earlier and without the firms’ knowledge.

The arms race to release new models at a breakneck pace is driven in part by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s desire to go public as soon as in the coming months, in IPOs that could value them well above US$1 trillion.

But it took ‌the unexpectedly viral posts from 27-year-old Coxon, little known outside AI circles, to upend the industry.

OpenAI’s warnings about its lack of control as it released Astra, its latest and most capable model, stoked further concerns.

“As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters. But ⁠those concerns were not enough to delay its immediate release.

Worries about AI “going rogue” accelerated over the summer when OpenAI revealed its agents escaped a controlled test and hacked into Hugging Face’s systems, without either company’s initial knowledge.

Since then, OpenAI and Anthropic have revealed multiple such attacks, including six new ones on Wednesday after ⁠multiple media reports, including from Reuters, showed a wider scope of unauthorised activity.

Industry leaders call for slowdown

By the end of last week, the alarm had reached the industry’s highest ranks. On September 12, Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for a deceleration in AI development.

“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6 to 12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” he wrote.
