He, along with the heads of some of the largest AI developers, including xAI’s Elon Musk, OpenAI’s Altman and DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis, all said ‌they supported allowing outside firms access to their systems to ensure safety and rational ‌AI development.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed suggestions that AI development should pause – a line he has taken before – arguing instead that increasingly powerful systems are essential for the technology’s progress.

Meta, whose CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, is credited with popularising the “move fast and break things” ethos, took the opposite view, arguing that each lab should be responsible for setting its own pace, rather than seeking out industry coordination.

“Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this,” wrote Zuckerberg in a social media post.

The industry’s self-reflection continued on Wednesday, with Microsoft’s AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman, cautioning that Anthropic’s development of models that imitate human consciousness was ill-advised.

“We’re all focused on the same aim, which is to try to control a superintelligence,” Suleyman told Reuters. “I think that’s going to be the greatest challenge that we face in the 21st century.”

Still, even as OpenAI appeared to embrace industry calls for a slowdown, there were reports that investor faith had not waned. The company is considering a new funding round that would double its valuation.

That new number: US$1.5 trillion.

item.title: [SCMP] US space weapons move has ‘broken taboo’, could spark new arms race, Beijing forum told
item.description:
The US deployment of space weapons has shattered a long-held taboo and risks igniting a fresh arms race, with the world at a “breaking point in history”, speakers at a major security conference in Beijing have warned.

Experts at the Xiangshan Forum this week also called for US-China dialogue on space security, just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping makes his first state visit to the US in more than a decade.

US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink – the civilian head of the department that oversees both the US Air Force and Space Force – acknowledged for the first time on Tuesday that the Pentagon had deployed weapons in space.
item.content:encoded:
The US deployment of space weapons has shattered a long-held taboo and risks igniting a fresh arms race, with the world at a “breaking point in history”, speakers at a major security conference in Beijing have warned.

Experts at the Xiangshan Forum this week also called for US-China dialogue on space security, just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping makes his first state visit to the US in more than a decade.

US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink – the civilian head of the department that oversees both the US Air Force and Space Force – acknowledged for the first time on Tuesday that the Pentagon had deployed weapons in space.

“We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said, according to a US Air Force statement. He did not give details on the systems involved.

Almudena Azcarate Ortega, senior programme analyst on space law and regulation with the Washington-based think tank Secure World Foundation, said the weapons were likely to be jammers or spoofers, which are essentially non-kinetic technologies.

A kinetic weapon would conflict with US policy against debris-creating activities, Ortega told the Xiangshan Forum on Wednesday.

The Outer Space Treaty – the cornerstone of international space law adopted in 1967 – bars its more than 110 signatory nations from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. However, it does not impose limits on the deployment of conventional weaponry.

“The Outer Space Treaty does not prohibit the deployment of conventional weapons in outer space, but … it has become a taboo, just like no first use of nuclear weapons in the eight decades since 1945,” noted Guo Xiaobing, director of the Centre for Arms Control Studies with the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations.

Hosting a panel discussion on outer space security governance on Wednesday, Guo said: “We also have a space taboo. That’s the taboo about the deployment of conventional weapons in space.

“That taboo was broken yesterday. We are at a breaking point in history.”

Ortega said that while the US deployment did not violate the Outer Space Treaty, “if the threshold rose to the level of a use of force, that would be a violation of Article 2.4 of the UN Charter”.

“So the reason why this is sort of a big deal is that no US official has ever acknowledged an actual weapons system in space before.

“It is a shift in terms of traditional US policy around counterspace capabilities. And it is also dangerous from a linguistic perspective,” she cautioned.

She said the comment could potentially be escalatory, causing others to deploy similar technologies, making space more contested and competitive.

“I do think that this is a bit of a step back in terms of everything that we’re trying to achieve at the multilateral level on space security [and] diplomacy.”

The 13th edition of the Beijing Xiangshan Forum – China’s most important annual defence gathering – was held from Tuesday to Thursday. It brought together defence officials, military leaders and global experts from over 100 countries.

Experts at the forum also argued that ambiguous space terminology had fuelled rising space competition between countries.

Gao Guozhu, director of Beihang University’s Institute of Outer Space Law, said opinions varied on what constituted a space threat.

“For example, the United States considers the use of anti-satellite weapons or technologies to pose a serious threat to space systems – or, more precisely, a serious threat to the countries that own those systems,” Gao said.

“China, by contrast, views the US policy of seeking dominance in outer space as a threat. In other words, China sees this as a strategic or policy-level threat. The two sides therefore differ in what they identify as a threat.”

Gao agreed that the US deployment of space weapons was “bound to trigger a new round of the arms race in space”.

“If a war in space breaks out in the future, the era of spacefaring civilisation that humanity has pursued for more than half a century could well become a thing of the past,” he warned.

US defence and intelligence assessments have long highlighted China’s pursuit of wide-ranging counterspace capabilities, including direct-ascent anti-satellite missiles, co-orbital systems, electronic warfare and directed-energy weapons, with some capabilities already considered operational.

Since 2024, the US has also claimed that Russia is developing space-based anti-satellite capabilities – which Moscow denies. Additionally, the US alleged in both its 2025 and 2026 annual threat assessment reports that Russia was developing a new satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon into orbit as an anti-satellite payload.

Senior Colonel Zhao Weibin, a prominent Chinese military scholar and member of the Beijing Xiangshan Forum Secretariat, said the risks of a space arms race had probably just become a reality.

“Once [the arms race] logic is activated, it’s hard to reverse. Because an on-orbit weapon will severely erode strategic mutual trust,” he warned.

“Planning countermeasures on the assumption of a worst-case scenario – may trigger an escalating spiral of action and reaction.”

In 2025, President Donald Trump unveiled the “Golden Dome for America”, a multilayered missile-defence architecture incorporating space-based interceptors (SBI) designed to intercept threats shortly after launch.

The SBI programme aims to place missile interceptors in low-Earth orbit, rather than solely using satellites to detect and track threats.

Gao said both the SBI programme and the deployment of space-based weapons had shattered the quiet global understanding on “no weapons in space”.

“What did we mean by strategic stability in the past? It meant that each side had the ability to destroy the other – a theory based on mutually assured vulnerability,” Gao said, warning that the present shift left adversaries with no diplomatic recourse.

“The problem now is that you are becoming increasingly powerful, while using that power to make me vulnerable and grind me into the ground. What am I supposed to do under those circumstances? I have no options left, and there is no longer any basis for dialogue.”

Experts are also calling for space cooperation to become part of the China-US constructive strategic stability dialogue initiated during the May Xi-Trump summit in Beijing.

Gao also highlighted the dangers posed by space weapons in case of a Taiwan conflict, pointing to commercial and military infrastructure in orbit.

“The US might use Starlink to provide services for Taiwan and we might disrupt it because we don’t think that’s OK. And the US, in order to stop China, could disrupt China’s BeiDou [satellite-based navigation] system,” he said.

Such an escalation would be very dangerous and could potentially lead to both sides attacking each other’s satellites, Gao warned.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the US – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons for its defence.

item.title: [SCMP] How will Beijing receive the most senior Taiwan official at Apec events this year?
item.description:
In a rare development, Taiwanese Labour Minister Hung Sun-han is expected to travel to Nanjing on Sunday, becoming the first cabinet-level official under William Lai Ching-te’s administration to visit mainland China.

Hung will attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) ministerial meeting on Monday to discuss employment, vocational training, social security and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs.

Hung will be the most senior Taiwanese official to visit the mainland for Apec events this year. The island’s vice-minister of economic affairs, Lai Chien-hsin, took part in the energy ministerial meeting in Beijing last week and then chief trade negotiator Yang Jen-ni participated in a trade ministers’ meeting in Suzhou in May.
item.content:encoded:
In a rare development, Taiwanese Labour Minister Hung Sun-han is expected to travel to Nanjing on Sunday, becoming the first cabinet-level official under William Lai Ching-te’s administration to visit mainland China.

Hung will attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) ministerial meeting on Monday to discuss employment, vocational training, social security and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs.

Hung will be the most senior Taiwanese official to visit the mainland for Apec events this year. The island’s vice-minister of economic affairs, Lai Chien-hsin, took part in the energy ministerial meeting in Beijing last week and then chief trade negotiator Yang Jen-ni participated in a trade ministers’ meeting in Suzhou in May.

While Hung’s visit is being closely watched for signs of a possible thaw in a prolonged cross-strait stand-off, analysts have cautioned against interpreting it as an icebreaking trip or a resumption of official exchanges between Taipei and Beijing.

The trip will also take place just days before US President Donald Trump is expected to host Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, putting Taiwan under renewed scrutiny as the two powers seek to manage their differences.

Ahead of his departure, Hung stressed that Taiwan was a full Apec member under the name “Chinese Taipei”. He said he would take part under the grouping’s established arrangements and the principles of “equal participation and reciprocal dignity”.

Nevertheless, with official cross-strait dialogue suspended, Hung’s visit carries symbolic weight because no cabinet minister – particularly a political appointee – has travelled to the mainland since Lai took office in May 2024.

“A small step by Hung Sun-han would be a big step for cross-strait relations,” said Lee Yen-hsiu, a lawmaker from the main opposition Kuomintang, a Beijing-friendly party.

Lee questioned whether the trip signalled a change in the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) approach towards Beijing after more than two years of promoting its “resist China, oppose China” agenda.

She said Hung’s visit could be seen as “a possible test by Lai of whether cross-strait relations could begin to thaw”.

DPP lawmaker Wu Szu-yao urged Hung to remain alert to “potential personal safety concerns and the possibility of unequal treatment or politically motivated difficulties” while on the mainland.

But DPP legislative caucus whip Chuang Jui-hsiung dismissed such concerns.

“Are you kidding? If holding Apec in China meant there was a threat to someone’s personal safety, it wouldn’t just shock Taiwan – the whole world would be shocked by China,” Chuang said.

Analysts said Taipei might hope the trip created an impression of easing tensions, particularly ahead of the Washington summit.

“It is especially important before the sensitive Trump-Xi meeting to create an impression that Taiwan is not a troublemaker and hopes cross-strait relations can ease,” said Wang Kung-yi, head of the Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, a Taipei-based think tank.

But Wang said the trip could not be regarded as a genuine advance because Hung was attending a multilateral meeting and not direct talks with Beijing.

“If there were really a breakthrough, there would inevitably be substantive interactions, such as Hung meeting mainland officials,” he said.

Li Da-jung, a professor of international relations at Tamkang University in New Taipei City, similarly argued that the arrangement was standard.

“Taiwan is a full member of Apec, and to maintain its position in the international organisation, it has to send officials to attend the meeting,” Li said, adding that participation also helped maintain the island’s international visibility.

More important for Taipei, he said, would be the consequences of the coming Trump-Xi summit.

“Its impact on Taiwan remained uncertain, but Taipei would be watching closely to see whether Washington’s approach to the island – including pending arms sales – is affected by Trump’s talks with Xi,” Li said.

Analysts also doubted Beijing would create difficulties for Hung over his entry arrangements.

“Long-established arrangements have already governed participation in Apec meetings, and this is mainland China’s third time hosting the leaders’ meeting after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014,” Wang said.

Hung should therefore be able to enter using his Apec invitation letter under existing arrangements instead of using a mainland-issued Taiwan compatriot permit, he added.

Beijing has skirted questions over whether Hung must hold the permit.

“Since 1991, Taiwan’s participation in Apec meetings and activities has been handled in accordance with the ‘one-China principle’ as well as the provisions and established practices of relevant Apec memorandums of understanding,” Chen Binhua, a spokesman for the State Council’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said last week.

Zhu Fenglian, a spokeswoman for the Taiwan Affairs Office, reiterated on Wednesday that under the one-China principle, the “Taiwan region” took part in Apec under the name “Chinese Taipei” and as a regional economy.

Taipei rejects that interpretation, saying its 1991 Apec accession memorandum contains no reference to the “one-China principle” and provides for participation on an equal basis with other members.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Wang said the DPP could benefit politically if Beijing created difficulties for Hung – and thus Beijing was unlikely to take action that could inadvertently help the party electorally.

Huang Kwei-bo, a diplomacy professor at National Chengchi University in Taipei, said the DPP government was likely to stress that Hung was attending an international meeting rather than engaging in bilateral cross-strait exchanges.

He also cautioned against using the trip as a barometer of cross-strait relations because Beijing, as this year’s Apec host, was expected to invite representatives from all member economies, and Hung was only visiting because the Apec meeting happened to be held on the mainland.

Huang said Taipei’s choice of representative to the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November would be a more significant test.

item.title: [SCMP] Young Nepalis battle climate dread in wake of flood disaster
item.description:
Alina B.K. should have been preparing for her end-of-year university exams, but news of devastating floods along the Nepal–Tibet border kept pulling her back to a troubling question: what kind of future awaits her?

The 21-year-old forestry student, who coordinates the Pokhara network of Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, said she struggled to concentrate as reports of death and destruction deepened her fears about a changing climate.

“With the floods and deaths happening around us, it is really hard not to feel anxious and emotionally overwhelmed,” she said.
item.content:encoded:
Alina B.K. should have been preparing for her end-of-year university exams, but news of devastating floods along the Nepal–Tibet border kept pulling her back to a troubling question: what kind of future awaits her?

The 21-year-old forestry student, who coordinates the Pokhara network of Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, said she struggled to concentrate as reports of death and destruction deepened her fears about a changing climate.

“With the floods and deaths happening around us, it is really hard not to feel anxious and emotionally overwhelmed,” she said.

The August 26 disaster, triggered by a glacier collapse, has left more than 1,400 people confirmed dead across Nepal and Tibet, with thousands still missing.

Scientists have not yet established whether the collapse was directly caused by climate change and several factors could have been involved. But experts say the disaster fits a broader pattern across the Himalayas, where rising temperatures accelerate glacier melt, weaken frozen slopes and increase the risk of cascading hazards such as ice-rock avalanches, landslides and flash floods.

Nepal faces these mounting risks despite contributing little to the emissions driving them. A 2022 World Bank report put its share of global greenhouse gas emissions at about 0.1 per cent, while warning that the number of people in Nepal affected each year by river flooding linked to climate change could more than double to 350,000 by 2030, from 157,000 in 2010.

For young Nepali activists like Alina, that means building a future in a country acutely exposed to a crisis it did little to create. The latest catastrophe has deepened anxieties that already shape their studies, family lives and future plans, adding urgency to their demands for climate justice.

A 2024 Unicef report, citing a U-Report poll of 2,506 young respondents in Nepal, said 46 per cent were very or extremely worried about climate change, with another 32 per cent a little worried.

Losses ‘can’t be counted’

Those concerns sit alongside the trauma experienced by survivors. Activists and development specialists say the emotional toll deserves greater attention, even as communities scramble for basic shelter and survival.

Bimal Regmi, a senior consultant for climate change and disaster risk management at Oxford Policy Management Nepal, said losses that were not just economic – from bereavement and psychological distress to the destruction of places of worship and community spaces – were often overlooked.

“People’s [lives] can’t be judged in economic value,” he said. “People’s culture, loss of biodiversity, mental and other stresses can’t be counted in US [dollars].”

For Alina, concerns about the future begin right outside her window in the Annapurna Rural Municipality of Kaski district, where Machhapuchhre – the twin-pointed Himalayan peak also known as Fishtail – dominates the skyline.

She long associated the mountain with snow and light. Recently, however, its appearance has changed dramatically.

“I used to see the white, shining mountains, but Machhapuchhre is becoming like a black rock,” Alina said.

She described hotter summers in a region where fans and air conditioning once seemed unnecessary, as well as erratic rainfall that had disrupted planting and reduced harvests for her family, who rely mainly on agriculture.

Alina said her forestry studies had heightened her awareness of ecosystem threats, making it harder to switch off. She said she often imagined what Nepal might look like in 50 years and where displaced mountain communities would go.

“Nepal is a small country,” she said. “So what will happen if the snow is melted? If the glacier outbursts, what will happen to the people from the mountains? Will the land of Terai [Nepal’s southern lowland belt] be enough for them, for all the shifted people?”

Everyday terror

In flood-ravaged regions, fear can become part of everyday life.

Aakriti Dotel, national network coordinator at Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, saw this first hand while researching disaster-related trauma in Melamchi in 2024.

She found children haunted by a mix of fear for the future and grief for the past. Many told her they were frightened by the sound of the river. Others had lost contact with friends who had moved away, while damaged infrastructure blocked their routes to school and destroyed their play areas.

Khusbu Paudel, a programme coordinator at Ipas Nepal focused on climate change and gender health, said the urgency of saving lives and recovering belongings often sidelined mental healthcare.

“In affected regions, people are more thinking only about how to save [their] life, how to get [their] belongings and everything,” she said. “And the people affected in the disasters … I think the psychosocial thing doesn’t come to priority for people.”

Although government agencies and other organisations were increasingly adding counselling services into disaster-relief health camps, Paudel said support remained inadequate and social stigma could discourage people from seeking help.

Efforts to bridge this gap followed the August disaster. Unicef said on Thursday that it was deploying psychiatrists, clinical psychologists and psychosocial counsellors alongside government teams to help affected communities.

Monica Neupane, a young climate activist who represented Nepal at the 2022 United Nations climate change conference Cop27 and has given a TEDx talk on climate anxiety, recalled meeting an elderly man during field research who kept a small umbrella beside his bed – ready to flee a sudden flood or landslide.

Neupane spent years trying to understand her own climate anxiety, eventually stepping back from activism to focus on her mental health. When she returned to community work, she realised how widespread the feeling was.

“I actually felt that they are also suffering from climate anxiety, and I was able to help them from my experience,” she said.

Turning anxiety into action

For Alina and Dotel, grass-roots organising offers a way to act on their concerns, although it does not dispel them.

“As youth, we have to make some solution, and we need [to] be an example so that others also can support and others also can cope,” Alina said.

Alongside her work with the youth network, Alina started the Climate Change Advocacy Group Annapurna with other young people in her community. With a small budget, the team delivers environmental education in local schools, organises clean-ups and uses art to show climate impacts.

“If we can obtain and reflect the climate change impact in a story or in a form of art, it … remains in [the] mind for a long time,” she said.

Dotel also introduces climate anxiety into her school presentations once pupils are old enough, connecting lessons about climate change with ways to take action.

Working with fellow organisers helps her feel less alone, though each new disaster tests her resolve.

“Again and again we are facing this kind of crisis and it demotivates us,” Dotel said.

While Alina believes local knowledge and education are vital for communities to prepare for future hazards, she said vulnerable people also needed support that goes beyond what young volunteers could provide.

“What vulnerable countries need is not simply sympathy or conventional development finance,” Alina said. “We need climate justice, including timely and adequate loss and damage finance and compensation for the losses and damages we are experiencing.”

item.title: [SCMP] Crouching dragons: the suicide divers Japan never sent to war
item.description:
Japan’s wartime kamikaze pilots remain among the most recognisable symbols of the Pacific war: young men flying aircraft into Allied ships on missions from which they were not expected to return.

Far less well-remembered are the fukuryu – suicide frogmen trained in the closing months of World War II to walk into the sea with mines on bamboo poles, then wait beneath the waves for an Allied invasion fleet.

Kanade Hamamoto was one of many Japanese people who had never heard of them, despite spending years on the same stretch of coast where they once trained.
item.content:encoded:
Japan’s wartime kamikaze pilots remain among the most recognisable symbols of the Pacific war: young men flying aircraft into Allied ships on missions from which they were not expected to return.

Far less well-remembered are the fukuryu – suicide frogmen trained in the closing months of World War II to walk into the sea with mines on bamboo poles, then wait beneath the waves for an Allied invasion fleet.

Kanade Hamamoto was one of many Japanese people who had never heard of them, despite spending years on the same stretch of coast where they once trained.

The 25-year-old photographer knew Inamuragasaki, on the Shonan coast south of Tokyo, only as a scenic seaside spot until a friend mentioned that the remains of a military base could still be seen near the cape, in tunnels cut into the cliff face.

“My friend’s comments kept nagging away at me after I got home, so I did an online search and came across the term ‘Fukuryu Special Attack Unit’ for the first time,” Hamamoto told This Week in Asia.

She has since turned that discovery into “ー・・”, a bilingual photo book published in 2025 that won the 50th Kimura Ihei Photography Award, one of Japan’s most prestigious honours for emerging photographers.

The title, rendered in English as “Arrived at the seabed”, refers to the Morse code-style signal – one long tug and two short ones – that the divers would use to tell colleagues on shore they had reached the bottom.

Once underwater, the fukuryu could communicate only through such coded tugs on a rope. Their bodies were sealed inside heavy diving suits, with weighted shoes and helmets fastened shut with four screws.

As those screws were tightened, surviving members of Japan’s wartime fukuryu units later described a piercing, high-pitched sound right next to their ears.

In his memoirs, former fukuryu Takaichiro Monna wrote that it felt “as if I were being placed in a coffin while I was still alive”.

Other survivors of the little-known unit, which was tasked with the last-ditch defence of the Japanese homeland in the closing stages of the second world war, reported that even years afterwards, they could still hear the whistling sound.

Few of the estimated 1,200 men who completed fukuryu training before Japan’s surrender on August 15, 1945, are likely to still be alive, but Hamamoto has helped return their story to public memory.

A different kind of kamikaze

The first organised kamikaze attack came during the Battle of Leyte Gulf, off the Philippines, in October 1944, when Lieutenant Yukio Seki crashed his Zero fighter into the US Navy escort carrier St. Lo, causing an explosion that sank the vessel in minutes.

Kamikaze air attacks on Allied shipping grew more frequent over the following months, alongside one-way missions by kaiten crewed torpedoes and shinyo motorboats laden with explosives.

The tide of the war could not be turned, however, and the fukuryu – meaning “crouching dragon” – were conceived as virtually the last line of defence against an Allied invasion of Japan.

The plan was simple: when an invasion fleet was sighted offshore, the fukuryu would wade out from the beaches, wait for a warship or landing craft to pass overhead, then strike it with a mine fixed to a five-metre-long (16.4 foot) bamboo pole.

The 15kg (33lb) explosive would be devastating to the enemy vessel – and to the frogman holding it.

In some places, underwater structures were installed a short way off the beach to store extra mines and offer the divers some shelter.

The 71st Arashi unit, based at Yokosuka, was tasked with defending the beaches of Sagami Bay with about 1,000 men. Additional units were stationed at Kure in central Japan and Sasebo in Kyushu.

Although the divers were never called upon to face an invasion fleet, since Japan surrendered first, their training was far from safe and at least some of the men died in accidents.

It is not clear how many were killed during training, however, because many records were destroyed after the surrender.

Surviving accounts describe isolated incidents, including one evening when bioluminescence at sea was mistaken for an approaching invasion fleet and the men were ordered into the water.

“When I read reports that said many of the bodies could not be recovered and many people were still missing, I began to wonder if they might still be there, somewhere beneath the sea where I had spent time since I was a teenager,” Hamamoto said.

“I felt their presence not as something that belonged to the past, but as something that exists in the present. I felt it not as something that concerned someone else, but as something that concerned me personally.”

While researching her book, Hamamoto concluded that the fukuryu were relatively unknown today for a number of reasons: firstly because the war ended before they saw combat, secondly because the unit’s records were destroyed and thirdly because the area where they trained was long off limits to civilians.

Garren Mulloy, a professor of international relations at Daito Bunka University and a specialist in military affairs, pointed to yet other reasons that the fukuryu frogmen’s stories had been largely overlooked for so long.

“When the first kamikaze aircraft started hitting warships in the Pacific in 1944, it was caught on film and shocked everyone who saw it,” he said. “There was also attention on how the kamikaze were first thought up, then the technology was developed and deployed, but with the fukuryu, it was just diving suits and a pole with a mine on the end.”

Sending young men to their certain deaths armed only with a mine illustrated the desperation of Japan’s military in the waning days of the conflict, Mulloy said.

Other last-gasp defences were planned too, including soldiers being ordered to crouch in beach foxholes and wait for enemy tanks to pass overhead before detonating a mine beneath them.

“I imagine that even in those extreme circumstances – with reckless training regimens and makeshift diving suits, as well as the grim necessity of carrying out a suicide mission – the waves and winds off Yokosuka must have been just as calm as they are today,” Hamamoto said.

“In that beautiful sea, human beings were attempting to kill their fellow human beings and, in the process, were losing their own lives.”

Preserving the memory of the fukuryu was essential to ensure that history did not repeat itself, she said. “I simply cannot bring myself to view this as a distant event that has nothing to do with me.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s rocket boom has made Hainan a space hub. Can launches fuel wider growth?
item.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.
item.content:encoded:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.

Long known for its coconuts, its namesake chicken and generations of emigrants who left for Southeast Asia in search of a living, Wenchang has been thrust onto the frontier of national development. Beijing’s space ambitions have turned the city into a showcase for rocket launches – and given Hainan a catalyst to reshape an economy long reliant on tourism and consumer services.

Today, the island province is working to build a more diversified and sustainable growth model and, together with its ambition to host a premier free-trade port, is embracing a hi-tech future increasingly centred on the space economy.

From coconuts to rockets: Hainan’s economic reboot

“Commercial space flight could give Hainan a clearer manufacturing focus while complementing its traditional strengths in tourism and consumer services,” said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government.

Home to more than 10 million people and comparable in size to Belgium, Hainan now boasts a growing industrial cluster known as Wenchang International Aerospace City. At its centre are two state-owned rocket launch facilities: one serving national programmes and another handling commercial missions.

The Wenchang Space Launch Site staged its first launch in 2016 and focuses mainly on lunar exploration and human space flight. Just a few miles away sits the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site, China’s first dedicated commercial launch platform.

Since its inaugural mission in November 2024, the commercial site has completed 21 launches and has sent 221 satellites into orbit, according to Xu Xikai, deputy head of the development department at Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch, the site’s operator.

Two more general-purpose liquid-fuel launch pads were also under construction and could host their maiden missions by the end of this year, Xu noted. Longer-term plans envision as many as eight large coastal launch pads, together with tracking facilities and systems for recovering rockets at sea.

We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains

Xu Xikai, Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch

Wenchang’s coastal geography gives it a major advantage. Massive rockets can be delivered directly by sea, bypassing the road, tunnel and bridge constraints faced by inland facilities. And at about 19 degrees north latitude, rockets gain an extra momentum boost from the Earth’s rotation, reducing fuel requirements or allowing heavier payloads, Xu explained.

“For large-diameter, heavy-lift rockets in the future, coastal launch sites will increasingly have an advantage,” he said.

Geography, however, is also one of Hainan’s economic weaknesses. The island has historically lacked a heavy industrial base, meaning much of the specialised hardware and construction materials required for space manufacturing must be shipped in.

Inside Wenchang’s manufacturing ambitions

The challenge for Hainan is transforming launch sites into the nucleus of a wider industrial ecosystem – and early signs are encouraging.

Wenchang International Aerospace City recorded a surge in revenue amid an “unprecedented” pace of rocket launches, according to a June report by Nanhai Net, a state-run news portal operated by the Hainan Daily Press Group.

The aerospace park’s revenue jumped 85 per cent in 2025 to 23.53 billion yuan (US$3.5 billion), while manufacturing output from its rocket supply chain more than doubled to over 8 billion yuan, the report stated.

Under a provincial action plan from 2025 to 2027, Hainan also aims to raise annual operating revenue at Wenchang’s aerospace cluster to 10 billion yuan by 2027, while building an integrated supply chain spanning rockets, satellites and data services.

The expansion comes as Beijing presses ahead with reforms to open the island further and develop new sources of growth – though competition is intensifying. Two other commercial launch sites have already begun operating in Gansu and Shandong provinces, while at least four more are under development nationwide.

To stay ahead, Hainan’s strategy is to push further up the industrial chain. Its action plan prioritises a “super factory” next to the launch pads, designed to produce up to 1,000 satellites annually. The location would allow freshly assembled satellites to move straight from production line to launch pad with very little transit time, the Star Market Daily, a Shanghai-based financial news outlet focused on technology and capital markets, reported in December.

Described by local authorities as Asia’s largest satellite-manufacturing facility, the industrial complex is also expected to support China’s Qianfan low-Earth-orbit constellation. A planned special bonded zone for satellite data would further leverage Hainan’s free-trade policies to attract data from overseas, according to the report.

“We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains,” said Xu of Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch.

The infrastructure buildout is already reshaping launch activity. After more than two years of development, the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site has moved from experimental testing to routine operations. It handled more than 30 per cent of China’s commercial satellite launches in 2025 and successfully carried out the country’s first offshore rocket booster recovery.

Business beyond the launch pad

Putting a rocket into orbit, however, is only one part of the emerging space economy. Ye Shiyang, a Wenchang native who chairs the company behind the Aerospace Supercomputing Centre in Wenchang International Aerospace City, argued Hainan must capture a larger share of the value generated after a rocket launches.

“Over the past few years, we have connected the entire chain – from collecting and receiving satellite data to storing, processing, applying and trading it,” Ye said.

Completed in 2023, the supercomputing centre occupies about 40,000 square metres (about 431,000 square feet), with about 22,400 square metres of floor space. A guide at the centre said it offered peak computing power of 100 petaflops – a measure of processing capacity – and was designed to accommodate about 2,000 server racks.

Meanwhile, three of the centre’s remote-sensing satellites operate as part of Jilin-1, which is described by its developer as the world’s largest commercial sub-metre Earth-observation constellation. The centre has also built 13 ground stations, according to a guide there.

The practical applications could be numerous. Satellite images processed in Wenchang can distinguish food crops from cash crops, identify fallow land and monitor crop growth, assess pest outbreaks and track the effects of typhoons. Such imaging tools can also help to detect water pollution, illegal logging and unauthorised land use.

These services, Ye argued, could generate steady demand from agricultural, environmental and land-management authorities, giving Hainan a revenue stream that is less dependent on the schedule of rocket launches.

The aerospace city is also developing a space tourism business. The Jixing Meteorite Museum, for instance, displays more than 400 specimens gathered from around the world, while exhibitions introduce visitors to satellite data and supercomputing.

“We are developing space tourism in response to market demand,” Ye said. “Visitors should not only watch a launch or see a rocket or satellite. They should also understand the industry and technology behind them.”

In 2025, tourism, modern services, hi-tech industries and tropical agriculture – Hainan’s four pillar sectors – accounted for 65.9 per cent of the province’s gross domestic product, according to the provincial government.

“The Wenchang launch site has already become a tourist attraction, and this could give Hainan an economic model built around tourism, consumer services and aerospace manufacturing – and give its manufacturing sector a much clearer direction,” said Peng of the Guangdong Society of Reform.

For a Wenchang native surnamed Xie, the transformation has been drastic. Growing up in a village in Longlou town, he once walked barefoot along unpaved red-earth tracks. Today, working as a taxi driver, he has watched the sprawling aerospace complex reshape the place he calls home.

As the launch site and surrounding projects expanded, local families were relocated and farmland acquired. While some households received hundreds of thousands of yuan in compensation, Xie noted how traditional livelihoods were quickly fading, leaving coconut processing as one of the few legacy industries remaining.

“Farmers around here barely farm any more,” he said.

In Longlou, the coconut palms still remain – quiet reminders of a past that existed before the rockets arrived, even as a new economy takes shape around them.

item.title: [SCMP] Brics summit ends with Xi’s AI offer, Modi’s warning on critical minerals as weapons
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded his brief trip to India on Sunday with an offer to help Brics members develop open-source AI and smart manufacturing.

Summit host Prime Minister Narendra Modi, meanwhile, warned against turning technology and critical minerals into economic weapons.

Experts said the exchange captured the wider picture of the Brics summit. Two days of diplomacy produced a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” pressure with a joint declaration, while heads of institutions Washington once dominated sat at a Global South table. Concerns over minerals and technology, however, exposed clear limits to that unity.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded his brief trip to India on Sunday with an offer to help Brics members develop open-source AI and smart manufacturing.

Summit host Prime Minister Narendra Modi, meanwhile, warned against turning technology and critical minerals into economic weapons.

Experts said the exchange captured the wider picture of the Brics summit. Two days of diplomacy produced a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” pressure with a joint declaration, while heads of institutions Washington once dominated sat at a Global South table. Concerns over minerals and technology, however, exposed clear limits to that unity.

Speaking on the second day of the summit in New Delhi, Xi identified open-source AI and smart factories as two out of five key initiatives to promote economic growth and technological development in the Global South.

He also said Beijing would offer to train young talent from other member states in advanced technology and innovation, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The bloc has grown rapidly in recent years and is being increasingly seen as one of the strongest voices for the Global South, as the United States becomes increasingly assertive on the world stage.

Against this backdrop, the Chinese leader also issued a rallying call for unity and cooperation within the bloc to counter geopolitical hostilities and disruptive forces that he warned were shattering the stability of supply and industrial chains.

“A world without rules is like an intersection without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder would be inevitable,” he was quoted as saying by Xinhua.

Global rules should be written jointly and applied equally to all countries without double standards, Xi added. “The logic of might makes right should have been discarded long ago.”

Xi’s offer covered some of the key areas of the rivalry between the US and China, where control of resources and technology is vital.

Open-source models and smart factories require magnets, batteries, chips and processing equipment, and the supply chain of the minerals needed to make them run overwhelmingly through China.

But the US is the key gatekeeper when it comes to advanced chips and chipmaking equipment, and has imposed a series of export controls on the most advanced technology.

That leaves many Global South countries caught between two forms of dependence. While Chinese support could be vital to helping Global South countries develop, many are worried about over-reliance on either Beijing or Washington.

Modi, chairing Sunday’s session, marked that fear without naming either side.

“The weaponisation of technology and critical minerals can hinder our shared progress. Therefore, we have emphasised inclusivity in the adoption of technology,” he said.

India already has first-hand experience of how supply chains can be used to exert economic pressure. After the deadly 2020 border clash between Chinese and Indian troops, fertiliser clearances slowed and supplies of some equipment were held up.

In 2025, when China put rare earth magnets under a global export-licence system during its tariff war with the US, Indian automotive production lines felt the impact immediately.

Xi, who arrived in New Delhi early Saturday afternoon local time, skipped a gala dinner hosted by Modi for Brics leaders. Meanwhile, a social media video posted by Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday captured a relaxed exchange on the summit sidelines between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov and Araghchi himself.

At one point, as Lavrov was speaking, Wang reached over to look at the badge pinned to Araghchi’s collar.

Analysts said New Delhi’s aim at the summit was simple: preserve Brics unity without letting its internal tensions take centre stage.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said divisions within Brics were natural – given differences in geopolitics, political systems, levels of development and national interests – and had become more pronounced as the group expanded.

Those differences did not prevent cooperation, he argued, saying consensus and divergence shared a “symbiotic and dialectical relationship”.

But geopolitical trust remained a major weakness, Liu noted, particularly between China and India, something he described as “the biggest problem within Brics”.

While members had found broad common ground on development and economic issues at this year’s summit, disagreements over critical minerals reflected India’s efforts to raise issues with China that were difficult to resolve bilaterally, he said.

“India is trying to maintain ties with both sides,” Liu said, citing its cooperation with China and Russia through Brics and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation while avoiding a break with the US and the West.

Liu said Brics cooperation could also give the Global South including China a greater say in shaping international rules in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence (AI) and space.

“Many of the current rules in these fields were shaped primarily by Western countries, with the Global South having limited influence over their formulation,” he said.

If Brics members and other Global South countries worked together to develop new rules, Western countries would have to take their views into account because they represented “huge markets” and “huge numbers of users”, he noted.

Despite US President Donald Trump’s threats of 100 per cent tariffs if Brics nations chose to “play games” with the dollar, the bloc pushed for local currency settlement and linked payment systems to keep trade moving if Washington were to use the dollar as a sanctions or tariff weapon.

However, member states remain divided over how and how much to move away from the US currency.

Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, said differences were inevitable given the members’ varying relationships with Washington.

“Such differences are a natural existence under the current circumstances, and they can only reach consensus through long-term interaction and mutual adjustment,” he said.

Lin said the unanimous adoption of the joint declaration also reflected the impact of US policies.

“The measures of the US government are certainly a very important external stimulus,” he said, citing tariffs, sanctions and the “America first” policy, which he said had “damaged the external environment for development across much of the Global South”.

He said Brics had a role to play in emerging areas where the US and other Western countries were “reorganising” their approach, but its ability to shape new global rules remained limited by “the diversity of interests among member states” and their differences.

item.title: [SCMP] How one company’s choice – resignation or the factory – left China’s young workers floored
item.description:
Weeks after sparking a nationwide outcry over its mass dismissal of recent college graduates, Xingyu – a major automotive lighting maker in eastern China – has severely penalised four of its executives and promised to help the former employees find new jobs.

Two of the firm’s top executives received salary deductions and two human resources managers were dismissed or demoted for their “misjudgment and hasty decision-making”, the company said in a lengthy statement detailing its recent “mistake” last week.

The saga began in early August, when the Shanghai-listed company, whose clients include international carmakers such as Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, presented more than 370 fresh graduates – who had joined the company a month earlier – with a stark choice.
item.content:encoded:
Weeks after sparking a nationwide outcry over its mass dismissal of recent college graduates, Xingyu – a major automotive lighting maker in eastern China – has severely penalised four of its executives and promised to help the former employees find new jobs.

Two of the firm’s top executives received salary deductions and two human resources managers were dismissed or demoted for their “misjudgment and hasty decision-making”, the company said in a lengthy statement detailing its recent “mistake” last week.

The saga began in early August, when the Shanghai-listed company, whose clients include international carmakers such as Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, presented more than 370 fresh graduates – who had joined the company a month earlier – with a stark choice.

They could either resign “voluntarily” and receive half a month’s salary, or stay and be reassigned from office-based technical roles to factory-floor work, including tightening screws.

According to the firm, 107 chose the former option. But the uproar that ensued has placed the company firmly in the centre of a media firestorm, with Communist Party news organ People’s Daily calling the move “a blatant trampling of social trust” in a commentary late last month.

The extensive public attention the incident aroused stood as a tangible reflection of corporate workforce contraction, youth employment pressure and growing incidents of labour disputes, phenomena occurring within a broader slowdown in the world’s second-largest economy, analysts said.

While neither the firm nor local authorities specified any violation of labour law by the short-term manoeuvre, which coincided with its application for a listing in Hong Kong, its adverse effects were evident, the analysts warned.

“The company’s planned Hong Kong listing is very likely to be blocked, because the negative impact is simply too damaging,” said Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing.

As for the employment of fresh graduates – an increasingly sensitive issue for Beijing amid a tough job market – “the fact that this incident has escalated to such a degree is also highly unfavourable. Big companies will become very cautious in their future hiring”, he said.

According to its statement, Xingyu had recruited more than 400 college graduates through campus hiring last autumn and this spring, while 372 formally joined the company in July.

About one month into their employment, the company’s human resources department conducted one-on-one meetings with each of them, presenting the binary choice. The decision resulted from a workforce optimisation plan “based on the company’s order pipeline and staffing needs”, it said.

The move sparked backlash from many former employees, who complained to domestic media that after being dismissed, they lost their status as fresh graduates and could only re-enter the job market as social hires with a termination record on their résumés.

Within China’s institutional framework, losing this status stripped them of many competitive job-seeking advantages.

The company and the municipal human resources bureau of Changzhou, where Xingyu is based, have so far arranged for 71 of those dismissed to join new employers, while an additional 22 passed interviews and received offer letters.

The remainder were either undertaking interviews or planning to pursue postgraduate studies, Xingyu said last week.

Previously, both the firm and the bureau responded with apologies and explanations over the incident but failed to quell widespread public scepticism.

On August 25, the bureau confirmed the controversial lay-off – after media reports went viral – noting that the negotiation process was “overly rigid and simplistic, lacking full and effective communication”.

Two days later, the firm issued a public apology, acknowledging “managerial errors in decision-making” and offering a package of remedies including three months’ worth of job-seeking living allowances, free dormitory accommodation and an additional six months’ salary compensation for those who remained unemployed.

At its half-year performance briefing on September 2, the company’s chairwoman and general manager, Zhou Xiaoping, apologised and said the company was “properly implementing remedial measures” under government guidance.

According to its earnings results, Xingyu posted revenue of 6.88 billion yuan (US$1 billion) in the first half of the year, up 1.87 per cent, year on year, with a profit of about 712 million yuan, down 7.78 per cent, year on year.

Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard

Nie Riming, Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law

Its 2025 sales figures showed that it held an 11.6 per cent share of China’s automotive lighting market, ranking first in the country, and accounted for 4.6 per cent of the global market share, ranking seventh.

Nie Riming, a researcher at the Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law, said the broader lacklustre job market was primarily why this incident generated such a huge response.

“Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard,” he said.

Another record-breaking army of university graduates – an estimated 12.7 million students – entered China’s job market this summer, up about 4 per cent from last year, according to official data. The youth jobless rate – covering those aged 16 to 24, excluding students – climbed to 17.9 per cent in July from 14.9 per cent in the previous month.

Nie noted that Xingyu’s immediate cash compensation alone could compare favourably with statutory minimums in Germany, where labour protections are generally stronger.

While China has relatively high-standard labour laws on paper, enforcement and compliance are uneven, especially among smaller firms, he said. Against this backdrop, listed companies like Xingyu – along with foreign-invested firms and state-owned enterprises – remain the primary sources of higher-quality jobs in China.

However, these relatively “well-behaved” companies had been steadily reducing their headcount in recent years, and after this incident, such formal, regulated positions were likely to become even more scarce, he added.

“For companies going forward, they will become increasingly cautious when hiring for compliant, formal positions,” he said.

“They will lean more towards non-standard employment arrangements – such as outsourcing and dispatching – to offload their staffing responsibilities. That, in turn, would further reduce formal direct hiring and reinforce labour-market dualisation.”

The most contentious issue remains fresh graduate status, as many recruitment policies, including those for civil service admissions, favour fresh graduates, he said.

“The way graduates are regulated has yet to align with the job market, and this disconnect must be resolved before it causes further frustration,” he urged.

As the economic slowdown persists in China, lay-offs have become a recurring theme in the workplace, and labour disputes are on the rise.

Labour dispute mediation and arbitration bodies at all levels handled 4.54 million cases nationwide in 2025 – a 7 per cent increase from 2024, following a 10 per cent rise over 2023, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security’s annual statistical bulletin.

Meanwhile, Xingyu’s lay-off controversy emerged after it refiled its updated H-share listing application with the Hong Kong stock exchange at the end of July, sparking market speculation that it was a short-term tactic to pad the company’s research workforce and make it look stronger for its listing ambitions.

Among the dismissed employees, about two-thirds held bachelor’s degrees, while the remainder held master’s degrees. The majority were assigned to research and development roles, as well as manufacturing and production positions, while a smaller number were allocated functional support roles, according to last week’s statement.

However, legal experts and academics considered it unlikely that this was the company’s primary intention, given that such a move would offer limited substantive gain while exposing it to significant compliance and reputational risks.

Such risks may soon materialise, such as hindering its listing progress, said Zhao Zhanling, a commercial lawyer from Beijing-based Javy Law Firm.

“The stock exchange and its advisers are likely to demand clarifications on the mass lay-offs, labour law compliance and internal control mechanisms,” he said. “Adverse media coverage may also invite regulatory questions, causing delays – though not necessarily scuttling the IPO altogether.”

The Shanghai Stock Exchange website showed that it issued a regulatory work letter to Xingyu on Wednesday, specifying regulatory requirements regarding the company’s “relevant matters”, without providing further details.

The saga could also lead to a loss of business opportunities, according to Tang, the Beijing researcher.

“It is possible that its international clients would respond positively to public outcry,” he said, “but that does not mean they would punish Xingyu – they may downgrade its supplier tier ... or impose more stringent supply conditions.”

Volkswagen China said earlier this month that it had initiated an investigation into the matter following intense media coverage.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s tech giants fuel the rise of AI tokens as a new corporate currency
item.description:
Every month, a Beijing-based ByteDance employee says he burns through close to a billion units of a new corporate currency – one that cannot buy a coffee or pay rent.

Yet, as he noted, that staggering volume “doesn’t even put me near the top of the consumption rankings in my department”.

That currency is not yuan, but artificial intelligence tokens.
item.content:encoded:
Every month, a Beijing-based ByteDance employee says he burns through close to a billion units of a new corporate currency – one that cannot buy a coffee or pay rent.

Yet, as he noted, that staggering volume “doesn’t even put me near the top of the consumption rankings in my department”.

That currency is not yuan, but artificial intelligence tokens.

“Using AI has become part of almost every task now,” said the employee, who requested anonymity as he was not authorised by the company to speak to the media.

A token – dubbed ciyuan in mainland China – is the basic unit through which AI services are measured and billed. Every prompt submitted to a model and every response generated consumes tokens, much like electricity is measured in kilowatt-hours.

As Chinese tech giants from ByteDance to Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings rush to encourage staff to integrate AI into daily workflows, tokens have become a new kind of corporate allowance. Employees are no longer just budgeting their time; they are also expected to budget their token use as proof of their AI literacy.

This surge in AI use in the corporate sector is being fuelled by a brutal price war. When Hangzhou-based AI unicorn DeepSeek slashed the price of its flagship V4-Pro model by 75 per cent in May, it highlighted the defining feature of China’s AI industry: an accelerating race to make intelligence cheap.

The overarching logic is that as token costs plummet, a broader economy built around ubiquitous AI adoption can finally take shape.

The token surge

For decades, Chinese companies bought software through fixed, predictable subscriptions – often called “per-seat” licensing. If a company bought 500 licences for an office software suite, the monthly bill remained the same whether an employee typed one sentence or 1,000 pages.

AI billing, however, scales proportionally with usage. While a short question might cost a regular user a few dozen tokens, a software engineer scanning an extensive corporate spreadsheet or building a computer program can burn through millions at a time.

The exact price of a token varies by the model. DeepSeek, for instance, later reversed course and raised its prices, charging 12 yuan (US$1.77) for every million output tokens during peak hours and 6 yuan during non-peak time for API access to its latest V4 models.

To adapt, Chinese tech companies are experimenting with new allocation methods.

In May, cybersecurity firm 360 Security Technology launched a companywide initiative to directly distribute a total of 100 million AI tokens across employee accounts, entirely eliminating managerial approval and reimbursement procedures.

Founder Zhou Hongyi has repeatedly argued publicly that AI tools must be integrated into ordinary workflows, rather than restricted mostly to specialised engineering teams.

In March, Tencent, developer of the Hunyuan model, handed out free tokens to employees through products such as QClaw, an internal AI tool. During testing, some individual quotas reportedly reached as high as 40 million tokens per day.

Alibaba, the Hangzhou-based e-commerce giant, launched a similar internal incentive scheme the same month, granting token allowances for in-house tools like its agentic platform Wukong and coding assistant Qoder.

Internal adoption is expected to climb further after Alibaba’s security team banned the use of Anthropic’s Claude Code earlier this month, citing data security risks.

Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

Rise of the token economy

This major corporate push has contributed to a massive explosion in token usage across the country.

According to the National Data Administration (NDA), China’s average daily AI token consumption surpassed 140 trillion in March, up from 100 billion two years earlier. That is equivalent to roughly 100,000 tokens per person based on the country’s population of about 1.4 billion.

The [Chinese] digital economy has gone through the stages of the data economy and the computing economy. Today, the token economy is emerging

Yin Hao, Chinese Academy of Sciences

In May, Premier Li Qiang said average daily token consumption in the country had reached hundreds of trillions by the end of the month.

Top Chinese policymakers have openly touted the emergence of a “token economy”.

When NDA head Liu Liehong convened executives from top domestic companies including Alibaba, Tencent and China International Capital Corporation at a token-economy symposium in May, he described tokens as the new accounting and settlement units for AI services.

At the China Internet Conference in Beijing last week, Yin Hao, an academician at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said, “The [Chinese] digital economy has gone through the stages of the data economy and the computing economy. Today, the token economy is emerging.”

Tokens were more than just a technical metric, they had become a new production factor connecting AI model capability, computing resources and commercial value, he said.

China Unicom viewed “token operation” as an important driver of efficiency across its businesses, company vice-president Qiu Baohua said in a speech at the conference.

Qiu said Unicom’s growing AI token consumption mirrored the expanding use of AI across its business.

AI agents had improved document drafting and contract retrieval efficiency by 70 per cent, he said, while AI now handled more than 85 per cent of calls to Unicom’s customer service hotline, reducing annual operating costs by more than 100 million yuan (US$14.8 million).

Other industry leaders also expressed optimism about the future of the token economy, with Huawei Technologies vice-president and head of data communication products Wang Lei saying the company believed it was “the greatest opportunity we can be certain of in an otherwise uncertain era”.

The developments reflect a growing belief among policymakers and technology companies that AI output is becoming an economic resource in its own right. As model usage spreads across coding, research, customer service and content creation, tokens are increasingly being used to measure, allocate and price access to that resource.

“Tokens are effectively the energy unit of the AI era,” said Zhou Zhengang, research vice-president at IDC China.

“Just as companies in the industrial era budgeted for electricity, companies in the AI era will have to budget for tokens,” added Lu Yanxia, research director at the market intelligence firm. “They are becoming a financial metric rather than simply a technical one.”

IDC’s latest market tracking report, published in May, projected that China’s model-as-a-service (MaaS) market would process 40,000 trillion tokens in 2026, an increase of about 20 times versus 2025.

The surveillance shift

The rapid expansion of token allowances, however, has also created a new flashpoint for corporate strife: unprecedented managerial surveillance. As AI usage surges across entire companies, bosses have gained unprecedented visibility into how employees work.

Some companies are now linking token consumption directly to employee performance evaluations.

Beijing-based internet company Kunlun Tech announced in February it would provide engineers access to top US coding AI agents, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code, while evaluating employees based on how many tokens they consumed.

This mirrors controversial productivity tracking methods seen in the US.

According to internal reports from late last year, Meta Platforms, the parent of Facebook and Instagram, briefly used an internal dashboard known as the “Claudeonomics” leaderboard to track AI token consumption across more than 85,000 employees before shutting it down after internal statistics were leaked.

Amazon similarly retired “KiroRank”, an internal leaderboard that ranked developers by AI activity. Some employees had been inflating token usage through unnecessary agent tasks to fake productivity, spiking compute costs without delivering real output, the Financial Times reported in late May.

Similar tensions are beginning to emerge in China.

Since June, Tencent has tightened internal AI allowances, requiring employees to seek fresh approval every two weeks for additional tokens. Quotas have been slashed to less than half of previous levels and are now increasingly tied to specific job functions and workloads, according to an employee working on AI agents.

Tencent did not respond to a request for comment.

For tech enterprises in both the US and China, the primary drivers are the same: intense financial pressure to increase engineering efficiency, speed up product releases and drive down development costs.

While corporate executives often pitch the token economy as a way to liberate workers from boring, repetitive tasks, some employees describe a more complicated reality. Part of the reason is that AI tools are not yet reliable enough to fully automate entire workflows.

Employees from various Chinese companies have reported a distinct gap between corporate optimisation targets and reality. AI tools remain prone to hallucinations – instances where models generate incorrect or fabricated data – meaning heavy token usage often translates to more oversight work for humans, not less.

“Cursor and Codex are basically used by everyone,” said a software engineer in Nvidia’s IT Software Engineering group in Shanghai, referring to popular AI-assisted coding tools. “But that does not mean the workload is lighter. I spend more time reviewing AI-generated output now.”

China’s state-owned telecoms giants are looking to monetise the AI boom by introducing tokens as a new unit of measurement in monthly bills, after having billed users by the gigabyte of data for years.

In May, China Telecom unveiled nationwide, token-based pricing packages on its official app, targeting everyone from enterprise developers to casual smartphone users.

Business packages, which support coding and AI agent deployment, range from 39.9 yuan to 299.9 yuan per month, with token allowances from 15 million to 250 million. Consumer packages, tailored for everyday tasks, start at 9.9 yuan per month for 10 million tokens and increase in price and volume to 49.9 yuan for 80 million tokens.

Beyond ‘big tech’

As the cost of running AI models continues to drop, the token economy is reshaping ecosystems beyond corporate cubicles – namely, venture capital and higher education.

In the start-up world, the traditional practice of exchanging cash for corporate equity is being supplemented by a more immediate need: access to raw compute.

In March, prominent Chinese venture capital firm ZhenFund, in partnership with start-up developer community Crossing, launched an initiative dubbed “Token Grant”.

Instead of offering standard cash financing, the programme awards early-stage AI developers 50,000 yuan worth of direct model-access credits. The initiative specifically targets solo founders and prototype-stage teams who are building AI agents or multimodal products before they approach institutional investors for cash.

“For early-stage developers, token credits often matter more immediately than cash itself,” said an angel investor, who requested anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. “A small team with sufficient compute access can now prototype agents, generate code, process video and test products without hiring large engineering teams.”

The replacement of cash with tokens has even reached the halls of higher education. In May, during a public panel discussion with Moonshot AI president Zhang Yutong, Tian Xuan, the dean of Peking University’s Guanghua School of Management, suggested that universities might eventually “stop giving scholarships and distribute more tokens instead”.

Additional reporting by Ben Jiang

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready for it?
item.description:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.
item.content:encoded:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.

Concerns about AI run the gamut from autonomous weapons, mass unemployment and machine-driven cyberattacks to deepfake-fuelled misinformation, algorithmic bias and a dangerous overreliance on automation.

South Korea has seen all this – and decided now is the time to hit the accelerator.

Under President Lee Jae Myung’s “AI for All” initiative, the government is preparing to hand every citizen free access to artificial intelligence, integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices and daily lives in a way few countries have attempted.

“The idea is to substantially lower barriers to access so that the benefits of the technology are distributed evenly rather than enjoyed by only some people,” Seoul’s Ministry of Science and ICT said in a statement to This Week in Asia.

The government, which has a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current financial year, has allocated an additional 250 billion won for the roll-out through 2027.

A beta version is set to launch later this month, introducing free, unlimited-access general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by three consortiums – led by telecoms giants SK Telecom, KT and Kakao – using hundreds of state-of-the-art Nvidia B200 graphics processing units lent to them by the government.

From next year, officials envisage the temporary trial will become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility, eventually connecting to government systems to allow citizens to book doctor’s appointments, go house hunting, get tax advice and the like, all through AI intermediaries.

To manage the risks involved, Seoul is relying on its landmark AI Basic Act, which came into force in January, to ensure human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments and clear watermarking of synthetic content.

Meanwhile, a state-funded AI Safety Institute has been tasked with serving as a technical watchdog to evaluate the pitfalls and ensure that public AI utilities remain trustworthy, secure and answerable to the citizens who use them.

“Going forward, the government plans to establish an autonomous reliability-assurance system”, the ICT ministry said in its statement, adding this would be based on the seven “AI Ethics Principles” it laid out last month: accountability, human-centredness, privacy protection and fairness among them.

South Korea hopes its “AI for All” push will help it become one of the world’s three leading AI powers, alongside the United States and China, with the government seeing the technology as an antidote to a shrinking workforce and as a way to strengthen its export-driven economy.

But the same society racing to put AI in every pocket is also confronting the consequences of what that means, as workers worry about automation eliminating jobs, police struggle to combat a surge in deepfake crimes and educators watch a generation’s reading scores slide.

Sovereignty is another concern. Of the roughly two-thirds of South Korea’s 51.6 million people who have tried or regularly use AI, 23.45 million are active users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, 8.45 million of Google’s Gemini and 2.41 million of Anthropic’s Claude, according to government figures.

Yet access to these platforms cannot be guaranteed, as the ministry noted in its statement.

“As we saw recently, foreign AI services can have their availability limited at any time depending on decisions made by foreign governments or companies,” it said, in a possible nod to Washington’s recent attempts to block access to the newest models.

In July, Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon unveiled plans for South Korea to develop its own cybersecurity-focused AI model by the end of this year, following the US clampdown.

Brewing with bots

At Unicup Coffee, an independent cafe vying for business against 11 low-cost chain rivals in Busan International Finance Centre, owner Bae Kyung-han, 31, credits AI with helping him beat the competition.

What began a year ago as a cost-saving experiment, with Bae teaching himself how to use generative AI to create promotional posters and menu images, has since taken over nearly every part of the business.

“It’s now running my research, proposal developments, communications and advertisements,” he said, adding that the AI system – his only office-based “colleague” – had also orchestrated a shift in focus towards bulk orders instead of walk-in customers.

Five employees handle customer orders, serving some 13,000 people a month and generating card sales that are, according to Bae, roughly double those of his competitors.

He has also built a second business around the technology, registering as a vendor under one of the government’s chosen AI consortiums to teach novices how to ask better questions of their chatbots.

“The biggest advantage of AI in the workplace is that it reduces the psychological burden of managing people,” Bae said, describing the relief of no longer having to coordinate schedules, repeat instructions or manage employees’ feelings.

“With AI, I can ask questions whenever I need to and revise plans whenever I want to. It’s just more efficient.”
