Yet he is still sceptical of the government’s AI strategy, questioning whether domestically developed models – even ones that are provided for free – would actually be able to wean people off premium foreign made tools.

“People who are used to using AI would likely pay for a more expensive US-based model like ChatGPT rather than use a free domestic service,” Bae said.

That is, unless the models were specialised and purpose-built for specific problems, as opposed to another general-purpose chatbot.

“That changes the conversation,” Bae said. “That could do wonders for businesses like mine.”

Elsewhere, at a jobs fair in Seoul’s Yonsei University, technology companies crowded the floor, competing for the attention of soon-to-be graduates before they had even finished their degrees.

Kwon Il-geun, an electronic engineering student hoping to work at semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix, said AI proficiency had never been more important.

“My skills in using AI tools have nearly doubled in the past year,” he said, comparing the shift to the first industrial revolution or the arrival of the personal computer. “This is just part of the changing times.”

No juniors needed?

Not everyone is sharing in the spoils, however. The number of young South Koreans aged 15 to 29 who were in work dropped by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to the central bank, which estimated that 94 per cent of that decline was in sectors highly exposed to automation, including publishing, IT services and computer programming.

And the Korea Development Institute, a government-run think tank, projected in July that AI could wipe out roughly 256,000 jobs a year within the next decade.

This has had a knock-on effect on students’ ambitions, with enrolment reportedly falling at academies teaching graphic design and coding, even as institutions preparing young people for stable public-sector careers enjoy booming interest.

At the SKY Entrance Exam Academy in Seoul, enrolment in its military and policy preparation track is up 70 per cent year on year.

Yun Ji-sang, a recent school leaver, is among those preparing to commit himself to five years of officer training and a military career of 15 years minimum.

“Some people think this is a long time to be trapped inside the military, but I just view it as a long time of having a stable job,” he said, noting that it was also one that came with a pension.

The number of young South Koreans in employment fell by 143,000 in August compared to the year before, the Chosun Daily newspaper reported on September 9, marking the 46th straight month of decline for those aged 15 to 29.

Meanwhile, the number of civil servants being recruited nationwide increased this year for the first time in five years, according to the Ministry of Personnel Management.

“I used to want to live as an entrepreneur who would travel abroad frequently and live freely,” Yun said. “But what use is that when we are constantly worrying about making a living?”

Conventional wisdom surrounding which jobs were most at risk from automation had been flipped on its head by the rise of generative AI, said Ko Hak-soo, a law professor at Seoul National University.

“When ChatGPT first emerged three or four years ago, there was widespread concern that jobs involving workers with relatively low levels of education … would be at highest risk,” he said.

“But now, there is a much stronger view that jobs requiring a great deal of human labour may actually be relatively safe while professional occupations, especially entry-level and junior workers in these fields, might gradually disappear.”

New roles were likely to emerge as AI became more integrated into workplaces, Ko said – while warning there was “little understanding of the reality of the shifting labour market”.

Kim Myuhng-joo, executive director of South Korea’s AI Safety Institute, said the disruption was already under way.

“Until just a few years ago, programmers were extremely highly valued, and their salaries were rising rapidly,” he told This Week in Asia. “But AI companies are increasingly using AI for coding … without needing as many junior-level developers.”

Kim further voiced concerns that a new cohort of workers coming of age in the “AI for All” era might never develop the skills needed to operate without the technology.

“In less than 10 years, we could see a new generation entering the workforce that is overly dependent on AI,” he said.

“Companies may expect these new employees to have the capabilities of previous generations, but they … could end up becoming people who are incapable of doing anything without AI.”

AI-fuelled abuse

South Korea’s most visceral fears surrounding AI stem not from the threat of rogue tech, however, but from the recent reality of criminal misuse.

The Nth Room case of 2020 – in which encrypted social media channels were used to produce, sell and distribute sexually exploitative material and blackmail victims – and subsequent scandals led to the country strengthening its deepfake laws in 2024.

Producing such material can now result in seven years behind bars or a 50 million won (US$37,000) fine, while possessing or knowingly viewing it can mean three years in prison or a 30 million won penalty.

Yet police still recorded 1,553 deepfake-related offences last year, accounting for over 35 per cent of all reported cybersex crimes, according to statistics presented at a recent forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea.

In the first half of this year alone, police apprehended 419 suspects for deepfake offences, 17 of whom were physically detained while awaiting trial.

The National Office of Investigation said in a statement that officials were “developing police response technologies at a pace that exceeds the speed at which technology itself is evolving”, including by expanding forensic video expertise and the use of AI-assisted detection tools.

Won Eun-ji is less convinced that technology alone will solve the problem. As director of Team Flame, which investigates digital sex crimes, she has spent much of this year infiltrating roughly 50 Telegram chat rooms alongside investigative outlet Newstapa, documenting how AI tools have swelled the ranks of anonymous perpetrators and lowered the age of victims.

“Even today, many initial leads in these investigations often come from victims themselves,” she said. “The police need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities.”

Kim, of the AI Safety Institute, said the government needed to prepare for the unintended consequences of increasing access to AI.

“Once AI becomes embedded in society, it is difficult to remove it,” he said, describing it as “an irreversible change”.

“We need to conduct thorough impact assessments from the beginning, considering what effects the technology might have and whether it could be misused, abused or overused.”

To combat crime, Kim said he would support police undercover investigations “depending on the circumstance” alongside greater use of invisible watermarking to trace AI-generated content back to its creator or means of distribution.

“Online platforms should take more active steps to identify online crimes” and prevent abuse material from being circulated, he said, adding the children “need to receive education on these issues as part of broader civic education and AI literacy”, starting in primary school.

Generation chatbot

Yet in the classroom, an upside-down hierarchy of knowledge has begun to emerge, according to Moon Sung-ho, the 16-year-old editor-in-chief of Tokipul, an independent student-run newspaper.

“In many cases, students actually know more about AI than teachers, resulting in students using AI to complete all of their assignments while teachers don’t really know how to stop them,” he said.

Song Keun-sang was among the educators who protested last year against the government’s short-lived 1.2 trillion-won plan to roll-out AI-powered textbooks.

“Once we actually tried using AI in the classroom, we realised that it wasn’t as useful as we had expected,” said the fifth-grade teacher at a school in South Chungcheong province.

While good teaching pushes students to learn more about the world, AI short-circuits this process, according to Song.

“It simply gives you the answers,” he said. “It doesn’t have much educational value.”

Song had once thought that AI might be useful to help isolated students or those struggling to make friends, but that changed after a child in neighbouring North Chungcheong province died by suicide following conversations with a chatbot.

“I wonder whether it is really beneficial for students to be exposed to chatbots that constantly cater to them and reassure them,” he said. “They are essentially designed to tell you what you want to hear, so you will never be challenged or face disagreements.”

The effects of this may already be starting to be felt. South Korean 15-year-olds topped global reading charts in 2006, as measured by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment.

Yet in 2025 they posted their lowest average reading score since the country first began taking part in the assessments in 2000, the OECD reported earlier this month.

“Other countries are starting to ban social media and other online devices for adolescents, but South Korea is moving in the exact opposite direction,” Song said. “We can already expect serious declines in academic achievement and literacy skills.”

The more pressing concern for him, however, is social rather than academic.

“Cooperation and communication between students ultimately develops the skills they will need to succeed in society later on,” he said, predicting that interacting with AI chatbots might make it “much more difficult to form relationships with other people.”

Moon has seen this happen among his own classmates and friend group, who once went to internet cafes and played football together, while also asking for help with homework assignments.

“Students these days increasingly ask AI chatbots about these questions,” he said. “It feels like it’s become more difficult to talk with people.”

This Week in Asia contacted South Korea’s Ministry of Education for comment on this article.

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China is playing it cool amid Trump’s disruption and churn
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the first part of a series, Mark Magnier looks at expectations in the US for the summit.

Chinese planners have been frustrated for months at the slow speed of decision-making and limited engagement by a distracted US administration as the days tick down to next week’s high-stakes summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

This may advantage Beijing by precluding trade and security concessions that require extensive groundwork, according to former US officials, analysts and people involved in coordinating the visit.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the first part of a series, Mark Magnier looks at expectations in the US for the summit.

Chinese planners have been frustrated for months at the slow speed of decision-making and limited engagement by a distracted US administration as the days tick down to next week’s high-stakes summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

This may advantage Beijing by precluding trade and security concessions that require extensive groundwork, according to former US officials, analysts and people involved in coordinating the visit.

“How are we going to get anything done if we can’t even agree on the basic logistics,” said a person involved in planning. “The Chinese are … not thrilled with it. But as a result, we have ever-shrinking expectations for the visit, and the Chinese are OK with that too.”

Any expectation of a massive soy deal or a large number of Boeing aircraft was a long shot, he added.

“The Chinese are all signalling that their expectations are very low, that there should have been more preparation,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director with the German Marshall Fund of the United States.

“It’s hard to identify anything that is a sure thing,” she added. “I haven’t heard the term ‘deliverable’ even used.”

But reduced expectations also speak to a US president who disparages planning in favour of in-person deals with his “gut” – and to increasingly frequent presidential summits.

“This is not a relationship where you can expect big numbers or major gift packages being announced any more,” said Yun Sun, China director at the Stimson Centre. “We seem to have unrealistic expectations that these two leaders should come together, sit down, announce the ending of all wars and world peace. That’s just unrealistic.”

While planning has picked up ahead of the first full US-China state visit in Washington since 2015, arrangements have been creaky as the White House juggles the Iran war, rising inflation and Trump’s declining popularity.

“There probably won’t be breakthroughs because Trump’s team is not capable of that,” said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst with the Eurasia Group. “But there also won’t be a breakdown.”

Drawn-out issues include a US$30 billion for US$30 billion, or “30-for-30”, reciprocal tariff reduction deal likely to be a summit cornerstone; extending a trade truce that expires next month; when, where, and on what issues meetings will be held; and who will meet an expected Chinese business delegation.

One impediment has been the small circle of White House decision-makers.

“It’s a bandwidth issue,” the person involved in planning said, citing a reluctance to involve the US president too early.

“You’ve got folks who don’t want to bring Trump into the discussion yet because they think he might land someplace different than they land,” he said. “The longer they put it off, the better people are going to be able to shape a contained visit.”

What each side hopes to achieve

For Trump, the summit is an opportunity to celebrate his power, host a strong leader he admires and bask in the pomp and ceremony he relishes.

“Trump wants a diversion, something showing he is a ‘big guy’ peer and managing China to good effect,” said Kevin Nealer, a partner with The Scowcroft Group consultancy. “My worry is they lack any affirmative agenda. There’s nothing we’re doing together and plenty that divides.”

Xi, meanwhile, can showcase China’s growing clout, solidify gains made on Taiwan and show that Beijing faced down the US on trade and prevailed.

“They want the world to see they can manage Trump and they want the world to say, ‘look, we’re being treated as the equal,” said Ryan Hass, China director at the Brookings Institution and former National Security Council (NSC) official.

“Part of their broader narrative is, we’re the new adults in the room; it’s the US that is the disrupter. They’ve got a lot of reasons that they want this to go right.”

Summit format to mirror Trump’s May trip to Beijing

The summit format will be a meticulous mirroring of Trump’s May trip to Beijing, lasting no more than 48 hours, with no additional stops, speeches or side trips out of the capital. This suits China’s equal footing messaging, analysts say. It also blunts criticism that Chinese business leaders accompanying Xi are outsourcing American jobs, since they are only replicating Trump’s entourage.

A key focus is likely to be the 30-for-30 tariff reduction framework. Washington wants to include US farm exports to appease Trump’s rural farm base hit by higher costs tied to the Iran war and his aggressive tariff policies.

It also wants China to export so-called 4A products to the US, such as apparel, footwear and televisions, to ease voter affordability concerns and address China’s failure to fully satisfy the 2020 phase one agreement. China, however, would rather export higher-value goods and has expressed interest in a package larger than US$30 billion that Washington reportedly balked at.

On the political front, China at one point offered over a dozen non-economic issues for discussion, according to one source, only to see these largely rebuffed, with the administration laser-focused on three: a possible November Xi-Trump meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen; a possible December meet-up at the G20 in Florida; and China’s help in pressuring Iran, something Beijing rejects given its ties with Tehran.

“It’s basically been the Chinese in a holding pattern, waiting for the US to stand up some sort of interlocutor,” the source, who declined to be named, said. “Two of those are logistics, and one of those is a non-starter … So, we have nothing to discuss on the political-diplomatic track.”

What was likely, analysts said, were some largely symbolic announcements on law enforcement, space, military communication and something on artificial intelligence, arranged this weekend by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng.

“We should have exceedingly low expectations for the AI dialogue. In all likelihood, it will be a one or two-hour conversation in consecutive translation between two men in their 60s and 70s,” said Jon Czin, a Brookings fellow and former CIA analyst. “Moreover, the administration does not have a coherent view on what – if anything – should be done about regulating AI at home, never mind in tandem with our principal competitor.”

Expect US-China trade truce to be extended

Another likely announcement is an extension of the trade truce Xi and Trump reached in South Korea last year. But even this had seen wrangling, analysts said. China pushed for a 24 or 27-month extension, while Washington sought six to 12 months, reportedly believing this boosted its leverage amid the lingering distrust over phase one outcomes.

Looming over the talks – and a source of Beijing’s growing confidence – is China’s tight control over global rare earth production essential for hi-tech products. While Beijing wants to cement its constructive strategic stability framework, those close to negotiations said Washington saw it more as a holding action until it eased China’s grip and potentially resumed its trade war.

“If it’s two years, it’s not strategic stability,” said the person involved in planning. “China has got one definition and Washington has got a very different definition.”

Taiwan not on the agenda

Taiwan was not expected to be contentious, sources said, given Beijing’s satisfaction with Trump’s suggestion in May that the US would not fight a war over Taiwan.

“If I were the Chinese, I would say “you got basically everything out of Trump that you are likely to get’,” said Zack Cooper, senior fellow with the conservative American Enterprise Institute.

“Anything else that he does carries at least a 50 per cent chance that he says something that you’re not going to like. So why poke this issue?”

Beijing will, however, likely convey its displeasure with any Taiwan arms sale soon after the summit – as seen with December’s record US$11 billion package – any interaction with Taiwanese officials or any record weapon sales.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is traditionally opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons.

Within the administration, meanwhile, mud wrestling and competing objectives abound. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been sidelined from most China discussions, partly given his prominent role in threatening 50 per cent tariffs against China leading up to “Liberation Day”. That backfired when China imposed rare earth restrictions.

“That revealed the American underbelly to the Chinese,” a Washington insider said.

Bessent remains the lead on the China file but has numerous other responsibilities, while US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer oversees the 30-for-30 framework, keen on helping achieve balanced trade and blunting Chinese exports that could further deindustrialise the US.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a long-time China hawk, meanwhile, had been noticeably quiet, potentially burnishing his anti-Communist credentials for any 2028 presidential run, analysts said.

This weekend’s expected Bessent-He meeting and Thursday’s call between Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi just days before the summit, also point to ineffective planning or outcomes.

“Maybe the Chinese are happy to have that,” said Cooper, a former NSC and Defence Department official. “But if anyone wanted a deliverable out of the summit, the last thing you’d do is wait until three days before arrival to try and hammer out the details.”

At least the two were talking, however, analysts said.

“Just to think how deeply hostile we were,” Sun said. “I’m not sure if it’s going to end well, but it’s already a miracle.

“The evaluation of whether this visit is a success should not just be contingent upon the big-ticket items.

“It’s also the overall stabilisation of the bilateral relationship, which people should remember could generate the largest nuclear war in human history. So on low expectations I would argue that no bad news is good news.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will China’s new local surtax provide relief for its regions’ fiscal headaches?
item.description:
As even China’s wealthiest provinces continue to run deficits and rely on the central government to make ends meet, Beijing is loosening the reins on the country’s highly centralised fiscal system, with legislation for a new tax category – the local surtax – under way.

Late last month, the Ministry of Finance unveiled a draft local surtax law for public consultation. The proposed tax would merge three existing levies – the urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge and local education surcharge – and would be charged on value-added tax (VAT) and consumption tax payments. Provincial governments would be allowed to set rates within an 11 to 13 per cent range.

Analysts described the move as a modest but constructive step in China’s broader fiscal reform agenda. While far from a cure-all for local financial distress, the change would give local authorities much-needed flexibility to manage their spending, they said.
item.content:encoded:
As even China’s wealthiest provinces continue to run deficits and rely on the central government to make ends meet, Beijing is loosening the reins on the country’s highly centralised fiscal system, with legislation for a new tax category – the local surtax – under way.

Late last month, the Ministry of Finance unveiled a draft local surtax law for public consultation. The proposed tax would merge three existing levies – the urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge and local education surcharge – and would be charged on value-added tax (VAT) and consumption tax payments. Provincial governments would be allowed to set rates within an 11 to 13 per cent range.

Analysts described the move as a modest but constructive step in China’s broader fiscal reform agenda. While far from a cure-all for local financial distress, the change would give local authorities much-needed flexibility to manage their spending, they said.

“It appears that the top leadership has heard the calls [for fiscal reform] and is aware that many localities, including coastal regions, are becoming cash-strapped,” said a frontline official with a local finance department in Zhejiang. Although the eastern province is among China’s most financially self-sufficient, it still posted a fiscal deficit of 360.6 billion yuan (US$53.8 billion) in 2025.

During China’s property boom, local authorities were able to rake in huge sums from selling land, enabling them to balance their books even as they handed over most tax revenue to the central government.

But a prolonged slump in the housing market has effectively closed off that source of income, leaving local governments under mounting pressure as they fund an expanding range of public services for a rapidly ageing population – from public transport to healthcare – and work to meet heavy bond repayment obligations.

The proposed local surtax marks the first move towards rebalancing the skewed fiscal relationship between China’s central and local governments – a long-term reform mandate laid out by the ruling Communist Party’s Central Committee at a plenum in July 2024.

“There is only one core reason the central government is pushing ahead with this reform this year – it’s time for fiscal rebalancing,” said Li Xin, a partner at Shenzhen-based DeHeng Law Offices. “Local authorities are under such acute fiscal strain that adjustments have become unavoidable.”

Turning fees into tax and making it an income stream for local authorities marks a step towards a bigger solution

Finance official, Zhejiang

How does the new surtax work?

Representing a “major component of China’s fiscal and taxation reform”, the proposed local surtax is poised to become “the largest single tax category” in China’s local tax system and a pillar source of income for provincial authorities, according to Tian Zhiwei, director of the Institute of Public Policy and Governance at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics.

But it was not designed to boost fiscal revenue, analysts from Moody’s Ratings said in a report this month, adding that the proposed local surtax rate was broadly aligned with the combined effective burden of the three existing charges it would replace, and that overall fiscal revenue was likely to remain broadly unchanged.

Under the current system, the urban maintenance and construction tax is levied at 7 per cent, 5 per cent or 1 per cent of VAT and consumption tax payments, depending on the taxpayer’s location, while the education surcharge and local education surcharge are fixed at 3 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively.

In 2025, the effective combined rate nationwide stood at 11.6 per cent, according to Xinhua, compared with the 11 to 13 per cent range proposed under the new legislation.

The reform would change the institutional status of these revenue streams from three sources distributed across tax, non-tax and government fund accounts to a single tax that would be fully retained by local governments, the Moody’s analysts said, adding that this would improve revenue transparency and simplify fiscal administration.

A key proposed change concerns the two education-related surcharges: by raising their status from fees to taxes, the reform would give provincial governments greater flexibility in spending the proceeds.

Currently, the two surcharges are earmarked for education-related spending, including the purchase of teaching equipment and school building renovations. If enacted, the new law would allow local authorities to use the revenue at their discretion.

In 2025, combined proceeds from the two education-related surcharges reached 396.4 billion yuan, according to Xinhua. If enacted, the reform would allow local governments to redirect the revenue towards repaying maturing debt and meeting civil service payrolls, with civil servants facing pay cuts and delayed salary payments even in some of China’s wealthiest regions.

“Turning fees into tax and making it an income stream for local authorities marks a step towards a bigger solution,” the Zhejiang official said, on condition of anonymity.

Meanwhile, experts said the reform would also streamline tax collection and cut compliance costs.

“On collection, three separate sets of rules will be consolidated into one … Taxpayers will only need to submit one tax return, lowering manpower-related costs for both businesses and tax authorities,” said Li, the Shenzhen lawyer.

With the two fees’ conversion into taxes, taxpayers who failed to pay or who underpaid their liabilities would face penalties, including overdue payment surcharges and fines, she added.

“This gives local tax authorities much stronger incentives to bolster tax collection,” Li said.

Relief for cash-strapped local governments?

In total, the three revenue sources generated 913.4 billion yuan last year, according to Xinhua. Although the proposed local surtax would be the largest tax source fully retained by local governments, its revenue would remain relatively modest.

Last year, domestic VAT revenue reached 6.9 trillion yuan (US$1.0 trillion), half of which is allocated to local governments under the current revenue-sharing arrangement.

Corporate income tax revenue totalled 4.1 trillion yuan, and personal income tax revenue amounted to 1.6 trillion yuan. The central government kept 60 per cent, leaving 40 per cent for local governments.

Consumption tax for the year brought in 1.7 trillion yuan. Imposed on certain categories of goods – such as alcohol, tobacco and fuel – the income generated goes entirely to the central government.

“The issue is that even with our income dropping, a big portion still needs to be turned over to the central government as state tax, leaving us with limited fiscal resources … The main complaint is that the state is taking too much,” said the Zhejiang finance official.

Daisy Xiao, director of Asia-Pacific international public finance ratings at Fitch Ratings, said the reform should modestly improve local revenue flexibility and spending discretion, but would be unlikely to materially ease structural pressure on local finances because debt growth had far outpaced the expansion of fiscal resources in recent years.

“The extra tax income would be small against persistent structural deficits, which are largely financed through special-purpose bonds linked to capital spending,” Xiao said.

“Even so, the measure is a constructive step in broadening more stable local revenue sources and giving local governments greater fiscal discretion,” she added.

More broadly, the move was consistent with China’s fiscal reform agenda and longer-term objective of reshaping local fiscal incentives away from property-related revenue and towards economic growth, consumption and sustainable tax bases, according to the Moody’s analysts.

“While incremental in nature, it represents a step in expanding provincial fiscal autonomy, supporting a more sustainable local revenue structure,” they added.

Rare autonomy for rate-setting

Under the proposal, provincial governments would be allowed to set the new rate within a range of 11 to 13 per cent, signalling greater flexibility.

“This is notable because most major tax rates in China are set by the central government, leaving local authorities with few levers to adjust revenue,” Xiao said.

Rate-setting discretion within an approved band would give provinces a limited additional countercyclical tool, allowing them to respond to changing revenue needs and local economic conditions, she added.

That is one reason why the central government gives provinces the discretion over setting tax rates – local authorities know their own circumstances best

Tian Zhiwei, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

Tian, from Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, said final tax rates would be the product of provincial governments’ “trade-offs”.

Authorities would need to strike a balance between retaining businesses and easing fiscal pressure: set the rate too high and they risk driving firms away; set it too low and they forgo revenue when public finances are already under strain, he said.

“That is one reason why the central government gives provinces the discretion over setting tax rates – local authorities know their own circumstances best,” Tian added.

Wealthier provinces may choose lower rates to strengthen their competitiveness, while fiscally weaker regions could opt for higher rates to bolster revenue, according to Moody’s.

“As a result, fiscal management could become incrementally more province-specific, reflecting local economic conditions and policy priorities,” the analysts added.

But the reform could also bring unintended consequences for some localities. Under the current urban maintenance and construction tax rules, a 7 per cent rate applies in urban areas, 5 per cent in counties and designated towns, and 1 per cent elsewhere, including rural areas and oil-producing fields.

As the proposed legislation would replace that system with a single rate across an entire province, businesses in counties and rural areas could face a higher tax burden, according to Li, the lawyer.

“From a provincial perspective, the overall tax burden may see little change, yet for individual companies, it translates into real-world cost increases.”

Additional reporting by Frank Chen

item.title: [SCMP] India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
item.description:
For 65 years, even as India and Pakistan fought wars, severed diplomatic ties and traded nuclear threats, one agreement held: the Indus Waters Treaty, which governs the river system sustaining roughly 300 million people across the subcontinent.

That was until April last year, when New Delhi suspended the pact in the aftermath of a deadly militant attack on tourists in Kashmir that it blamed on Islamabad.

Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry.
item.content:encoded:
For 65 years, even as India and Pakistan fought wars, severed diplomatic ties and traded nuclear threats, one agreement held: the Indus Waters Treaty, which governs the river system sustaining roughly 300 million people across the subcontinent.

That was until April last year, when New Delhi suspended the pact in the aftermath of a deadly militant attack on tourists in Kashmir that it blamed on Islamabad.

Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry.

On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that Delhi had no legal basis for suspending the water-sharing agreement, adding that India must also limit construction on the Ratle Hydroelectric Plant being built in Kashmir.

The court’s five-member panel was unanimous: none of the grounds India cited justified suspending or terminating the agreement.

It was a clean sweep for Islamabad, which brought the case after Delhi froze cooperation on the Indus and its tributaries – vital rivers that irrigate Pakistan’s agricultural heartland.

A role reversal

India has long cast Pakistan as the region’s rule-breaker, accusing it of harbouring militants and flouting international norms. But last month’s ruling flips that script, observers say.

“This is particularly attractive to Pakistan, as it turns a long-standing Indian tactic upside-down,” said Daniel Markey, a senior fellow with the Stimson Centre think tank’s South Asia programme, adding that the tribunal’s decision gave Pakistan “a diplomatic opportunity to exploit”.

“Even if Pakistan is only partially successful, it will relish the chance to muddy the waters and claim some high ground,” he said, describing the ruling as another front in a rivalry now “playing out in different forums, including this tribunal”.

Within hours of the ruling being issued, Delhi had rejected it outright, insisting that its decision to hold the treaty “in abeyance” would stand.

Islamabad’s reaction was equally swift and considerably more triumphant, with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar declaring on social media that the ruling “vindicates Pakistan’s consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside”.

Delhi disputes the court’s right to rule at all, however, calling it “illegally constituted” because the Indus treaty specifically requires both parties to agree on how an arbitration panel is formed.

“India is challenging the authority of the mechanism,” said Uttam Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses in Delhi.

Describing the stand-off as a contest over “sovereignty vs consent”, Sinha said India’s ambition was not to “turn off Pakistan’s water” completely but to finally exploit its own treaty rights on hydropower, storage, irrigation and the like.

“For decades, India had treaty rights and provisions on paper but had not developed the infrastructure necessary to harness them fully,” he said.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and senior fellow at King’s College London’s Department of War Studies, said Delhi was trying to “hide behind a technicality”, having previously turned to the very same court when it suited its own interests – notably in the case of Kulbhushan Jadhav, an Indian national sentenced to death by a Pakistani military court on espionage charges in 2017.

How can India now say that it will not comply? Politically, this will be very embarrassing

Ayesha Siddiqa, political scientist

“How can India now say that it will not comply?” Siddiqa asked. “Politically, this will be very embarrassing, though like the United States, it can refuse to honour the judgment.”

India’s actions are certainly not without precedent on the world stage.

Sriparna Pathak, an associate professor of international relations at O.P. Jindal Global University in India, points to the US’ 2019 exit from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty after Russia deployed a banned cruise missile system as one of several precedents for unilateral treaty suspension.

“States routinely invoke countermeasures … when they judge the other party’s conduct has destroyed the treaty’s object and purpose,” she said, citing a legal principle under which a fundamental shift in circumstances can void an agreement.

But Pathak is clear-eyed about what is really at stake. India has tied the treaty’s suspension to a demand that Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” end its support for cross-border militancy – a condition that is political rather than legal.

“That is a political precondition, not a technical one,” she said. “Compliance with The Hague order would undercut that position.”

It is a dilemma India has long tried to avoid by keeping bilateral disputes, especially over Kashmir, out of international forums altogether – wary that outside mediation legitimises exactly the kind of “internationalisation” Delhi has spent decades resisting.

Weaponised water

Behind the legal arguments lies the reality that water has become a lever for coercion.

In June, India’s minister of water resources, C. R. Patil, vowed that “not a single drop” would flow to Pakistan – prompting Islamabad to accuse Delhi of “weaponising” a shared resource and to warn, as it had in April, that any attempt to block or divert rivers would be treated as an “act of war”.

For now, at least, the threat is mostly rhetorical. India’s existing infrastructure cannot yet shut off Pakistan’s water supply, according to Markey, nor can it “single-handedly cause flooding”.

But as Delhi expands its hydroelectric and water storage capacity, its leverage will grow – and so will the inherent risks.

Bigger Indian dams and barrages would create “a more likely target for Pakistani military attacks in the event of future India-Pakistan hostilities”, Markey said.

“A return to the negotiating table looks unrealistic at the moment, but it will be the wiser course of action over time,” he added. “Neither side will readily benefit from pulling water to the centre of their bilateral dispute.”

Sinha, meanwhile, resisted the idea of a looming “water war”, preferring instead to describe what was happening as the “strategic securitisation of water” – a contest fought not with weapons but with infrastructure, data, timing and design.

That contest is now unfolding across the Indus River system, a vast basin of Himalayan tributaries spanning China, India and Pakistan upon which hundreds of millions of lives depend – and the latest flashpoint in a deep-rooted, acrimonious rivalry.

item.title: [SCMP] Why I am grateful for Asean’s endless meetings
item.description:
I remember 2011 well. Indonesia was chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and I was serving as deputy foreign minister for Asean cooperation. I learned a great deal, although if I had to summarise the experience in one word, I would say: meetings.

Asean members meet. They talk. They disagree. They issue statements. Then, quite remarkably, they meet again. We meet in conference rooms, coffee shops and restaurants. We speak by telephone and online. And when matters become particularly serious, there is always durian.

To outsiders, Asean consensus can appear tedious. Where is the breakthrough? Why does everything take so long?
item.content:encoded:
I remember 2011 well. Indonesia was chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and I was serving as deputy foreign minister for Asean cooperation. I learned a great deal, although if I had to summarise the experience in one word, I would say: meetings.

Asean members meet. They talk. They disagree. They issue statements. Then, quite remarkably, they meet again. We meet in conference rooms, coffee shops and restaurants. We speak by telephone and online. And when matters become particularly serious, there is always durian.

To outsiders, Asean consensus can appear tedious. Where is the breakthrough? Why does everything take so long?

Yet the longer I work in diplomacy, the more I appreciate the willingness to meet again, especially after a disagreement. Agreement is important, but it is not the only measure of successful diplomacy. Sometimes, the achievement is simply that disagreement does not end the conversation. This is what I understand as the habit of dialogue.

Working in Beijing, I see something familiar around Chinese dinner tables. A round table has no visible head, creating a sense of equality. Yet it does not remove order. Everyone has a place and everyone is expected to contribute.

Those who have conducted business in China will understand that many important decisions are shaped around such tables. Trust is built gradually, through conversation, shared food and the willingness to spend time understanding one another.

I wonder whether this habit offers a modest lesson for a world accelerating towards multipolarity. I use the word “accelerating” because the changing distribution of global power appears to demand immediate adjustment. Yet multipolarity does not tell us how power will be exercised or what kind of order will emerge.

China’s vision of an equal and orderly multipolar world recognises this challenge. Its Global Governance Initiative similarly places sovereign equality at the centre. But how can sovereign equality become a working practice? How can countries create order without simply recreating hierarchy?

Perhaps Asean can offer part of the answer.

International order needs power to sustain it, but it also needs limits on how power is used. Institutions make those limits more durable. Countries accept restraint because predictability benefits everyone: they know broadly what others may do, what they are unlikely to do and how disagreements will be managed.

The difficulty arises when power shifts. Established powers may fear that restraint gives rivals room to advance. Rising powers may question rules they had little opportunity to shape. When countries no longer believe restraint will be reciprocated, rules begin to give way to transactions. Every concession has a price. Every act of self-restraint starts to look like a favour that must be repaid.

Cooperation does not require countries to agree on everything. It requires them to preserve the means of working through what they cannot agree upon

This is especially complicated because power today takes many forms. One country may possess greater military strength, another greater manufacturing capacity, another financial influence, advanced technology or essential mineral resources. Strength in one area often exists alongside dependence in another.

Countries will not always share the same interests. But perhaps they can develop a shared understanding of how their different forms of power should be exercised.

Indonesia has Asean’s largest population and economy. By accepting consensus, Indonesia accepts a restraint on its weight. This restraint is useful because, as Bilahari Kausikan, a good friend of mine, has explained, consensus reassures smaller members that Indonesia cannot impose decisions upon them. It also reassures Indonesia that smaller members cannot simply combine to outvote it.

Each accepts limits in exchange for reassurance. No one gets everything but no one is expected to surrender everything either. This matters in a region of different political systems, cultures, levels of development and national interests. Such diversity complicates collective decisions. It also makes Southeast Asia difficult for any outside power to capture entirely behind a single agenda.

Its members may not converge on every interest, but they can converge on certain procedures, protocols, principles or concepts, for example, the non-use of force, a zone of peace, freedom and neutrality, a nuclear-weapon-free zone, Asean centrality and Asean-plus.

We have learned, imperfectly, how to disagree without immediately reaching for the divorce papers.

There are, of course, limits to Asean’s experience. Consensus can take time. Dialogue can become repetitive. Meetings can produce more meetings, sometimes followed by preparatory meetings for the next meeting. I would therefore hesitate to present Asean as a complete model for the global order. Its lesson is more modest: cooperation does not require countries to agree on everything. It requires them to preserve the means of working through what they cannot agree upon.

The habit of dialogue helps sustain this process. Equality gives every country a voice. Humility helps each country listen and recognise that it may not possess the whole answer. Repeated interaction gradually creates predictability.

Admittedly, habitual dialogue cannot erase power differences. It cannot resolve every dispute. But it can do something essential. It can create time when decisions are moving too quickly. It can lower the temperature when tensions are rising. And it can help countries adjust to power shifts without allowing every disagreement to become a crisis.

This is why I view the first Indonesia-China comprehensive strategic dialogue, held in Jakarta last month, with hope. Its importance lies not only in what was discussed but in the habit that made the discussion possible.

And there is quite a momentum to protect. Since 2015, the bilateral trade volume has tripled and Chinese investment has risen over 12-fold. At this pace, US$300 billion of trade in the next four to five years is within reach.

Through my years in China, I have walked its streets, met its people and spoken to many who will inherit whatever we build today. I do not know whether I have done enough. But I take some comfort in believing I have helped nurture the habit of dialogue. As long as we remain willing to meet again, we will always have something on which to build.

item.title: [SCMP] Saudi oil pipeline closure puts Asia’s economic resilience to the test
item.description:
Asian economies heavily dependent on imported energy are facing an even sharper squeeze after the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline removed a key escape route from the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, deepening an energy shock that has already pushed crude oil above US$100 a barrel.

Analysts said the loss of that bypass would hit Asian refiners first before feeding through to inflation, currencies and economic growth across the region.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, confirmed that the pipeline was shut as a precaution following an attack last week but did not disclose the extent of the damage, the number of affected pumping stations or a timetable for restarting operations, according to a Rystad Energy report on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
Asian economies heavily dependent on imported energy are facing an even sharper squeeze after the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline removed a key escape route from the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, deepening an energy shock that has already pushed crude oil above US$100 a barrel.

Analysts said the loss of that bypass would hit Asian refiners first before feeding through to inflation, currencies and economic growth across the region.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, confirmed that the pipeline was shut as a precaution following an attack last week but did not disclose the extent of the damage, the number of affected pumping stations or a timetable for restarting operations, according to a Rystad Energy report on Monday.

The closure leaves Saudi Arabia with fewer ways to keep crude moving to Asian buyers, raising the risk of delayed or reduced deliveries if the outage drags on.

Benchmark Brent crude oil, which surged to US$108 a barrel following the attack, was trading at US$104.6 during Asian evening hours on Friday, up more than 70 per cent year to date.

Before the attack, Saudi crude reaching Yanbu on the Red Sea coast could bypass the contested Strait of Hormuz, with tankers then able to head south through Bab el-Mandeb towards India and the rest of Asia or move north towards Egypt.

Rystad said Saudi Arabia had increasingly favoured the northern route because of the growing threat of attacks by Houthi militants.

Flows through Bab el-Mandeb should decline because fewer Saudi cargoes would be available to sail south, although the reduction would be partly obscured by already loaded vessels and non-Saudi traffic, Rystad added.

Asian oil refiners have the greatest direct exposure. Most Chinese and Indian customers had been instructed to lift September barrels from Yanbu, while Japanese and South Korean customers had increasingly been offered supplies through Sidi Kerir, an alternative route, the report said.

The market should therefore first see delayed or reduced deliveries into China and India, it said.

Janiv Shah, vice-president at Rystad, told This Week in Asia that Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam were among the most exposed to the oil supply disruption because of their dependence on imported energy and the resulting impact on transport, manufacturing and electricity costs.

“Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh are more vulnerable through inflation, foreign exchange rates and balances, while India faces a substantial increase in its overall import bill,” he said, adding that while Japan and South Korea were also highly import-dependent, they had stronger financial and strategic stock buffers.

Shah warned the development was likely to weigh on Asian countries’ economic growth.

“A short-lived price above US$100 per barrel should slow growth, but prices remaining elevated for multiple months would raise inflation, weaken consumption and increase fiscal pressures. The likely outcome is slower, more inflationary regional growth rather than an immediate recession,” he said.

The recent disruption would challenge global supply and demand “as we flip from a relatively balanced market currently to one that is heavily undersupplied in the next few months”, said the Rystad report.

An Oxford Economics report published on September 10 noted that neither an oil price shock nor higher trade tariffs imposed by the US had derailed Asia’s economic growth this year, driven by demand for AI-related hardware.

However, it predicted the region’s growth would drop by around 0.4 percentage points to 4.2 per cent next year, noting that Asian governments had absorbed much of the initial energy shock to protect consumers.

“Asian economies would feel the shock unevenly but the direction is clear. Southeast Asia would be particularly exposed because it sources close to 60 per cent of its crude from the Middle East,” said Ausaf Sayeed, India’s former ambassador to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

He noted that regional officials had estimated the pipeline would remain largely out of service for three to five weeks.

The pressure would spread through several channels, including larger import bills and current account deficits, higher prices for food, fuels and fertiliser, as well as weaker currencies and heavier subsidy outgo for their governments, he added.

US tariff threat

India, Asia’s second-largest crude oil importer, is facing a double whammy.

The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed legislation that could enable President Donald Trump to impose sanctions on Russia and up to 100 per cent tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. It will need Trump’s approval to be made into law.

India and China have been among the largest buyers of Russian oil.

Analysts believe China will keep buying Russian oil because overland pipelines protect its supply compared with maritime supplies, and the benefit of cheaper oil is likely to outweigh the US tariff threats.

Sayeed said the proposed legislation gave Trump the authority to grant waivers on the grounds of national interest. “The bill does not automatically impose a 100 per cent tariff on every country that buys Russian energy.”

Nevertheless, India will have to grapple with the dilemma of buying more expensive crude oil from elsewhere or potentially exposing its exports to substantial US tariffs.

“The immediate effect is therefore heightened policy and commercial uncertainty, not an already operative 100 per cent tariff,” he said.

India’s Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement on Thursday expressing concern about the proposed US legislation.

“India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people. It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics,” the statement said.

“This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.”

Russian oil supplies were not just another commercial option for India but an important diversification source when flows through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb were under stress, said Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at Indic Researchers Forum.

The loss of Saudi supplies also made other South Asian countries – Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh – vulnerable as energy imports affected their limited fiscal space, Sayeed said.

“Countries with weaker currencies, limited foreign-exchange buffers and large fuel subsidy burdens will feel a prolonged period above US$100 per barrel oil price more acutely than richer East Asian economies,” said Uday Chandra, a professor at India’s Ashoka University.

item.title: [SCMP] How will Beijing receive most senior Taiwan official to attend Apec events this year?
item.description:
In a rare development, Taiwanese Labour Minister Hung Sun-han is expected to travel to Nanjing on Sunday, becoming the first cabinet-level official under William Lai Ching-te’s administration to visit mainland China.

Hung will attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) ministerial meeting on Monday to discuss employment, vocational training, social security and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs.

Hung will be the most senior Taiwanese official to visit the mainland for Apec events this year. The island’s vice-minister of economic affairs, Lai Chien-hsin, took part in the energy ministerial meeting in Beijing last week and then chief trade negotiator Yang Jen-ni participated in a trade ministers’ meeting in Suzhou in May.
item.content:encoded:
In a rare development, Taiwanese Labour Minister Hung Sun-han is expected to travel to Nanjing on Sunday, becoming the first cabinet-level official under William Lai Ching-te’s administration to visit mainland China.

Hung will attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) ministerial meeting on Monday to discuss employment, vocational training, social security and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs.

Hung will be the most senior Taiwanese official to visit the mainland for Apec events this year. The island’s vice-minister of economic affairs, Lai Chien-hsin, took part in the energy ministerial meeting in Beijing last week and then chief trade negotiator Yang Jen-ni participated in a trade ministers’ meeting in Suzhou in May.

While Hung’s visit is being closely watched for signs of a possible thaw in a prolonged cross-strait stand-off, analysts have cautioned against interpreting it as an icebreaking trip or a resumption of official exchanges between Taipei and Beijing.

The trip will also take place just days before US President Donald Trump is expected to host Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, putting Taiwan under renewed scrutiny as their two powers seek to manage their differences.

Ahead of his departure, Hung stressed that Taiwan was a full Apec member under the name “Chinese Taipei”. He said he would take part under the grouping’s established arrangements and the principles of “equal participation and reciprocal dignity”.

His visit nevertheless carries symbolic weight because no cabinet minister – particularly a political appointee – has travelled to the mainland since Lai took office in May 2024, with official cross-strait dialogue remaining suspended.

“A small step by Hung Sun-han would be a big step for cross-strait relations,” said Lee Yen-hsiu, a lawmaker from the main opposition Kuomintang, a Beijing-friendly party.

Lee questioned whether the trip signalled a change in the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) approach towards Beijing after more than two years of promoting its “resist China, oppose China” agenda.

She said Hung’s visit could be seen as “a possible test by Lai of whether cross-strait relations could begin to thaw”.

DPP lawmaker Wu Szu-yao, however, urged Hung to remain alert to “potential personal safety concerns and the possibility of unequal treatment or politically motivated difficulties” while on the mainland.

But DPP legislative caucus whip Chuang Jui-hsiung dismissed such concerns.

“Are you kidding? If holding Apec in China meant there was a threat to someone’s personal safety, it wouldn’t just shock Taiwan – the whole world would be shocked by China,” Chuang said.

Analysts said Taipei might hope the trip created an impression of easing tensions, particularly ahead of the Washington summit.

“It is especially important before the sensitive Trump-Xi meeting to create an impression that Taiwan is not a troublemaker and hopes cross-strait relations can ease,” said Wang Kung-yi, head of the Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, a Taipei-based think tank.

But Wang said the trip could not be regarded as a genuine advance because Hung was attending a multilateral meeting and not direct talks with Beijing.

“If there were really a breakthrough, there would inevitably be substantive interactions, such as Hung meeting mainland officials,” he said.

Li Da-jung, a professor of international relations at Tamkang University in New Taipei City, similarly argued that the arrangement was standard.

“Taiwan is a full member of Apec, and to maintain its position in the international organisation, it has to send officials to attend the meeting,” Li said, adding that participation also helped maintain the island’s international visibility.

More important for Taipei, he said, would be the consequences of the coming Trump-Xi summit.

“Its impact on Taiwan remained uncertain, but Taipei would be watching closely to see whether Washington’s approach to the island – including pending arms sales – is affected by Trump’s talks with Xi,” Li said.

Analysts also doubted Beijing would create difficulties for Hung over his entry arrangements.

“Long-established arrangements have already governed participation in Apec meetings, and this is mainland China’s third time hosting the leaders’ meeting after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014,” Wang said.

Hung should therefore be able to enter using his Apec invitation letter under existing arrangements instead of using a mainland-issued Taiwan compatriot permit, he added.

Beijing has skirted questions over whether Hung must hold the permit.

“Since 1991, Taiwan’s participation in Apec meetings and activities has been handled in accordance with the ‘one-China principle’ as well as the provisions and established practices of relevant Apec memorandums of understanding,” Chen Binhua, a spokesman for the State Council’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said last week.

Zhu Fenglian, a spokeswoman for the Taiwan Affairs Office, reiterated on Wednesday that under the one-China principle, the “Taiwan region” took part in Apec under the name “Chinese Taipei” and as a regional economy.

Taipei rejects that interpretation, saying its 1991 Apec accession memorandum contains no reference to the “one-China principle” and provides for participation on an equal basis with other members.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Wang said the DPP could benefit politically if Beijing created difficulties for Hung – and thus Beijing was unlikely to take action that could inadvertently help the party electorally.

Huang Kwei-bo, a diplomacy professor at National Chengchi University in Taipei, said the DPP government was likely to stress that Hung was attending an international meeting rather than engaging in bilateral cross-strait exchanges.

He also cautioned against using the trip as a barometer of cross-strait relations because Beijing, as this year’s Apec host, was expected to invite representatives from all member economies, and Hung was only visiting because the Apec meeting happened to be held on the mainland.

Huang said Taipei’s choice of representative to the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November would be a more significant test.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Singapore’s big-box gyms are losing to niche fitness studios
item.description:
Property agent Raymond Heng had suspected True Fitness was struggling, but he did not expect the gym he had visited for more than a decade to disappear overnight.

The closure was not entirely surprising given the region’s fiercely competitive fitness industry, but its abruptness left Heng, 47, in disbelief after paying S$8,800 (US$6,900) for a lifetime membership in 2013.

“I guessed that they might not have been doing that well since branches have been closing over the years, but I did not expect the whole chain to disappear just like that,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
Property agent Raymond Heng had suspected True Fitness was struggling, but he did not expect the gym he had visited for more than a decade to disappear overnight.

The closure was not entirely surprising given the region’s fiercely competitive fitness industry, but its abruptness left Heng, 47, in disbelief after paying S$8,800 (US$6,900) for a lifetime membership in 2013.

“I guessed that they might not have been doing that well since branches have been closing over the years, but I did not expect the whole chain to disappear just like that,” he said.

Heng is among the many fitness fans left searching for a new gym after True Fitness abruptly ceased all operations in Singapore last week. Parent company Kontafarma China Holdings cited cost pressures and intense market competition for winding up the business.

Industry experts said the closure did not necessarily point to a saturated market in Singapore, but instead reflected shifting consumer preferences. Gym-goers are increasingly splitting into two camps: those seeking value and convenience, and those looking for specialised experiences beyond traditional big-box facilities.

Low-cost, 24-hour chains and niche boutique studios offering structured, guided classes are squeezing traditional full-service fitness centres from both ends of the market.

While the large-format gym model was attractive two decades ago, the market had fragmented, said Jack Tong, an assistant professor of business at Nanyang Technological University.

Operators now had to compete on all fronts, including experience and the sense of community they provided, he added.

“This leaves traditional full-service gyms potentially squeezed in the middle. They may find it difficult to compete with low-cost gyms on price while also struggling to compete with specialised operators on experience,” Tong said.

Natthavut Srinara, a lecturer and consultant at EHL Hospitality Business School in Switzerland, said that the old business models were falling out of favour. “Demand is now spread across many formats and price points, which makes the middle of the market increasingly difficult.”

Following True Fitness’ closure, budget and boutique gyms moved quickly to court displaced members, with franchises like Body Fit Training and Anytime Fitness waiving sign-up fees and offering complimentary sessions.

Price vs experience

A short walk from a closed True Fitness branch, Stella Loh laces up her boxing gloves.

Three times a week, the 60-year-old rotates between strength and Muay Thai classes at Hybe Fit, a hybrid training gym where curated programmes and attentive instructors make workouts less intimidating.

“Technique and safety are more important than simply lifting heavy weights,” Loh said.

Boutique studios like Hybe Fit have been popping up across Singapore in recent years, offering specialised workouts and personalised coaching that mass-market gyms rarely provide.

Hybe Fit co-founder Nuovo Tan said the studio had welcomed an increasing number of members seeking structured training since opening in the city state’s Orchard Road shopping district last month.

“We have [had] some conversions from open gyms, such as those who have been going to the gym for a while but don’t see progress due to a lack of a proper programme or guidance,” Tan said.

The popularity of functional fitness events like Hyrox has also provided a boost, with studios launching targeted programmes to prepare participants. Ground Zero, which launched as a spin studio in 2017 during the global rise of indoor cycling gyms, has expanded its offerings to include functional fitness and strength training while remaining open as a gym between classes.

Ground Zero founder Jeong Fok said their community-driven nature was a key selling point for boutique gyms.

“People who train at such studios want somewhere they can call their own, meet like-minded people, and actually feel like they belong … It almost becomes a modern-day version of a club or community space,” Fok said.

“I think that’s also connected to the rise of events like Hyrox – people just aren’t participating individually any more.”

But these specialised experiences come at a premium. An unlimited monthly pass at Hybe Fit costs S$360 – dropping to S$300 on an annual plan – while weekly access at Ground Zero ranges from S$70 to S$80.

Consumers’ willingness to spend substantial sums on fitness was no surprise, Srinara said.

“Consumers are becoming much more specific about what they want,” he said. “Premium customers are willing to pay more for better service, wellness experiences and networking opportunities.”

At the other end of the spectrum, price and accessibility top the priority list for Justina Tay, 26. The consultant pays S$95 a month for an Anytime Fitness membership, giving her 24-hour access to roughly 160 locations across Singapore.

“Convenience is the most important to building a consistent routine and Anytime Fitness has the most number of outlets,” Tay said.

The chain operates on a franchise model, with fitness group Inspire Brands Asia the master franchisee for Southeast Asia since 2020. Inspire Brands Asia did not immediately respond to requests for comment from This Week in Asia.

Calls for stronger protections

The sudden closure of True Fitness – which reportedly left customers suffering losses exceeding S$600,000 – has renewed calls for stricter consumer protection standards around long-term prepayments.

Holly Yang, a professor of accounting at Singapore Management University, said that while financial distress was evident in public filings from Kontafarma and True Fitness, ordinary consumers could not be expected to scrutinise financial statements before buying a gym membership.

In Singapore, financial records for companies such as True Fitness and True Yoga are available via the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority for a fee. However, tracking cross-border corporate structures is challenging.

Singapore operates a voluntary accreditation scheme called CaseTrust, under which participating firms that collect qualifying advance payments must implement prepayment protection measures. A government-run Consumer Protection Review Panel is currently evaluating whether existing safeguards for high-value packages are adequate.

Yang urged regulatory authorities to consider making insurance requirements mandatory for large advance membership fees.

“[The] information existed, but people had no reason to think they needed it, and no costless way to obtain it,” she added.

Kontafarma China Holdings, which is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange, has been contacted for comment.

item.title: [SCMP] Why the ICC is cracking down on ‘fake news’ as Duterte trial looms
item.description:
As Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes-against-humanity trial looms, an international tribunal faces the challenge of managing a sprawling prosecution case around the health of an 81-year-old former president of the Philippines, on top of shielding the proceedings from a highly charged media environment.

Those pressures came into focus at an International Criminal Court (ICC) status conference on Wednesday, when Presiding Judge Joanna Korner urged prosecutors to trim their witness list and evidence ahead of the November 30 trial opening while delivering a blunt warning against lawyers using the media in ways that could fuel “fake news”.

Legal experts say such warnings are not unusual in international criminal cases, but the breadth of Korner’s remarks reflects the particular difficulty facing the court as its proceedings are scrutinised, interpreted and sometimes distorted across the Philippines’ political and social media landscape.
item.content:encoded:
As Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes-against-humanity trial looms, an international tribunal faces the challenge of managing a sprawling prosecution case around the health of an 81-year-old former president of the Philippines, on top of shielding the proceedings from a highly charged media environment.

Those pressures came into focus at an International Criminal Court (ICC) status conference on Wednesday, when Presiding Judge Joanna Korner urged prosecutors to trim their witness list and evidence ahead of the November 30 trial opening while delivering a blunt warning against lawyers using the media in ways that could fuel “fake news”.

Legal experts say such warnings are not unusual in international criminal cases, but the breadth of Korner’s remarks reflects the particular difficulty facing the court as its proceedings are scrutinised, interpreted and sometimes distorted across the Philippines’ political and social media landscape.

Duterte was arrested in the Philippines and surrendered to the ICC in The Hague in March 2025. In April this year, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber confirmed all three counts of crimes against humanity against him – involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed as part of his war on drugs between November 2011 and March 2019 – and committed him to trial.

He appeared in person at the pretrial conference for the first time, looking thinner but walking unassisted and without a cane. News agencies said he waved to the audience and smiled slightly but did not speak.

Blunt reminder

During the case conference, Korner bluntly told defence and prosecution lawyers: “We see no reason why counsel should feel it necessary to make any comment to the media. The appropriate forum for counsel to raise matters is in the courtroom. Trials are not conducted by the court of public opinion, but by this court during the course of the proceedings.”

She criticised in particular Duterte’s former counsel Nicholas Kaufman, who she said had made “wholly inappropriate” personal comments in at least three media interviews about decisions by the Pre-Trial Chamber and Appeals Chamber despite “a reminder to him to remember that he had a professional duty to be respectful and courteous to the chamber”.

Korner noted that “this case has attracted, not surprisingly, a substantial amount of media interest in the Philippines in particular” – in mainstream and social media – “as to have provoked suppliers of what is undoubtedly fake news and obviously fake news”.

“The first thing we wish to emphasise is the need for the media to report to the public accurately and fairly what is said in court and above all to avoid speculation,” Korner said.

Two legal experts on the ICC told This Week in Asia that Korner’s reminder was not unique to Duterte’s case, although the former president’s rise to power and continuing political influence have been closely intertwined with social media.

For British legal expert Tom Smith, who has been closely following Duterte’s case and other ICC proceedings, the judge’s warning “is not unprecedented”.

“What is striking here is the breadth and bluntness of Judge Korner’s warning, and her explicit recognition of the Philippine disinformation environment,” said Smith, an associate professor in international relations at the University of Portsmouth and academic director of the Royal Air Force College.

“This was not simply concern about an indiscreet lawyer. Kaufman’s interviews were feeding an enormous political and social media ecosystem in which incomplete or inaccurate claims about the ICC could be turned into supposed facts within hours.”

Smith stressed that the court had not imposed a formal gag order on the media, but warned of “a danger for the ICC”.

“If the lawyers stop speaking and the court does not communicate the proceedings clearly and quickly, the resulting information vacuum will be filled by the Duterte political network,” Smith said.

“The ICC cannot defeat disinformation simply by asking everyone to remain silent. It must explain its own decisions far more effectively to Filipinos.” .

The ICC had issued warnings in previous cases, said Ruben Carranza, a senior expert at the International Centre for Transitional Justice, which advises victims in cases before war crimes tribunals such as the ICC, including on reparations.

Carranza recalled that in the case of former Kenyan president Uhuru Kenyatta, his indicted co-accused were warned by ICC judges “to not issue statements to the media or to the public that would tend to incite more political violence in Kenya”.

‘Enormous’ amount of evidence

Korner also told prosecutors to “think long and hard” about trimming some 15,000 exhibits – including documents and videos – and their witness list covering 57 separate incidents.

Lead prosecutor Julian Nicholls said prosecutors had already begun cutting both, after initially estimating they would need between 175 and 200 hours just to present witnesses.

Duterte’s lead counsel Peter Haynes called the volume of evidence “enormous” and raised concerns about duplicate and incomplete records.

Legal experts said such large volumes of material were not unusual in crimes against humanity cases, where prosecutors must prove not only individual killings but also a broader attack on civilians and the accused’s connection to it.

Carranza indicated that Haynes was familiar with handling an enormous amount of evidence, as Haynes had handled the case of the convicted Congolese politician Jean-Pierre Bemba Gombo on appeal where he had to review “over 5,700 pages of evidence and [testimonies of] more than 70 witnesses”. Bemba was acquitted in 2018.

“This case is also unusually documentary because Duterte was president and the Philippine police and government generated extensive records,” Smith said. “Even the prosecution acknowledged that there is more material than in other cases its lawyers have handled.”

The defence, however, had “legitimate concerns [about] … duplicate records, individual pages being treated as separate exhibits and incomplete documents”, Smith added.

“The raw number tells us very little about the strength of the case. Sixty-two thousand disclosed items are not the same as 62,000 pieces of compelling evidence.”

Smith said the prosecution’s estimated courtroom hours also excluded cross-examination and procedural arguments, meaning the trial could run substantially longer once proceedings began.

His “cautious” estimate was: “Two to four years from the opening of the trial is more realistic, particularly if health disputes and appeals continue.”

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea’s president rejects US request for Iran war support
item.description:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has drawn a clear line against any US request for Seoul to join the war against Iran, explicitly ruling out the dispatch of troops or military assets that could involve his country in the conflict.

The stance comes amid mounting public opposition to any military deployment and growing pressure from Washington for Seoul to contribute to efforts to secure freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Lee’s government faces the difficult task of balancing its security alliance with the United States against the risks of becoming entangled in a distant conflict that could expose South Korean forces, citizens and commercial interests to Iranian retaliation.
item.content:encoded:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has drawn a clear line against any US request for Seoul to join the war against Iran, explicitly ruling out the dispatch of troops or military assets that could involve his country in the conflict.

The stance comes amid mounting public opposition to any military deployment and growing pressure from Washington for Seoul to contribute to efforts to secure freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Lee’s government faces the difficult task of balancing its security alliance with the United States against the risks of becoming entangled in a distant conflict that could expose South Korean forces, citizens and commercial interests to Iranian retaliation.
