“There will be no dispatch of troops or military assets that would lead to involvement in a conflict. There will be no engagement or involvement in war. I can say that clearly,” Lee said during a televised press conference on Friday. “We’ve been sticking to this principle, and this principle won’t change.”

His remarks represent the clearest signal yet of Seoul’s position regarding US President Donald Trump’s demands. Washington argues that countries benefiting from American operations in the Strait of Hormuz should contribute to the military effort.

South Korea initially appeared to be weighing a role in the strategic waterway, sending a fact-finding team to the Middle East while balancing US pressure against Iranian threats of retaliation. A security briefing on the team’s findings – originally scheduled for Thursday – did not take place ahead of Lee’s press conference.

Lee ruled out sending combat troops or placing them under foreign command, an issue of particular sensitivity as his administration seeks to regain wartime operational control over South Korean forces from the US military leadership by 2030.

He acknowledged that distinguishing between defensive protection and military involvement could be challenging, but he said Seoul would not cross that line.

“Let me make it clear once again: there will be no deployment for war,” Lee said.

However, Lee said South Korea would maintain “the minimum level of activities” to protect its merchant ships, crude oil transport routes and citizens abroad, pointing to the deployment of the Cheonghae Unit – a naval anti-piracy task force operating in Middle Eastern waters.

He said the government was considering ways to strengthen the unit’s defensive capabilities without escalating into direct military intervention.

Trump’s pressure

South Korea’s president noted that several other countries had deployed military assets near the Strait of Hormuz, with some committing to post-conflict recovery while others focused strictly on protecting commercial shipping and their citizens.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Lee “firmly stated his stance against dispatching military assets or troops to the raging war”.

But he noted that Seoul had promised to support post-war efforts to restore freedom of navigation through the strait, a route that accounted for roughly 70 per cent of South Korea’s crude oil imports before the war and a significant share of its natural gas and petrochemical feedstocks.

“His statement on this issue will help put domestic controversies and concerns to rest, although Washington is unlikely to be happy with it,” Yang said.

Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, said Lee had made it clear that a deployment would only be for “post-conflict multinational stabilisation efforts”, such as mine clearing.

The Trump administration has repeatedly singled out South Korea over its reluctance to help the US in its war against Iran. Speaking to reporters at the White House last month, Trump recounted a conversation in which Lee rejected his request for support.

“I called him, I said, ‘Would you like to give us a little hand? We don’t need help with Iran. But if you would like, give us a hand with Iran.’ He said, ‘No thanks’,” Trump recalled. “And I said, ‘Wait a minute. We have 39,000 soldiers over there guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbour. And you’re not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran?’ That’s strange.”

South Korea hosts about 28,500 US troops.

A delicate balancing act

Aside from Hormuz, the two allies are currently navigating several other major economic, trade and security issues.

These include the implementation of South Korea’s commitment to a US$350 billion investment package in the United States – which includes US$150 billion for shipbuilding – regulatory scrutiny over US-listed technology platforms such as Coupang and stalled progress on Seoul’s acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines.

Against this backdrop, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun left for Washington on Thursday for talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Domestically, Lee is also under pressure. Jhee Byong-kuen, a political-science professor at Chosun University, said that the president was “putting his foot down” on the deployment issue to avoid further damaging his sliding approval ratings, which took a hit from recent real estate reforms.

Hundreds of South Korean civic, religious and labour organisations have held rallies demanding that the government reject US demands. Opposition to military action has also surfaced within the ruling coalition.

“Even US public opinion polls show that 66 per cent of Americans do not support this war. We could be driving our young people into a situation where their lives and safety are jeopardised,” said Woo Won-shik of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, a former National Assembly speaker.

South Korea sent about 320,000 troops to the Vietnam war – the second-largest foreign force after the US – and sent 3,600 personnel from the non-combat Zaytun Division to northern Iraq in 2004 under liberal president Roh Moo-hyun.

The Iraqi deployment sparked deep domestic political divisions and severely eroded Roh’s support base. Roh later reflected in his memoir, Destiny: “I authorised the deployment not because I believed it was right, but because it was an unavoidable choice … The Iraq troop deployment will go down in history as a wrong decision.”

Professor Jhee said: “President Lee must have learned a lesson from former president Roh’s bitter experience”.

item.title: [SCMP] 3 new pastry chefs in Hong Kong who are redefining desserts with innovative twists on classics
item.description:
Upon entering a restaurant, the way you are greeted and seen to your table provides that vital first impression. But come the end of a meal, it is up to dessert to ensure diners leave on a high note, no matter what came before.

“It’s the finale … a bad dessert can ruin the meal,” insisted Anne McManus, then executive pastry chef at Manhattan’s Maloney & Porcelli, in an interview in 2000.

Since the pandemic, as Hong Kong’s F&B industry deals with a labour shortage and a change in dining habits, the role of many pastry chefs has shifted. No longer is their sole focus crafting plated desserts. Now, they are frequently a more involved member of the wider chef’s team, responsible too for innovation and polishing recipes for takeaway.
item.content:encoded:
Upon entering a restaurant, the way you are greeted and seen to your table provides that vital first impression. But come the end of a meal, it is up to dessert to ensure diners leave on a high note, no matter what came before.

“It’s the finale … a bad dessert can ruin the meal,” insisted Anne McManus, then executive pastry chef at Manhattan’s Maloney & Porcelli, in an interview in 2000.

Since the pandemic, as Hong Kong’s F&B industry deals with a labour shortage and a change in dining habits, the role of many pastry chefs has shifted. No longer is their sole focus crafting plated desserts. Now, they are frequently a more involved member of the wider chef’s team, responsible too for innovation and polishing recipes for takeaway.

Despite these changes, Hongkongers’ fascination with sweet treats remains strong, and not all restaurants are abandoning the old ways. This summer, three new faces are making waves in the dessert scene, facing down the challenges and looking to leave a lasting impression.

Eve Minialai – Louise

Born in Hong Kong but having relocated to France with her family at just one year old, Eve Minialai spent her formative years in Europe’s culinary heartland.

After an apprenticeship at La Violette in Paris in 2014, the then future pastry chef perfected her craft with stints at Hotel Plaza Athénée alongside the legendary Alain Ducasse, and as a pastry sous chef at Pavyllon Paris under patissier Thomas Moulin and owner Yannick Alléno.

Working with some of the most celebrated chefs in the world provided Minialai with a thorough education, albeit a particular French one.

“Everything is different working in Paris,” she says. “The management style, the mentality and the market are all different to anywhere else in the world … including satisfying the French palate, with their stronger preference for crispy textures over Hong Kong’s preference for smoother textures.”

Now back in Hong Kong, in her first role in the city as head pastry chef for French fine dining restaurant Louise, Minialai is channelling all her abilities into crafting desserts for a clientele that also prefers them “sweet but not too sweet”. As a result, Minialai, an avid fan of contemporary pastry, has been creating innovative takes on traditional desserts. “My creations are the classics but with modern nuances. I don’t want to fixate on change for the sake of change,” she says.

The use of a calamansi sorbet in her crepes Suzette is a case in point. Swapping the traditional ice cream for a sorbet brings a refreshing zing of citrus tang that cuts through the buttery orange sauce. The Paris-Brest works according to the same principle. There’s an explosive abundance of roasted hazelnuts in every bite, but set against crunchy praline and a tender choux pastry exterior, the result is sufficiently sweet.

Minialai enjoys working with variations on a common theme. Her new Pineapple dessert is just that – a varying array of preparations of the tropical fruit: roasted, pickled, infused and more. The Rice is similar, featuring everything from a Niigata rice pudding to caramelised puffed rice, each take offering bewitching and contrasting textures.

Leo Faler – Cristal Room by Anne-Sophie Pic

Although barely 30, Leo Faler, head pastry chef at Cristal Room by Anne-Sophie Pic, has spent much of his career working alongside culinary masters. Born in Normandy, he did all his pastry training in France, eventually working alongside Yannick Alléno before moving to Singapore, and subsequently Hong Kong, for roles with Anne-Sophie Pic.

“I learned to make desserts with my mother when I was small,” Faler tells us. “Growing up in a family surrounded by home-grown fruits and vegetables for sweets and bakes helped me understand the science and art of desserts, especially the healthier options that bring a smile without [you] feeling bloated or unhealthy.”

Working for the likes of Anne-Sophie Pic, Faler now has to design a list of desserts that highlight the French chef’s signature style and flavour profiles. Often, for each new menu, the signature mille-feuille blanc gets a makeover, together with the creation of a chocolate dessert, an item featuring fruit and nuts, and a further optional fruit-based dessert that rotates according to what’s available that season. “The seasons are the most honest source for inspiration,” Faler says in summary.

After two years in Hong Kong, Faler believes he has established a sound understanding of local tastes. His Pineapple Vacherin, for instance, pairs pineapple with lovage, a herb with vegetal notes most similar to celery. This dessert combines herb-cooked pineapple cubes with a sorbet of pineapple, as well as lovage, green lovage tuile and lovage powder dusted on French meringue and pistachio shortbread. Its refreshing balance of sweet and sour provides a beguiling invitation to appreciate the popular European herb.

Raspberry and Seaweed is another playful harmony of flavours. The fruit comes in forms of a pâte de fruits confit, gastrique and sorbet, each sweetly paired with the micro cress and ice cream of sea fennel, with deep-fried dried seaweed sprinkled all over the dessert for a dry crunch. The striking contrast of flame red and forest green yields a highly photogenic dessert, and a beloved melange of herbs helps bring out the sweetness of the raspberries.

When I first started, I tried to jam in everything to show my guests that I could do it all. It was only later I came to agree with the notion that ‘simplicity is best’

Astoria Koh, Caprice

Faler’s recent Chocolate dessert introduces a playful twist on traditional after-dinner chocolate mints. Featuring five different kinds of mint, a soft chocolate sponge cake and minty chocolate mousse are stacked up against chocolate crèmeux and tempered chocolate in a vibrant mix. Another of his desserts saw a spread of pandan-infused coconut tapioca and coconut pandan sorbet pay homage to his time in Singapore.

“At the beginning, guests often responded that our desserts were too sweet, with ingredients too unfamiliar to them, such as rose geranium, rhubarb and tonka beans. We respect our guests’ palates and we’ve learned to slowly introduce these ingredients to them while making sure to remember what they enjoy the most. After all, our job as pastry chefs is to create sweet satisfaction for our guests.”

Astoria Koh – Caprice

Despite having worked at Caprice for seven years, where she is a crucial member of the chef’s team led by Guillaume Galliot, seasoned pastry chef Astoria Koh has only recently come into the spotlight.

Starting out, the Singaporean native worked part-time in a local bakery in the Lion City while majoring in interior architecture and design at university. The job helped her gain expertise, both theoretical and hands-on, in breads and pastries. Once she graduated, she chose to make pastries her career.

Determined to pursue her dream, Koh moved to Macau to work under Galliot when he was at City of Dreams’ The Tasting Room. She spent five years there working with him designing degustation menus, where the sweets needed to cohere with savoury courses. She returned to Singapore for a nine month stint working for Joël Robuchon before an offer arrived to reunite with Galliot, by then in Hong Kong, at Caprice, where she has been ever since.

“When I first started, I tried to jam in everything to show my guests that I could do it all,” Koh says. “It was only later that I really came to agree with the notion that ‘simplicity is best’. It’s never easy to execute but I’m up for the challenge.”

Koh introduces to us a trio of desserts that are now staples at Caprice.

The Strawberry is an annual dish that changes style and content each time strawberry season comes round. The 2025 version leverages the flexibility of the fruit – presenting it in the form of ice cream, yogurt mousse and consomme, accented with a fanned display of gariguette strawberries and semolina sable for texture. Visually straightforward, the dessert relies on surprises in texture and flavour to impress – the strawberries’ sweetness is balanced with just the right amount of tartness from the yogurt and lemon cream.

The festive Chocolate dessert is a playful interpretation of pairing chocolate and caramel, where the caramel cremeux and praline sable match well with chocolate mousse, whipped ganache, dark chocolate ice cream, and a sharp passion fruit caramel. That tartness can often be found in Astoria’s creations, lending a balancing element to tame the inherent sweetness in desserts, creating an alchemy, if not illusion, of a less-sweet dessert while also offering a wider range of textures too.

If there is one skill Koh hasn’t quite mastered yet, it’s customer interaction. She rarely shares her creations on social media, instead creating a feed filled with travelogues and K-pop concerts

“Being a chef is hard work but … I learned that I can do my best work when I can be myself when I’m not in the kitchen,” she says. “I feel my hobbies and fondness for K-pop give me room to breathe and relax. They often get me pumping and filled with high spirits to work harder when I come back from concerts.”

Koh says she is working on becoming more sociable and better at introducing her work through interactions with her guests, adding that whatever nerves she displays on the outside, inwardly, sharing the nuances of her creations makes her feel invincible as a chef. Clearly, her efforts to get her where she is today have been worth the long hours of dedicated practice.

item.title: [SCMP] Bail out or downsize? Malaysia’s stark choice as AirAsia losses mount
item.description:
Malaysia could struggle to preserve some domestic air links if low-cost carrier AirAsia is forced to scale back operations, analysts have warned, as rival airlines would have little commercial incentive to take over unprofitable routes.

That reality could leave the government facing a stark choice: allow domestic flight services to shrink or step in with subsidies for essential routes, rather than assuming competitors will automatically fill any void left by the country’s largest budget airline.

The concern has taken on added urgency as AirAsia seeks fresh financing following a sharp rise in jet fuel costs, which contributed to heavy losses across its wider airline group.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia could struggle to preserve some domestic air links if low-cost carrier AirAsia is forced to scale back operations, analysts have warned, as rival airlines would have little commercial incentive to take over unprofitable routes.

That reality could leave the government facing a stark choice: allow domestic flight services to shrink or step in with subsidies for essential routes, rather than assuming competitors will automatically fill any void left by the country’s largest budget airline.

The concern has taken on added urgency as AirAsia seeks fresh financing following a sharp rise in jet fuel costs, which contributed to heavy losses across its wider airline group.

The government had already sounded out full-service flag carrier Malaysia Airlines and hybrid operator Batik Air on whether they could expand into AirAsia’s domestic routes should its financial position worsen, Reuters reported on Wednesday.

Both carriers indicated a willingness to take on more routes, but doing so at scale could require them to assume AirAsia’s existing aircraft leases, according to two sources familiar with the discussions.

Batik Air chief executive Chandran Rama Muthy separately told national news agency Bernama that the carrier was able to “bring aircraft in quickly” to help meet domestic demand if required.

According to data from the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia, AirAsia handled a third of all passengers passing through Malaysian airports in the first quarter of the year, compared with 17.1 per cent for Malaysia Airlines and 10.3 per cent for Batik Air.

Malaysia has no other large-scale budget operator; Firefly, the next largest domestic carrier, accounted for just 4 per cent of traffic.

Domestic difficulty

Analysts said rival airlines were most likely to prioritise adding capacity to commercially attractive routes, leaving thinner, secondary domestic services vulnerable.

Wang Kun, an assistant professor at Hong Kong Polytechnic University’s Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, said international routes within Southeast Asia were generally more attractive to carriers because of established demand and existing low-cost competition.

“If the expected commercial return is insufficient, other airlines may choose not to enter the route or may provide less capacity unless an appropriate support mechanism is available,” Wang said.

He added that even profitable routes could not be replaced overnight, as expansion would depend on aircraft availability, staffing, airport slots and other operational bottlenecks.

Fu Xiaowen, a transport economist and head of the same department, agreed that while competitors would probably move into AirAsia’s profitable routes over the medium to long term, they could not stretch existing fleets and crews indefinitely.

“There’s a safety limit on the number of hours a pilot can fly,” Fu said, adding that the government could protect essential links by allowing fewer flights rather than trying to match AirAsia’s previous schedules.

Wang said routes deemed essential but not commercially viable could be sustained through targeted passenger or seat subsidies, government purchases of capacity or competitive tenders in which airlines bid to operate them.

Malaysia already uses such a model: the federal government pays 209 million ringgit (US$50 million) annually to subsidise rural air services in Sabah and Sarawak. Those routes are now operated by state-owned AirBorneo, which took over the operations from Malaysia Airlines’ regional arm, MASwings, in January.

Extending such frameworks could protect vital domestic links without requiring a broader state bailout of an airline.

Fu said government intervention would come with significant costs, including to taxpayers and through the precedent it set for future rescues.

“But if you do not intervene, it’s going to create a disruption to the whole economy,” he added, pointing to the effects on passengers, creditors, suppliers and local government.

Fuel squeeze

The contingency planning comes as AirAsia’s parent group faces mounting financial pressure caused by this year’s surge in global fuel prices.

While Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air were similarly exposed to the rising costs, AirAsia faced the spike largely unhedged after shelving its hedging plans in January. By April, chief executive Bo Lingam acknowledged the carrier could not afford to hedge at prevailing prices.

Jet fuel prices surged to average US$183 a barrel in the second quarter amid market disruptions due to the Iran war.

AirAsia Group subsequently reported a headline net loss of 830.5 million ringgit, which included 331 million ringgit in foreign-exchange losses. The group said its core short-haul operations in Malaysia remained profitable, with losses concentrated in its long-haul business and regional subsidiaries in Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia.

Wang said budget airlines were particularly vulnerable to fuel price volatility because fuel made up a large share of their variable operating costs compared with full-service carriers, which generated additional revenue from services including meals and checked baggage.

AirAsia’s second-quarter accounts show current liabilities of 18.4 billion ringgit against 954 million ringgit in cash reserves at the end of June.

The carrier is seeking up to US$1 billion in international debt and 700 million ringgit in local credit lines, though sources cited by Reuters say it needs at least US$3 billion.

In a September 2 statement, AirAsia Group said its fundraising was primarily aimed at debt restructuring, refinancing and consolidating its balance sheet.

Fu said the exact size of the funding shortfall would heavily influence policymakers’ response.

“If they are close to a deal, the government only needs to provide some support,” Fu said, while a much larger shortfall could be a signal for the government to proceed more cautiously.

Wider economic costs

Mohd Harridon Mohamed Suffian, an associate professor at Universiti Kuala Lumpur, said AirAsia’s low-fare model supported a wider network of small businesses, hospitality vendors and technical subcontractors dependent on passenger volumes.

“AirAsia employs thousands of workers, and there are numerous subcontractors,” he said.

Allowing AirAsia to collapse would be “financially calamitous” for Malaysia’s economy, Harridon said, though he stressed that the carrier should first try to raise funds privately. Should state-backed guarantees or loans eventually be needed, Harridon added, the government “should have a say in AirAsia’s financial operations”.

AirAsia had previously said it did not comment on market speculation. However, deputy group chief executive Farouk Kamal told Reuters the airline remained focused on business continuity and continued to see strong demand.

Any job losses would also reverberate through an already saturated aviation labour market.

A representative for the National Union of Flight Attendants Malaysia said on September 10 the country was “overflooded with aviation professionals, especially technical engineers and pilots”, adding that qualified Malaysian staff were also being recruited by overseas operators, particularly airlines in the Middle East.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia confronts complexities of schizophrenia after school killing ruling
item.description:
When Cindi suffered her first severe psychotic episode a decade ago, she could no longer tell where reality ended and her imagination began.

“My reality and fantasy [were] all distorted. I had no idea what was real, what was not,” the 38-year-old, who asked to be identified only by her first name, told This Week in Asia.

“It was so severe to the point that I couldn’t even recognise my own family members. My mother was there, my brother was there, but they didn’t feel like my mother or my brother.”
item.content:encoded:
When Cindi suffered her first severe psychotic episode a decade ago, she could no longer tell where reality ended and her imagination began.

“My reality and fantasy [were] all distorted. I had no idea what was real, what was not,” the 38-year-old, who asked to be identified only by her first name, told This Week in Asia.

“It was so severe to the point that I couldn’t even recognise my own family members. My mother was there, my brother was there, but they didn’t feel like my mother or my brother.”

Her experience has taken on new resonance in Malaysia after a court acquitted a 15-year-old boy of murdering his schoolmate Yap Shing Xuen, 16, on the grounds that severe schizophrenia had left him legally insane when he killed her at their school in Bandar Utama, outside Kuala Lumpur, last October.

Yap was found dead in a school toilet after suffering at least 180 stab wounds, according to a forensic report, in a killing that shocked Malaysia and intensified concerns over safety in the country’s schools.

On Monday, the Shah Alam High Court accepted testimony from forensic psychiatrist Ian Lloyd Anthony that the teenager had severe schizophrenia and was incapable of understanding the nature of his actions or that they were wrong.

His lawyer Kitson Foong earlier told This Week in Asia that the boy’s condition had gone untreated for several years before the attack.

“The court held that, because of his illness, the child offender did not know the nature of what he was doing and did not know that it was wrong or against the law,” Foong said.

After his acquittal, the boy was sent to Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta, a psychiatric hospital in Perak state, for treatment, counselling and medication.

Foong said the boy would remain there until he was assessed to no longer pose a threat to society, with any eventual release dependent on medical and psychiatric reports presented to the Sultan of Selangor.

But much of the anger since the ruling has centred on the word “acquitted”, with some Malaysians questioning why the boy should escape a murder conviction and others arguing that an insanity verdict had been mistaken for freedom.

In one online forum, the verdict quickly split opinion. Some users called for the death penalty and invoked “a life for a life”, while others stressed that the boy had not simply walked free and remained in psychiatric custody.

Yap’s mother, Wong Lee Ping, has also urged the public to back a petition calling on Malaysia’s Attorney-General’s Chambers to appeal against the acquittal, saying her family had few avenues of its own to challenge the decision.

“We are neither judges nor prosecutors. We are simply a family who has lost our daughter,” Wong said on social media, adding that the family wanted the proper legal process, including any available right of appeal, to be considered.

Cindi said she understood why the case frightened people because her own first psychotic episode in 2016 took her to a place she still struggles to explain.

At one point, frightened and feeling alone, she took out knives. After her mother locked her in an outside kitchen, Cindi repeatedly stabbed the door trying to get out.

“I felt very out of control, basically,” she said. “It’s like I’m witnessing everything from a different point of view, but I don’t know why or how to explain why I do this. I feel like I’m just looking at what I’m doing, but I cannot stop it … by then it was too late because I’ve already done the action.”

Police eventually took her to a psychiatric ward, where she was observed for about two weeks before being diagnosed with schizophrenia.

She then went seven years without another psychotic episode and today works, raises a five-year-old son and attends therapy, although severe stress can still trigger symptoms.

During a recent episode, Cindi called a crisis hotline and told her family she needed their help. As someone on the line talked her through what she was experiencing, she said the negative voices gradually stopped and she began to feel normal again.

“With the right intervention, with the right medication, with the right support, we are just as normal as anyone else,” she said.

Diagnosis in the dock

About 27 million people worldwide, or roughly one in every 300, live with schizophrenia, according to the World Health Organization, which lists persistent delusions and hallucinations among symptoms that can profoundly alter how a person perceives reality.

Mariani Md Nor, a psychologist and vice-chancellor of SEGi University, said severe psychosis could seriously impair judgment and a person’s understanding of their actions, but that was not the experience of everyone diagnosed with schizophrenia.

“We should not assume that schizophrenia means violence. Most people with schizophrenia are not violent,” she told This Week in Asia.

“The risk may increase when someone is experiencing severe untreated psychosis, particularly when other factors such as alcohol or drug misuse are involved. In fact, people with serious mental illness can also be victims of violence, discrimination and stigma.”

We need to be careful about taking one case and allowing it to shape how we see everyone living with schizophrenia

Chua Sook Ning, clinical psychologist

A review published last year examining 47 longitudinal studies involving more than 203,000 people with psychosis found that a previous criminal history had the strongest association with later violence, followed by substance misuse, with many treatment-related factors linked to a lower risk.

Clinical psychologist Chua Sook Ning, founder of mental health organisation Relate Malaysia, said the danger after a case such as the Bandar Utama killing was that the diagnosis itself could become the explanation for what happened.

“A diagnosis can become a very easy one to reach for. That can make schizophrenia sound as though it explains the violence by itself,” she said.

“Most people with mental illness aren’t violent, and acts of violence can occur in the absence of mental illness, so we need to be careful about taking one case and allowing it to shape how we see everyone living with schizophrenia.”

Cindi has felt those assumptions in her own life. She kept her diagnosis private for almost a decade and said the father of her son refused to marry her because his family was afraid of her schizophrenia.

“Schizophrenia is a treatable disease. It’s lifelong, but it’s treatable,” she said, adding that she now had an accepting workplace, supportive friends and continued access to therapy.

Much of her attention now is on raising her son, whom she hopes will never have to experience the same illness and upheaval that have marked the past decade of her life.

“I just hope that my son doesn’t get it. That’s all,” Cindi said. “I don’t want my son to go through the same suffering that I have … so let the struggle end with me.”

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia faces reckoning over maritime safety after deadly ferry disaster
item.description:
Indonesia’s latest ferry disaster has exposed persistent weaknesses in maritime safety oversight, experts have said, with poor enforcement and inadequate supervision continuing to leave passengers vulnerable across the sprawling archipelago.

The capsizing of the Virgo Transport 8 in the Java Sea on Sunday has intensified scrutiny of a system that analysts say too often comes under pressure only after deadly accidents, rather than preventing them.

Six people have been confirmed dead and 129 remain missing after the passenger and cargo ferry capsized amid high winds and rough seas while travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s latest ferry disaster has exposed persistent weaknesses in maritime safety oversight, experts have said, with poor enforcement and inadequate supervision continuing to leave passengers vulnerable across the sprawling archipelago.

The capsizing of the Virgo Transport 8 in the Java Sea on Sunday has intensified scrutiny of a system that analysts say too often comes under pressure only after deadly accidents, rather than preventing them.

Six people have been confirmed dead and 129 remain missing after the passenger and cargo ferry capsized amid high winds and rough seas while travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.

According to Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency, 243 people – 213 passengers and 30 crew members – were aboard the vessel when the captain reported bad weather at about 2am local time on September 13.

A total of 108 people were rescued after personnel from agencies including the Indonesian Army and the Search and Rescue Agency were deployed, in the latest of a string of maritime incidents that have renewed questions over how Indonesia regulates and enforces safety at sea.

The latest disaster follows a string of other maritime incidents in recent months.

In August, five people died after a ferry caught fire off the island of Madura, while a blaze aboard another ferry travelling from Bali to Lombok killed one person. In July, a ferry sank in the Bali Strait leaving 19 people dead and 16 missing, and another ferry went down in waters close to South Sulawesi, killing three people with 14 still missing. In May, a tourist boat capsized close to Bengkulu City in Sumatra, resulting in eight deaths.

Following the latest sinking, lawmakers and experts have called for a comprehensive investigation into the incident and a tightening of maritime safety regulations.

In a statement provided to This Week in Asia, Usman Hamid, the head of Amnesty Indonesia, described the Virgo Transport 8 incident as “a humanitarian tragedy” that exposed the state’s failure to protect the safety rights of sea transport users.

Hamid called for an “immediate, independent, impartial and thorough investigation” to determine whether negligence by regulators, the vessel’s owners or other parties had contributed to the disaster, adding that anyone found responsible should be held legally accountable.

He also pointed to survivor testimony that no emergency alarm sounded when the ship capsized in the middle of the night while many passengers slept in cabins below deck.

“The availability of life jackets has also come under scrutiny,” Hamid said, citing survivor accounts that some passengers could not find them and that many people on life rafts were not wearing them.

Data from Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency showed 601 maritime incidents between January and August this year that required search and rescue deployment, including passengers falling overboard, engine failures and fires aboard vessels. In 2025, there were a total of 450 incidents from January to December.

Rise in incidents

Soerjanto Tjahjono, head of the National Transportation Safety Committee, told This Week in Asia he could not comment on the Virgo Transport 8 incident as it was still under investigation but that data compiled by the independent government agency also showed maritime incidents in Indonesia were on the rise.

“However, we do not yet have a definitive conclusion for why that is,” he said.

“What we do know is that extreme weather should never be blamed. We have to learn how to deal with the weather at sea and avoid it. It is not a reason for accidents, but it can be a contributing factor. There are also technical issues such as human factors.”

Tjahjono said the committee was currently conducting a wider investigation into boat safety, and aimed to publish a list of recommendations in the coming months.

One family member still anxiously awaiting news of a loved one aboard the Virgo Transport 8 is Fredy Manuhua, whose younger brother Stefiansa Manuhua, 44, played keyboard in the boat’s band to keep passengers entertained during the voyage.

Manuhua, 48, said he last contacted Stefiansa on Friday and later heard about the ferry incident around 7am on Sunday.

“I went straight to the port in Surabaya and the ferry company confirmed it,” he said. “I have been waiting there ever since and will not leave until there is news.”

Lack of oversight

Aji Suraji, director of postgraduate programmes at the University of Widya Gama in Malang, who specialises in transport safety and engineering, told This Week in Asia that maritime safety was a shared responsibility.

“It is the responsibility of boat operators to ensure that all the standard operating procedures on their vessels are being followed,” Suraji said. “However, it is also the responsibility of external stakeholders such as the Department of Transportation to make sure that vessels are adhering to these procedures.”

While the Department of Transportation had tightened some regulations in recent years, particularly regarding the compilation of accurate boat manifests, Suraji said there was still room for improvement.

“Adhering to standard operating procedures and external oversight of these are weak points in Indonesia when it comes to transport safety,” Suraji said, adding that “there needs to be more control and supervision, with clear and enforced sanctions in place”.

Suraji lamented that too often, transport safety in Indonesia gained attention only when incidents such as the Virgo Transport 8 happened and went viral. “But after that, people forget and are too forgiving. We need to be better at identifying potential issues before they happen and anticipating them.”

The incident has left Manuhua grappling with questions such as why no alarm apparently sounded, and why the captain of the Virgo Transport 8 and 11 crew members left the vessel and were rescued while other passengers were still aboard.

“I hope there will be a full investigation, and I will push for anyone to face the full extent of the law if they were at fault,” he said.

“I am devastated by what has happened. I am so close to my brother and I pray every night to our parents, and tell them that he is still lost and to please send him back to us.

“There are still so many things that we want to do together. I am not ready to lose him.”

item.title: [SCMP] Filipino fishers count the cost of South China Sea dispute
item.description:
For fishermen like Joey Marabe in the Philippine province of Zambales, the geopolitical contest playing out in the South China Sea can be measured in dwindling catches and shrinking incomes, as the presence of Chinese vessels around a contested shoal increasingly limits where they can work.

“It’s a huge drop. Before, a lot of us who could go out to Scarborough Shoal used to bring home around 15,000 pesos (US$238) a week, a comfortable amount for our families,” said Marabe, a resident of Masinloc town and provincial coordinator for the national fisherfolk federation Pamalakaya.

“But now, since we’ve been restricted from going out that far, and we’re limited to our own nearer waters … we’re down to 600 to 700 [pesos], struggling hard just for one day.”
item.content:encoded:
For fishermen like Joey Marabe in the Philippine province of Zambales, the geopolitical contest playing out in the South China Sea can be measured in dwindling catches and shrinking incomes, as the presence of Chinese vessels around a contested shoal increasingly limits where they can work.

“It’s a huge drop. Before, a lot of us who could go out to Scarborough Shoal used to bring home around 15,000 pesos (US$238) a week, a comfortable amount for our families,” said Marabe, a resident of Masinloc town and provincial coordinator for the national fisherfolk federation Pamalakaya.

“But now, since we’ve been restricted from going out that far, and we’re limited to our own nearer waters … we’re down to 600 to 700 [pesos], struggling hard just for one day.”

The decline in earnings has coincided with rising fuel and operational costs, piling further pressure on fishermen who say they are being pushed into overcrowded waters closer to shore.

At the centre of their struggle is Scarborough Shoal, or Huangyan Island – a coral atoll and rich fishing ground known in the Philippines as Bajo de Masinloc.

Claimed by both countries, the shoal lies about 124 nautical miles (230km) west of Zambales and has been under Beijing’s de facto control since a tense, months-long stand-off in 2012.

In 2016, a Hague-based arbitral tribunal ruled that Scarborough Shoal was a traditional fishing ground for several nations and declared that China had unlawfully prevented Filipinos from fishing there. The tribunal did not rule on sovereignty over the feature.

Beijing rejects the ruling as “illegal, null and void”, maintaining that the shoal is Chinese territory and that its coastguard patrols are legitimate exercises of sovereignty.

That maritime presence has intensified recently. The Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative recorded 933 Chinese coastguard ship-days – a unit of measurement equal to one vessel operating in an area for one full day – around Scarborough Shoal in the first half of 2026 alone, almost matching the 1,099 ship-days logged across the whole of 2025.

For Filipino crews, the patrols make reaching or remaining at the shoal risky. Fishermen report being chased, ordered away, targeted by water cannons or having their anchor lines cut.

Beijing says its coastguard acts lawfully within Chinese jurisdiction, defending the use of warnings and blockades against Philippine vessels it accuses of intruding into its waters.

Reduced access to the shoal is only one part of a wider economic crisis hitting Zambales fishing communities. Declining nearshore fish stocks, rising fuel prices, temporary no-sail zones for military exercises and coastal dredging are all taking a heavy toll.

“No fisherman can come near the shoal,” said Leonardo Cuaresma, head of the New Masinloc Fishermen’s Association, adding that Chinese ships patrolled the area “24/7”, forcing many Filipinos into crowded municipal waters where catches were smaller.

“Some go hook-and-line fishing here in municipal waters, but only catch two or three kilos, sometimes as much as five kilos, because almost all our municipal waters really have weak fish stocks now,” he said.

Rising fuel costs have made longer journeys harder to sustain. Marabe recalled how crews used to travel 80 to 100 nautical miles offshore in convoys, whereas most now opted for short, quick trips to save fuel.

Rough seas add another layer of difficulty. The southwest monsoon, locally known as habagat, has long forced fishermen to scale back trips, but Marabe said falling earnings were pushing some to take greater risks.

“We usually comply with guidelines on when we can and cannot fish … but we have to force ourselves and try for our families’ needs,” he said.

Local waters were also temporarily disrupted by Balikatan, the annual joint military exercises between the Philippines and the US, which included live-fire drills and temporary no-sail zones off Zambales.

Cuaresma said the fallout outlasted the exercises, which scared away fish and damaged sensitive coral ecosystems.

Dredging concerns

Fishermen are also worried by extensive river and estuarine dredging across Zambales. Government officials have defended sediment removal as part of flood control measures, saying the extracted sand generates provincial revenue and supplies infrastructure and land reclamation projects, including Manila Bay and the international airport in Bulacan, north of Manila.

But environmentalists and fishing communities warn that large-scale extraction could alter river and coastal ecosystems, particularly during extreme weather.

These concerns intensified after heavy rainfall and lahar – volcanic mudflows – caused severe flooding in parts of the province.

In August, the Zambales Ecological Network called for an investigation after torrential floods collapsed a bridge in San Marcelino town, cutting off the village of Santa Fe. The group questioned whether changes to the Santo Tomas sediment system caused by dredging had affected natural drainage patterns during extreme rainfall.

Marabe said dredging made the water murky. “Silt and everything ends up in the sea,” he said. “And that kills a lot of fish and marine life.”

Fernando Siringan, a professor of marine and coastal geology at the University of the Philippines Marine Science Institute, said industrial noise and suspended sediment could disturb marine habitats and spawning grounds.

“If you have a boat that’s loud, and material gets suspended in the water, it’s the noise and the suspended material that directly impact the presence of fish,” Siringan said.

Dredging has also become politically contentious after reports surfaced last year alleging the involvement of Chinese companies.

Representative Leila de Lima sought a congressional inquiry into foreign contractors involved in the operations, including China Harbour Engineering Company, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Communications Construction Company.

Government officials have disputed allegations of Chinese involvement and rejected claims that Zambales sand was being used to build artificial islands in the South China Sea.

For Marabe, however, the more immediate concern is making fishing viable again.

He said longer-term support should include resources for small-scale fishermen, such as shared cold storage to preserve their catch, alongside greater protection for those trying to make a living at sea.

“We’re grateful for the five kilos of rice [from the government]. But that’s not what we’re truly after,” Marabe said. “We need protection as fishermen, to be allowed to go out to sea and not be left behind. That’s the freedom we want.”

item.title: [SCMP] Teodoro for president? Philippine defence chief draws 2028 election buzz after China clash
item.description:
Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr has won a burst of online support among Filipinos who see him as one of Manila’s most outspoken senior officials against China, with some already asking whether it could give him enough political momentum to carry him into the 2028 elections.

His latest boost came after a viral moment at the Seoul Defence Dialogue on September 8, where he read out a handwritten note reiterating Beijing’s rejection of the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling while on stage.

Forum organisers said the note came from a military attaché at the Chinese embassy in Seoul, who had passed it to a staff member and asked that it be given to Teodoro, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap.
item.content:encoded:
Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr has won a burst of online support among Filipinos who see him as one of Manila’s most outspoken senior officials against China, with some already asking whether it could give him enough political momentum to carry him into the 2028 elections.

His latest boost came after a viral moment at the Seoul Defence Dialogue on September 8, where he read out a handwritten note reiterating Beijing’s rejection of the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling while on stage.

Forum organisers said the note came from a military attaché at the Chinese embassy in Seoul, who had passed it to a staff member and asked that it be given to Teodoro, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap.

Teodoro read parts of the note aloud, including Beijing’s position that the 2016 award was “illegal, null and void”, before saying the move was disrespectful to the forum’s South Korean hosts and showed disregard for international law.

“So, perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do … This is actual coercion, bullying and aggression,” he said.

Beijing hit back, with Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning accusing Philippine officials of “grandstanding and lying” and urging “certain people in the Philippines” to stop undermining China-Philippines relations and stability in the South China Sea.

China does not accept the 2016 ruling by an arbitral tribunal in The Hague, which found Beijing’s claims to historic rights within the nine-dash line had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

Beijing argues the tribunal had no jurisdiction because the case involved territorial sovereignty and maritime delimitation and says the Philippines abused the Unclos dispute settlement mechanism by bringing the case unilaterally.

The Seoul episode followed Beijing’s June sanctions on Teodoro, his wife and child over what China said were erroneous remarks that undermined its interests and damaged bilateral relations.

The move barred them from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau and restricted Chinese organisations and individuals from dealing with them, but Teodoro remained defiant, saying the sanctions would not stop him from doing his job.

Even before his latest viral moment, some social media users in the Philippines had begun urging Teodoro to run for president, vice-president or the Senate in 2028.

On Facebook, a page entitled “Filipinos for Gibo Teodoro 2028” had sprung up by June and had 35,000 followers as of the time of writing. One user commented “if Sec Gibo decides to run for President, we should all support him”, while another said: “He’s my President in 2028.”

His Seoul response also drew support from public figures, including Senator Erwin Tulfo, who said Teodoro had done “the right thing”, and Senator Panfilo Lacson, who said the episode showed what Teodoro’s “brilliant mind” could bring to the world stage.

But political observers said Teodoro’s path to higher office would depend on whether he could translate a burst of online attention into sustained support – a challenge made clearer by his previous unsuccessful runs for national office.

Teodoro was criticised over disaster rescue operations after Typhoon Ketsana in 2009, when he was defence secretary, before running the following year as president Gloria Macapagal Arroyo’s official candidate and finishing in fourth place.

After that defeat, he largely shunned politics until 2022, when he offered to be the vice-presidential running mate of Davao City mayor Sara Duterte-Carpio.

When Duterte-Carpio decided to seek the vice-presidency herself, Teodoro instead ran for one of 12 Senate seats up for election that year under the poorly funded People’s Reform Party, but finished 15th and missed out.

Dr Ranjit Rye, founding president of poll firm Octa Research, told This Week in Asia that Teodoro was “not yet” ripe for the vice-presidential race but said a Senate run could be more realistic.

In Octa’s July poll of the public’s senatorial preferences, Teodoro placed No 29, with 11.2 per cent of respondents saying they would vote for him, while WR Numero Research’s June survey put him at No 35, with 6 per cent support.

Barry Gutierrez, who was spokesman to former vice-president Leni Robredo and is himself an ex-congressman, said survey numbers were “the most immediate measure” of viability, though not the only one.

“Unfortunately, Secretary Teodoro’s numbers are fairly low across the board at this point,” Gutierrez told This Week in Asia, adding that Teodoro “is not even considered in publicly released presidential surveys”.

“To me this indicates that, as of now, he is not top of mind when it comes to choices for the top posts in 2028,” he said.

Ronnie Holmes, Pulse Asia president and a professor of political science and development studies at De La Salle University, said the pollster “will include his name for a long list on presidential preference in our third-quarter survey”.

“I can’t comment on viability until we see the survey results,” Holmes said.

Gutierrez said Teodoro’s numbers could improve if his recent prominence became “the start of a more sustained visibility as a national leader”, but added that this would require “a sustained and consistent effort over time, and not simply one viral moment two years before the elections”.

“Gilberto Teodoro is qualified to run for higher office in 2028. He has the credentials and experience,” said Manuel Mogato, a defence and security analyst.

“But experience, expertise, and his high qualifications are not enough. Winnability is also important,” Mogato said, adding that current opinion polls suggested Teodoro still had significant ground to make up before 2028.

University of the Philippines political-science professor Dr Jean Franco said Teodoro was “definitely viable given his background, experience, and competence”, but that his association with Macapagal Arroyo, elite family background and lack of mass appeal could count against him.

“I believe, however, that if he is paired with a strong presidential candidate and if he has good campaign strategists, he can be a strong contender. He can carry the China issue, which I believe is something that resonates across classes,” she said.

Asked by radio station DZBB on September 11 whether he was eyeing an elective post, Teodoro said he was keeping his options open because “you know it’s hard to plan now. It’s hard to plan because I am focused on my work here”.

item.title: [SCMP] Japan’s Natuna port proposal highlights Indonesia’s balancing act on China
item.description:
Japan’s proposed port upgrades in Indonesia’s Natuna Islands reflect Tokyo’s push to bolster South China Sea security without building an overt military footprint. However, analysts stress that the move does not mean Jakarta is siding with Japan in its efforts to contain Beijing.

Japan, which earlier this year eased its restrictions on lethal weapons exports, is ramping up security cooperation with Indonesia – a crucial bellwether for Southeast Asia.

The expanding partnership includes joint defence industry development, intelligence cooperation and expanded military exercises in strategic waterways.
item.content:encoded:
Japan’s proposed port upgrades in Indonesia’s Natuna Islands reflect Tokyo’s push to bolster South China Sea security without building an overt military footprint. However, analysts stress that the move does not mean Jakarta is siding with Japan in its efforts to contain Beijing.

Japan, which earlier this year eased its restrictions on lethal weapons exports, is ramping up security cooperation with Indonesia – a crucial bellwether for Southeast Asia.

The expanding partnership includes joint defence industry development, intelligence cooperation and expanded military exercises in strategic waterways.

Citing Japanese government sources, Kyodo News reported earlier this month that Tokyo was planning to use its official development assistance to help upgrade Indonesia’s fishing ports to allow patrol vessels to operate in more areas.

According to the report, one potential location will be the Natuna Islands, which lie along the southern edge of China’s nine-dash line – a boundary outlining Beijing’s expansive claims in the South China Sea.

In a commentary, state-owned Global Times framed Japan’s offer as a geopolitical tactic to expand Tokyo’s intelligence gathering and strengthen its presence in the South China Sea.

“Japan seeks to push countries like Indonesia to the front lines of South China Sea rivalry, while hiding behind the scenes to orchestrate its ‘proxy gambit’,” it said.

“This allows Japan to avoid risks of direct confrontation yet reap intelligence and strategic dividends. Indonesia and other Asean nations must be particularly vigilant against this ‘wolf in sheep’s clothing’ ploy,” it continued.

The Natuna Islands lie to the northeast of Sumatra and west of Borneo in the South China Sea. The archipelago and its adjacent waters – officially named the North Natuna Sea by Indonesia in 2017 – sit astride a key shipping route. The area is also a hotspot for commercial fishing.

Chinese, Vietnamese and Indonesian fishing vessels, often escorted by coastguard ships, have occasionally clashed over marine resources in recent years.

Chen Xiangmiao, a research fellow at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, noted that Jakarta’s push to upgrade the remote resource-rich islands served both economic and sovereign ends.

He said that policymakers in Jakarta had long been wary of foreign military presence in the region, especially the Chinese.

“Indonesia has sought to develop Natuna Islands, particularly its fishing resources, and has looked to expand its military presence in the region so as to consolidate its control in the region,” he said.

Chaula Rininta Anindya, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Indonesia, noted that the project was expected to address the “grey-zone” tactics Jakarta faced in the North Natuna Sea by bolstering frontline maritime deterrence.

However, she said the plan was broader than a simple response to South China Sea issues.

Rather, she said, it reflected Indonesia’s attempt to enhance its “Large Islands Defence” strategy through the dual use of ports – hosting civilian vessels as well as military and coastguard fleets when needed.

Under its “Free and Open Indo-Pacific” strategy, Tokyo has prioritised helping Southeast Asian partners build capacity and increase awareness of maritime threats so they can safeguard critical sea lanes.

Heng Yee Kuang, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Public Policy, said efforts to upgrade fishing ports were a result of the Japan-Indonesia summit in March.

At that meeting, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi emphasised cooperation in the fisheries industry, especially as Indonesia faced challenges related to illegal fishing and smuggling in the South China Sea, according to Heng.

He added that the initiative illustrated the continuity of cooperation between the two countries, as Japan had provided patrol boats for the Indonesian coastguard since the early 2000s.

The stakes for Japan are significant. Roughly 80 per cent of its energy imports and much of its maritime trade flow through the South China Sea, making stable sea lanes a core national interest.

“Indonesia’s importance to Japan has grown because of its geostrategic archipelagic location astride maritime chokepoints and key shipping lanes within Japan’s Free and Open Indo-Pacific Vision. Helping Indonesia address its maritime challenges is also in Japan’s enlightened self-interest,” Heng said.

However, Beijing has become increasingly alarmed by Tokyo’s growing security footprint in the region amid a downturn in Sino-Japanese ties.

Chen said that by offering security aid to Southeast Asia, Tokyo might be trying to distract Beijing from territorial disputes in the East China Sea.

“In a sense, Japan is … hoping to use the Southeast Asia region to relieve pressure or draw attention away from the East China Sea,” he said.

“More importantly, I think Japan is now engaged in a full-spectrum competition against China, not just in northeast Asia but in Southeast Asia as well, in terms of the economy, the military and diplomatic influence,” Chen said.

In the past two years, Japan and the Philippines have signed two deals to strengthen the logistics and sustainment capabilities of their armed forces, including the Reciprocal Access Agreement, which came into force last September.

At a defence ministers’ meeting in Jakarta in May, Japan and Indonesia signed a defence cooperation agreement covering military personnel development, defence industry collaboration and a mechanism for integrated defence dialogues. It institutionalises exchanges between senior officials and operational-level engagements between Japan’s Self-Defence Forces and Indonesia’s armed forces.

More crucially, the two sides also agreed to explore cooperation on defence equipment and technology aimed at boosting maritime deterrence, opening the door to future Japanese arms transfers.

Anindya said Indonesia’s role as the largest country in Southeast Asia – by size and by population – and its critical role as a co-founder of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) had made it an agenda setter in the region.

“It seems that Japan is expecting Indonesia to share a common understanding on the issue in the region, then the message could be conveyed as well at the regional level,” she said.

She added that military cooperation between Indonesia and Japan should not be seen as an alliance to counter China but a pragmatic strategy by Jakarta to work with its partners around the world.

“Indonesia is simply being pragmatic, and I believe it does not want to risk escalating tension with China. Indonesia will be careful in establishing cooperation with various countries and will remain committed to its ‘free and active’ foreign policy,” she said.

Heng noted that Japan and Indonesia did not yet have an intelligence-sharing framework for sensitive information.

He said Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto had also been careful to balance relations with China, “so Beijing can be reassured on this point”.

item.title: [SCMP] Is Japan’s Okinawa finally moving past anti-base politics?
item.description:
Okinawa has handed a landslide victory to a conservative who accepts Tokyo’s plans for relocating a controversial US airbase – delivering a blow to 12 years of anti-base politics in Japan’s southernmost prefecture.

Genta Koja’s victory on Sunday over two-term governor Denny Tamaki raised a question cutting to the heart of Okinawa’s post-war politics: is it finally starting to move on from the US military base issue?

Koja, a 42-year-old conservative backed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party, campaigned on economic revival and accepting Tokyo’s plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station from densely populated Ginowan to the coastal Henoko district in Nago, both on Okinawa Island.
item.content:encoded:
Okinawa has handed a landslide victory to a conservative who accepts Tokyo’s plans for relocating a controversial US airbase – delivering a blow to 12 years of anti-base politics in Japan’s southernmost prefecture.

Genta Koja’s victory on Sunday over two-term governor Denny Tamaki raised a question cutting to the heart of Okinawa’s post-war politics: is it finally starting to move on from the US military base issue?

Koja, a 42-year-old conservative backed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party, campaigned on economic revival and accepting Tokyo’s plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station from densely populated Ginowan to the coastal Henoko district in Nago, both on Okinawa Island.

Tamaki, by contrast, had opposed the base project for his entire tenure as governor, a stance he inherited from his late predecessor after winning 2018’s election on an anti-base platform.

Exit polls conducted by Kyodo News on Sunday found that nearly half of voters ranked economic revitalisation as their top concern, while barely one-fifth of respondents cited issues related to US bases.

That was reflected in the election results. Koja, a former deputy mayor of Okinawa’s capital Naha, defeated Tamaki with 59 per cent of the vote, officials said on Monday.

He will become the prefecture’s first governor born after its return to Japanese sovereignty by the United States in 1972 and the first in over a decade not to have built his career on opposition to US military bases.

Generational rift

Okinawa has been seen as a bastion of pacifist, left-leaning opposition forces for years.

Despite accounting for less than 1 per cent of Japan’s total land area, it hosts roughly 70 per cent of the land dedicated exclusively to US military facilities in the country – a burden that has made it central to arguments over the US-Japan alliance.

Tamaki and his All Okinawa movement, a broad political and civic alliance that opposes the relocation and construction of US military bases on Okinawa Island, had long framed the dispute as a test of local autonomy against central authority.

Sunday’s result illustrated a generational divide, according to Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Social Science.

While voters over 60 largely backed Tamaki and All Okinawa, “younger voters were more concerned about the economy”, he said.

The outcome reflected “pragmatism as well as frustration” with Tamaki for failing to stop new base construction, Maslow said – though that did not mean voters were unconcerned about national security implications.

Japan’s “Nansei shift” – the build-up of defence capabilities across its southern islands – was expected to continue under the new governor and “this will place an even higher burden on Okinawa”, he said.

Masato Kamikubo, a political scientist and professor at Ritsumeikan University, said successive LDP governments dating back to Shinzo Abe’s administration had cut subsidies to Okinawa in an attempt to “bully” the prefecture for its confrontational approach to central authority.

A younger generation is now beginning to create a new form of politics

Masato Kamikubo, political scientist

“Faced with rising prices and other economic difficulties, Okinawan voters appear to have wanted a way out of the present situation and therefore prioritised the economy over the military base issue,” he said.

The election result reflected a move away from the decades-old contest between conservative and liberal blocs, Kamikubo said, arguing that All Okinawa’s “crushing defeat” revealed a movement built on ideological resistance struggling to hold a new generation’s attention.

“A younger generation is now beginning to create a new form of politics from the grass roots, moving beyond the traditional divide between left and right,” he said. “This election may have symbolised that emerging transformation.”

Meanwhile, Takaichi’s firm stance on national security, particularly the tough line she had taken on China, also resonated with Okinawan voters, Kamikubo said.

“Okinawa is on the front line in confronting the perceived threat from China,” he said, noting that liberal politicians such as Tamaki and the All Okinawa movement had done little more than appealed for peace.

“Some voters are anxious about whether these groups would actually be able to protect them in the event of a crisis.”

Tokyo’s cash carrot

On Monday, following Koja’s victory, Takaichi pledged to raise Okinawa’s budget to more than 300 billion yen (US$1.94 billion) from around 260 billion yen in recent years.

Kamikubo said he expected her “to present Okinawa as a model demonstrating that economic growth can be achieved and rising living costs overcome when the central and prefectural governments work together”.

“For a prime minister struggling with declining approval ratings, the victory in Okinawa will be seen as a significant glimmer of hope,” he added.

A recent poll by national broadcaster NHK found public approval of Takaichi’s cabinet at 53 per cent, down from 66 per cent in November last year, amid concerns about inflation and the rising cost of living.

Koja’s economic focus and his image as a fresh face – in contrast to Tamaki, who staked his political legacy on opposing the US military presence – had all helped at the polls, said Rintaro Nishimura, a Tokyo-based senior associate at strategic advisory firm The Asia Group.

But Sunday’s result did not mean that Okinawans no longer cared about the base issue, he said, nor that they would accept every central government policy.

“He [Koja] has been clear in how he views his role: a coordinator who will seek out the most practical and best option for the people of Okinawa,” Nishimura said.

Still, the LDP backing a winning candidate for governor in a historically anti-LDP prefecture was “a good narrative for Takaichi to build on”, he said – particularly heading into next year’s local elections, as it helped counter concerns that the party was unpopular at the local level.

Masaaki Gabe, a professor emeritus at the University of the Ryukyus in Okinawa, said many Okinawans had voted out of dissatisfaction with rising prices and economic hardship rather than security concerns.

“The sense of immediacy regarding a potential conflict stemming from the Taiwan Strait crisis remains relatively limited,” he said, adding that further militarisation of Okinawa was likely to be “tolerated” by a significant segment of voters.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but are opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force.

The two central challenges facing Okinawa today were poverty and the burden of hosting US bases, Gabe said.

“Regardless of who serves as governor, these two challenges continue to exist with unwavering force and successive prefectural administrations have been compelled to confront them,” he said, adding that “the central government holds the upper hand on the base issue and its control over policy is unlikely to be shaken”.

Okinawa consistently ranks as the least economically developed of Japan’s prefectures, with average incomes and employment roughly 20 to 30 per cent behind mainland standards.

item.title: [SCMP] Brics members find common ground on AI, trade and alternative payment expansion
item.description:
Brics members agreed in New Delhi on Saturday to continue the push to expand trade and payments in local currencies to counter US pressure.

The member nations also found enough common ground to overcome some of their biggest diplomatic splits.

In addition, Chinese President Xi Jinping used his address at the Brics summit to deliver a thinly veiled critique of US policies, calling on members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
Brics members agreed in New Delhi on Saturday to continue the push to expand trade and payments in local currencies to counter US pressure.

The member nations also found enough common ground to overcome some of their biggest diplomatic splits.

In addition, Chinese President Xi Jinping used his address at the Brics summit to deliver a thinly veiled critique of US policies, calling on members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.

Xi proposed an initiative on “AI-empowered new industrialisation” designed to deepen collaboration on industry and supply chains, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The call came as the bloc was celebrating its 20th anniversary, having grown from a small economic framework into what Xi calls “the most influential cooperation platform for emerging markets and developing countries in today’s world”.

At the same time, the gathering is being held against a backdrop of regional and global turmoil, from the war in Ukraine and the Middle East conflict to protectionism and tariff tensions. And its unity is being tested by divisions such as Iran’s repeated attacks on fellow members, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.

Xi’s attendance at the summit is the latest in a flurry of diplomatic activities preceding his trip to the United States, efforts that are expected to give him the upper hand in his meeting with his US counterpart, Donald Trump.

Brics, a bloc of developing nations, has increasingly been viewed as a counterweight to Western-led institutions and a platform for building an alternative international order.

Part of that push includes cross-border payments. The group’s Payment Task Force had studied “cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels” and would keep working on payments that were “fast, low cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent and safe”.

But the leaders were also clear about just how far they were prepared to go as the declaration said there was “no one-size-fits-all approach” and that national priorities must be respected.

As well as the host, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, other high-profile attendees include Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian.

For China, Brics is also seen as a platform to advance Beijing’s vision of a multipolar world and cement its standing as a leader of the Global South.

In that vein, Xi said Beijing was willing to work with Brics countries to play a “due role” in bringing peace to the Middle East, calling on the group of emerging economies to oppose bloc confrontation and the “infringement upon the sovereignty of other countries and interference in their affairs”.

His call for AI cooperation also highlights Beijing’s efforts to advance its own framework, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), widely seen as its answer to Washington’s Pax Silica Initiative.

The two countries are vying for AI dominance and Pax Silica is Washington’s approach to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains among allied nations.

Xi invited all Brics countries to join Waico to shape global AI governance and development.

“China stands ready to work with all parties to jointly produce more research and development and application outcomes, and to deepen cooperation across industrial and supply chains,” he said.

“Facts will prove that ‘decoupling and severing supply chains’ cannot hinder our development process, and ‘small yards with high fences’ will only confine oneself and fragment the world,” Xi said, in a veiled swipe at the US.

“We must firmly … strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence, encourage open source and collaborative sharing and push practical cooperation to new heights.”

Xi said the Global South was growing stronger and urged Brics countries to “firmly stand on the right side of history” and lead the international order towards a more just and equitable direction, away from unilateralism and power politics.

Member nations unanimously adopted the 45-page “New Delhi Declaration 2026” on the opening day of the summit, with Modi saying that no member had objected to the text.

In a thinly veiled challenge to Washington’s stance, Xi urged the Brics members to criticise protectionism and unilateralism, calling on emerging economies to defend international institutions such as the United Nations and the World Trade Organization against tariff threats, treaty withdrawals, and efforts to carve out exclusive global trade alliances.

“We must oppose withdrawing from organisations, breaking treaties, and starting anew by setting up separate mechanisms,” Xi said.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said Xi’s call for Brics to become “a vanguard for peace and stability” was especially relevant, given India’s efforts, as the group’s chair, to avoid being drawn into geopolitical conflicts.

Xi urged Brics countries to pursue “common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security”, reject cold war thinking and bloc confrontation, and oppose violations of sovereignty and interference in internal affairs.

He also called for constructive efforts to resolve regional hotspots, saying China was ready to work with Brics partners to “contribute to peace and stability in the Middle East and Gulf region”.

Liu said the political and security dimension, part of the three pillars of Brics cooperation, had become increasingly important as global tensions intensified.

“In today’s turbulent global environment, the political and security pillar is especially critical. As Xi emphasised, Brics should play a constructive role in mediating and easing regional tensions to advance global and regional peace.”

Modi, who chaired the opening session, said the voice of developing economies could not remain “a courtesy” and that emerging countries had to write the rules of global governance.

Brics, he said, was “not against anyone” but instead was for everyone.

“The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid,” he added.

“Power and decision-making sit at the top. Those who live with the consequences sit at the bottom, they are affected by every decision, excluded from every one of them.”

China will assume the organisation’s rotating chair next year.

In a sit-down after the summit, Xi told Modi that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”.

The grouping first took shape in 2006 when Brazil, Russia, India and China began informal talks before it was officially established in 2009. South Africa joined in 2010, turning the bloc from Bric to Brics.

The grouping has undergone two expansions since, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2024 and Indonesia in 2025. Brics now covers nearly half the global population and about a third of the world’s GDP.

Over the years, the bloc has evolved into a political platform for intergovernmental cooperation in areas ranging from finance and trade to culture and justice.

It has also become increasingly vocal about overhauling global systems, including proposing alternatives to US dollar-based payment systems, a suggestion that prompted warnings from Trump.

But its expansion has also brought fresh challenges to the bloc, with analysts suggesting that there are now more competing voices which have slowed its progress and made it harder to reach a consensus on issues.

Additional reporting by Orange Wang, Nayan Seth, Alyssa Chen, Shi Jiangtao and Victoria Bela

item.title: [SCMP] J-50 designers reveal leapfrog tech for China’s next-gen stealth fighters
item.description:
China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations.

That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month.

The institute is associated with the development of the Chinese next-generation aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50, which first appeared in flight-test imagery in December 2024, although the paper does not mention the J-50 by name or confirm that the aircraft will incorporate any of the described technologies.
item.content:encoded:
China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations.

That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month.

The institute is associated with the development of the Chinese next-generation aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50, which first appeared in flight-test imagery in December 2024, although the paper does not mention the J-50 by name or confirm that the aircraft will incorporate any of the described technologies.

China’s future fighters, including the J-50 and J-36, are considered rivals to the US Air Force’s sixth-generation main fighter programme, the F-47, being developed by Boeing.
