The lead researcher is chief flight-control designer Zhang Dong at the institute, and his team’s paper – rare for its public details – was published in a peer-reviewed journal Aircraft Design in August.

China’s next-generation stealth fighter programmes were undergoing a “leapfrog transformation from being able to fly steadily to being able to win in combat”, wrote Zhang and his colleagues.

Zhang’s study presents a future of pilots handing over control during periods of extreme workload or incapacitation, quantum navigation technologies supporting operations in satellite-denied environments and crewed fighters coordinating attack, reconnaissance and protection missions with reconfigurable wingman drones.

The team’s institute is part of the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China, which oversees much of the country’s aircraft research and development.

Its subsidiary, Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group, is also developing the J-36 fighter, widely regarded as another candidate for China’s next-generation sixth-generation combat aircraft.

In 2025, an investigation by defence news website, The War Zone, using satellite imagery found that the Chengdu J-36 and the Shenyang J-50 aircraft were both based at an experimental military airfield near Lop Nur, a highly secretive site for aerospace test flights that has often been compared to the United States’ Area 51.

Their simultaneous presence at the same base suggested that China’s military was actively supporting the parallel development of the two programmes.

Zhang’s paper presents a rare technological road map for future combat aircraft, describing a fundamental restructuring of the flight-control system from a device concerned mainly with flight quality into a core enabler of collaborative engagement, intelligent manoeuvre and mission effectiveness.

The change reflected what the authors described as three successive eras of air combat.

In the earlier “energy manoeuvrability” era, victory depended heavily on physical manoeuvring performance in close-range combat, while flight-control systems were largely closed and centralised, with specialised hardware and software designed mainly to keep the aircraft stable, controllable and responsive to pilot inputs.

The rise of long-range radar, stealth shaping and precision-guided weapons shifted combat towards “information manoeuvrability”, where detecting, tracking and attacking an opponent before being detected became increasingly important.

Fifth-generation aircraft such as the F-22 and J-20 use full-authority digital fly-by-wire systems and increasingly integrate flight control with fire-control and propulsion systems through high-speed data links.

The authors argued that the next phase was “cognitive manoeuvrability”, in which artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and distributed networking allowed air combat to move from platform-versus-platform competition towards system-level contests involving manned-unmanned formations.

This changes what flight control is expected to do.

“The functional positioning of the flight control system is undergoing a fundamental restructuring – from a platform controller merely pursuing flight quality to a core enabler of collaborative engagement management, intelligent manoeuvre decision-making and closed-loop mission effectiveness,” Zhang and his co-authors wrote.

The first major capability is autonomous flight control.

Instead of making pilots constantly turn high-level battle plans into precise stick movements, the new system would let on-board intelligent algorithms do that job automatically, translating tactical orders into smooth, continuous flight actions while keeping the aircraft safely within its physical limits, even during extreme manoeuvres.

The aircraft would constantly monitor its own health by fusing data from sensors such as inertial navigation, airspeed indicators, control-surface positions and engine performance.

This would allow it to assess its flight state, estimate remaining manoeuvrability and detect potential problems before they develop into emergencies.

The system could then automatically adjust control settings and redistribute on-board resources while strictly enforcing safety boundaries to avoid stalls, loss of control or stuck control surfaces.

In particularly stressful situations, the aircraft could take over from the pilot.

The paper proposes allocating control authority between humans and autonomous systems so that pilots can spend less effort on low-level aircraft handling and more on battlefield assessment and tactical decisions.

During periods of excessive workload or if a pilot loses the ability to control the aircraft, the system could take control and continue executing the intended tactical task while prioritising flight safety.

The second major change concerns navigation.

Future combat aircraft may need to operate when satellite navigation is jammed, disrupted or unavailable, prompting the researchers to identify quantum inertial navigation, visual navigation, geomagnetic navigation and terrain matching as potential technologies for passive autonomous navigation.

The paper proposes combining data from various sensors to reduce errors and prevent failures caused by the degradation or loss of any single sensor under severe electromagnetic interference.

Quantum inertial navigation is therefore presented as part of a broader effort to give aircraft an independent sense of movement and position, rather than as a replacement for GPS.

The study framed these technologies as areas requiring further engineering research and implementation, rather than saying a quantum navigation system had already been deployed on a Chinese fighter.

The biggest shift, however, may come from the way multiple aircraft work together.

Future formations could pair crewed fighters acting as command nodes with uncrewed wingmen assigned to reconnaissance, attack and protection roles. Flight-control systems would coordinate their positions, routes, electromagnetic spectrum use and weapons-launch windows while dynamically allocating tasks between aircraft.

The authors saw this as more than a traditional formation controlled by a single leader.

If an aircraft suffered a malfunction or combat damage and left the formation, the remaining aircraft could automatically reorganise, replace the missing node and redistribute its unfinished tasks.

The system used consensus-based coordination and a dynamic “virtual leader” replacement mechanism to maintain autonomous operation without relying on a permanent central node.

Zhang and his team said single-aircraft autonomous control guaranteed survival in complex environments, while swarm coordination delivered multiplied combat effectiveness.

The paper pointed towards a more heterogeneous air-combat network rather than a simple arrangement of one crewed fighter and several identical drones.

It further highlighted large collaborative wingmen alongside various aircraft and autonomous platforms, suggesting a future architecture in which crewed fighters, larger unmanned aircraft and smaller autonomous systems could perform different functions within the same network.

Aircraft such as the Chinese Y-20 transport aircraft, the J-20 fighter and even the H-20 stealth strategic bomber, which is believed to be under development, could potentially form part of such a combat network.

However, Zhang and his team did not say whether the “combat group”, or the crewed “lead aircraft” and unmanned wingmen, would consist mainly of large numbers of drones or a combination of the larger aircraft described above.

The Shenyang Aircraft Corporation and the paper’s authors did not respond to a request for comment.

Based on the paper’s publicly available discussion, the researchers suggested retaining conventional systems engineering as the safety backbone while using intelligent tools for tasks such as parameter optimisation, test expansion, automated testing and defect detection, with early trials conducted on lower-cost uncrewed platforms before broader adoption in major aircraft.

But the researchers do not advocate handing the aircraft’s most safety-critical functions directly to artificial intelligence (AI).

Instead, they identified a basic engineering conflict between intelligence and flight safety.

Data-driven algorithms can be difficult to explain and verify, and they might not apply in every situation, especially in extreme scenarios.

Applying such systems directly to the innermost control loops could therefore introduce unpredictable risks.

The proposed solution was a layered architecture.

“Engineering practice widely adopts a hybrid architecture with a closed core and open periphery,” the team wrote, allowing high-reliability, real-time functions to remain tightly controlled while more flexible software functions could be upgraded and connected across different platforms.

Under this model, the inner loop would retain conventional, highly deterministic controls for functions such as attitude stabilisation, control-surface actuation and hard flight-envelope protection.

AI would operate mainly in the outer loop, handling tactical decision-making, trajectory optimisation, multi-aircraft coordination and payload adaptation, while rigid safeguards would constrain its commands so that its recommendations remain inside a safe operating envelope.

The researchers called for further work on open layered architecture, verifiable intelligent flight control and cross-domain cooperative control, supported by large-scale simulation and flight-test data to improve the robustness and verifiability of intelligent models.

item.title: [SCMP] Young Chinese turn to Mao Zedong for life advice, 50 years after his death
item.description:
When you are denied a pay rise, when you feel anxious about your children’s education, or when you are alienated by colleagues, Chairman Mao can help.

At least, that is what China’s online influencers and their hundreds of thousands of followers believe.

Wednesday marks the 50th anniversary of the death of Mao Zedong, founding father of the People’s Republic of China. Chinese authorities have not announced any plans to mark the date, as former state leaders are usually commemorated on the anniversaries of their birth.
item.content:encoded:
When you are denied a pay rise, when you feel anxious about your children’s education, or when you are alienated by colleagues, Chairman Mao can help.

At least, that is what China’s online influencers and their hundreds of thousands of followers believe.

Wednesday marks the 50th anniversary of the death of Mao Zedong, founding father of the People’s Republic of China. Chinese authorities have not announced any plans to mark the date, as former state leaders are usually commemorated on the anniversaries of their birth.

The only special arrangement in place is at the Chairman Mao Memorial Hall in Beijing, which will open for an extra three hours on Wednesday. Visiting slots for the week are fully booked.

Despite the official silence ahead of the anniversary, it is hard to ignore the quiet comeback of Mao’s popularity in the country.

In recent years, younger generations of Chinese have rediscovered Mao as their life coach. They organise online book clubs devoted to his works, spread the gospel through artificial intelligence-narrated videos, and affectionately refer to him as jiaoyuan, or “teacher”, a title Mao himself once said he preferred.

His views are regularly cited in times of US-China tensions. Last year, when the Trump administration imposed a 104 per cent tariff on Chinese goods, social media users searched for the term jiaoyuan, described imperialism as a “paper tiger” – one of Mao’s best-known slogans – and quoted his collection of speeches, On Protracted War.

While much of this youthful sentiment aligns with China’s official narrative about Mao as a symbol of national independence, especially in the face of US-led international pressure, experts say Beijing is also wary that Mao’s teachings could feed into scepticism about the country’s economic policies and its interpretation of Marxism.

Mao in youth culture

For Mao’s most vocal online admirers, the former state leader is a symbol of resilience, courage and dedication to the common people.

One blogger on the arts and culture forum Douban praised Mao’s selflessness, especially the fact that he sent his own son to the battlefield.

“He stood with us, the people, at all times,” she wrote.

The 29-year-old blogger, who asked to be referred to only by her surname Liu, describes herself as an “ordinary company worker”. She said she had read most of Mao’s works and applied them to her own life.

“Don’t regard a mistake as merely a disgrace; see it as an asset,” she said, quoting the late leader. She added that this perspective had taught her not to criticise herself too harshly.

I believe [Mao’s] spirit in heaven can bless young students like us, help us make progress and achieve our ideals

Li Muqi, Chinese university student

Young people can also be spotted paying tribute to Mao at a giant monument in Changsha, Hunan province. Li Muqi, a second-year student at Hunan Normal University, has made a habit of visiting the enormous statue before final exams to pray for good luck.

“I believe his spirit in heaven can bless young students like us, help us make progress and achieve our ideals,” Li said.

According to public data, the number of annual visitors to the site has more than tripled in about a decade, from 5.88 million in 2016 to 19 million last year.

It is hard to estimate the number of Mao’s young followers in China today, but a glimpse is possible through growing library loans and merchandise sales. At Beijing’s prestigious Tsinghua University, the Selected Works of Mao Zedong topped the library loan list last year, open records show.

On Taobao, one of China’s largest online shopping platforms, a shop selling enamel mugs with Mao’s portrait sold more than 20,000 units in the past year.

Wealth gap and nationalism

The deeper reason for the interest in Mao is that young people are becoming increasingly disillusioned by today’s China and cannot achieve their aspirations, according to analysts.

In June 2023, the official urban unemployment rate for young people aged 16 to 24 hit a record high of 21.3 per cent. Fearful for their futures, university graduates have started joking that they have to “degrade themselves” and consider blue-collar jobs with low pay.

“I think a lot of people have realised that this isn’t something that could simply be solved with the cake being made bigger,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University in Australia.

He said that Mao’s theories on class struggle and conflict were still relevant today, as young people facing immense pressure, a wealth gap and few employment opportunities sought an explanation or simply comfort.

This has been accompanied by a rise in nationalism in recent years. Many admire Mao for his foresight in areas such as the development of nuclear weapons, satellites and the industrialisation of inland provinces – achievements that have helped China compete and defend itself against outside forces.

During recent US-China tensions, members of the public have regularly cited Mao’s teachings.

For example, a Baidu blog post from last year stated that thanks to the former leader’s strategy, China “holds the ace” for winning the trade war. Despite tariffs, China has developed its domestic industry chain, made alliances with other countries and used rare earths to counterstrike – all moves out of Mao’s playbook on protracted war, according to the blogger.

An April commentary in the Monthly Review, a New York-based independent socialist magazine, said Mao’s legacy offered a “powerful counternarrative to the Western-centric story of globalisation”.

“He represents the possibility of an alternative path to modernity, one that does not require submission to the economic and political dictates of Washington.”

Mao reimagined

Rana Mitter, S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, noted that young people’s interpretation of Mao’s teachings generally did not include the violence of the Cultural Revolution.

When asked about the Cultural Revolution, Douban blogger Liu said she had mainly read Mao’s works to see the logic of his writing, how he worked and his attitude towards life, and she had not done “systematic research on historic events”.

Rebecca Karl, professor of history at New York University, said that for young people, the Cultural Revolution “reads as a liberatory moment”, rather than the “doom and gloom that we know from mainstream narrative convention and state repudiation”.

One reason young people have an incomplete view of Mao is due to censorship.

The Mao era came to an end with his death in 1976. In the years that followed, his legacy was officially defined by the Communist Party.

A 1981 party resolution under Deng Xiaoping, China’s leader at the time, established the basic framework: Mao was credited with major achievements and with laying the foundations of modern China, but his later rule was heavily criticised, particularly for the Cultural Revolution, which was described as a “catastrophe”.

Under President Xi Jinping, the emphasis has shifted towards more recognition of Mao’s achievements. Xi argued in 2013 that Mao’s three decades of rule “could not be repudiated” by the reform era.

Tiptoeing around Mao

Chinese authorities are prepared to tackle anyone who deviates from the official assessment of Mao’s legacy, and the government censors those who openly criticise him.

But at the same time, Beijing has been careful not to let Mao-related discussions get out of hand, especially those concerning his more radical ideas and the Cultural Revolution.

Analysts said that while the Mao revival among young people would not grow into a larger movement, it would persist as a form of self-expression.

“His return signifies that the fundamental questions he posed about China’s path are not relics of a bygone era. The questions of class, of social justice, and of who truly holds power in society have not been resolved by decades of market reforms … The revolutionary agenda, it seems, remains unfinished,” the Monthly Review commentary said.

Gao, the professor of Chinese studies, said the trend was a collection of mixed feelings mostly confined to the digital realm, and it would not be allowed to develop into something larger.

However, facing the problems of today, young people turn to Mao because “there’s no new path to take”, according to Gao.

“When the entire world is changing – and even chaotic – there’s no alternative narrative,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Exclusive: The Boar brings authentic British pub experience to Hong Kong’s Central
item.description:
If a good pint is what you’re after, Matt Richardson may have a solution. As one of the brains behind The Boar, a new British public house (where the shortened form and better-known term, “pub”, comes from) and restaurant in Central, he has been working to bring an authentic watering-hole experience to Hong Kong – even travelling to Ireland to perfect the Guinness pour in time for the establishment’s September 1 opening.

“I’m going to Dublin in two weeks, just to study it,” Richardson tells me about his late-August plans to visit the Guinness Storehouse. We’re sitting inside his office on Elgin Street, just one step from his latest venture. “Between me going right to the source and us [ensuring] that we’ve got the best beer lines, coolers and cleanliness … that’s the best we can do, that’s what makes a great Guinness. Every little bit counts, because the liquid in the barrel is not even the main element.”

Originally from Milton Keynes, northwest of London, Richardson has kept himself busy in the nine years he’s been in Hong Kong. He is the founder and managing director of Big Top Hospitality, the group behind Australian restobar Bourke’s, American-style saloon Honky Tonks Tavern, Mediterranean seaside terrace Terracotta Lamma, fresh pasta bar Twist in Sheung Wan, and bagel joint and delicatessen Mendel’s.
item.content:encoded:
If a good pint is what you’re after, Matt Richardson may have a solution. As one of the brains behind The Boar, a new British public house (where the shortened form and better-known term, “pub”, comes from) and restaurant in Central, he has been working to bring an authentic watering-hole experience to Hong Kong – even travelling to Ireland to perfect the Guinness pour in time for the establishment’s September 1 opening.

“I’m going to Dublin in two weeks, just to study it,” Richardson tells me about his late-August plans to visit the Guinness Storehouse. We’re sitting inside his office on Elgin Street, just one step from his latest venture. “Between me going right to the source and us [ensuring] that we’ve got the best beer lines, coolers and cleanliness … that’s the best we can do, that’s what makes a great Guinness. Every little bit counts, because the liquid in the barrel is not even the main element.”

Originally from Milton Keynes, northwest of London, Richardson has kept himself busy in the nine years he’s been in Hong Kong. He is the founder and managing director of Big Top Hospitality, the group behind Australian restobar Bourke’s, American-style saloon Honky Tonks Tavern, Mediterranean seaside terrace Terracotta Lamma, fresh pasta bar Twist in Sheung Wan, and bagel joint and delicatessen Mendel’s.

With five restaurants already in his portfolio, the British restaurateur is finally opening something that connects him to his roots, but with a name that pays homage to his time in both Hong Kong and Britain. “Boars are the largest land mammals in Hong Kong, but you can also find them all around the UK,” explains Richardson. “Here, they’re kind of loved, aren’t they? You walk up The Peak, and people are super excited to see a little family of boars walking around. I quite enjoy it.”

Behind the pass, he has brought on two British chefs with fine-dining pedigrees: executive chef Graham Long, who has worked in Michelin-rated kitchens across London and launched culinary concepts for luxury hotels in Hong Kong. Day-to-day kitchen operations are run by head chef Jake Bennett, who cut his teeth at several Simon Rogan restaurants, including three-Michelin-star L’Enclume in Britain’s Lake District. Most recently, he was at The Baker and The Bottleman, in Wan Chai.

“I jumped on board as soon as I found out [Richardson was opening a pub],” says Long. He recalls how the pair began brainstorming the making of The Boar over a few pints.

“I’ve always felt that pubs were missing in Hong Kong to a degree. You’d think there would be more, given Hong Kong’s history and the expat community that’s here.”

Despite its name, however, the pub and dining room will not be serving wild boar. In Hong Kong, it’s illegal to kill or capture the animal. In Britain, they were hunted to extinction several hundred years ago, before being reintroduced into the ecosystem in recent decades by farms. “I’ve cooked it professionally before. It’s not that common any more, but we used to get it from our game dealer. I actually prefer normal pork, to be honest, but it’s nice,” Long admits.

So, if boar is not on the menu, what is? Classic pub grub, of course, including Welsh rarebit, sticky toffee pudding and pork cheek and lobster pie, as well as courses that speak to British sensibilities, such as Eton mess and coronation chicken salad.

With both chefs coming from haute-cuisine backgrounds, the dishes reflect their technical discipline. “We want to make the best version of everything. Yes, we’re going to do fish and chips, but we want to make sure it’s the best fish and chips we can possibly do,” Long explains.

As for their Scotch eggs, these will be made with British sausage meat, black pudding and Japanese eggs, then fried to order. “You know, nothing beats a Scotch egg. Hopefully, nothing will beat our Scotch egg,” says Long.

The Boar will offer two menus, with “downstairs” serving casual bites such as prawn cocktail toast, the signature BLT sandwich, Guinness and treacle bread with salted English butter, broccoli and Stichelton tart, and more, while “upstairs” hosts a more formal dining format, with celeriac and mushroom Wellington, roasted turbot chop, baked Chilean sea bass and chargrilled rib-eye steak to look forward to. (Sunday roasts are in the works, too.) “It’s where we get to have a little bit more fun, be a bit more chef-y, have a few more luxury ingredients and a more sit-down experience,” says Long.

One of the highlights of the upstairs menu is the roasted duck, dry-aged for two weeks in-house – no short cuts, all processed by the Boar team – and served with buttered turnips, carrots, a sauce of port and citrus, and toller’s pie, a play on the timeless shepherd’s pie in reference to the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, a medium-sized gun-dog breed traditionally trained by hunters to find, flush out and retrieve shot game.

Moving into Flaming Frango’s old space on Elgin Street, the two-storey location, with an expansive ground floor and quirky structural nooks, has just the right bones to make it feel like a British pub – but Richardson has a fresher take in mind.

“We want it to feel more like a modern pub, because we feel it would be unjust to try and transport something you’d find from the laneways in London [to Hong Kong] – that would be too theatrical,” says Richardson. Instead, he explains he was inspired by his favourite pub, The Pelican, a Michelin Bib Gourmand spot in London’s Notting Hill neighbourhood.

“It’s a totally different experience from what people might know of the pub world, but the aesthetics, the feel, is that,” he says. “So, downstairs, think brighter colours and nice wood textures, but lots of nods to the things you might recognise from a pub back home, like the way we do the edgings on the tables and footrests and textures. And then when you move upstairs, this will have a different feel – more green, a bit more opulent.”

For Long and Richardson, The Boar is more than just another restaurant opening. “I spent most of my adult life in London and, generally, when I wasn’t working in a kitchen, I was in a pub,” recalls Long, whose time in the city included a stint at two-Michelin-star Pied à Terre, then helmed by Shane Osborn.

“Wherever you grow up, everyone has their local pub,” Long says. “[A pub is] shaped by the community that it’s in.”

Richardson agrees: “When I’m back home [in Britain, the go-to pub is] just wherever my friends are.”

Creating that sense of community here in Hong Kong – where both restaurateur and chef have settled, and for not an insignificant amount of time – is top of their minds when it comes to shaping the destination. “We let the food, the drinks and the genuine hospitality speak for themselves,” says Richardson, adding that every visit to The Boar “feels like coming home”.

item.title: [SCMP] Nancy Kwan’s enduring legacy, six decades after the release of The World of Suzie Wong – interview
item.description:
To many, Nancy Kwan Ka-shen is the actress who rose to international stardom for her role in the 1960 film The World of Suzie Wong, based on the book of the same name, about a sex worker in Wan Chai who meets a wealthy American (played by William Holden). Kwan’s story, however, is far richer than any single role.

From breaking barriers for Asian actors in Hollywood and standing her ground in an industry that was rigid and often prejudiced, to founding her own ballet studio, producing films and television advertisements across Southeast Asia, and starring in more than 50 films spanning decades, she has lived a life of relentless creativity, resilience and grace.

Now 87, Kwan’s path to celebrity was as serendipitous as it was extraordinary. In August 1959, she stumbled upon a casting call for The World of Suzie Wong.
item.content:encoded:
To many, Nancy Kwan Ka-shen is the actress who rose to international stardom for her role in the 1960 film The World of Suzie Wong, based on the book of the same name, about a sex worker in Wan Chai who meets a wealthy American (played by William Holden). Kwan’s story, however, is far richer than any single role.

From breaking barriers for Asian actors in Hollywood and standing her ground in an industry that was rigid and often prejudiced, to founding her own ballet studio, producing films and television advertisements across Southeast Asia, and starring in more than 50 films spanning decades, she has lived a life of relentless creativity, resilience and grace.

Now 87, Kwan’s path to celebrity was as serendipitous as it was extraordinary. In August 1959, she stumbled upon a casting call for The World of Suzie Wong.

“I thought it was dreadful because all I did was giggle,” she tells me over a FaceTime call from her home in Los Angeles, in the United States. “I was really quite silly. I was surprised I got a job at all. But they seemed to like it, so I ended up in Hollywood doing more screen tests. Eventually, I got the role.”

Initially, France Nuyen had been cast, but when the French-American actress withdrew, Kwan’s ballet-trained poise and expressive presence made her the perfect replacement. The film catapulted her to global fame, subtly transforming Hollywood’s perception of Asian women at a time when “yellowface” – casting non-Asian actors in make-up to portray Asian characters – was still widespread.

Even decades later, her magnetism remains palpable. Behind her, a poster of Suzie Wong seems almost to lean towards the camera, a reminder that the character and the woman who portrayed her remain inseparable in the public memory. Yet Kwan’s memoir, last year’s The World of Nancy Kwan, reveals a keen awareness of her own agency, her understanding that her story is as much about heritage and personal resilience as it is about fame.

Born in 1939 to Kwan Wing-hong, a prominent, Cambridge-educated Chinese architect, and Marquita Scott, a British model and aspiring actress who would leave the family before the start of World War II but later reconnect with her daughter in the US, Nancy grew up in a family whose legacy was intertwined with Hong Kong’s development and global affairs.

Her great-grandfather, Kwan Yuen-cheung, was the city’s first Western-trained dentist; her great-grandmother, Lai Amui, survived the mainland’s Taiping rebellion (1850-64) to become one of the first Western-trained nurses in Hong Kong. Her great-uncle Kwan King-leung studied alongside Dr Sun Yat-sen and later served as physician to the Empress Dowager of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911). “I don’t know if great-uncle Kwan King-leung’s friendship with Dr Sun Yat-sen endured, but I think it is extraordinary that the man who is considered the father of modern China spent his formative years in the Kwan household,” Kwan writes in her memoir.

Kwan also recalls how, although she has only hazy memories of it, her father (who later remarried) had to hide her and her brother in wicker baskets to travel to Macau by boat and then onwards to mainland China to flee the war after Japan’s attack on Hong Kong in 1941 – an event remembered locally as “Black Christmas”.

Later, Kwan learned that her father had served covertly with the British Army Aid Group, assisting soldiers stranded behind enemy lines in their escape from Japanese forces. Some media have even described him as a “Chinese James Bond”. The family returned to Hong Kong in 1945, resuming their lives amid the city’s post-war recovery.

Hollywood was never Kwan’s first passion. Ballet had captivated her from childhood, and she trained in Britain, attending the prestigious Royal Ballet School, in London.

“I’ve always continued with ballet,” she says. “Then I branched out – jazz and other kinds of dance. Nowadays, I take tai chi.”

That disciplined movement would define her screen presence, most memorably in Flower Drum Song (1961).

“Hermes Pan, the choreographer, told us, ‘Don’t dance like this; this is jazz.’ We did jazz because that’s what the piece called for. It was all about keeping ballet at bay,” she recalls, a glimmer of mischief in her eyes.

At the time of filming, Kwan had no idea how historic the movie would become.

“I just thought, ‘Oh, Flower Drum Song, all great.’ But it was the first time a major Hollywood studio made a film with a mostly Asian cast – that was a real achievement. I didn’t know the business that well back then,” she admits. “It wasn’t until my friend [the late Chinese-American actor] Benson Fong told me, ‘Nancy, this is the first time they’re making a film with an all-Asian cast,’ that I thought, ‘Wow, OK, this is bigger than I realised.’ It was very exciting.”

Decades later, that trail-blazing spirit echoed in the meteoric success of Crazy Rich Asians, the 2018 film adapted from Kevin Kwan’s 2013 novel, starring a predominantly Asian cast and capturing the global imagination. The connection is more than thematic: Kevin is Nancy’s cousin.

“Nancy really paved the way for me to pursue my own creativity,” Kevin, 53, tells me over the phone. “The first time I saw her in Flower Drum Song, I could hardly believe my eyes – just this glamorous creature in my own family. It was always inspiring.”

He fondly remembers the rare glimpses of authentic Hong Kong and the nuanced female characters Nancy brought to the screen. He recalls her performance in the late-1980s miniseries Noble House, adapted from the James Clavell novel, that was shot in Hong Kong, which also starred Pierce Brosnan and Deborah Raffin, as it offered him an immersive look at his heritage.

“It was remarkable to see her playing a sassy, empowered secretary, and years later, seeing her in Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story [1993] as Lee’s boss was another milestone,” he says. “She was there at every significant stage, paving the way for younger talent, for stories like my own.”

Kevin attributes her success to her perseverance.

“She never gave up, no matter the hardships or controversies. She was the first woman to return to Hong Kong and run her own film studio, and she got through everything with determination. Even now, in her 80s, she carries herself with the energy and poise of someone decades younger – not just physically, but in spirit,” he says.

Nancy navigated Hollywood’s entrenched racial attitudes, which often reduced Asian actors to exoticised caricatures. She admired Anna May Wong – considered to be the first Chinese-American film star in Hollywood, in the 20s – and her ability to get through the barriers she faced.

“I didn’t know much about her until I came to Hollywood and found out she was really the first Asian actress from Los Angeles,” Nancy recalls. “I think I met her niece – she comes to a lot of my screenings and book signings – a very lovely girl. I read up on Anna May Wong and even did a documentary about her, doing the voice-over, so I learned a lot about the struggles she faced, especially when they didn’t use Asian actors – they used Caucasians dressed up as Asians, like Luise Rainer in The Good Earth [1937]. She was trying to work during that era, and it was very difficult. When we did Flower Drum Song, the producer told me [Wong] was going to have a role, and I was so excited to work with her. Sadly, she passed away just a few weeks before filming.”

Private life and career are intertwined in Kwan’s reflections. Decades spent in Los Angeles, a brief return to Hong Kong to manage her father’s company and the routines of long-term partnership and care illustrate a life shaped by both focus and balance.

“I came back when my father was ill and, sadly, he passed away,” she recalls. “After that, I was offered the chance to run a company in Hong Kong. I thought, ‘Why not?’ But I quickly realised it wasn’t for me. Being a CEO meant more lunches and meetings than actual work – I wanted to be on the ground, doing things myself. By then, my son was ready to start high school, so that’s why I moved back to Los Angeles.”

Her memoir is filled with vivid, intimate stories of Hollywood encounters. She recounts her then-boyfriend Maximilian Schell, in a fit of jealous rage, hurling his “Best Actor” Oscar at her, and the time she turned down the lead opposite Elvis Presley in Blue Hawaii (1961).

“I was asked to meet someone at Paramount Studios about a film,” she recalls. “I didn’t know it was Elvis. I walk onto this empty stage, and then suddenly, he appears with a few of his friends. He sat me down and sang the ‘Hawaiian Wedding Song’ – I was floored. He was such an entertainer. Of course, I applauded and made a fool of myself.”

Despite the allure, Kwan politely declined. “I told them I’d already signed for Flower Drum Song. Both roles were historic in their own way, but I felt committed to this one,” she says.

She fondly remembers meeting Ursula Andress, who casually mentioned she was about to star in a “B” movie called “007” with Sean Connery, and her own friendship with Bruce Lee, whom she first met in Hong Kong and grew close to while filming The Wrecking Crew (1968), for which he served as martial-arts adviser.

“He was going to teach Sharon [Tate] and me some kung fu for a fight scene. That’s how I got to know Bruce quite well. We would hang out at the house, and he often told me about his plans to return to Hong Kong and make martial-arts films,” she remembers.

That now-famous fight scene between Tate and Kwan is immortalised in Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 film, Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, in which Margot Robbie, playing Tate, is shown watching that exact scene in a cinema. In her memoir, Kwan also reflects on Tate’s kind nature and tragic death, revealing the personal impact it had on her.

The memoir confronts other heartbreaks. Kwan opens up about the loss of her son and “best friend”, Bernie Pock, whom she shared with her first husband, Peter Pock.

Born in Austria and raised in Hong Kong, Bernie was fluent in Cantonese, adored and mastered martial arts and was described as wise beyond his years. Known for his kindness – he once sheltered a homeless boy – Bernie was a stunt performer in Los Angeles when he was diagnosed with Aids, contracted from a woman he loved and later married, before he died, in 1996, aged 33.

Even in the shadow of loss, Bernie refused to let their story end in tragedy. Together with Kwan and her new husband, Vienna-born actor and producer Norbert Meisel, now aged 96, the family completed a final project: Rebellious (also known as The Biker Poet), a 1995 film about a biker discovering himself, a testament to Bernie’s creativity and enduring spirit.

In the years since, Kwan has devoted herself to Aids awareness advocacy, channelling her grief into purpose. She also wrote Celebration of a Life: Memories of My Son (1997), a memoir that honours Bernie and preserves his memory.

Arthur Dong, the Oscar-nominated filmmaker and American Book Award-winning author of Forbidden City, USA (2014), has interviewed Kwan on many occasions over the past 20 years. He recalls the magnetic presence she brought to every set.

“Nancy candidly confronts the xenophobic and sexist attitudes that once branded her a ‘real-life China doll’, despite the pivotal influence of producer and mentor Ray Stark, who promoted her as a ‘girl of many nations’.”

Kwan became a symbol of possibility for actors navigating Hollywood’s rigid and often Eurocentric standards.

“I am from the East and West. My father is Chinese, my mother is English, and bringing that together … I feel very proud. The world is getting smaller, we recognise each other more and I wish I had even more cultural roots to embrace. It’s a wonderful thing,” she reflects.

“Nancy was among the most beautifully photographed women of the 60s,” notes Dong.

“That she was biracial made her worldwide popularity even more historic, particularly in the image- and race-conscious world of entertainment.”

Her pragmatism has always stood out to him. “In 2004, when I asked her to sum up the roller-coaster trajectory of her career, she replied, ‘What’s fair in life? There’s no fairness. As an actor, you have to keep that in mind; otherwise, you might as well not be in this business. Nothing lasts forever. Times change.’”

Even in her mid-80s, Kwan retains vitality and joy. Asked what she does to relax, she replies, “Probably tai chi, meditation […] that is the way I am.”

Her energy and elegance are palpable. “I’ve been in the business a long time now. I made my mark in the 60s, and now it’s [the mid-2020s]. It’s been a long journey, and I’ve met so many people along the way. Many Asian actors I know are still working, thank goodness, and television has opened up opportunities for them.”

Any advice for budding artists? “Just work hard,” she says. “Do what you can, steadily. Go out there. The film business is changing, too.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong Science Park celebrates 25 years of innovation and growth
item.description:
A particular kind of energy settles over Hong Kong Science Park on a weekday morning: researchers, deep in conversation, cross footbridges with laptop bags slung over shoulders; engineers transport prototypes between buildings, hunting for the next set of testing conditions; the air is rich with the buzz and hum of a community that has, over a quarter of a century, grown from reclaimed land at Pak Shek Kok into the largest start-up incubation platform in the city.

Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) kick-starts its silver-jubilee celebrations this year, and that industrious atmosphere is precisely what its new chairman, Cordelia Chung, wants people to understand about what has been built here. Not a laboratory, not a gadget: an ecosystem driving growth – one she intends to carry into its next phase.

Chung took up the chairmanship on July 1, arriving with a résumé that speaks of more than two decades inside one of the largest technology companies in the world. At IBM, she held senior leadership roles and steered the mainland China, Hong Kong and Asean markets, served as the vice-president and general counsel for Asia-Pacific, and was appointed to the IBM chairman and CEO’s Global Strategy Council as its first Asian female executive, contributing to worldwide direction setting across more than 140 countries. Her international background – having lived and worked in Tokyo, Singapore, Shanghai, Beijing and Hong Kong – brings a broader outlook.
item.content:encoded:
A particular kind of energy settles over Hong Kong Science Park on a weekday morning: researchers, deep in conversation, cross footbridges with laptop bags slung over shoulders; engineers transport prototypes between buildings, hunting for the next set of testing conditions; the air is rich with the buzz and hum of a community that has, over a quarter of a century, grown from reclaimed land at Pak Shek Kok into the largest start-up incubation platform in the city.

Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) kick-starts its silver-jubilee celebrations this year, and that industrious atmosphere is precisely what its new chairman, Cordelia Chung, wants people to understand about what has been built here. Not a laboratory, not a gadget: an ecosystem driving growth – one she intends to carry into its next phase.

Chung took up the chairmanship on July 1, arriving with a résumé that speaks of more than two decades inside one of the largest technology companies in the world. At IBM, she held senior leadership roles and steered the mainland China, Hong Kong and Asean markets, served as the vice-president and general counsel for Asia-Pacific, and was appointed to the IBM chairman and CEO’s Global Strategy Council as its first Asian female executive, contributing to worldwide direction setting across more than 140 countries. Her international background – having lived and worked in Tokyo, Singapore, Shanghai, Beijing and Hong Kong – brings a broader outlook.

She is no stranger to HKSTP, either, as her tenure on the board of directors, from 2017 to 2023, will show. Among Chung’s long list of achievements, receiving the Medal of Honour from the Hong Kong government in 2024, for her role in propelling the city’s innovation and technology (I&T) development, is arguably one of the most meaningful.

It is that blend of corporate governance and lived experience in a future-focused sector that shapes Chung’s vision for HKSTP, along with her sense of service to the community, instilled early on during her formative years at a convent school, which guides her intentionality to empower and enable talents.

China’s 15th five-year plan outlined high hopes for the continued advancement of Hong Kong’s I&T industry as an international hub for science and technology, and for it to deliver results. But Chung does not reach for a single headline figure to convince the audience of her ambition, instead framing her philosophy around four qualities: breadth, depth, height and strength.

“Hong Kong’s economy has relied heavily on finance and service industries, but facing global challenges, industrial transformation is now imperative. What we’re currently looking for is the breadth of I&T. We want to fully integrate I&T into traditional industries in order to expand Hong Kong’s industrial base,” she says, explaining that expanding talent development, nurturing that passion early and planting the seeds will provide a clear pathway for the next generation.

Once breadth is established, depth comes into play. “Besides pursuing advanced technology, we also aim for a wide application of technology,” she says, pointing to the investment in AI computing capacity as the base for something broader than any one company’s product road map. “It offers hope for transformation to traditional industries that have reached a bottleneck.” She counts off some of Hong Kong’s foundational economic pillars: “Financial services, construction, real estate, education – all of them can be pushed forward with technology, and it can be applied to so many different disciplines.”

Height, the third quality, is where Chung’s own international career shines through most clearly. Hong Kong’s unique East-meets-West positioning must be leveraged to “proactively attract businesses and talent from around the world. At the same time, we must lead the world by helping local and mainland Chinese I&T ventures expand to global markets”.

Last but not least, strength describes the pace and density she wants HKSTP to sustain. “It’s easier to create synergy when talent, capital and different resources are highly concentrated,” Chung says. Bumping into experts from different fields while walking through the park’s corridors and campuses encourages exchange and intellectual confluence. Removing friction at each stage of a company’s growth and creating a support network to match innovators with investors allows the start-ups to have the “sprint energy” to break through and thrive.

Chung’s vision is grand, and to understand her framing of the next chapter, it helps to trace how HKSTP arrived at this one.

Its roots stretch back to the 1970s, when the first of three industrial estates – in Tai Po, Yuen Long and Tseung Kwan O – was established, starting a lineage that eventually produced the Hong Kong Industrial Technology Centre Corporation in 1993.

It was not until 2001 that the government consolidated these assets under the HKSTP umbrella as the city’s flagship innovation and technology body, with the Hong Kong Science Park at Pak Shek Kok as its centrepiece.

With a quarter of a century under its belt, that foundation has grown into a multi-location operation spanning around 240 hectares (593 acres) of dedicated infrastructure. With a network of more than 210 investors and over 500 public- and private-sector partners, HKSTP credits these relationships with keeping talent, technology and capital moving through its community.

In the past eight years alone, HKSTP has demonstrated rapid acceleration, raising more than HK$170 billion (US$21.7 billion) in funding for its start-ups, with its Corporate Venture Fund leveraging private capital at a ratio of roughly one to 13. Under Chung’s predecessors, the number of companies based in the park rose from around 600 to more than 2,600, 14 unicorns were nurtured and 23 start-ups went public. HKSTP counts more than 26,000 professionals from 26 markets among its ranks, including success stories such as SenseTime and Lalamove, all built and scaled within its own ecosystem.

From its origins as an industrial asset manager, the evolution of HKSTP into a global technology catalyst has been defined by game-changing milestones. Following Hong Kong Science Park’s opening in June 2002, early operations focused on building research and development (R&D) capacity across four pillars: electronics, biotechnology, precision engineering and IT. Back then, Hong Kong’s technology scene was primarily designed to serve as an innovation engine for the city and the Pan-Pearl River Delta, reimagined in 2019 as the Greater Bay Area.

An iconic symbol of this ambition arrived in 2010. Following Charles Kao Kuen’s Nobel Prize win the previous year for groundbreaking achievements in fibre optics, HKSTP named its central landmark – the striking ovoid Charles K. Kao Auditorium, affectionately dubbed the “Golden Egg” – in honour of Hong Kong’s own laureate, inspiring generations of local talent.

In 2019 came the announcement of InnoHK, a flagship government initiative enabling research collaborations in artificial intelligence, robotics and healthcare with top global universities, while 2021 saw the repositioning of the three traditional industrial estates in Tai Po, Yuen Long and Tseung Kwan O as modern InnoParks.

It was a pivotal era that culminated in a historic visit by President Xi Jinping, in 2022, cementing the park’s role in the national innovation agenda.

HKSTP’s momentum has only accelerated. It extended its physical footprint with a Shenzhen branch in Futian district the following year and, in 2025, the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou Innovation Cluster was ranked No 1 in the world.

If Chung supplies the vision for the road ahead, HKSTP CEO Terry Wong Ping-sau is responsible for the daily mechanics of getting there. Wong has more than 30 years of international executive experience across advanced mobility, smart cities, infrastructure and energy, including in markets such as Australia and Saudi Arabia, but he describes his own first year in the role as a process of listening intently before acting.

“I spend a large amount of time almost every day meeting stakeholders, including universities, the government, start-ups, corporations, partnerships and investors,” he says, adding that he celebrated his one-year anniversary at HKSTP in much the same way. In fact, that instinct for stakeholder management is not so different from the discipline required to deliver an infrastructure project, despite the subject matter. Big budget, small budget, international, or local matters not. “We have to have a strategy, be clear about what we want to achieve, and work together so that big teams share the same goal.”

What has changed is the expanded terrain that HKSTP now covers, a point that dovetails with Chung’s own emphasis on breadth as a strategic priority. “We have a broad technical arena,” says Wong. “Market development, AI and robotics – it’s so broad, no one can say they’re an expert in all of this.”

But there is a method to the madness of managing that range. HKSTP has organised its support around four pillars that play to Hong Kong’s natural advantages: life and health technology, AI and data science, green technology and advanced manufacturing. Support is calibrated to a company’s stage of growth, moving from early incubation, global connections and talent scouting through to business development, early capital and elite programmes, as well as venture-capital networks designed to help mature firms expand abroad. Wong describes this as a journey “from ideation to IPO”, spanning over 20 initiatives, including funding, proof-of-concept support, business matching and market access.

Central to delivering that support is Inno.OS, the corporation’s own platform, blending hardware, software and services to help companies build value. Physical infrastructure is equally important. Beyond Hong Kong Science Park, the three InnoParks, dedicated to advanced manufacturing, offer plug-and-play production facilities that let companies move quickly from R&D into commercial output. A GreenTech Hub focuses on sustainability, and a new I&T facility, InnoPole, has been announced at the San Tin Technopole, in the Northern Metropolis area of the New Territories, where Chung has separately been appointed to the board of the dedicated company overseeing the site.

Successful support systems must also consider the well-being of the innovators at the heart of progress. InnoCell, a 17-storey smart-living and co-creation space next to Hong Kong Science Park, was built to house the talent on which the ecosystem depends. It embodies what HKSTP describes internally as a “Work, Live, Play, Learn” philosophy: proximity between researchers, engineers and entrepreneurs, whether in a laboratory or a shared kitchen, produces the kind of chance encounter that formal programming cannot manufacture. InnoCell is a physical expression of the same principle Chung raises when she talks about strength: put enough talent and capital within walking distance of one another, and ideas begin to take shape.

Nowhere is that philosophy more apparent than in life and health technology. More than 350 companies within the HKSTP ecosystem are involved in such fields as drug discovery and digital health. PanopticAI, a start-up founded by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) alumni, has developed a camera-based monitoring solution capable of reading vital signs, including heart rate, blood pressure and respiration rate, from little more than a short video clip. PanopticAI won clearance from the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for contactless pulse and respiratory rate measurement on its mobile application, making it the first Hong Kong company to secure such approval for a piece of software as a medical device. Early adopters now include Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong and healthcare firm Bupa.

Another example is Koln 3D, a Hong Kong Science Park company that has become the first medical metal 3D-printing manufacturer in the city, producing patient-specific body implants used in reconstructive surgeries as far afield as Central Asia and Europe. Its AI-powered technology can accurately tailor-make bone replacements and 3D models.

Starting out in 2013, Koln 3D has since expanded its production into the Greater Bay Area and Switzerland, and partnered with hospitals in Singapore, France and Kazakhstan – exactly the kind of internationalisation Chung and Wong say they want to accelerate across the Hong Kong Science Park portfolio.

Meanwhile, Lalamove, an on-demand delivery platform that grew from a local start-up within Hong Kong Science Park into a unicorn that operates in 17 markets across Asia, the Americas and the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, tells the story of scale centred on international expansion.

Founded in 2013, Lalamove, formerly known as “EasyVan”, joined HKSTP’s incubation programme early on to connect with technology partners and unlock investments that accelerated its development. Within 18 months, the company received two major capital injections and expanded to mainland China and other Asian markets. In April, it successfully tested its low-altitude-economy logistics solutions in complex urban environments, flying a cargo-carrying drone from Hong Kong Science Park, over Tolo Harbour, to the Mars Centre in the Tai Po InnoPark.

Positioning Hong Kong as a connector is an instinct that runs through HKSTP, supported by its own cross-border work. HKSTP presents itself as a two-way avenue for Hong Kong and mainland Chinese innovators seeking to expand internationally, while also helping overseas companies enter the Greater Bay Area, mainland China and beyond. Its Shenzhen branch has attracted more than 90 innovation companies, helped raise over 800 million yuan (US$119 million) in funding and supported more than 170 companies moving northbound into the mainland and 80 moving southbound into Hong Kong.

“Whatever we do, the market here is too small, anyway,” says Chung. “We need to have that broader, connective outlook.”

HKSTP says its Global Connect programme has brought together more than 8,000 stakeholders, advisers and innovators, while its Global Mixer programme has taken more than 200 partner companies to over 20 exhibitions in more than 10 countries, from Las Vegas to Dubai to Singapore.

“We can provide what we call a one-stop service,” says Chung. “If you have an idea, we can incubate you, we can give you money. When we think you’re doing a good job, we can help you accelerate. We can introduce investors, lawyers, bankers, tax consultants, accountants – the full suite of things that you need to really grow your business. If what you do is something that can be produced, you can actually land in one of our InnoParks and do the pilot production there and test it out.

“It’s about building the bridge, making sure people are connected, making sure that the people who have the ideas meet the people who can make it happen.”

She explains that the park’s bridging ability can “support the scale and eventual maturity of the entire I&T landscape in Hong Kong. We’re ready; the infrastructure is ready. We’re not going from zero to one, we’re [going] from one to 10 or one to N”.

For companies coming from different starting points, Wong notes, the support required is rarely identical. “For companies from mainland China, their main objective is to expand overseas, and they already have good products that are selling in China.” What HKSTP offers is help understanding global regulatory standards and linking them with the right industry players. Newer, earlier-stage companies tend to need more fundamental support: introductions to researchers, help refining a prototype, or access to corporate partners willing to run pilot trials. “Instead of doing it on their own, the people in our park get access to different stakeholders,” Wong says. “We proactively curate the people they actually need.”

Chung brings the governance experience and the outward-facing conviction to argue that Hong Kong’s next phase depends on breadth of talent, depth of adoption, height of ambition and strength of concentration. Wong brings the operational discipline to turn that framework into an organisation whose real product is connective tissue: the funding relationships, the mentorship networks and the physical proximity that let Hong Kong’s researchers and entrepreneurs turn ideas into products, and products into global businesses.

For an organisation that has spent 25 years building that infrastructure, both physical and relational, Chung’s four-part vision reads less like a slogan and more like a checklist for the next page. Breadth, so that more of Hong Kong’s economy and more of its young people have a stake in the outcome. Depth, so that the technologies built here change how entire industries operate. Height, so that Hong Kong’s position between mainland China and the rest of the world becomes a genuine advantage. And strength, so that the density of talent and capital already gathered keeps generating the kind of collaboration no five-year plan can fully script in advance.

Chung feels confident about the future because she has seen first-hand the path that lies ahead and where it can lead, during her years as a board member of HKSTP. “When I first joined, the start-up population here was around 600. Now, we have over 2,600. It has really grown. But is it enough? I don’t think it’s enough. So, that is one thing that I want to steer: for us to become much more energetic in this area,” she says. “In the last 10 years, 20 years, we have created a solid foundation. Now, we can take it to the next level.”

Much can change in the next 25 years. In fact, the chairman is counting on it. Chung muses on the next chapter with good humour: “I have to think of my own age, if I still have the ability to …” She trails off, deep in thought, imagining the possibilities.

“In 25 years’ time, I hope that the various science parks in the entire Greater Bay Area will be truly integrated. With laws and regulations completely streamlined, HKSTP will be the largest innovation cluster globally,” she smiles. “A day at Hong Kong Science Park will look like being in the leading science and technology hub in the entire world: a SuperPark.”

HKSTP kicks off its 25th anniversary on August 31 with its “Together to Next” prelude celebration, honouring the visionaries, partners and innovators of the I&T community. To register for the event, click here

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Anwar traded reform for power. Now Umno wants it all
item.description:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.

The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.
item.content:encoded:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.

The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.

PKR’s victory in the 2022 general election came at the cost of the very reforms it had promised to deliver, as Anwar had little choice but to negotiate compromises with erstwhile rivals, including former ruling party Umno, to steady his administration. Those trade-offs did not go unnoticed.

Anwar’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, of which PKR is a founding and principal member, has suffered a series of bruising defeats across three state elections since November – and whatever platform the prime minister gave a once-deflated Umno has turned the party into the greatest threat to his rule.

Staring down the possibility of being turfed out of Putrajaya after just one term, PKR members are left wondering how to reverse the trend, especially as surging Malay nationalist sentiment carries a resurgent Umno forward.

“The delegates are all confused. They need clear direction,” a senior party leader told This Week in Asia, speaking anonymously due to the sensitivity of the matter.

“Before, it was about coming to power and raising Anwar as prime minister. Now what?”

Senior members who attended last weekend’s congress pointed to a disconnect between Anwar, his party’s top leadership and the rank and file, who have been left without a common purpose to rally around.

That gulf became apparent during Anwar’s opening speech at the congress last Saturday.

Delegates gave only a lukewarm response as their party president and prime minister listed out, at length, his administration’s successes in bolstering growth and investment numbers.

It was only when Anwar touched on the multibillion-ringgit scandal at the Tabung Haji pilgrim fund – made public last month – that the crowd roared to life, with some delegates passionately demanding retribution against Umno, the party in power when the alleged offences occurred.

That reaction offered the clearest indication yet that the prime minister and PH need to coalesce around a clear message if they hope to slow Umno’s momentum, and that of its nascent partnership with the opposition Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS).

“You see Umno and PAS talking about uniting the ummah [Muslim faithful], and claims that [PKR coalition partner] DAP is out to wrest power from the Malays. It’s simple messaging that people can easily understand,” the senior PKR leader said.

When comparing investments and other economic indicators, Anwar scored higher than past leaders, he said. “But the people here don’t understand all that. You need to present things using simple language.”

House of cards

The problems trace back to November 2022, when Anwar was named prime minister by former king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah on condition that he form a unity government that included allies and rivals alike, to avoid a hung parliament.

The arrangement threw a lifeline to Umno, which had just suffered its worst electoral outing, winning fewer than 30 of parliament’s 222 seats.

From there, Anwar has been accused of setting aside his reform agenda and steering his government rightward, mirroring the previous Umno administration’s penchant for cracking down on sexual minorities and free speech in a bid to win over a Malay-Muslim majority suspicious of his motives.

Despite growing outrage from long-time supporters, the prime minister enjoyed a period of relative political stability over the first half of his five-year term, as economic growth and foreign investment hit record highs.

But that proved to be merely the calm before the storm.

The first salvo was fired in the Sabah state election last November, when Anwar’s PH coalition was all but wiped out. Hardest hit was the Democratic Action Party (DAP), the largest party in Anwar’s federal coalition, which lost every seat it contested.

Over the past two months, PH’s tenuous grip on power has truly sunk in, as it suffered back-to-back defeats at the hand of fellow federal partner, Umno.

Umno cruised to an extended supermajority in the southern state of Johor in July, then struck an informal alliance with Islamist rivals PAS to wrest control of Negeri Sembilan state from PH earlier this month.

The losses in the three state elections were the first tangible signs that Anwar and PH were in real trouble, after years of complaints from civil society groups and PH’s own support base about the lack of reforms following decades of promises.

Wong Chen, a three-term MP who quit PKR this month after being unceremoniously removed from a government post and cut off from his constituency fund, said the current trend pointed to PH losing the next national poll, which must be held by February 2028 at the latest.

If they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support

PKR defector Wong Chen on his former party

Wong, who later joined fellow former PKR leader Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama party, said the recent string of electoral losses proved that Anwar’s personal popularity was not enough to guarantee PH’s survival against Umno and PAS.

“They have to start accepting the fact that if they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support to be a strong opposition,” Wong said.

The losses did trigger a response from Anwar. Last weekend, he pledged that the government would proceed to repeal the controversial University and University Colleges Act 1971 – which student activists have long said stifles freedom of speech and expression – and fulfil promises to impose a two-term limit on the prime minister and separate the powers of the attorney general and public prosecutor.

But those pledges may amount to little if they only translate into legislative change, according to Timothy Wong, a senior analyst with government affairs consultancy BowerGroupAsia.

“There needs to be real action behind institutional reforms rather than relying solely on legislation to convince the majority,” he said.

“They will need to do more to convince a politically fatigued electorate, especially urban and middle-class voters who are feeling increasingly disenfranchised by the country’s politics.”

Complicating matters further is Anwar’s continued reliance on Umno, which long-time Malaysia watcher James Chin says has every reason to sabotage the prime minister’s reform push, leveraging its cabinet positions – and the budgets that come with them – to bolster its own electoral chances.

“If you want to do real deep reforms, you have to inform the cabinet. And of course Umno, which has a lot of ministers in cabinet, will try to sabotage it or not agree to it, so you’re stuck,” said Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

“He [Anwar] knows deep down inside that Umno is plotting to win the next election and replace him as prime minister.”

Cracks in PH

Anwar caught a break, of sorts, last weekend, when delegates at DAP’s own convention voted decisively to remain within the governing coalition, after months of speculation the party might walk away.

But that lopsided vote belied the seething dissent within DAP’s ranks over how Anwar has managed the ruling coalition – especially his perceived favouring of Umno.

“Instead of bringing the coalition partners together, what has he done? He has divided us, pitted one against the other and empowered Umno. We cannot afford to ignore that,” DAP leader Sangeet Kaur Deo told her party’s convention.

“We cannot run away from the fact that today, under our government, Malaysia is more divided on racial lines than ever before. We cannot deny that there are scandals relating to corruption that have escalated during the time that we have been in power.”

Within PKR itself, the complaints are just as pointed. Some argue Anwar’s political instincts have curdled into self preservation.

His decision, in closing the party congress last Sunday, to announce an extra 222 million ringgit (US$54.6 million) in annual constituency allocations for MPs – money used for everything from pothole repairs to cash handouts for the needy – struck many grass-roots members as besides the point.

It did nothing to address the growing anger over stalled reform, critics say – with no explanation offered either for why three PKR MPs seen as loyal to Rafizi had their own allocations slashed.

Rafizi quit PKR after losing the deputy presidency to Anwar’s daughter, Nurul Izzah, in a contest he claimed was rife with nepotism.

Nurul Izzah has since stepped back too, beginning what the party has called a “leave of absence” to pursue her studies after serving her final days as her father’s deputy at the congress.

The extra funding fits a pattern: over the past two years, Anwar has pushed to increase cash handouts and maintain costly fuel subsidies despite the strain on public coffers, in a bid to win broader support.

One grass-roots leader offered a warning from history. “You can’t keep giving people freebies and expect them to love you. Look at what happened during BN’s time,” he said, invoking the Umno-led Barisan Nasional coalition that lost power in 2018 at the height of the 1MDB corruption scandal despite its own cash-handout scheme. “They still lost. We are doing exactly the same thing now.”

These internal rifts may not trigger an outright collapse of PH, but analysts warn that pressure from DAP and PKR supporters will keep mounting as long as Anwar prioritises political stability and his relationship with Umno over the reform agenda.

“The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out as an electoral alliance,” said public policy adviser Kamles Kumar, associate director for Malaysia at strategic advisory group Asia Group Advisors.

“If electoral losses continue, the question will increasingly shift from whether PH can stay together to whether staying together still benefits each component party.”

And the next test for PH is not far off. The Melaka state election, which must be called by February next year, is already looming and the Umno-led BN – which holds 21 of the state assembly’s 28 seats – has signalled its terms for any future deal: PH can have a shot at the seven seats BN does not currently control, but nothing more.

The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out

Kamles Kumar, public policy adviser

According to one Melaka-based PKR grass-roots leader, the party leadership is seriously considering the offer, even if it means accepting a subordinate role to Umno.

Yet this appears badly out of step with sentiments on the ground. “The top are talking about negotiating with BN, but we’ve already seen what happened in the two past state elections. On the ground, people are already sharpening their knives,” the insider said.

“As far as the grass roots are concerned, we have two choices. Fight and lose, or not do anything and die [politically].”

Anwar has promised party delegates he will listen: to their opinions, their suggestions and even their criticism.

For a party that spent 20 years fighting to put him in power – and is now watching that power slip through its fingers – the question is no longer whether he hears them.

It is whether, after everything, just listening will be enough.

Additional reporting by Iman Muttaqin Yusof

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese defence chief skirts flashpoints at Xiangshan Forum ahead of Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
With just a week to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun opted for the diplomatic path in his address to China’s premier security conference on Wednesday.

Speaking at the annual Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, Dong took veiled swipes at Washington and its allies but – unlike last year – appeared to pull his punches, skipping mentions of contentious issues such as Taiwan and the South China Sea.

He also said Beijing would share its experience in “military building” and “provide assistance within our capabilities” to foreign armed forces, a rare public offer by the country’s top defence officials.
item.content:encoded:
With just a week to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun opted for the diplomatic path in his address to China’s premier security conference on Wednesday.

Speaking at the annual Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, Dong took veiled swipes at Washington and its allies but – unlike last year – appeared to pull his punches, skipping mentions of contentious issues such as Taiwan and the South China Sea.

He also said Beijing would share its experience in “military building” and “provide assistance within our capabilities” to foreign armed forces, a rare public offer by the country’s top defence officials.

Beijing seems increasingly confident of its military prowess heading into the People’s Liberation Army’s centenary next year, with a belief that it is closing the military gap with Washington.

At the same time, there are signs of improving defence ties between the two powers. A senior Pentagon official said earlier that US-China military communication was “stronger than it has been in years”.

At the forum, Dong described the global landscape as complex and international security as “fragile”, saying there was an “urgent need” to improve global security governance.

“We must promote an equal and orderly multipolar world and an economic globalisation that is universally beneficial and inclusive, forging a new path to security based on dialogue rather than confrontation, partnership rather than alliance and win-win outcomes rather than zero-sum games,” he said.

While he did not name any country, Dong alluded to the US and its actions in the Middle East on several occasions, including urging “major powers” to shoulder the responsibility of maintaining global stability and upholding multilateralism, and calling on countries to “resist reckless moves that use security as a bargaining chip”.

“We must not tolerate provocations that attempt to hijack the overall interests of countries and regions for private gain or the interests of small cliques. We must work together to rein them in,” he added.

“The persistence of global conflict serves as a sobering reminder that … force cannot resolve the root of the problem. Coercion and pressure only widen rifts and create more difficulties.”

His comments took tacit aim at the United States as the Donald Trump administration resumed strikes against Iran in a bid to end a conflict now in its seventh month.

Dong instead positioned Beijing as a “responsible major country” that has maintained an impartial stance, capable of acting as a “positive and stabilising force” in resolving conflicts.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi hosted his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Beijing on Wednesday.

Even as Dong took veiled jabs at the US, his tone was markedly more measured than at the same forum last year.

A year ago, he still did not name any country but described military alliances as groups driven by “selfish interests”.

Urging countries to stand up against “disguised hegemonic logic and bullying acts”, he also said the time that the world was overshadowed by a “cold war mentality, hegemonism and protectionism” – phrases Beijing routinely uses to describe Washington’s actions.

Unlike last year, when Dong asserted that the return of Taiwan to Beijing was “an integral part of the post-war order” and that Beijing was “ready to thwart any external military interference”, he left out Taiwan from this year’s speech.

Zhou Bo, senior fellow at the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, described Dong’s tone on Wednesday as “relatively mild” but stressed that the omission of Taiwan did not mean the issue was any less important.

“Not mentioning Taiwan does not mean that China is less concerned with the issue,” said Zhou, a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army. “It doesn’t mean that China is not paying attention to it.”

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Beijing has repeatedly said that Taiwan is its core interest and a “red line” that must not be crossed in Sino-US relations. The issue is expected to be raised again by Xi when he sits down with Trump next week.

Nor did Dong make any mention of the South China Sea. Last year, he criticised “extra-regional powers” for using freedom of navigation to stir up tensions in the disputed waterway.

According to Zhou, Dong’s offer to help with military development in other countries reflects Beijing’s growing confidence in its military.

That offer came a day after Dong hosted senior officials attending the forum, including the defence ministers of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Myanmar, according to China’s defence ministry.

The PLA has also held a series of joint training exercises with other militaries, including those of Belarus, Egypt, Singapore and Thailand in the past month.
