Meanwhile, according to Zheng Yongnian, dean of the school of public policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, it was good for the world that the US and China had agreed to establish stable relations since Trump’s visit to China in May.

Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University’s school of international studies, said the forum was aimed at promoting security cooperation between Beijing and the world, so Dong’s speech could not solely focus on “these contentious issues”, referring to the omission of Taiwan and the South China Sea.

Beijing’s offer to help build other militaries stemmed from the turmoil roiling global affairs, Zhu added, saying that while China could deepen cooperation through multilateral platforms, it also needed to work together with smaller states if they faced internal problems.

“This also demonstrates China’s responsibility as a major country in the face of various current tensions,” he said.

With China-Japan relations still strained following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks on Taiwan in November last year, Dong said the world “must bear in mind the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against … hegemonism, militarism and historical revisionism”.

Among other things, the Chinese defence chief also called for countries to deepen cooperation in areas including joint exercises and training as well as engage in dialogue on artificial intelligence, outer space and the deep sea.

The three-day Xiangshan Forum is expected to gather defence delegations from close to 100 countries, regions and international organisations. The forum, seen as Beijing’s answer to Singapore’s annual Shangri-La Dialogue, marks its 20th anniversary this year.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore court rejects 90-year-old’s spousal support claim against ex-wife, 89
item.description:
A Singapore family court rejected a 90-year-old man’s claim for spousal maintenance from his 89-year-old wife, noting that both of them are in the twilight of their lives.

The court also noted that the man would receive more than S$2 million (US$1.6 million) from the matrimonial pool, comprising the couple’s assets to be divided in the divorce, and his wife was a retiree living on a pension.

The former couple were married for more than 64 years and have three children, all aged above 60, a judgment published on Wednesday said. They were not named in the judgment, as is usual for a family court ruling.
item.content:encoded:
A Singapore family court rejected a 90-year-old man’s claim for spousal maintenance from his 89-year-old wife, noting that both of them are in the twilight of their lives.

The court also noted that the man would receive more than S$2 million (US$1.6 million) from the matrimonial pool, comprising the couple’s assets to be divided in the divorce, and his wife was a retiree living on a pension.

The former couple were married for more than 64 years and have three children, all aged above 60, a judgment published on Wednesday said. They were not named in the judgment, as is usual for a family court ruling.

Most of the value in the matrimonial pool came from their joint asset, a S$5.8 million house.

The couple married in January 1960 and were granted an interim judgment for divorce in September 2024. There were no issues of custody or child maintenance since their children are adults.

Dealing with the division of matrimonial assets, Justice Dedar Singh Gill added about S$14,500 in the man’s name to the pool. Most of this is from his Central Provident Fund (CPF), Singapore’s mandatory social security savings scheme.

He added about S$80,000 from the woman’s assets to the pool, including almost S$20,000 in CPF.

Disputed contributions

The woman argued that she had contributed 100 per cent to the matrimonial home and financed it alone.

She said she had bought their previous property under the Teacher’s Estate housing scheme, which provided homes for educators. The sale proceeds from this property were used fully to buy the matrimonial home, to which her husband contributed “nothing”.

The man sought a 50:50 division of all matrimonial assets, claiming to have contributed to both the Teacher’s Estate property and the matrimonial home.

However, the judge noted that neither side’s account was supported by documentary evidence.

The woman sought a ratio of 80:20 in indirect contributions in her favour, arguing that she bore virtually all the financial and non-financial burdens of the family throughout the marriage.

She said she was the main provider during the first half of the marriage when both of them worked, paying for the children’s tuition and courses, family holidays and a domestic worker to care for the children when she was at work.

She also said that she gave her son S$50,000 to start a business that failed, and footed the bills for her children’s weddings.

After she retired in 1992, she claimed that her husband had no income and contributed “nothing” while she supported the household from her pension of about S$2,400 a month. She gave her husband half of this amount each month, she added.

She also said that she was the primary carer for her children, cooking for the family and supervising the various domestic helpers and overseeing the repairs and maintenance of the household.

The husband sought an equal or near-equal division of indirect contributions, claiming that until retirement, both parties had pooled their incomes in joint accounts. From these, all the household expenses were paid.

After retirement, he said the expenses were paid from their pooled savings in joint accounts, and thereafter from his wife’s joint accounts with their son and oldest daughter.

He said he did his “fair share of being involved in the care and upbringing of the children”.

Justice Gill said the indirect financial contributions for the first half of the marriage were difficult to determine, given the couple’s differing versions of events without objective evidence.

However, the position is clearer for the second half of the marriage after their retirement.

It was undisputed that the man had no income beyond his monthly annuity of S$485.75 from insurer NTUC Income, and that the only income stream was the woman’s monthly pension of about S$2,400, of which she gave her husband half.

The woman also produced payment records showing that she paid the property tax bills up to 2024, as well as receipts for household bills she continued to cover on her own.

Family carer

The judge also found that the wife contributed the greater share in indirect non-financial contributions, with detailed evidence of her caregiving and home-making.

She was the primary carer of her children from birth and even when she worked, helping them with their homework and managing their schooling and activities.

She also ran the household, cooked for the family, organised family gatherings, and trained and supervised the various domestic workers they hired.

“The husband, on the other hand, does no more than assert in general terms that he did his fair share,” Justice Gill said.

“He descends to no particulars of caring for the children, their schooling, their health or their emotional needs. I also consider it significant that the husband neither disputed most of what the wife says she did for the family nor offered any competing account of his own.”

He assessed indirect contributions at 70:30 in favour of the woman.

The woman sought a 2 per cent increase of her share of the matrimonial pool, saying that her ex-husband had illegally excluded her from the home from March 2025 and placed a padlock on the gate. The man, however, claimed that his ex-wife and their oldest daughter moved out of their own accord.

Justice Gill noted that this complaint of illegal exclusion surfaced for the first time only in written submissions, and both parties would obtain substantial sums from the pool in any event. He declined to raise the woman’s share of the assets on this basis.

In total, the ratio across direct and indirect contributions was computed to be 60:40, in favour of the woman. Accordingly, she was to get S$3.5 million, while her ex-husband obtained S$2.4 million.

The man sought maintenance as an incapacitated former husband under the Women’s Charter, pointing to his medical and mobility issues, his inability to earn a livelihood, his minimal income and his wife’s departure from the matrimonial home. This has left him to cover the home’s expenses alone.

If he did not get maintenance, the man asked for a lump sum equivalent to 5 to 10 per cent of his share of the matrimonial assets.

The judge rejected the man’s claim for spousal maintenance and his request for the lump sum payment. He said that both parties are in the twilight of their lives, with neither having any earning capacity nor any expectations of improving their financial positions through work.

Both of them rely on monthly pensions or payouts as their financial source, and they will each have very substantial sums from the matrimonial pool, Justice Gill added.

The sum of more than S$2 million that the man will obtain is “more than sufficient to meet the needs of a 90-year-old retiree for the remainder of his life”.

“Once the division takes effect, he will be amply provided for. In these circumstances, I do not think an order for maintenance against the wife, herself an elderly retiree living on a pension, would be just or necessary.”

The man sought reimbursement from his ex-wife’s share for the property tax he paid on the house for the years of assessment 2025 and 2026, saying that she had paid nothing since moving out in March 2025.

The judge acknowledged that the man should not necessarily bear the entire property tax simply because he lived there, but found his argument for his ex-wife to pay the full bill untenable.

He said that the property tax for the two years must be borne equally by both parties.

The home is to be sold on the open market within six months, with them having joint conduct of the sale.

Each side will bear its own costs.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] How will the Okinawa governor’s race result reshape China’s local messaging?
item.description:
The leadership change in Okinawa could deal a quiet blow to Beijing’s attempts to leverage local opposition to remilitarisation and the US-Japan military alliance, according to analysts.

They added that the shift would compel Chinese academics and state media to recalibrate their messaging and approach towards the strategically vital Japanese prefecture.

Genta Koja, the 42-year-old backed by Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party to become Okinawa’s new governor, defeated incumbent Denny Tamaki on Sunday. This brought an end to eight years of Tamaki’s leadership, characterised by vocal pacifism and active regional diplomacy with Chinese cities that historically maintained ties with Okinawa.
item.content:encoded:
The leadership change in Okinawa could deal a quiet blow to Beijing’s attempts to leverage local opposition to remilitarisation and the US-Japan military alliance, according to analysts.

They added that the shift would compel Chinese academics and state media to recalibrate their messaging and approach towards the strategically vital Japanese prefecture.

Genta Koja, the 42-year-old backed by Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party to become Okinawa’s new governor, defeated incumbent Denny Tamaki on Sunday. This brought an end to eight years of Tamaki’s leadership, characterised by vocal pacifism and active regional diplomacy with Chinese cities that historically maintained ties with Okinawa.

For Beijing, which has long cultivated relationships with Okinawan leaders who challenge Tokyo’s defence policies, Koja’s win represents the loss of a sympathetic subnational partner.

Analysts said the election result served as a reality check for China’s external messaging, requiring it to adjust its approach towards Okinawan voters who were prioritising bread-and-butter issues over opposition to American military bases.

Okinawa prefecture is made up of around 40 inhabited islands and has a population of 1.5 million. It hosts roughly 70 per cent of all US military facilities in Japan despite accounting for less than 1 per cent of the country’s land area.

The United States seized Okinawa from Japan after World War II. Washington returned administrative control of the islands to Tokyo in 1972, but it has maintained a substantial military presence that serves as a crucial node in checking Beijing’s regional ambitions.

Before Japan annexed it in 1879, Okinawa was known as the Ryukyu Kingdom, an independent maritime kingdom that paid tribute to China during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties.

In July 2023, Tamaki visited Beijing as part of a Japanese trade delegation and paid respects at the historic Ryukyu Kingdom cemetery in Beijing’s Tongzhou district.

Concerns have grown in Japan that Beijing may play the “Ryukyu card” – invoking the islands’ history to question Japanese sovereignty over Okinawa and counter Tokyo’s position on Taiwan.

Positioned within the “first island chain”, which stretches along the East Asian coastline from the Kuril Islands down to Borneo, Okinawa acts as a barrier limiting the People’s Liberation Army’s access to the Pacific Ocean. It is expected to play a vital strategic role in the event of a Taiwan conflict.

In addition to the American presence, Japan’s Self-Defence Forces have been expanding their deployments in Okinawa as part of Tokyo’s “southwest shift” – a defence strategy that bolsters the region with new missile systems, radar installations and troop deployments.

Tamaki firmly opposed the construction of new American military facilities on Okinawa Island and also opposed a plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station in southern Okinawa to the Henoko coastal area in the north. Koja supports this controversial plan but has also called on Tokyo to provide a clearer timeline on when the Futenma station will close.

For decades, local Okinawans have protested against the American military presence, with residents long complaining of noise pollution, security risks and recurring cases of sexual assault by US servicemen.

Xu Weijun, an associate research professor at the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou, said that with Tamaki’s exit, China would lose an important interlocutor who could speak on behalf of the prefectural government to “publicly emphasise dialogue and oppose the expansion of US military bases”.

“Koja’s victory could weaken the leverage Beijing has long relied on to constrain Tokyo through Okinawa’s local politics,” he said.

Xu noted that Koja would be far more mindful of Tokyo’s foreign policy stance and would be likely to scale back reciprocal visits to China that carried obvious political symbolism.

He is also expected to draw stricter boundaries on local matters that concern Beijing, such as the Ryukyu narrative, Taiwan and Japan-US military base arrangements, according to Xu.

In recent years, Chinese state media have played up the historical ties between China and the ancient Ryukyu Kingdom while emphasising tensions between Okinawa residents and the US military.

Chinese academics and state media have even suggested challenging Tokyo’s control of Okinawa. While Beijing has not openly done so, state media have increasingly called for more research into historical and legal claims over the islands.

Xu said that following Tamaki’s defeat, it would be difficult for Chinese media and intellectuals to continue using the narrative that Okinawans generally opposed US-Japan security arrangements. Koja’s victory at least showed that a candidate who did not oppose the air station’s relocation could still win, he added.

“This shift can weaken the credibility and factual foundation of China’s previous narrative, which relied on invoking Okinawan public opinion to criticise Japan-US military activities.”

Xu suggested that Beijing should shift from emphasising the divergence between the prefectural government and Tokyo to focusing on the social consequences of the military build-up.

“China’s focus should be on how these arrangements increase the local burden, exacerbate regional tensions and pose threats to the lives and property of Okinawan residents,” he said.

Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, cautioned against overstating the impact of the election on China’s approach.

“China does not have a formal Okinawa policy in official diplomatic terms, and the change in Okinawa’s leadership may not constitute a shock to existing policy from Chinese cities that have civilian exchanges with Okinawa,” he said.

“During Tamaki’s tenure, he maintained relatively friendly communication channels with China at both the central and local levels. How Okinawa now adjusts and develops its relationship with China will certainly be a test for the incoming governor.”

Yet Koja’s victory signals a recalibration of Okinawan priorities that may still offer Beijing room for regional engagement.

Exit polls conducted by Kyodo News showed that only 21 per cent of voters prioritised issues related to US military bases, while nearly 50 per cent chose economic revitalisation when deciding who to vote for. Over half of the respondents said they supported the Futenma relocation.

During the campaign, Koja pledged to double Okinawa’s average income – which remains among the lowest of all prefectures – expand the local government budget for childcare and increase tourist spending on the island.

According to Xu, Koja’s success stemmed from tapping into Okinawa residents’ economic anxieties.

“This suggests that his administration will still need to preserve commercial ties with China and remain open to advancing tourism, business and cultural cooperation,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Politics aside, young Vietnamese are warming to China
item.description:
Vietnam is often held up as proof of China’s underwhelming soft power in Southeast Asia: a millennium of resistance against Chinese domination, a border war within living memory, unresolved maritime disputes and elite surveys that consistently show Vietnamese respondents’ deep distrust of Beijing.

Yet beneath these strategic tensions, a quieter shift is under way. Young Vietnamese are warming to Chinese culture, language, lifestyles and economic opportunity. From crowds queuing for Labubu toys to a scramble for Chinese-language jobs, and from Chinese content going viral on social media to record numbers of Vietnamese students choosing to study at Chinese universities, China is being woven even more tightly into the everyday lives of young Vietnamese.

Four converging forces underpin this shift: cultural attraction, new-media connectivity, facilitation by both governments and economic incentives.
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam is often held up as proof of China’s underwhelming soft power in Southeast Asia: a millennium of resistance against Chinese domination, a border war within living memory, unresolved maritime disputes and elite surveys that consistently show Vietnamese respondents’ deep distrust of Beijing.

Yet beneath these strategic tensions, a quieter shift is under way. Young Vietnamese are warming to Chinese culture, language, lifestyles and economic opportunity. From crowds queuing for Labubu toys to a scramble for Chinese-language jobs, and from Chinese content going viral on social media to record numbers of Vietnamese students choosing to study at Chinese universities, China is being woven even more tightly into the everyday lives of young Vietnamese.

Four converging forces underpin this shift: cultural attraction, new-media connectivity, facilitation by both governments and economic incentives.

China’s cultural appeal rests on a mix of cultural familiarity and contemporary trendiness. Chinese dramas have long been a fixture of Vietnamese television and Vietnam is now among Asia’s largest markets for them, their reach amplified by digital distribution. Content from major Chinese streaming platforms such as iQiyi, Tencent Video and Youku is carried on Vietnamese platforms such as VieOn and FPT Play, delivering China’s entertainment industry directly into Vietnamese homes and onto Vietnamese smartphones.

Meanwhile, some Vietnamese celebrities have found wider fame on Chinese reality shows, while hit Chinese formats have been adapted for Vietnamese audiences.

China’s appeal has also spilled into Vietnam’s shopping and lifestyle. Many Chinese brands have won over young Vietnamese with trendy designs and affordable prices. Mixue, the Chinese ice cream and tea chain, had expanded to more than 1,300 Vietnamese outlets by late 2024, making Vietnam its second-largest overseas market. Chagee, Cotti Coffee, KKV and Pop Mart have followed suit, turning shopping centres in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City into showcases of “Made in China” cool.

Algorithmic ambassadors

None of this cultural traction would travel as far, or as fast, without new media. TikTok counts more than 70 million monthly active users in Vietnam, out of 460 million across Southeast Asia, and sits within a broader Chinese digital ecosystem that channels content on Chinese culture and daily life to regional audiences. Vietnamese-language content on TikTok and Facebook – including from Vietnamese influencers living in or travelling through China – offers viewers a window onto Chinese cities, landscapes and the rhythms of life and work in the country.

This bottom-up, peer-driven pull is unfolding alongside a renewed official push for closer people-to-people ties. Since the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations and the designation of 2025 as the “Year of Vietnam-China Humanistic Exchange”, officials on both sides have promoted youth engagement. The joint statement during President Xi Jinping’s state visit in April 2025 invited Vietnamese youth to join “Red Study Tours”. More than 1,000 have done so, visiting sites commemorating the two countries’ shared revolutionary history – among them the former base of the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League in Guangzhou – alongside hi-tech hubs that showcase China’s modern development and technological achievements.

Two-way travel has expanded too, supported by growing rail and air links. Since August, Vietnamese citizens have been able to transit China visa-free for up to 10 days, and the Vietnam–China Tourism Cooperation Years 2026–2027 initiative aims to further strengthen people-to-people ties. The numbers are impressive: Chinese visitor arrivals to Vietnam surged 41.3 per cent to 5.3 million in 2025, making China Vietnam’s largest source of tourists, while Vietnam had become China’s fourth-largest source market by mid-2026.

Education diplomacy tells a similar story: the number of Vietnamese students in China has more than doubled, from 11,300 in 2018 to about 25,000 today – still trailing the numbers in South Korea (43,300), Japan (36,300), Australia (33,000) and the United States (31,300), but expected to climb further as Beijing promises at least 1,000 government scholarships and 1,000 Chinese-language teachers to Vietnam.

Mandarin pays

Underpinning all this is economic pragmatism. Vietnamese attraction to China rests not only on what China represents, but also on what engaging with it offers. As Chinese investment has poured into Vietnam, Mandarin has become a sought-after skill for young Vietnamese. Vietnamese recruitment platform Joboko reported roughly 13,000 openings for Chinese-speaking professionals in 2025, up 50 per cent on the year before, with fluency commanding better pay in industrial estates and Chinese-invested companies. LinkedIn, TopCV and VietnamWorks each list thousands of Chinese-language roles in Vietnam, with monthly salaries ranging from US$500 to US$2,000 – attractive pay by Vietnamese standards.

Demand is such that Vietnam recorded the world’s highest number of registrations for the HSK Chinese-proficiency test in the first quarter of 2025. At some Vietnamese universities, Chinese-language programmes now post higher admission scores than English ones, reflecting surging youth interest. English remains the default foreign language taught from primary school and is moving towards compulsory status by 2030, while Chinese is increasingly picked up later for its practical economic value. But anecdotal evidence points to growing parental demand for early Chinese learning and Vietnam has said it will pilot Chinese, Japanese and Korean lessons for preschoolers to prepare for future workforce competitiveness.

Young Vietnamese people’s growing embrace of China coexists with deep-rooted patriotic sensitivities

All this unfolds as Hanoi emphasises the more productive dimensions of its relationship with Beijing, while keeping long-standing South China Sea tensions in the background. This favourable climate may have helped, but young Vietnamese people’s growing embrace of China coexists with deep-rooted patriotic sensitivities. The 2025 boycott of Chagee after its app and website displayed China’s disputed “nine-dash line” and the removal of some Chinese dramas displaying the same map show how quickly those sensitivities can resurface. Yet such episodes have merely interrupted rather than reversed the broader trend. Chagee is back in Vietnam, just as bilateral ties have recovered from the turbulence of the 2010s, when the maritime dispute overshadowed the relationship.

Whether this societal warming can cushion or withstand the next downturn in relations remains to be seen. Vietnam’s history suggests that affinity with China and resistance to its power have never been mutually exclusive. A younger generation is now living that old paradox on new terms: drawn more directly and intimately into China’s orbit of culture and opportunity, while retaining the instinct to push back when national interests collide.

Hoang Thi Ha is a Senior Fellow and Co-coordinator of the Regional Strategic and Political Studies Programme, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. Pham Thi Phuong Thao is a Senior Research Officer at the Asean Studies Centre, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] No pit stops: Chinese coal mine makes big upgrade with autonomous electric trucks
item.description:
In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).

In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash.

Today, however, an observer at the edge of the same pit could see a convoy of electric mining trucks rumble deep into the mine. A closer look would reveal something remarkable: no one behind the wheel.
item.content:encoded:
In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).

In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash.

Today, however, an observer at the edge of the same pit could see a convoy of electric mining trucks rumble deep into the mine. A closer look would reveal something remarkable: no one behind the wheel.

This is the scene in Yimin – one of the five largest open-cast coal mines in China – which launched the world’s first large-scale fleet of cabless, electric autonomous mining trucks in May last year.

More than a year on, the performance of the 100-vehicle fleet offers a chance to assess how the technology has fared beyond the pilot stage – and whether it can be scaled up further to help upgrade China’s traditional energy sector.

“The autonomous electric trucks have helped us cut operating costs, improve safety and increase efficiency,” said Zhao Yaozhong, deputy manager for technology at the mine.

Beyond easing recruitment difficulties caused by harsh working conditions, the deployment has – more importantly – improved safety by reducing the scope for human error, analysts and industry insiders said. This consideration takes on particular importance amid renewed scrutiny of mine safety following a spate of recent accidents.

The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment

Zhao Yaozhong, deputy mine manager for technology at Yimin

Custom-built by heavy machinery maker Xuzhou Construction Machinery Group to withstand extreme cold, the self-driving trucks operate over a 5G network and Huawei Technologies’ cloud-based AI dispatching system, allowing them to navigate the mine and optimise routes in real time, according to the companies.

Automated swapping stations replace depleted batteries in about six minutes, while a dedicated solar microgrid supplies electricity, allowing the fleet to achieve zero-carbon status and run constantly.

“The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment,” Zhao said.

He noted that many mining accidents over the years had been linked to human factors, such as emotions or failures to follow operating procedures. Zhao contrasted this with the autonomous trucks, which he said executed commands precisely once given instructions to haul coal or overburden – the layer of rock and dirt covering a mineral deposit.

Coal mine safety has fallen back under the regulatory microscope in China following a gas explosion in May at the Liushenyu Coal Mine in Shanxi province. The blast killed 82 people, making it the deadliest coal mine disaster in more than a decade.

Aside from safety, the autonomous solution also offered cost savings, Zhao said, remaining cheaper to operate than conventionally driven trucks even after factoring upfront investments in the vehicles, battery-swapping stations and 5G cloud platform, as well as maintenance costs.

The savings have come mainly from lower labour and fuel costs, with the deployment replacing a crew of nearly 270 truck drivers with a smaller maintenance and support team – equivalent to about 220 fewer positions – and saving an estimated 13,300 tonnes of diesel.

Zhao said operating costs for the autonomous trucks were about 6.5 yuan (US$0.97) per cubic metre for hauling coal and overburden, compared with roughly 12 to 14 yuan per cubic metre for conventional haul trucks – almost half the cost.

Since the fleet was deployed in May last year, it has hauled about 28 million cubic metres (988.8 million cubic feet), saving nearly 200 million yuan (US$29.8 million) in operating costs, he added.

Coal has long been the backbone of China’s energy system, powering the country’s rapid industrialisation and still accounting for more than half of its energy consumption. Its dominant role has also helped cushion China from this year’s global energy shock, which saw a rapid increase in oil prices triggered by the US-Israel war with Iran.

Wang Hongzhi, head of the National Energy Administration (NEA), said at a press conference in June that “coal is our biggest source of confidence in maintaining a stable energy supply”, saying China should build up its major coal production bases in line with its national circumstances.

Meanwhile, upgrading and transforming the traditional energy sector has also become part of Beijing’s broader energy strategy.

A blueprint released by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA for China’s “new energy system” during the period covered by the country’s 15th five-year plan called for a “modern coal supply chain”, with wider adoption of green mining practices and the development of smart mines tailored to local conditions.

In another blueprint intended specifically for the coal industry over the period, the two agencies set a target to further advance smart mining across the sector and raise the share of production capacity at smart mines to 75 per cent by 2030.

Analysts from Citic Securities said regulators’ focus on ensuring a safe and stable coal supply amid energy security concerns was driving smart mining, which could also help address labour shortages and cut costs for coal companies.

“The industry’s development is therefore driven not only by central policy coordination and local development plans, but also by coal companies’ own willingness to upgrade,” the analysts said in a report on smart mining last year.

They estimated that smart upgrades could reduce mine staffing by 20 to 30 per cent, with the investment potentially paying for itself in about seven to eight years on labour savings alone.

Since its deployment in May 2025, the Yimin fleet has moved beyond the pilot phase, taking on more demanding operations as the mine prepares to add 200 more trucks by the end of this year.

Initially used to haul topsoil and rock on the surface, the trucks began hauling coal in November, Zhao said. The mine also relocated its battery-swapping stations into the pit to test whether the trucks could navigate more challenging terrain, such as the confined spaces of the coal-preparation plant.

“We need to verify the system’s stability, because we plan to deploy 200 more trucks by the end of this year,” he said.

For Yimin, the experience suggested that technology was no longer the main barrier to wider adoption. But replicating the model across China’s coal mines was another question, with differences in geology, infrastructure and power supply likely to determine how quickly it can scale.

“The technology behind autonomous electric mining trucks is ready for nationwide deployment, but the biggest challenge is whether individual mines have enough power infrastructure to support them,” Zhao said.

Yimin, China’s first coal-and-power integrated project, has an advantage in electricity supply, with the mine able to draw power directly from the affiliated Yimin power plant.

“For other mines, such as those in [the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region], the biggest issue is whether they have enough power supply,” he noted, adding that government efforts to encourage mines to develop microgrids combining solar and wind power with energy storage could offer a potential solution.

Developing smart microgrids in mining areas that coordinate power generation, grids, electricity demand and energy storage is also listed in the coal industry’s five-year plan, which calls for the integrated development and operation of solar and wind power, coal-mine gas generation, energy storage and smart control systems.

According to the Citic Securities analysts, autonomous trucks at open-pit mines and mining robots for underground operations were among the two most mature applications combining artificial intelligence with mining hardware in China, while home-grown large language models for mining provided the technological foundation for such integration.

“We expect … mining-specific large models to incorporate generative AI, further enhancing data analysis and decision-making capabilities while improving safety and energy efficiency in mining operations,” the analysts said.

item.title: [SCMP] Tiananmen vigil leaders jailed for up to 7 years, group fined HK$1.5 million
item.description:
Three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil have been sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail under the national security law for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

Three High Court judges on Friday also ordered the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China to pay a HK$1.5 million (US$191,300) fine in three months, as they brought the high-profile trial at West Kowloon Court to a close.

The alliance, former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted last month after the judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including what used to be the only large-scale commemoration on Chinese soil of Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989.
item.content:encoded:
Three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil have been sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail under the national security law for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

Three High Court judges on Friday also ordered the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China to pay a HK$1.5 million (US$191,300) fine in three months, as they brought the high-profile trial at West Kowloon Court to a close.

The alliance, former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted last month after the judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including what used to be the only large-scale commemoration on Chinese soil of Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989.

Lee, 69, and Chow, 41, were sentenced to seven years and seven years and three months behind bars, respectively.

Former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months after pleading guilty ahead of the trial.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the rule of law could only be upheld by imposing severe penalties on the accused.

“The law never allows anyone to blatantly harm their country and compatriots under the guise of promoting human rights, democracy and freedom,” he said.

Central government authorities in Hong Kong hailed the tough sentences as a manifestation of the city’s rule of law, while warning “external forces” against smearing the court’s decisions.

A spokesman for the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office said the alliance and the defendants “had long incited public hostility, hatred and disaffection towards the state regime”, adding that their offences had seriously challenged the constitutional order of Hong Kong and gravely violated the city’s national security law.

“They must be severely punished in accordance with the law,” the spokesman said.

The foreign ministry’s arm in Hong Kong said the alliance had undermined the central government’s authority “at both ideological and practical levels”.

Beijing’s liaison office said the defendants deserved severe penalties for attacking the party’s leadership, while the country’s Office for Safeguarding National Security in Hong Kong described the ruling as “widely supported” by society.

Ho is expected to complete his sentence in April 2028, assuming he is not granted a one-third reduction by prison authorities on the basis of good conduct during his incarceration.

Lee Cheuk-yan may be released in September or October 2029, whereas Chow may have to serve her sentence until early 2030. The pair intend to lodge an appeal.

Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, said the sentences did not only punish the alliance and its former leaders, but also those who subscribed to the group’s beliefs or previously attended its annual vigil at Victoria Park in Causeway Bay.

“I think free speech is already a thing of the past,” she said. “They were given such heavy sentences even though they had never resorted to any unlawful means.”

Chow’s mother, Medina Chow Lau Wah-chun, said her daughter had only intended to “speak the truth”.

The elder Chow added that she was not free to speak her mind because of a police investigation against her.

Justices Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Jong-herng and Anna Lai Yuen-kee said the case was serious and warranted five to 10 years’ imprisonment under a two-tier sentencing regime of the national security law.

They noted the offence lasted for 14 months after the law took effect on June 30, 2020, during which the defendants persisted with their offensive conduct on social media and during public events at a time when Hong Kong remained “turbulent and unsettled”.

“Despite the defendants’ belief that their agenda of ‘ending one-party dictatorship’ might be in breach of the [Chinese] constitution and the national security law, they recalcitrantly pursued their course of conduct and strenuously promoted their agenda. This was a premeditated act,” the judges said in a 19-page written ruling.

The European Union said about the sentencing: “This ruling undermines confidence in the rule of law and harms Hong Kong’s reputation.”

The United Nations Human Rights Office said the jailing of the trio highlighted the ever-increasing restrictions on civic space in Hong Kong, including harsh measures taken against civil society actors, since the National Security Law was passed in 2020. The office’s High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk called for these sentences to be quashed.

Meanwhile, the court adjourned handling the prosecution’s request to confiscate the “Pillar of Shame” sculpture, created by Danish artist Jens Galschiot, pending further arguments.

Galschiot has repeatedly demanded that the eight-metre-tall (26-foot) artwork be returned to him since it was seized by police’s National Security Department in 2023.

Steve Li Kwai-wah, the department’s chief superintendent, argued the sculpture belonged to the alliance and was used to incite others to undermine the party.

“I think the rationale is very simple. You created something and gave it to someone else. Can you ask to take it back any time you want?” Li said.

Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung said that any item relevant to the commission of an offence should be confiscated.

In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Galschiot said he intended to request his government to take diplomatic action so that the sculpture could be returned to “its rightful owner”.

Former trade union leader Carol Ng Man-yee, who was released from prison last year after serving 45 months for a subversion offence, and former alliance standing committee member Tang Ngok-kwan were among those who attended the brief hearing on Friday.

Ng said she felt relieved the three defendants finally got to know when they might be released, but said she was still saddened by the outcome.

Tang Ngok-kwan urged the public to continue to honour those who died in the 1989 crackdown in a “reasonable and lawful” manner.

The alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to commemorate the event and called for democratic reforms across the border and the end of one-party rule.

Police prohibited the vigil for the first time in 2020 on public health grounds related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2021 event was banned for similar reasons before the alliance disbanded in September that year.

item.title: [SCMP] What’s a Northern Metropolis-like project doing in Malaysia? Lessons for Hong Kong?
item.description:
Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours.

Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure.

Inside YTL’s sprawling Green Data Centre Park, massive operational blocks stand beside numerous others under construction. The park supplies high-performance computing power and artificial intelligence (AI) chips to global technology giants, sitting squarely within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), a landmark 350,000-hectare (865,000-acre) project officially established in January 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours.

Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure.

Inside YTL’s sprawling Green Data Centre Park, massive operational blocks stand beside numerous others under construction. The park supplies high-performance computing power and artificial intelligence (AI) chips to global technology giants, sitting squarely within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), a landmark 350,000-hectare (865,000-acre) project officially established in January 2025.

Covering an area more than four times the size of Singapore, the JS-SEZ aims to generate 260 billion Malaysian ringgit (US$63.9 billion) for Johor’s regional economy by 2030 and create more than 20,000 high-skilled jobs, anchored by the coming 4km Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link designed to slash travel times and cement cross-strait integration.

For Malaysia, the early trajectory of Hong Kong and Shenzhen remains the foundational blueprint.

Lee Ting Han, Johor’s state executive councillor for investment and trade, told the South China Morning Post that despite distinct political frameworks, the wealth gap between Singapore and Johor mirrored the historic economic disparity between Hong Kong and Shenzhen.

“Similarly, it is pretty much like the early days of Hong Kong and Shenzhen, where the economic disparity between the two regions was so wide … what we are trying to do now is see whether there’s a way for us from a business standpoint to make it more integrated from trade relationships to investment culture,” Lee said.

He acknowledged that building the JS-SEZ presented unique regulatory challenges because Johor and Singapore operated as sovereign nations without an overarching central authority such as Beijing to coordinate rules.

However, Johor is studying how Shenzhen strategically transitioned over decades from labour-intensive assembly to capital- and technology-intensive hubs by leveraging Hong Kong capital to build home-grown tech giants in the same vein as Huawei Technologies and DJI.

As Asia’s premier financial and technology centres construct massive border-spanning growth corridors, Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis and Malaysia’s JS-SEZ offer a compelling case study in mutual learning.

While Malaysia looks to emulate Hong Kong’s long-standing success in frictionless border flows and joint state-directed planning, the city stands to learn key lessons from Johor’s aggressive strategy in nurturing talent pipelines and deploying state-backed infrastructure to secure a low-cost, high-reliability energy grid for power-hungry tech industries.

Key to Johor’s rapid rise is its approach to energy, an area where Hong Kong could draw valuable operational insights. Highlighting the power requirements of data centres, Lee noted that Malaysia’s utilities were largely state-backed.

This allows the government to take a long-term, strategic view by investing heavily in power infrastructure upfront, insulating critical digital hubs from the short-term profit pressures faced by purely private, commercial utility entities.

Malaysia adopted a forward-looking approach by making heavy infrastructure investments ahead of the cycle.

Chew Chong-sin, a former Mengkibol state assemblyman who has analysed the region’s economic integration, noted that by combining Singapore’s global financial and connectivity hub status with Johor’s land, energy, and industrial capacity, the zone aimed to mirror Shenzhen’s early evolution into a technology powerhouse.

However, he cautioned that significant operational hurdles persisted – most notably easing severe bottlenecking at the world’s second-busiest land checkpoint and resolving head-on competition in ports and logistics – even as the coming RTS Link aimed to streamline cross-border mobility by 2027.

Crucially, the zone was positioning itself to absorb global supply chain diversification, offering a neutral, disaster-free base for multinationals and mainland Chinese enterprises looking to de-risk, Chew said.

He added that this momentum had already drawn increased interest from Hong Kong firms, including sustainable aviation fuel producers and hospitality enterprises.

As Malaysia and Singapore finalise a comprehensive 10-year master plan, he said that the zone’s ultimate success would depend on maintaining the strict execution discipline needed to translate high-level blueprints into lasting economic integration.

To spur investment ahead of its full master plan launch in late 2026, authorities introduced sweeping tax incentives starting January 2025.

Firms deploying at least 500 million ringgit in high-growth fields such as AI, quantum computing and aerospace enjoy a 5 per cent preferential corporate tax rate for years, paired with stamp duty waivers.

These incentives have caught international attention.

A representative from a Mexico-based construction and information technology enterprise, who did not wish to be named, confirmed to the SCMP that the company would visit Malaysia to explore data centre sites, citing the country’s strong connectivity within Asean, widespread English proficiency and attractive tax environment.

Following stops in Kuala Lumpur and coming visits to Johor, he commended Malaysia’s proactive tech push.

Turning to Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis, however, the representative observed that while the city retained distinct institutional advantages, its position within China imposed inherent geopolitical limitations when manufacturing high-end, sensitive semiconductor chips.

The Northern Metropolis has been touted repeatedly as a top priority for Hong Kong’s administration, capped most recently by a visit from Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, who underscored Beijing’s call to accelerate construction.

The megaproject aims to transform 30,000 hectares into a major housing hub and an economic growth engine.

Both the Northern Metropolis and the JS-SEZ are strategically positioning themselves as multifaceted growth engines that integrate international education hubs, hi-tech innovation corridors and vibrant ecotourism circles.

Joining the call for deeper integration, Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers Hong Kong, said the city could take reference from Johor as a benchmark for cross-border development by aligning its land-grant policies with Shenzhen and leveraging universities to spearhead innovation.

She noted that Johor’s experience showed how robust research and technology ecosystems relied heavily on close synergies with academic institutions.

To build a sustainable tech ecosystem, Lee urged authorities to synchronise housing and talent policies with project completion timelines, anticipating a resurgence in demand as new infrastructure came online.

Given the intensive energy requirements of advanced technology and data centres, she recommended that the government initiate joint feasibility studies with mainland Chinese authorities on cross-border electricity supply to secure a reliable, green power source for the city’s tech sector.

Echoing the push for seamless integration, former lawmaker Edward Lau Kwok-fan argued that Hong Kong should draw inspiration from the JS-SEZ by speeding up the implementation of bespoke legislation for the Northern Metropolis to unlock the fluid movement of people, goods, capital and data.

He also called on higher education institutions to take greater initiative.

“I feel universities have not done enough yet. In the future, universities could evolve towards an industry-oriented development path,” said Lau, a member of the Advisory Committee on the Northern Metropolis.

“Universities need to reflect. There is a need to rethink course offerings and review academic programmes going forward.”

In response, Hong Kong’s Development Bureau said that the Northern Metropolis operated as a strategic cross-boundary hub under the “one country, two systems” governing principle, utilising coming Hetao-specific legislation to facilitate fluid cross-border resource sharing within the Greater Bay Area.

The bureau highlighted that by pairing the city’s five global top-100 universities and a planned 1,000-hectare university district with Shenzhen’s industrial scale, Hong Kong provided a platform, backed by common law, capable of rapidly converting lab discoveries into mass production.

The Education Bureau also said in a reply that it was encouraging University Grants Committee-funded universities to revamp their academic offerings, backed by a fund launched in 2023 to drive digital teaching reforms.

The Chinese University of Hong Kong said in a reply that it offered AI degree programmes across its engineering and science faculties, which delivered structured training to foster AI talent equipped for real-world innovation and academic research.

The SCMP also reached out to the University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

Under the 2025-28 triennial planning cycle, local universities were introducing 27 new undergraduate degree programmes tailored to STEAM fields, the bureau said.

STEAM refers to an educational approach that combines science, technology, engineering, the arts and maths.

Addressing Hong Kong’s internal bottlenecks, lawmaker Aaron Bok Kwok-ming, a former president of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers (HKIE), stressed that the city had to aggressively tackle its ongoing engineering talent shortage similarly to Malaysia.

To supply future high-value talent for the JS-SEZ, the Johor Talent Development Council acts as a centralised talent engine by partnering with universities, institutions and agencies to deliver industry-aligned upskilling, matching programmes and specialised training.

Bok called for targeted manpower forecasts, particularly in electronic engineering, to pinpoint exact deficit areas as Hong Kong advanced its innovation ambitions.

He urged government leaders to conduct official, comprehensive surveys rather than relying on industry estimates, while establishing structured pathways to entice overseas Hong Kong engineers back home and expanding domestic university training.

According to a manpower forecast report by Hong Kong’s Construction Industry Council released in 2023, the sector is expected to face a shortage of about 6,000 to 6,500 professionals by 2027, with civil, mechanical, structural and environmental engineering listed among the most severely affected specialisms.

Drawing on the forecast report, the HKIE noted in 2023 that the city would face a shortfall of about 3,000 professional engineers over the five years through 2027, stressing that engineers played an indispensable role in supporting the government’s push for new industrialisation and biotechnology.

This deficit is already affecting local businesses. Some tech companies previously said that while they struggled to find veteran talent, such as experienced electronics engineers, locally in Hong Kong, they could easily recruit skilled professionals on the mainland.

Addressing these industry concerns over projected workforce shortages, including the estimated shortfall of 3,000 engineers, engineer and former technology minister Alfred Sit Wing-hang said that emerging technologies such as AI, robotics and building information modelling required more sophisticated technical expertise rather than diluted entry criteria.

Sit added that as Hong Kong’s economic landscape underwent a structural shift towards advanced manufacturing and technology-driven industries, local universities and professional bodies were actively overhauling their training frameworks.

AI had increasingly become a core component of undergraduate engineering curricula, while new certification programmes were being developed to upskill mid-career professionals in fields such as smart industrial engineering and automation, he said.

On the energy front, lawmaker and energy sector expert Chan Siu-hung noted that Hong Kong already possessed top-tier infrastructure for data centres and computing hubs, but suggested the government could accelerate the roll-out of power infrastructure blueprints to match coming industrial investments.

On the city’s digital expansion, he noted that major development zones such as the Lok Ma Chau Loop and the San Tin Technopole were well positioned, with strong power supply nodes.

Responding to queries on energy security, the Environment and Ecology Bureau said that the government had signed Scheme of Control Agreements (SCAs) with the city’s two power companies.

Under these agreements, the suppliers are obliged to support the development of Hong Kong including the Northern Metropolis, by providing, operating and maintaining sufficient electricity-related facilities to meet the needs of various industries.

Chan stressed that actual energy demand would ultimately depend on incoming corporate investments.

“To ensure long-term energy security, Hong Kong’s two power suppliers need to finalise power agreements with mainland supply, securing cross-boundary supply options while advancing low-carbon energy goals,” he said.

“Officials should provide clearer and earlier timelines for these infrastructure plans to give operators certainty.”

item.title: [SCMP] Indo-Chinese cuisine in Hong Kong: a delicious dialogue of cultures and flavours
item.description:
On September 12 and 13, world leaders and ambassadors are due to gather in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit, with President Xi Jinping expected to be among them – his first visit to India since 2019. It is a moment of cautious optimism in a relationship that has see-sawed between tension and thaw for the better part of a decade, marked by such events as the 2017 Doklam (Donglang) stand-off and the 2020 clashes in the Galwan valley.

But as politicians cook up deals and diplomacy, two chefs in Hong Kong would rather let the food do the talking. In July, chef Palash Mitra of Prince and the Peacock and chef Theign Phan of Grand Majestic Sichuan fired up their tandoors and woks, trading notes on the almost 2,000-year-old conversation their cuisines have been engaged in, long before anyone put it on an agenda.

Growing up in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state in eastern India, Mitra never thought of Chinese food as a separate cuisine. It was simply stitched into the city’s culinary fabric.
item.content:encoded:
On September 12 and 13, world leaders and ambassadors are due to gather in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit, with President Xi Jinping expected to be among them – his first visit to India since 2019. It is a moment of cautious optimism in a relationship that has see-sawed between tension and thaw for the better part of a decade, marked by such events as the 2017 Doklam (Donglang) stand-off and the 2020 clashes in the Galwan valley.

But as politicians cook up deals and diplomacy, two chefs in Hong Kong would rather let the food do the talking. In July, chef Palash Mitra of Prince and the Peacock and chef Theign Phan of Grand Majestic Sichuan fired up their tandoors and woks, trading notes on the almost 2,000-year-old conversation their cuisines have been engaged in, long before anyone put it on an agenda.

Growing up in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state in eastern India, Mitra never thought of Chinese food as a separate cuisine. It was simply stitched into the city’s culinary fabric.

He remembers the Chinese food carts his family would visit on special occasions, and “Shubhon”, the man behind the wok, whose real name was Chen Shiobin. By day, Shubhon worked at a rifle factory; by night, he sold street bites, peddling in fluent Bengali, bargaining at the market in Bengali, laughing in Bengali.

“He was as much a part of Kolkata as the tram lines and the Durga Puja pandals. He was simply one of us,” says Mitra.

It’s easy to think of Indian and Chinese gastronomies as detached empires. But beneath the surface, a dialogue has been under way for more than a millennium. On ancient maps, the two are interwoven through the maritime lanes of the spice trade and the mountain passes of the Silk Road. It is believed that India initiated the exchange, sending black pepper to China during the first two centuries AD. Later, the favour was returned: China dispatched cassia bark and star anise along the same routes. By the time Hakka and Cantonese settlers arrived in Kolkata – then named Calcutta – more than 200 years ago, and adapted their woks to local ingredients to give birth to a composite cuisine now beloved across the subcontinent, Chinese and Indian communities had been using food as the language of negotiation for generations.

“Indo-Chinese is not a hybrid that belongs nowhere,” Mitra asserts. “It belongs specifically to Kolkata, a city that has always absorbed the world and made it its own.”

Global trade had shaped Kolkata for centuries. Portuguese merchants brought chillies, potatoes and cashews in the 1500s, and the English East India Company followed in the 1600s, chasing the spice trade. By the time the city was established, in 1690, other settlers, such as Armenians, had already brought their own kitchens and their own gods.

Kolkata’s Chinese community, concentrated in Tangra, the “new” Chinatown, peaked at 40,000 around the time of World War II. Settlers had arrived in waves, starting in the late 18th century, first making a home in Tiretta Bazaar, the “old” Chinatown, and then again throughout the 19th century and early 20th century, fleeing war and invasion. Many worked in the tanning industry, a profession that higher-caste Hindus considered “polluting”, leaving a niche that the Hakka filled. As tanneries in the Tangra neighbourhood closed or relocated over the years, the community increasingly turned to food to sustain their livelihoods.

Like many new immigrants, the Chinese adapted their cuisine, adding more chillies, more garlic and more ginger to suit Indian palates, while keeping the non-negotiables – wok, high heat and soy sauce – close to the hearth. A menu at an Indo-Chinese restaurant is what Mitra calls “gloriously Calcuttan”. While early Kolkata institutions such as Eau Chew pioneered the genre in the 1920s, the now-classic Hakka wheat noodles dish was later popularised by the grass-roots, family-run kitchens of Tangra. In 1975 came chicken Manchurian, invented at the Cricket Club of India, in Mumbai, when the Kolkata-born chef Nelson Wang paired the Indian trinity of ginger, garlic and green chilli with soy sauce and cornflour instead of garam masala. Chilli paneer – cubes of firm cheese fried with peppers and green chilli – emerged in the late 20th century as a vegetarian adaptation of familiar Indo-Chinese poultry recipes.

Mitra carried those memories with him when he arrived in Hong Kong. “It was only when I was dining at Luk Yu Tea House that I realised chilli chicken did not exist in China,” he says. “[Chicken] Manchurian was an Indian invention. Hakka noodles, as we knew them, did not belong to any province on a map [of China]. Instead, I found dim sum and Cantonese broths.”

It was the culinary equivalent of an American landing in Hong Kong and discovering fortune cookies were never Chinese to begin with. “Looking back, I laugh, because I had unknowingly grown up loving a cuisine that bore very little resemblance to the Chinese food I encountered in Hong Kong. Living on both sides of that divide has been a rare gift,” he reflects.

Phan speaks that same dialect of living between cultures – born in Malaysia, raised in Singapore, now cooking Sichuan food in Hong Kong. She recalls a childhood of tucking into roti prata at hawker centres, fish-head curries with her father and banana-leaf meals where she learned to eat with her hands.

“[Indian food] was always bold, flavourful and communal,” she says. “It was only after I started cooking professionally and travelling that I realised how incredibly diverse Indian cuisine is. What I knew growing up was just a small glimpse.”

Phan’s father is Hakka, so learning about the Kolkata community resonated with her. She had seen the same dynamic play out in Peranakan cuisine, born from Chinese-Malay intermarriage.

“Neither cuisine was created because people wanted to invent something new; they developed naturally because communities settled in a new place and began cooking with what was around them, while holding onto parts of their own identity,” she says.

At a time when a quick scroll on social media can (virtually) transport you to a Chongqing hotpot joint, it’s easy to forget the ingredients themselves have already travelled farther. While huajiao (Sichuan pepper) is native to Sichuan province, chilli peppers arrived from Mesoamerica. It took centuries of seafaring and cross-continental trade to bring them together in a single pot.

Mala, one of Sichuan’s most famous flavour profiles, is defined by the chillies that hit the tongue first, delivering a building burn that lingers, and the huajiao that numbs the tongue, a tingling that feels almost electric. It’s a dialogue between two different kinds of fire, connected through ancient routes.

But just as it would be a mistake to generalise Indian food as “curry” – a British catch-all for a whole universe of Indian cooking – it would be equally reductive to sum up Sichuan cuisine, which has 24 official flavour profiles, such as the sweet, sour, salty, savoury, spicy and numbing guaiwei (“strange flavour”) and the fish-free yuxiang (“fish-fragrant”), as just mala.

With such vast and layered traditions on both sides, how do two chefs even begin to find common ground? “Both cuisines understand the importance of balance,” says Phan. “Even when a dish is spicy, it’s never just about heat. You’re looking for aroma, depth, acidity, texture and fragrance all working together.”

In Indian cookery, this plays out in the methodical blooming of whole spices in oil before adding aromatics and garam masalas. In Sichuan fare, the same instinct runs through layers of aromatics and the slow heat of chillies and peppercorns.

Both traditions also share a deep understanding of fermentation – the funky depth of doubanjiang (fermented broad-bean paste) meets the sharp tang of Indian pickles and kasundi (fermented mustard). More importantly, they are unafraid of fire. “Whether it’s a tandoor or a blazing wok, both cuisines rely on high heat to create smokiness, caramelisation and complexity,” Mitra adds.

When the two chefs travelled through India together earlier this year, these parallels became tangible, and the trip became the foundation for two four-hands dinners at Prince and the Peacock and Grand Majestic Sichuan. In Mumbai, Phan ordered crab cooked two ways and found herself naming Sichuan flavour profiles: garlic paste and fragrant-spicy. “I could taste cardamom, peppercorns, cassia bark, coriander seeds – not just chilli, but layers of dry spices working through the sauce,” she says.

In hotel restaurants across the country, the international menus told the same story: Sichuan stir-fried vegetables, triple Sichuan fried rice (an Indo-Chinese dish with “Manchurian” gravy), kung pao prawns, mapo tofu. “It really shows India’s love of Sichuan food – the flavours have been embraced so naturally,” says Phan.

For Mitra, the trip was also a homecoming: “I probably ate Hakka noodles almost every day we were in India.”

Mitra’s cravings naturally found their way onto his four-hands menu – but with a twist. During recipe trials in Jamnagar, in Gujarat state, he was making a bowl of Hakka noodles when a leftover Goan xacuti spice blend caught his eye. He added a little without thinking and found that “the coconut rounded everything out, while the stone flower brought an earthy note that worked surprisingly well with the soy [sauce] and chilli” – and so the spice blend stayed. Both flavours are products of migration and adaptation; xacuti carries Portuguese influence into Goa, while Hakka noodles carry Chinese technique into Kolkata.

Chilli paneer was another classic discussed from the start. “We always knew we wanted chilli paneer on the menu because it’s such an iconic Indo-Chinese dish,” Mitra says. But Prince and the Peacock doesn’t have the kind of set-up that produces wok hei (“breath of the wok”), so he turned to the grill. Paneer hits the hot metal with a hiss; onion and capsicum blister and pop as the skewers turn. “It still tastes recognisably like chilli paneer, but the grill gives it a different character,” he says. It’s the same spirit that built Tangra’s kitchens: when you don’t have the right tool, you invent a new way to use the one in front of you.

At Grand Majestic Sichuan, Phan had the woks to spice things up. In Mumbai, she had a Bombay duck chilli fry and thought about how to translate its fragrant heat, sweetness and savouriness through a Sichuan lens for the collaboration, eventually landing on the flavours of kung pao. What emerged keeps the crisp-fried fish and the punchy chilli of the original, but reroutes it through the sweet-sour-nutty dialect of kung pao.

Other dishes in their four-hands collaboration, such as the chilled soup of chaas and tangerine peel, look forwards, rather than backwards. Chaas, a spiced buttermilk drink meant to cool the palate, takes on a faint bitterness and citrus fragrance from the dried tangerine peel, a combination Mitra and Phan describe as “completely new”. It is a dish that requires both chefs in the same kitchen, with no particular interest in staying inside the lines.

“Sharing a meal creates a different kind of connection,” says Mitra. “Food has always travelled more freely than politics.”
